News.title: Crazed ‘Islamist radical’ & mum-of-four, 36, stormed nursery with gun and fired at two teachers in sick kidnapping plot
News.content:
GUN PLOT Crazed ‘Islamist radical’ & mum-of-four, 36, stormed nursery with gun and fired at two teachers in sick kidnapping plot







Next

A MUM-of-four suspected of Islamist radicalisation allegedly tried to shoot two teachers after storming a nursery school armed with a gun and knife.

The woman, 36, allegedly pointed her weapon at a headmistress and repeatedly pulled the trigger before threatening her with a blade during an hour-long attack.



She then allegedly slapped another teacher before cocking her gun and pointing it at her.

The Tunisian-born mum, who was living illegally in France, has been charged with attempted murder and kidnapping following Monday’s attack in Nice.



Prosecutors revealed she had previously been identified as a suspected Islamist radical and placed under house arrest.

The woman, whose two children attend the nursery, arrived demanding an urgent meeting with the headmistress.



Once inside her office, she reportedly raised allegations that one of her children had been sexually assaulted before pulling out a handgun.

She allegedly slapped the headmistress, pulled her hair and struck her again after tucking the weapon into her belt.

The suspect then pointed the gun at her and pulled the trigger, but no shot was fired.

She reportedly claimed the weapon contained just two bullets.



The woman then allegedly hit the headmistress in the face with the gun before pulling out a knife and pressing it against her cheek.

Despite the violence, prosecutors said she remained calm throughout the ordeal and left the office an hour later.

After confronting the second teacher, she fled the school but was tracked by CCTV and arrested at her nearby home.



Officers recovered a Laguiole knife and several passports, some suspected to be fake, during a search in which she briefly attempted to escape.

The handgun has not been found.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told MPs on Tuesday that the weapon was “fortunately a fake”.

But prosecutors said footage appeared to show “an automatic pistol”, while the headmistress testified that she “felt it was made of metal”.

During two days in police custody, the woman denied carrying out the violence but admitted pulling the trigger several times.



She insisted she knew the weapon was unloaded and reportedly expressed remorse over the terrifying ordeal.

The woman was formally charged on Wednesday with attempted murder of a teacher, kidnapping, carrying a weapon and fraudulent possession of administrative documents.

She was remanded in custody as investigators continued probing her motive.

Prosecutors revealed the woman had previously been deported to Tunisia in 2019 but was arrested again in France in 2023.

Despite being banned from French territory, she remained in the country and regularly reported to police.



She also has two previous convictions.

The suspect is separated from the father of her two youngest children, who has been charged with attempted homicide and habitual domestic violence in a separate case in which she is a civil party.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Nice prosecutor Damien Martinelli confirmed the charges following the attack.

Education Minister Édouard Geffray said he would visit Nice “at the end of the week” and promised victims “the long-term protection and support they need.”

News.title: Christa Pike’s lawyers warned rare cancer could complicate lethal injection MONTHS before botched execution
News.content:
Next

CHRISTA Pike’s lawyers warned that a rare form of blood cancer could make her lethal injection agonizingly painful months before she survived a botched execution.

The chilling warning was laid out in court documents filed nine months before the convicted killer was left hospitalized following the failed procedure.



Pike, 50, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs on September 30 after executioners reportedly struggled to establish working IV lines.

But a January 8 court filing reveals her attorneys had already raised serious concerns about her medical conditions and the risks of administering the deadly drugs.



According to documents obtained by People, Pike suffers from myeloproliferative disorder, a rare form of blood cancer that causes the body to produce too many blood cells.

Her lawyers warned that her platelet count was significantly elevated, potentially putting her at greater risk of serious complications.

They argued that attempting to execute her by lethal injection was “very likely to result in unnecessary and superadded pain and suffering, terror, and disgrace.”

The complaint claimed Pike’s condition, known as thrombocytosis, could increase her risk of developing severe pulmonary edema.

The potentially deadly complication causes fluid to build up in the lungs, making breathing extremely difficult.

Her attorneys warned that the sensation could resemble drowning or suffocation.



“A pulmonary edema is not simply painful or uncomfortable; it can create a sense of suffocating or drowning that has been likened by experts to the sensation intentionally induced by the practice of waterboarding—an unambiguous form of outright torture,” the filing stated.

The legal team also highlighted Pike’s history of difficulties with blood draws and needle insertion.

They claimed prison medical staff routinely used butterfly needles to draw her blood because of problems accessing her veins.

Her attorneys argued that the smaller needles could reduce the risk of unnecessary suffering during the execution.

They also criticized Tennessee’s updated execution protocol for failing to guarantee lawyers immediate telephone access if something went wrong.



Those fears appeared to materialized on September 30.

Execution team members reportedly struggled to establish functioning IV lines before administering two rounds of pentobarbital.

Pike allegedly complained during the procedure: “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open.”



She later reportedly asked: “Does this happen like that?”

Despite receiving the drugs, Pike survived and was rushed to hospital, where she remained for ten days.

Her lawyers believe faulty IV lines caused the drugs to leak into the tissue of her arms rather than enter her bloodstream properly.

Both arms were reportedly left swollen, burned and blistered.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee subsequently suspended the state’s remaining executions for 2026 and ordered an independent investigation.



Pike was discharged from hospital on October 9 and returned to the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center.

Her attorneys have since filed an emergency motion challenging her alleged return to solitary confinement, claiming she has been denied meaningful human contact.

The filing also describes a “roach-infested shower” that Pike claims puts her at risk of infection.

In her first lengthy statement since the failed execution, Pike described her continuing ordeal.

“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” she wrote.



“My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak.”

She also acknowledged the suffering of her victim’s family.

“I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured.”



Pike has spent more than three decades behind bars for the brutal 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

She was just 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, lured Slemmer into a wooded area at a Tennessee job training camp.

Prosecutors said Pike, who believed Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, tortured the teenager before attacking her with a box cutter and a chunk of asphalt.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shipp, then 17, received a life sentence with the possibility of parole, while Pike was sentenced to death.

Her fate now remains uncertain as Tennessee investigates the failed execution.

News.title: Model’s HEAD ‘found immersed in pot of soup seized by cops’ after she was ‘killed & dismembered by ex-husband’
News.content:
Next

THE bloodied head of a model was found immersed in “liquid in a large soup pot,” a court has heard.

Abby Choi, 28, was found dismembered in a Hong Kong apartment in 2023 three days after she was reported missing.



Her ex-husband Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 32, his father Kwong Kau, 69, and his brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are charged with her murder.

Senior forensic pathologist Kwok Ka-ki saw two pots on the hob in Choi’s kitchen when she arrived at the scene of the crime.



When she examined them at the mortuary, she found a head immersed in liquid in one of them.

The court was also told that there was a hole on the right side of the head caused by a fracture produced by blunt-force impact.

The injury was consistent with a blow from a hammer, Dr Ka-ki explained.

Two “freshly” severed legs were also found in the fridge, and had no signs of decomposition.

“In the bathroom she [the pathologist] found suspected human tissue, including material on an electric saw,” Hong Kong media reported.

“A container of water in the bathroom held a small piece of suspected tissue floating on the surface.”



She confirmed the legs matched the characteristics of an adult woman, consistent with Choi’s age and medium build, concluding that both came from the same person.

The victim was a known socialite and model who rubbed shoulders with Hong Kong’s showbiz and business elites.

Her murder and the gruesome details that have since been revealed as part of court proceedings sent shockwaves through the wealthy financial hub.



Choi, who was a mother of four, went missing in February 2023.

Three days later, body parts believed to be hers were recovered at a house in the city’s Tai Po district.

A neighbour told the court last month that they remember hearing the sound of an electric chainsaw the night the victim disappeared.

They also claimed a foul smell started coming from the ground-floor flat, according to local media.

Prosecutors also told the court that the whirring sound and horrific smell were a result of Choi’s body allegedly being dismembered.



The defendants had no intention of eating the boiled remains – they just wanted to render them unidentifiable, prosecutors added.

Carrots and radishes were allegedly added to the mixture to cover up the pungent stench, the court heard.

Prosecutors told the jury earlier this week that Choi and her ex-husband’s family had financial disputes over a luxury property worth £5.7million.



She had allegedly decided to register the property under the name of her ex-father-in-law years ago to avoid paying higher taxes.

Prosecutors claimed her relationship with the Kwongs had been going downhill ever since she tried to sell the home in 2022.

Kwong Kau, a former police sergeant, allegedly became “resentful” over her decision to try and sell the apartment, the court heard.

The defendants allegedly decided to kill Choi because they wanted to keep the property, prosecutors alleged.

“We say three of them decided they would do it together,” they said.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

All defendants deny murder but have each admitted preventing the burial of her body.

If convicted, the three face life in prison.

News.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after BBC revealed rape allegations
News.content:
Married at First Sight UK will not return, Channel 4 has said, following a BBC Panorama investigation into the hit reality TV show.

The show's budget will be reinvested in "distinctive new programming", the broadcaster's chief executive Priya Dogra said on Thursday, and she repeated her apology to the women involved in the investigation, for the "distress they have clearly felt".

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis earlier this year, after a Panorama programme which revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

A review was commissioned by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster, with details of the allegations we had heard.

The show was left reeling after the Panorama investigation in May, in which three women made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny.

One woman said her onscreen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her onscreen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - accused her onscreen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading, and that it acted appropriately in all these cases.

Channel 4 had initially told Panorama that all the allegations were "wholly uncorroborated".

News.title: Drunk and dangerous e-bike riders face on-the-spot fines under crackdown
News.content:
People riding drunk or dangerously on e-bikes â and those who jump red lights - could face on-the-spot fines under plans to curb anti-social behaviour.

Firms which run shared e-bike schemes will also be expected to manage their fleets better and provide designated parking areas to keep pavements safe.

They could also be required to take out insurance so people can claim compensation if they are hit by someone on a shared bike.

It's part of a crackdown on what ministers called the "wild west" of e-biking â with a patchwork of rules across the country often leaving the streets unsafe for pedestrians.

A consultation launched on Thursday sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.

The first e-bikes were launched in Exeter in 2016 and arrived in London a year later, growing to become a popular commuter option.

According to the Greater London Authority, 37 million trips were taken on dockless e-bikes last year â a third more than the previous year.

Shared e-bikes - such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt - make short journeys quick and convenient.

While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes can only be left in specific areas, others have looser rules.

Under the government's proposals, local leaders will be able to license schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks.

Measures could include requiring operators to have a parking plan and to manage fleet sizes and operating areas, so bikes aren't overcrowding streets.

The consultation will also consider ways to tackle antisocial and illegal behaviour, to prevent users from riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements. There will also be clear consequences set out â such as fines for this type of behaviour.

The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the e-bike clampdown was a "small but important everyday fix" which would make streets safer.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the changes would "stop nuisance parking, tackle antisocial behaviour and make journeys safer".

Bosses at Lime, Voi and Bolt all welcomed the proposals, adding that consistent standards being applied across the country would provide clarity and certainty for operators, riders and the general public.

News.title: Pound rises to its highest level since the Brexit referendum
News.content:
The pound has risen to its highest overall level since the Brexit referendum over a decade ago.

Sterling has risen notably in recent weeks against the euro and the dollar, ahead of an expected rise in interest rates.

The most-watched measure of the value of the British currency against a basket of 18 of the world's main currencies this week reached its joint highest level since the June 2016 referendum, according to Bank of England figures.

The value reached 86.4 on an index where 100 equals the value in 2005. The Bank will officially confirm the calculation on Thursday.

News.title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
News.content:
US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled.

The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit.

Sherri Chrichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.

A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.

Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained.

"We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.

It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.

But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.

The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.

News.title: New £200m fleet of publicly funded trains in Wales barely used after three years
News.content:
A new fleet of publicly funded trains that cost more than Â£200m still remain mostly unused more than three years after the first one was delivered.

They were initially promised to be fully up and running by 2022 but Transport for Wales' (TfW) boss has said he expects all of the tram-trains will be in full service by the end of 2027.

Data obtained by the BBC reveals that less than half of the 36 fleet - what TfW call the "final piece" in their Â£2bn South Wales Metro project - have passed rigorous statutory testing.

TfW chief executive James Price said he wants trains that work "100% well, 100% of the time" before putting them into full service.

News.title: Watch: Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
News.content:
Italian chef Davide Tamburella was fired from a Brisbane restaurant in May after the establishment's management expressed concerns about a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.

Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function.

It was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.

At the time, the chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".

Australia correspondent Katy Watson explains what led to Tamburella's dismissal.

Read more about Davide Tamburella's story.

News.title: Anthony Zurcher: Trump is weakened but still wields power for now
News.content:
As the dust was still settling on the Democratic midterm wave that crashed across America, the official White House account posted a photograph on X of a stern-looking Donald Trump standing behind his desk in the Oval Office.

"Trump is still your president," the caption read.

It's the kind of message Trump surely wants to project â of a president firmly in charge and unbowed despite a dramatic electoral setback.

Left unsaid was that even without control of Congress, American presidents still have broad powers that they can exercise. And Trump has already shown that he is more than willing to push the boundaries of his executive authority.

But also unacknowledged was that the clock is ticking on Trump's presidency â and it will get increasingly more difficult for him to use the powers at his disposal.

News.title: Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
News.content:
From coast to coast, voters across the US have been grappling with the soaring cost of essentials. That anger was palpable on the ground in key races.

"Gas prices, grocery prices, everything's going up," one North Carolina voter told the BBC ahead of the elections, adding that she had switched her vote from Republican to Democratic this election.

Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices. Average US retail diesel prices in early October were just shy of the record of $6.52 (Â£4.83) per gallon seen in September, according to government data.

Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year, according to data from voter polls.

And more than six in 10 respondents laid the blame for that at the feet of Trump, saying they thought higher than usual prices were because of the president's policies.

News.title: England captain Harry Kane signs new Bayern deal
News.content:
England captain and Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane has signed a new contract with Bayern Munich that runs until 2029.

The 33-year-old striker was in the final 12 months of the four-year deal he signed after his Â£86m move from Tottenham in 2023.

He scored a club record 61 goals in 51 games last season as Bayern completed a league and cup double.

"I feel right at home at FC Bayern. I love the club, the fans and the city of Munich," said Kane.

"We have a fantastic team and, in Vincent Kompany, a fantastic manager. It makes me very proud to be part of this club.

"My whole family is very happy here. I was keen to stay. I'm now looking forward to the future and I want to win many more titles with this great club."

Kane's contract secures his future at Bayern until shortly before his 36th birthday and ensures he will remain with the club through Euro 2028 and to within a year of the 2030 World Cup.

The Leytonstone-born forward remains 47 goals short of equalling Alan Shearer's Premier League record of 260 and extending his deal in Germany decreases his chances of returning to break that mark.

By signing Kane to a new deal, Bayern have warded off any approach from Barcelona, who had a long-standing interest, while clubs in Saudi Arabia were also linked with the centre-forward.

Kane scored 73 goals in 65 matches for England and Bayern in 2025-26 and was crowned the world's best male player at the Ballon d'Or ceremony last month.

He has scored 102 goals in 102 Bundesliga matches, winning three successive Golden Boot awards and two league titles.

News.title: Parliament faces 'grave risks' as more asbestos discovered ahead of revamp decision
News.content:
More asbestos has been discovered in Parliament, the BBC has learnt, as MPs come under pressure to sign off on a major revamp of the crumbling home of UK democracy.

Known asbestos items in the Palace of Westminster and wider parliamentary estate, such as insulation, roofing, floor tiles and ropes, now number more than 1,650 - an increase of 500 since 2021.

It comes as the government considers holding a vote on refurbishing Parliament, which could cost up to Â£40bn and take 61 years, after years of indecision and delay.

The Commons public accounts committee this week warned it was "crunch time" for Parliament's restoration, with every additional year of delay costing taxpayers Â£420m.

More asbestos items were found during surveys in preparation for the long-awaited refurbishment project, parliamentary authorities said.

Asbestos has been identified as one of the main reasons for the refurbishment, given the dangers to human health when its fibres are airborne. While asbestos is largely fireproof, surrounding fire and heat can release fibres over long distances.

In the past five years, 700 items of asbestos have been removed from Parliament but the total has still risen, a Freedom of Information request by the BBC found.

Under Health and Safety Executive guidelines, most of it is classed as low risk in concealed areas, meaning it is less likely to be disturbed, but almost 200 items are classed as medium risk meaning they may require remedial works.

A spokesperson for UK Parliament said its "absolute priority is the safety of the those who work on and visit the parliamentary estate" with improved asbestos monitoring, new awareness training, and plans to further remove it.

Kris Gledhill, the son of former Labour MP Alice Mahon who died in 2022 of malignant mesothelioma - a type of cancer linked to asbestos exposure - told the BBC "asbestos should never be considered low risk".

News.title: Investigation after 'hundreds' of letters found dumped
News.content:
"Our teams will work to recover and process the items so they can be returned to the postal network and delivered to customers," a Royal Mail spokesperson said.

Durkan described the discovery of large amounts of personal mail dumped in the countryside as "absolutely shocking".

"Multiple bags of undelivered mail have been discovered dumped on a country road," he said.

"It is my understanding that there were other similar bags strewn around the area.

"There must be a full investigation into this appalling situation, proper accountability."

Durkan said many of the letters appear to have been sent by health trusts, government departments and banks, and are likely to contain confidential, sensitive information.

He now fears some people may have missed important correspondence, potentially affecting their access to essential services.

In a statement, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said they received a report on Wednesday "in relation to the discovery of postal mail at a location in the area of Mobuoy Road".

"Follow-up enquiries by police led to the subsequent discovery and seizure of a further quantity of mail.

"Police enquiries are ongoing, and officers are liaising with Royal Mail in respect of the matter."

News.title: Second buyer makes rescue bid for Poundland as retailer faces collapse
News.content:
A second buyer has made a rescue bid for Poundland as the discount retailer teeters on the brink of collapse, with thousands of jobs at risk.

London-based Xyra Group has offered to pay off half of Poundland's outstanding debts - a key sticking point in takeover talks so far - immediately. The rest would be deferred.

With Poundland close to collapse, US-based owners Gordon Brothers have already rejected a rival bid from an Irish property group which would have saved its 12,000 staff.

Gordon Brothers said the business has faced years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable".

Sources familiar with the offer said Xyra is offering to immediately pay off Â£12.5m of an outstanding Â£30m loan on Poundland's books.

The offer came as Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds held crunch talks with Gordon Brothers about the future of the business, urging the investment firm to protect staff however possible.

Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for Â£1 last June, committed at the meeting to prioritise offers which protect its shops and workers.

The company said: "We are pursuing all avenues through the sale process to find a solution which protects as many jobs as possible and preserves value. Work continues at pace, engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties."

Xyra is offering to pay off a higher proportion of Poundland's outstanding debts than Martin Property Group, which previously submitted a bid that Gordon Brothers rejected.

But doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer, as there is little evidence they meet Gordon Brothers' tests, including whether they have the money and whether they would be good long-term owners of Poundland.

Sources pointed to the appointment of Andrew Brode to Xyra's board as a sign of its credibility. Brode works for RWS - a company that provides AI solutions for businesses.

Judith MacKenzie, head of Downing Fund Managers, told the BBC Brode is "well known and very credible" among small businesses in the UK.

But she said there is "hardly any information" publicly available about Xyra. "So, although some of the people look good, I can't find any evidence to say that they've got the money to back it up yet," MacKenzie added.

Gordon Brothers said: "Our intent throughout the comprehensive sale process has been to protect as many jobs as possible and preserve value in order to deliver the best available outcome for all the people, creditors and local communities who care about this business as much as we do."

Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of Poundland has not yet been made.

Though Xyra made an offer to take over the whole business, it is unclear whether it would keep Poundland together as its owner or break the company up.

Several Poundland suppliers have said they would also go bust if the retailer collapses. Its founder Steve Smith said two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, those who solely work for Poundland, would be caught up in the collapse.

He added that not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall.

News.title: Family pay tribute to 'ray of sunshine' daughter killed by bus
News.content:
The family of a girl killed after being hit by a bus in Ayrshire have remembered their daughter as "a ray of sunshine" and said they are devastated by her death.

Sophia Aitken died on Tuesday after being struck by a Stagecoach bus at Lauchlan Way in Kilwinning.

The 12-year-old Kilwinning Academy pupil was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement released through Police Scotland her family said Sophia was "loved by everyone who knew her", adding that "a light has gone out, and it will never return."

Inquiries into the crash are ongoing. There were no other reported injuries in the incident.

Sophia's family said: "We are devastated at the loss of our darling daughter Sophia. She was a ray of sunshine, and was loved by everyone who knew her.

"We are comforted by the messages from the community. We would like to ask for privacy to grieve at this difficult time."

News.title: Police to escort fire crews in latest crackdown on Bonfire Night disorder
News.content:
Police officers are to be embedded in fire stations and will travel with crews to tackle potential attacks on firefighters during Bonfire Night.

The move is part of Scotland's biggest police operation since the visit of President Donald Trump last summer and a response to a "unique" combination of safety concerns.

As many as 1,700 officers could be deployed to deal with fireworks-related disorder, a European football match involving Celtic and potential protests in Glasgow.

Additional public order vehicles and drivers are being brought in from 18 English and Welsh police forces under mutual aid arrangements.

Emergency services have long recommended organised displays as the safest and often most impressive way of enjoying fireworks.

News.title: UK commits to 'time-bound' talks on slavery apology
News.content:
The UK has signed up to "structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith" talks that address the "historical harms" of the transatlantic slave trade, Commonwealth leaders in Antigua have said.

The formal conclusions marking the end of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, known as the communique, is the joint text setting out what has been agreed.

The 18 page document, external includes a paragraph in which the leaders "welcome the agreement of the Government of the United Kingdom to engage in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms".

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened the door to a formal apology on behalf of the UK for its role in the slave trade, while ruling out the prospect of reparations.

Officials said the timeframe for the talks would be agreed at a later date, though the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has suggested they are likely to conclude in around a year.

Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders' summit in Manchester next November, Miliband told BBC Newscast, external: "Broadly speaking, yes."

News.title: British man infected with Ebola in DR Congo to be flown back to UK
News.content:
A British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo will be flown back to the UK.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.

It is not clear when the flight will take place.

Earlier, a UK government spokesperson said there were "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and that the risk to the public remains low.

Reuters news agency reported the infected man is a healthcare worker, citing an internal document BBC News has not seen.

Imported Ebola cases are extremely rare in the UK and have resulted in no deaths.

There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

A UK government spokesperson said: "The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated.

"Further information will be shared in due course as appropriate. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low."

There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa.

It has since become the deadliest in the country's history, with a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.

News.title: World's tiniest car up for auction for £60k – here's what can fit inside
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A Peel P50, officially recognised as the world's smallest production car, is expected to fetch as much as £60,000 at auction.

Iconic Auctioneers, of Ashorne, Warwickshire, has put an estimate of £40,000 to £60,000 on the microcar, which goes under the hammer on 14 November.

The three-wheeled vehicle measures just 4.5ft long and 3.5ft wide – enough room for one adult and one shopping bag.

The P50 was built by the Peel Engineering Company, which produced it on the Isle of Man in 1964.

When new, the car retailed at £199, equivalent to £3,635 today.

open image in gallery The olive green microcar that is up for sale ( Iconic Auctioneers/BNPS )

It was designed as a city car with a top speed of nearly 40mph. There is no reverse gear – instead, the driver must use a handle at the rear to lift the back end and swing the car around by hand.

The car was advertised as “almost cheaper than walking” due to its fuel economy.

The Guinness Book of Records gave the P50 official recognition as the world's smallest production car in 2010.

However, the design never took off, and only about 50 were built between 1962 and 1965 before the model was scrapped.

Fewer than 30 survive today, making them coveted by wealthy petrolheads.

open image in gallery Model Karen Burch at the wheel of a Peel P50 in Earl’s Court in 1962 ( Getty )

The olive green car now being sold was imported new into Finland in 1964, and stayed there until earlier this year.

An Iconic Auctioneers spokesperson said: "Officially recognised as the smallest production car in the world and freshly arrived from Finland, this Olive Green Peel P50 tells a remarkable story.

"The Guinness Book of Records has officially recognised the Peel P50 as the 'World's Smallest Production Car'.

"From its harbourside base in the town of Peel on the Isle of Man, the Peel Engineering Company was a specialist producing boats and motorcycle fairings for the likes of Norton and BMW.

"Dreamed up by the company's founder, Cyril Cannell, the P50 was designed as a 40mph city car for 'one adult and a shopping bag' and was unveiled at the 1962 Earl's Court Cycle and Motorcycle Show with one wheel at the front and two at the rear.

"This layout was soon switched and with a 49cc two-stroke Zweirad Union/DKW engine driving the rear wheel through a three-speed manual gearbox, with the production model launched in 1963.”

open image in gallery The Peel P50 has three wheels and a handle at the rear used to lift and turn the car ( Iconic Auctioneers/BNPS )

The olive green Peel is “presented in unrestored and highly original condition wearing its years proudly”, the auctioneers said.

“Recently repatriated to the UK from Finland and ripe for a complete restoration, few Peel P50s can tell their story as well as this one."

Alex Lucocq, car specialist at Iconic Auctioneers, added: “The Peel P50 holds a special place in the hearts of many car enthusiasts and collectors.

“In the past 20 years, it has achieved something of a cult-like status. Well-known car personalities like Jeremy Clarkson have sung its praises, and for good reason – it represents the brilliance, creativity and eccentricity of the British car industry in the early 1960s.

“This desirability and the vehicle’s scarcity – only 30 are thought to exist today worldwide with them rarely coming to market – means an original, authentic Peel P50 is today often worth more than many British sports cars of the era.”

The auction takes place on 14 November.

News.title: Grade-II listed townhouse where Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein could be yours for £800,000
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Grade-II listed townhouse where Mary Shelley completed her renowned novel Frankenstein is on the market for offers over £800,000.

Located in Marlow, Buckinghamshire, the three-bedroom property was once part of the home the author shared with her husband and poet, Percy Bysshe Shelley.

Mary and Percy moved into Albion House shortly after marrying in March 1817, and remained there for nearly a year.

The author, then aged just 19, had begun writing Frankenstein during a famously gloomy summer in Switzerland the previous year.

She completed the novel while living in Marlow, before it was published anonymously on 1 January 1818.

open image in gallery The home in Marlow, Buckinghamshire ( Jam Press/Bonners & Babingtons )

The house was also a creative retreat for Percy, who worked on some of his best-known poetry during their stay.

When the Shelleys moved into the original Albion House, their household also included Mary's stepsister Claire Clairmont, children and servants.

During the couple's stay, Mary also gave birth to her and Percy’s daughter Clara in September 1817.

But life wasn't entirely idyllic. Despite its picturesque surroundings, Mary reportedly found the property cold and damp, while the couple also struggled financially.

The Shelleys' stay in Marlow proved short-lived. They left England for Italy in March 1818, just months after Frankenstein was published.

open image in gallery The kitchen is a far cry from the facilities available during the Shelleys' time ( Jam Press/Bonners & Babingtons )

The historic building was subsequently divided into four homes, including the three-storey Shelley Cottage, which is now being sold by Bonners & Babingtons.

Dating in part to the 18th century, the property retains exposed wooden beams, fireplaces and a distinctive white exterior.

It offers approximately 1,177 sq ft of accommodation, with three bedrooms, a modern kitchen and an enclosed courtyard garden.

The chain-free home, on West Street, has had its asking price reduced and is now available for offers over £800,000.

A plaque outside the property commemorates the famous couple, who lived here between 1817 and 1818.

open image in gallery A plaque outside the property commemorates the famous couple ( Jam Press/Bonners & Babingtons )

According to the estate agent, the site may originally have been occupied by a late 16th-century house, before being rebuilt during the 18th century.

Behind the historic exterior is a bright sitting room with white armchairs, a sofa, wooden flooring and a fireplace.

The attractive hallway features herringbone-style wooden flooring, rustic doors and a wine rack tucked beneath a counter.

The kitchen is a far cry from the facilities available during the Shelleys' time, boasting grey cabinetry, a substantial range cooker and a dining table.

A glazed roof floods the room with natural light, creating an airy contrast to the period features found elsewhere in the historic property.

One of the bedrooms features an ornate cast-iron fireplace, shuttered windows and a large double bed.

open image in gallery One of the bedrooms features an ornate cast-iron fireplace, shuttered windows and a large double bed ( Jam Press/Bonners & Babingtons )

Although the interiors have been modernised, details like these evoke the property's earlier life, while built-in bookshelves, framed artwork and a distinctive tiger-patterned rug give this bedroom a literary feel.

A further bedroom is tucked beneath the sloping roof, with white-painted beams, a small shuttered window and a cosy double bed.

The bathroom reveals a fitted bathtub with overhead shower, white mosaic wall tiles and a traditional sash-style window.

A timber outbuilding provides additional storage, while the town centre and River Thames are close by.

News.title: South Korean army faces backlash over soldiers being taught the catwalk
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

South Korea’s Army has acknowledged that a training programme at an elite special forces unit, in which soldiers were taught to walk and pose like fashion models, was inappropriate.

The event – called the K-Walking Performance Military Festival – was held at a gymnasium inside the Army Special Warfare Command’s 1st Special Forces Brigade base on 29 October, according to local media reports.

Footage obtained by broadcaster TV Chosun from a YouTuber who previously served in the special forces showed female models wearing camouflage outfits and high heels demonstrating catwalk techniques to groups of male soldiers.

The soldiers copied their movements, including walking with one foot placed in front of the other, turning their bodies and striking poses with bent arms. They later took turns walking forward and posing while the models watched, The Korea Herald reported.

The footage prompted criticism on social media, with some questioning why an elite military unit responsible for high-risk operations was spending time on runway techniques.

“Given the nature and responsibilities of a unit tasked with special operations, it’s hard to understand the purpose of this training,” one user wrote on X.

People Power Party lawmaker Park Choong-kwon also criticised the programme.

He wrote on his Facebook: “North Korea is carrying out land mine provocations and firing combinations of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and multiple rocket launchers, yet the Ministry of National Defense under the Lee Jae Myung administration is bringing in fashion models to teach special forces soldiers how to walk.”

He said, according to The Korea JoongAng Daily: “With the president himself lacking a clear sense of national security, the minister [talks vaguely as if he] is performing musicals, a corps commander is ordering troops to stand guard with unloaded rifles and front line commanders are arranging special lectures on catwalk techniques.”

Mr Park argued that the soldiers themselves should not be held responsible for the programme.

“The rank-and-file soldiers are not to blame,” he said. “The military must take responsibility for the humiliation these elite troops must have felt. Yet the unit made excuses, saying the training was intended to help soldiers develop proper posture and walking techniques to establish basic military bearing.”

The incident became fodder for online users. Some users suggested that the footage could damage the country’s international reputation. One user wrote that the incident “could make international headlines” and that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un “would collapse laughing if he saw this”.

The Army initially described the event as part of a personal development programme organised twice a year. The brigade said its intention was to help soldiers improve their posture, walking techniques and general military bearing, according to Chosun Daily.

However, an Army official admitted that the programme had not been properly assessed before it was organised.

“The training was a hands-on programme led by outside instructors as part of personal development training held once every six months,” the official said.

“However, the programme content was inappropriate because it did not suit the characteristics of the unit or the needs and expectations of its soldiers, and it had not been properly reviewed beforehand.”

“We will gather soldiers’ opinions from the planning stage of future personal development training programs and carefully review the appropriateness of the training content,” the official added.

The 1st Special Forces Brigade was among the units deployed during former South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol’s declaration of martial law on 3 December 2024. The brigade’s commander at the time Lee Sang-hyun is currently on trial over charges connected to the declaration.

News.title: Multiple flights in Europe diverted because of bomb threats after earlier hoaxes
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Multiple flights in Europe made emergency landings on Thursday after being diverted because of bomb threats, authorities said. The incidents followed hoax bomb threats earlier this week that prompted searches, diversions and in one case a military escort.

More than a dozen flights from cities including Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw were confirmed to have been targeted with bomb threats, most diverted to other airports for emergency landings while others landed safely at their destinations. So far inspections have not turned up hazardous or suspicious materials.

Such threats are not new, but the latest incidents come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and other disruptions, like attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems, drone incursions in Europe and mysterious triggers to alert apps. Authorities have warned that hybrid threats abound.

Czech police said searches of another four planes that landed in Prague after being targeted by bomb threats were clear. They have not given details on where the flights originated.

Earlier, a flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in western France because of a bomb threat, the French prime minister’s office said. The flight landed safely at the base in Evreux in Normandy, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office said. All 151 passengers and six crew members were safe and military bomb disposal teams were examining the plane, the office said.

It added that it was following the situation in real time. No other information was immediately released.

Authorities report ‘abstract threats’ to several airports

A LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at its destination, where inspections found no hazardous or suspicious items, the airline said. A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed safely in Bucharest following a bomb threat, airport spokesman Teo Postelnicu said.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome landed safely at Rome's Leonardo da Vinci airport at around 9:30 a.m., escorted by Italian air force fighter jets, according to an airport official with knowledge of the situation. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly.

An emailed bomb threat had been received, and security clearance procedures by police bomb disposal experts were completed, with no explosives found, the official said.

A flight to Warsaw landed in Vienna following a mail to Polish authorities containing an abstract threat, said Stefan Loidl, a police spokesperson in Lower Austria province. Nothing was found and the plane continued to Warsaw.

He said there was also an abstract threat to Vienna Airport concerning four other flights, which he declined to identify, but operations were not disrupted.

Polish authorities checked a LOT flight that was about to depart from Warsaw to Paris on Thursday morning after a threat was reported at Warsaw’s Chopin Airport, said airport spokesman Piotr Rudzki. No threat was ultimately identified. One runway at Chopin airport was temporarily closed while authorities carried out standard security procedures.

Three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, had to make emergency landings because of bomb threats on board. Two of the flights, one from Copenhagen, Denmark, and the other from Madrid, landed safely at Sofia’s Vasil Levski Airport, airport officials told reporters. The third Sofia-bound flight, from London’s Stansted Airport to Sofia, had been diverted and landed safely at the airport in Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s second-largest city, Plovdiv Airport CEO Krassimir Peshev said.

Hoaxes prompted similar searches earlier this week

Several flights across Europe received hoax bomb threats earlier this week that prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, an escort by the Italian air force until landing, officials said.

The flights included Polish airline LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair. The hoax threats came after a plane headed for Bulgaria was diverted to Hungary after receiving a similar bomb threat while in the air. No one was injured.

——-

Charlton reported from Paris and Biller from Rome. Associated Press writers throughout Europe contributed to this report.

News.title: Rolls-Royce Spectre Series II review: the ultimate luxury electric car gets better
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In my view, two car companies sit above all the others: Ferrari and Rolls-Royce. One makes the ultimate sports cars, the other the ultimate luxury cars. Other manufacturers might think they have something to rival them, but I don’t think anything gets particularly close. By and large, both have also been very good at sticking to what they do best and never stepping on each other’s toes.

Spend time in a Rolls-Royce and you soon understand that position. I drove the Spectre through some of the wealthiest parts of South Buckinghamshire, where an expensive car is hardly an unusual sight. Even there, it felt exceptionally rare. I found myself wondering whether another Rolls-Royce had passed through those towns and villages that day, or even that week – that’s the sort of exclusivity we’re talking about.

The Spectre has been something of a surprise hit for Rolls-Royce, although the combination does make perfect sense. Electric power brings the silence, effortless shove and lovely waftiness that you expect from a Rolls-Royce. The familiar Power in Reserve display, rather than an unseemly rev counter, seems especially at home here – you’re reminded of what’s still available, which is rather more in keeping with the car’s character.

First introduced in 2022, the Spectre remained Rolls-Royce’s second best-selling model globally in 2025. Series II brings more power, revised battery-cell technology and a maximum claimed range of 390 miles, together with more ways to personalise the car. The fastback shape, clean bodywork and split headlights remain, while a new solid paint colour called Ethereal Blue joins the choices.

There’s a more elaborate new finish, too. Gradient Two-Tone paint changes colour from one end of the car to the other, instead of dividing the colours horizontally. It took more than six months to develop and can take four days to apply, with four colour combinations over a black base. New forged alloy wheels, measuring 584mm in diameter, have crisp, faceted surfaces with 2.5mm radii. Each can take six hours to finish by hand, with part-polished or fully polished finishes available.

My car was rather more restrained, but no less beautiful in Mustique Blue and Silver. The view down that long bonnet was glorious, while the quality of the exterior finish out of the Goodwood factory was sensational. It was a very tasteful reminder that personalisation doesn’t have to mean going completely overboard.

How we tested

I spent 48 hours with the Spectre Series II around Buckinghamshire, covering roads from my home in South Bucks all the way up to Milton Keynes. That meant everything from the M1 and M25 to town roads, suburban streets and country lanes, where the Rolls can feel very wide. I also carried out the usual Fowler car park test, although a nice pub stood in for the supermarket this time. I even took the dog for a ride, with seat coverings firmly in place, obviously.

The weather was about as far from the Côte d’Azur as you could imagine. It was filthy, and I felt a little guilty taking such a lovely car out in it, but the Spectre kept me thoroughly cosseted and didn’t once complain. Along the way I tried the controls and Rolls-Royce’s own audio system, had a six-foot-plus friend try the rear seats and stopped at an Ionity rapid charger, where the highest charging rate I saw was 162kW.

Rolls-Royce Spectre Series II: from £280,000, Rolls-roycemotorcars.com

open image in gallery The interior of the Spectre II hasn't changed much and remains like nothing else ( Steve Fowler )

Independent rating: 9/10

Pros: Wonderful sense of occasion, quiet, effortless performance, sumptuous interior and beautiful craftsmanship

Wonderful sense of occasion, quiet, effortless performance, sumptuous interior and beautiful craftsmanship Cons: Occasional firmness over town roads, technology could have moved further forward, size and huge doors need care in tight spaces

Rolls-Royce Spectre Series II specifications:

Price: from £280,000

from £280,000 Battery size: 112.4kWh

112.4kWh Maximum claimed range: 390 miles

390 miles Charging: 195kW DC, 10 to 80 per cent in 28 minutes

Battery, range, charging, performance and drive

The Spectre Series II has a 112.4kWh battery and two electric motors, with a combined 593bhp and 1,015Nm of torque. That’s 115Nm more than the original Spectre, although the way the power arrives is much more interesting than the number itself. Acceleration is wonderfully measured: a more gentle, smooth, linear shove rather than a sudden kick. There was never any shortage of it on the roads I drove on, either – put your foot down and it just keeps coming.

open image in gallery The Spectre Series II's coupe shape stretches to 5,490mm in length ( Steve Fowler )

Rolls-Royce quotes 0–62mph in 4.5 seconds, or 0–60mph in 4.4 seconds, with a top speed of 155mph. Those are brisk figures for a car weighing 2,925kg, but the Spectre encourages a far gentler manner of motoring. The big steering wheel and the steering itself aren’t especially reactive; you soon settle into the car’s relaxed rhythm, and I found it surprisingly simple to drive. It’s a big thing to pilot, certainly, but it isn’t unwieldy.

The more powerful Black Badge Series II produces up to 671bhp in Infinity Mode, with Spirited Mode (what a wonderful name) allowing up to 1,100Nm. Its quoted 0–62mph time is 4.3 seconds, or 4.1 seconds to 60mph.

For most of the time, the ride delivers exactly the sort of gliding progress you’d hope for. Waftiness, if that’s a word, is in plentiful supply. There is another side to it, though – around town I was occasionally surprised by a firmer response, and a pothole could send a shimmy through the car.

It’s eerily quiet, although it isn’t completely silent. I remember Rolls-Royce engineers explaining to me that they could make a car completely quiet but deliberately allowed some sound in to help avoid travel sickness and let the driver know a little about what was happening outside, including the weather. The Spectre certainly leaves you well insulated from the worst of it, whilene-pedal driving fits its gentle character beautifully, too.

Rolls-Royce says revised battery-cell technology increases range by up to 18 per cent and cuts charging times by up to 14 per cent. The standard Series II’s claimed range spans 362 to 390 miles, depending on specification, while the Black Badge’s quoted range starts at 359 miles and reaches the same 390-mile maximum.

Maximum DC charging power is somewhat disappointing at 195kW, with a 10–80 per cent charge quoted at 28 minutes on a suitable rapid charger. On a 50kW charger, the same top-up takes a claimed 107 minutes. AC charging is supported at up to 22kW, with an empty-to-full charge taking five hours and 45 minutes for the standard car, or five hours and 30 minutes for Black Badge.

open image in gallery Even in dreadful British weather, the Spectre Series II's style and luxury shone through ( Steve Fowler )

My stop at an Ionity rapid charger didn’t produce the headline rate: 162kW was the highest figure I saw. I could still very happily imagine gliding down to the south of France in the Spectre, with an occasional charging stop along the way. Buckinghamshire in dreadful weather gave me plenty of reason to wish I was heading in that direction.

Interior, practicality and boot space

The Spectre Series II is a two-door, four-seat coupé measuring a sizeable 5,490mm long, 2,144mm wide, 1,585mm tall with a 3,210mm wheelbase and a 12,700mm turning circle. Those dimensions help explain why it feels so substantial, particularly on a country lane. The boot holds a pretty measly 380 litres.

open image in gallery Rear space in the Rolls-Royce Spectre Series II is surprisingly generous – and there's the stars in the roof to enjoy, too ( Steve Fowler )

The sizeable rear-hinged doors are part of the occasion, although they need some care. Park beside another car or an obstruction and you can find yourself sliding through the gap rather than making the grand entrance you might have had in mind. My Fowler car park test took place at a nice pub, and even a Rolls-Royce has to deal with the realities of parking beside other people.

Once you’re in the driver’s seat, putting your foot on the brake closes the door. The passenger’s door has a closing button on the centre console, next to the driver, which struck me as an odd place for it.

The seats themselves are huge, comfortable chairs, and that applies in the back as well as the front. A friend who’s more than six feet tall was perfectly happy in the rear, with good space once they were settled. Getting there requires the front seat to slide forwards, which happens at a suitably leisurely pace; like so much else in a Rolls-Royce, it glides, and gliding takes time. My car also had ventilated massage seats, the deepest lambswool footmats you can imagine and privacy glass for the rear.

My test car combined Grace White, Black and Charles Blue inside, with gorgeous Obsidian Tulip veneer. I particularly liked the proper physical key, trimmed in the same light Charles Blue leather as the cabin – it’s a small detail, but a lovely one to have in your hand. Everything inside felt considered and restrained, and the build quality was sensational. You can go an awfully long way with the personalisation, but this car showed how tasteful the result can be. And yes, there’s an umbrella tucked into each door.

Series II adds some interesting alternatives to the familiar leather-and-wood approach. Duality Twill is a rayon fabric made from bamboo, inspired by the bamboo grove in Le Jardin des Méditerranées on the French Riviera, beside Sir Henry Royce’s former winter home, Villa Mimosa. Its embroidered pattern draws on the founders’ interlinked R initials and the ropes of sailing yachts. It’s available in Lilac, Chocolate, Black or a new Sage green, with more than 50 thread colours. A complete interior can involve 2.6 million stitches, 10 miles of thread and up to 25 hours of work.

The new Placed Perforation leather takes a different approach. Its pattern, inspired by clouds in moonlight, contains 78,138 holes across the shoulders and headrests of the front and rear seats, in sizes of 0.8mm, 1mm and 1.2mm. With the illuminated-door option, the pattern becomes less dense around the lights, intended to suggest stars appearing through clouds.

open image in gallery The Spectre's boot holds a pretty measly 380 litres ( Steve Fowler )

There’s also the option of a high-gloss Brindled Walnut veneer, made by combining wood from non-fruiting walnut trees that would otherwise be burned with eucalyptus fibres left over from fine-paper production. The material is compressed and cut into veneer sheets to create a striped pattern. Glass flakes in the lacquer, beneath a final clear coat, give it a shimmering depth.

There are options, and then there are Rolls-Royce options!

Technology, stereo and infotainment

The Spectre’s cabin is a very Rolls-Royce blend of old and new, and that includes, wait for it, buttons. Plenty of them. I applaud the restraint in keeping so many functions out of the touchscreen, although it can still take a while to work out which button does what. Familiarity with BMW’s systems also makes some of the technology’s origins fairly easy to spot.

open image in gallery The dash blends old-school Rolls-Royce style with plenty of modern features ( Steve Fowler )

I was disappointed that Series II hadn’t moved things on a little further in this respect. The materials and the way everything is put together feel very special, but that doesn’t remove the opportunity to improve the technology. I don’t expect Rolls-Royce to lead every new development; I do expect it to offer advances that bring a useful benefit to the people sitting in the car.

The audio system is a good example. It’s Rolls-Royce’s own and it sounds seriously good, among the best systems without Dolby Atmos that I’ve listened to. You’d hope for something pretty impressive at this level, and that’s what you get. Even so, the absence of the latest audio technology is a shame. I enjoyed listening to it enormously while still wishing the update had gone that little bit further.

The digital interface is called Spirit and you get a beautifully animated Spirit of Ecstacy graphic as it starts up. My car had Apple CarPlay, DAB radio, wireless phone charging and connected services, alongside Parking Assistant Plus, Rolls-Royce’s Advanced Driver Assistance Systems and a universal garage-door opener. The voice assistant, Eleanor, is activated by a button on the steering wheel and can help with requests such as adjusting the temperature or finding a charging station.

Some of the most visible changes involve illumination. The interior panel and clock gallery now extend across the fascia, alongside a new illuminated artwork made up of 8,108 individual points of light. Its flowing wave pattern is inspired by mist over the South Downs near Goodwood. There’s a new clock, too, with metal hands and a clear design influenced by aircraft instruments. Beside it, an inset glass display houses a solid stainless-steel Spirit of Ecstasy figure lit from below.

open image in gallery There are buttons inside – and plenty of them. But the tech could do with a bit of an update ( Steve Fowler )

Outside, the illuminated grille might be a little too chintzy for some tastes, but you can switch it off. The same goes for the stars in the headlining. I enjoyed the initial spectacle, although later the cabin lights had me wondering whether I was seeing light from a car behind. I turned them down. It’s lovely to have the theatre available, but I was glad I could settle it all down to suit me.

Prices and running costs

The price? Don’t be vulgar. We can at least give you a steer, although ordering one also means joining a very long queue. A Spectre Series II starts at around £280,000, with Black Badge at around £325,000. Rolls-Royce says the average Spectre works out at roughly £400,000 once all the personalisation has been added, so the starting figure is only part of the story.

open image in gallery The Rolls-Royce Spectre Series II only charges at a maximum of 195kW – slow by today's standards ( Steve Fowler )

Some owners request more than 20 individual Bespoke details, and only the Phantom attracts more demand for Rolls-Royce’s personalisation work. The company’s Private Offices offer further scope to create something individual. Examples include a Starlight Headliner showing the constellations on the day a couple first met, marquetry celebrating a much-loved dog called Bailey, and interiors echoing the colours and textures of an owner’s home. Another commission took its inspiration from the colour associated with a client’s favourite jewellery designer. One owner in Korea has even created a gallery at home in which to display the car.

Black Badge adds its own choices. New Iced Black exterior detailing gives a satin-like finish to much of the brightwork, including the grille surround, window surrounds, bumper inserts, badge surround, handles and Spirit of Ecstasy. The grille vanes stay polished. There’s also a new seven-spoke wheel design with a polished outer ring and glass flakes in the finish, plus an Iced Matte Black option created using a special high-temperature curing process.

Running costs sit in a rather different context when Rolls-Royce says a typical Spectre is the second Rolls in a seven-car garage. Its research found average annual mileage of around 4,000 miles, similar to the Wraith, Dawn and Phantom Coupé, with owners charging almost exclusively at home. The Spectre is often driven alone and increasingly used for the simple pleasure of driving it.

That doesn’t mean every Spectre spends its life tucked away. Rolls-Royce describes a European owner covering more than 30,000 miles in two years, against a typical 4,000 miles a year. A collector in Los Angeles uses theirs daily and particularly enjoys the journey downhill from their house to their garage: regenerative braking means the car arrives showing more range than it had at the start.

The Spectre’s battery has a 15-year, unlimited-mileage warranty, while the car itself has four years’ unlimited-mileage cover for private use.

The verdict: Rolls-Royce Spectre Series II

The Spectre Series II is a truly sumptuous motor car, with a sense of occasion that nothing else quite matches. What’s more, electric power suits a Rolls-Royce beautifully, and this one makes relaxed progress feel very special indeed. It’s surprisingly simple to drive, too, even if you’re always aware of its size on a narrow lane or in a car park.

There are reservations: the ride can be unexpectedly firm around town, the big doors need room and I’d have liked the technology to move further forward. But the comfort, craftsmanship and effortless performance make you feel very special indeed. Series II nudges the Spectre forward in the ways it needs to, even if there’s still room to improve the tech. My biggest disappointment was having to give it back so soon.

FAQs

How long does it take to charge?

Rolls-Royce quotes 28 minutes for a 10–80 per cent charge on a suitable rapid charger, with a maximum DC rate of 195kW. The same charge takes a claimed 107 minutes on a 50kW charger. At the maximum 22kW AC rate, a full charge takes five hours and 45 minutes for the standard Spectre Series II, or five hours and 30 minutes for Black Badge. My highest observed rate at an Ionity rapid charger was 162kW.

How much does it cost and is it worth it?

The Spectre Series II starts at around £280,000, with Black Badge at around £325,000. Rolls-Royce says a typical Spectre reaches roughly £400,000 after personalisation. The comfort, craftsmanship, quiet performance and sense of occasion are wonderful, although I’d like more up-to-date technology and the ride can be unexpectedly firm around town. It’s a very special car, and one I wished I could have kept for longer.

Does Rolls-Royce replace batteries for free?

The Spectre’s battery comes with a 15-year, unlimited-mileage warranty, which Rolls-Royce has extended to new and existing cars. Any repair or replacement needs to qualify under the warranty’s terms; it isn’t an automatic promise of a brand-new battery whenever the range drops. The car itself has a four-year, unlimited-mileage warranty for private use.

Why trust us

Our team of motoring experts have decades of experience driving, reviewing and reporting on the latest EV cars, and our verdicts are reached with every kind of driver in mind. We thoroughly test drive every car we recommend.

News.title: Court rules that ER and The Pitt have ‘clear similarities’ after legal challenge from ER creator’s widow
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A US appeals court has permitted the lawsuit launched by Michael Crichton’s widow against the TV series The Pitt to proceed.

Sherri Crichton, the widow of the late author and creator of the TV series ER, began legal procedings against The Pitt in 2024, before the first season aired. The lawsuit contends that The Pitt is in effect an unauthorised reboot of ER, something that Warner Bros Television (WBTV) and the show’s producers have denied.

In a new ruling filed on Wednesday (4 November), a panel of three judges denied an appeal from The Pitt producers to have the case thrown out, stating that “there are clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER”.

open image in gallery Noah Wyle in 'The Pitt' ( HBO )

Also among the defendants are John Wells, an executive producer of The Pitt who formerly served as showrunner on ER ; lead Noah Wyle, who starred in ER before fronting The Pitt, and R Scott Gemmill, an executive producer and writer on ER who is the showrunner and an executive producer of The Pitt.

Michael Crichton’s 1994 contract with WBTV for ER – which was originally based on his experiences as a medical student – included a stipulation preventing any spin-offs being produced without his approval. With Crichton having died in 2008, his estate now assumes this authority.

Wyle and the show’s producers have spoken openly about the new series’ origins, stating that The Pitt came about after plans for a prospective reboot of ER fell through.

In the new court ruling, judges found that the two shows evinced various similarities, including the emergency room setting, the use of “frequently incomprehensible” medical jargon, overlapping simultaneous crises and gory injury recreations.

The document also notes that both series featured “exhausted” medical staff who suffer “emotional outbursts”.

“Each includes a young doctor, fresh from medical school and incompetent,” it states.

The defendants have argued that these shared qualities were “generic”, and can be found in any series “involving emergency room doctors”.

“It cannot be that all shows set in an emergency room are derivative of ER,” they contended.

open image in gallery George Clooney on 'ER' ( Getty )

Speaking on Amy Poehler’s Good Hang podcast, Wyle previously claimed that they had a “near-miss” with rebooting ER”, and had “uncoupled ourselves from that IP”.

The US court concluded: “We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case.”

Failing a settlement, the lawsuit will now proceed to a jury trial. However, Wyle, Wells and Gemmill were removed from the list of defendents, with the court ruling that they were unaware of the potential for a rights violation in the creation of The Pitt.

“I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators and their families and estates, being presented to a jury,” Sherri Crichton told Variety.

The Pitt has been a significant critical and ratings hit for HBO since its premiere in 2025, winning the Emmy Award for Best Drama for two years running. It returns for a third season in January next year.

News.title: Trump issues ominous warning as Democrats get another chance to impeach him. Will they take it?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump has warned that any attempts to impeach him would “destroy” the Democratic Party after his party lost its control of Congress.

Trump and the Republican Party were hit by a “Blue Tsunami” in Tuesday’s midterms, looking on in horror as the GOP’s majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate were washed away on a wave of public anger.

As of Wednesday morning, the opposition Democrats had picked up 25 additional seats in the House and seven in the Senate, taking them well clear of the 218 and 51 seats they needed to claim the upper hand in the twin chambers of Congress.

Asked whether he was concerned that the legislative bodies would move to impeach him, Trump issued a defiant and ominous warning: “Not even a little bit. I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that.

“Impeachment for no reason, what for having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in its history.”

The results have left an uncharacteristically downtrodden Trump conceding defeat, lashing out at his own candidates and media allies and already looking ahead to the prospect of a Democrat-run legislative making life difficult for him in the final two years of his second term.

The newly emboldened Democrats are likely to interpret the outcome as a mandate from an unhappy electorate to go after the Trump administration. They are expected to wield the powers of the congressional committees to launch probes into the president and his inner circle.

Trump is already the first American president to be impeached twice, so whether the Democrats will seek to do so again is a natural question.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump suffered a disastrous midterms, leaving him vulnerable to a possible impeachment push from rejuvenated Democrats on Capitol Hill ( Getty )

The Republican was first impeached by the Nancy Pelosi-led House in 2019, after a whistleblower reported him for threatening to withhold $400 million in congressionally-approved military aid to Ukraine on an official call with that country’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, unless the latter opened an investigation into Joe Biden’s son Hunter’s business dealings in Kyiv.

Trump went on to be acquitted in the Senate, a scenario that was repeated when he was impeached for an unprecedented second time after his supporters stormed the Capitol on January 6, 2021.

Republicans like Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz have both said they fully expect the Democrats to try for a third impeachment. The betting markets Kalshi and Polymarket are offering odds of 77.2 percent and 80 percent respectively as of Wednesday morning. However, the noise from the other side of the aisle has been much more muted.

New Yorker Hakeem Jeffries, who is about to become the first Black speaker of the House, was asked about the prospect by ABC News in September and said only: “We haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out.”

Speaking to The New Yorker’s Political Scene podcast earlier this week, influential Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin was equally cagey, telling host David Remnick impeachment was just one of many “tools” his side might choose to use on the Trump administration.

open image in gallery Hakeem Jeffries, the next House speaker, has refused to either rule out a new impeachment push or directly commit to it ( Getty )

New-minted Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who just beat Trump favorite Jon Husted, also expressed disapproval during his campaign, saying: “I can’t speak for everybody else but I would not support an impeachment of Trump. There’s just simply no reason for that, no matter what happens in the midterms.”

The difficulty of securing a conviction in the Senate – which requires a two-thirds majority to remove a president on grounds of treason, bribery or, more vaguely, “high crimes and misdemeanors” – might well dissuade the Democrats from having another go, even with their enhanced majority, which will see the likes of James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed and Josh Turek joining the ranks come January.

There is also a feeling that impeaching Trump allows him to push a victimization narrative and declare a “witch hunt”. This could ultimately only serve to rally his base around him at a time when it appears to be at its most fractured for a decade, judging by Tuesday’s outcome.

“Impeaching Trump is a bad idea,” Matt Bennett, co-founder of Third Way, a centrist Democratic think-tank, told The Times. “I want to be clear that we believe that Trump commits five impeachable offences before breakfast every morning. So this is not a question of his culpability.

“This is a question of political reality, and the reality is there’s literally zero chance that he will be removed from office unless he does something even more egregious.”

open image in gallery California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, leader of the House Oversight Committee, responded to Tuesday’s midterms triumph with a two-word tweet: ‘LAWYER UP’ ( Getty )

Nevertheless, California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, leader of the House Oversight Committee, responded to the midterms triumph with a two-word tweet, “LAWYER UP,” - making his intentions plain.

This might be through other means than impeachment, however, with Democrats likely to take an interest in accusations of corruption and personal enrichment leveled against the president.

Targeting him at one-remove by impeaching one of his top Cabinet secretaries might also prove a more fruitful avenue, with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, for instance, already the subject of articles of impeachment filed by outgoing Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie – and a direct threat from Jeffries.

“One of the first things we’re going to do in the majority, we’re going to run Pete Hegseth out of town,” the new speaker said on the campaign trail in Pennsylvania recently.
