World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football
World.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo announced his intention to ⁠retire from ⁠the Portugal national team in a social media post, bringing to ⁠an end one of the most illustrious international careers in the history of football.

The 41-year-old ⁠said on Thursday he would “hand back the number 7 shirt” after the November international break.

Ronaldo captained the team to their first major trophy at Euro 2016 ‌and helped them win the 2019 and 2025 Nations Leagues.

“It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made only with the head. They are also made with the heart,” said Ronaldo.

“If ⁠I ever made you happy, ⁠if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, ⁠then it was all worth it.”

Ronaldo thanked his family, the Portuguese ⁠people and the teammates, coaches ⁠and staff he worked with over his 23-year career with national team.

“Portugal will always be a part of me,” ‌he captioned the announcement video.

Ronaldo has made 234 appearances for Portugal and scored 146 goals. ‌He ‌holds the all-time record for international appearances and for international goals.

He fell out with national coach Jorge Jesus last month after he refused to use him in a Nations League match. Ronaldo immediately left the team camp.

More to follow.

World.title: Serbian officers arrested for using ‘excessive force’ against protesters
World.content:
Ten suspects are accused of abusing and torturing several people in the garage of a government compound in Belgrade.

Nine active Serbian police officers and one former officer have been arrested over accusations of using excessive force against students last year during protests that culminated in October’s electoral defeat of former President Aleksandar Vucic.

The Serbian Ministry of Interior announced Wednesday’s arrests, alleging that the suspects abused and tortured several people in the garage of a government compound in Belgrade in August 2025.

In a statement, the ministry said the suspects were on duty when they “used force and threats to inflict severe pain and suffering on several injured people, in order to obtain information, intimidate and unlawfully punish them”.

Anticorruption protests began in Serbia after 16 people were killed when the canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad collapsed in November 2024. The collapse was seen as symptomatic of alleged widespread corruption under Vucic, who served as president for 12 years before conceding defeat last month after parliamentary elections.

The ministry has released only the initials of the suspects but said they served in an elite unit. According to state broadcaster Radio Television of Serbia, the commander of the Special Antiterrorism Unit, Igor Zmiric, was among the detainees.

Since last month’s vote, the winning student-led protest movement has demanded reforms within state institutions, including the police and intelligence services. Protesters have also called on top officials to resign, accusing them of colluding with Vucic while he was in power.



Hopes that Belgrade would join the European Union have increased since October’s elections as the bloc offered to hold further accession talks if Serbia’s new government strengthens democracy.

In a 2025 report on Serbia, Amnesty International warned that protesters, journalists and civil society organisations “continued to face intimidation, harassment and unlawful surveillance as authorities sought to rein in widespread discontent”.

The rights group said protesters were subjected to excessive force in “multiple cases across the country”.

World.title: ‘Helpless’: The families facing winter in tents on the beach in Gaza
World.content:
An innovative idea to turn damaged cooking pots into seawater barriers is providing families in Gaza with some relief, but it’s far from enough.

Share ‘Helpless’: The families facing winter in tents on the beach in Gaza on social media

Khan Younis, Gaza – A few metres from the sea, near al-Qarara port on Gaza’s coast, Anas al-Shami, 33, is trying to keep his family of six warm and dry in a dilapidated tent. It offers little protection from wind and rain, while the damp seeps into their bedding and belongings at every moment. The swelling waves in the sea also pose a constant threat as winter approaches.

The beach was not al-Shami’s choice of place to live, but the refuge his family took shelter in after being displaced from their home quickly became overcrowded. They can’t afford anything safer than this tent.

Now, he and his family are living in constant fear of a repeat of last winter’s flooding.

Al-Shami and his family were forced to leave Bani Suheila, east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, when it became part of Israel’s so-called “Yellow Zone” beyond which Palestinians are not permitted to go.

“I searched for land in displacement areas where I could pitch a tent, but overcrowding and high rental costs made that impossible,” he tells Al Jazeera. “I was therefore forced to stay on the beach, despite the dangers facing my family and me.”

Al-Shami recalls last winter, when seawater and rain flooded his tent while the family was asleep. He would wake to find his children lying in water. Their bedding and belongings were repeatedly soaked, leaving him unable to protect them from the cold as the tent turned into a pond.

Despite trying all year, the family has been unable to find anywhere else to go, leaving them facing another winter on the beach.



“My children’s repeated exposure to water, cold and damp caused serious illness which threatened their lives,” he says.

‘I feel helpless in front of my children’

It’s a familiar story along this stretch of coastline.

Ibrahim Abu Tair, 47, whose family has also been displaced from eastern Khan Younis, is sharing a cramped tent with his seven children on the port’s shoreline. The dilapidated shelter lacks any basic necessities and offers little protection from the cold, rain and wind.

“What hurts me most is feeling helpless in front of my children,” he says. “I cannot provide winter clothes to protect them from the cold or even a dry mattress for them to sleep on.”

The strong wind and the sound of the rising waves keep him awake at night, he says, and he is terrified of another flood like last year’s, when water inundated the tent and forced the family to endure the cold in the open. His greatest wish is to find safe shelter where his children can sleep without fear.

Some families have found a makeshift solution to keep the water at bay.

By filling damaged cooking pots with earth, they have forged a barrier against encroaching seawater alongside the tents.

Mayasem Association, an aid organisation which works in cooperation with World Central Kitchen, has seized on this innovation and is now producing these pot-barriers for families in this area close to al-Qarara port.

The initiative reuses large pots rendered unusable by repeated exposure to flames, corrosion and holes. Three pots, donated by World Central Kitchen, are filled with soil and stacked on top of one another, reaching approximately 150 centimetres in height to form barriers that hold back the incoming water and prevent waves from reaching shelter sites.

“The initiative initially involved building barriers to protect the association’s safe space, which hosts its education programmes, school, cultural activities, arts and heritage programmes,” Khalil Abu Lahia, the association’s emergency response coordinator, tells Al Jazeera. “The idea later developed into an attempt to protect the displaced families’ tents along the coastal strip.”

A winter fraught with risk

While this is an example of the innovative thinking which can help families who are destitute and at risk in Gaza, it is nevertheless only a temporary measure which cannot make up for the widespread lack of safe shelter.



The initiative comes amid a warning from Gaza’s Winter Emergency Committee of a worsening humanitarian catastrophe, as tents and caravans remain in critically short supply as Israeli authorities continue to prevent their entry into the Gaza Strip, alongside the delivery of critical construction materials and fuel.

The committee has reported that Israeli forces have also destroyed about 70 percent of municipalities’ essential operational equipment and 90 percent of civil defence rescue equipment. The fuel crisis means machinery and generators will soon stop functioning altogether, further limiting the ability to respond to floods, carry out rescue operations and clear roads.

In all, there are about 200,000 dilapidated tents sheltering hundreds of thousands of displaced people, including children, women and people with disabilities.

Some 7,800 of them are located in extremely hazardous areas, the committee has warned, including on dry riverbeds which may now flood, rainwater collection ponds and beaches exposed to crashing winter waves. These need to be urgently relocated to safer locations.

About 2,000 cracked buildings are also at risk of collapse, threatening families who have sought refuge inside them. Building materials, caravans, shelter and fuel are all urgently needed, the committee says.

World.title: Congress defeat: How Trump’s allies are distancing themselves from Iran war
World.content:
US Vice President JD Vance blames the war for the midterm rout as Democrats prepare to use Congress to rein it in.

Share Congress defeat: How Trump’s allies are distancing themselves from Iran war on social media

Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war on Iran for the Republican Party’s sweeping defeat in Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of the United States Congress.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X on Wednesday.

Senator Ted Cruz, a longtime Iran hawk, also turned on the conflict, saying in an episode of his podcast on Wednesday that it “should have been brief, decisive, and over”.

This week, President Donald Trump has insisted that he has no regrets. “I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he told The Wall Street Journal about launching a war on Iran alongside Israel in February.

So, why are Trump’s allies breaking ranks, and what does it mean for the war? Here’s what you need to know:

What have Trump’s allies said?

Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and heir apparent to Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, questioned whether the war had been worth the political cost.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote.

Citing an unnamed pollster, Vance said ending the Iran war and “changing our relationship with Israel” were two of the top four answers given ahead of this week’s midterms by Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 but planned to vote for Democrats this year.

Cruz’s criticism came from another direction. The war had “dragged on too long”, he said in a post on X, adding that Washington “should never, under any circumstances, give the Ayatollah billions of dollars”.



He was apparently referring to the June memorandum of understanding signed by Washington and Tehran, which included a $300bn fund to help rebuild post-war Iran among several topics for discussion in wider peace talks. The proposal for the fund triggered hefty pushback from conservative lawmakers, including Cruz, who said it amounted to a massive payout for the Iranian regime.

The June agreement, which provided for a ceasefire at the time, quickly fell apart, however.

Trump told reporters at the White House on Wednesday that Vance’s assessment was “largely true”, blaming higher fuel prices, as a result of the war, for Americans turning against his party. But the president insisted the war was necessary to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Why are they distancing themselves?

Republicans are positioning themselves for the 2028 presidential election, which Trump will not be able to run in, as he will have served the maximum of two terms as president.

Paul Musgrave, associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera there are “major internal divisions within the Republican Party” over the war.

The US decision to attack Iran triggered a global fuel crisis with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has cost the US taxpayer an estimated $47bn so far. This means candidates for 2028 likely need to distance themselves from the war if they have any hope of winning.

But Musgrave said hawks such as Cruz and the late Senator Lindsey Graham had, in fact, long pushed for a war on Iran. Now that they have one, “it has been a disaster internationally and domestically for them”, he said, but “they can’t walk away”. Instead, they are limited to criticising its length and execution.

Vance, however, “is trying to represent a more isolationist wing of the Republican Party, and is willing to walk away from the war and probably other commitments to win favour with a large part of the Trump base”, Musgrave said.

“This is all about positioning for 2028 and the future of the Republican Party,” he said.

John Feehery, a former Republican congressional staffer, told Al Jazeera the Iran war “was a big part” of the defeat, alongside energy prices, healthcare and corruption. The race to succeed Trump has already begun, he said, pointing to Vance and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis.

What can Democrats do to make the most of this?

Limit the money available for continuing the war, and squeeze the people running it.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said on Wednesday that “this war must end”, pointing to Congress’s control of funding.



“The Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” he told a news conference in Washington, DC.

Congressman Ro Khanna proposed a continuing resolution “prohibiting the financing of any combat activities of the US military in Iran”, ending the war “like we did for Vietnam”.

Musgrave said appropriations would be “a principal lever”, especially given “the havoc that has been wreaked with the defence budget by the spiralling expenses of the war in Iran”.

Feehery, meanwhile, noted that the defence budget and an extension of the debt limit would both need bipartisan support to pass.

Official hearings and investigations, over which Democrats now wield a great deal more power by dominating both chambers of Congress, could also “make the war unpopular and harass or drive from office several key players”, Musgrave said.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is also in the firing line. Outgoing Republican Senator Thom Tillis told CBS News that Hegseth would face a “reckoning” for his part in the Iran war, while Democratic Representative Jason Crow labelled the defence chief as “incompetent and corrupt”.

But Musgrave warned that the bigger fight will likely be over the Trump administration’s refusal to obey congressional spending limits. “I expect many more fights over that than even over the War Powers Act,” he said, referring to the law that requires presidents to gain Congress’s permission before launching a war overseas, but which many presidents have managed to circumvent in the past.

Is the US still preparing for war?

Yes, even as diplomatic efforts and Qatar-led mediated talks continue.

On Tuesday, as Americans voted, US forces struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, the first attack there since June. US officials described the strikes as “defensive”.

US media, citing officials, also reported that the military’s Central Command had prepared for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, when three US aircraft carriers would be in the region.

Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of Gulf State Analytics, said Trump “prides himself in leaving everyone, including the Iranians, constantly guessing”.

With the midterms behind him, “Trump may conclude that he has nothing to lose and choose to significantly escalate this crisis”, Cafiero told Al Jazeera.

Democrats “won’t even take power until January 2027”, he noted. “So perhaps Trump will see these upcoming months as a window of opportunity to act very aggressively toward Tehran.”

Tehran has already promised to respond to any attacks.

Diplomacy is moving in parallel.

Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said Washington and Tehran “remain committed to the negotiation process”, though Iran called the latest US response to Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing”.

Cafiero said Doha’s mediation “can only prove successful if a willingness to compromise on core issues exists on both sides”. He added: “Israel will do all it can to play spoiler to any diplomatic arrangement that Qatar may ultimately help facilitate.”



Trump told The Financial Times on election night that he had no immediate plans to order new attacks.

World.title: England’s Harry Kane extends Bayern Munich contract until 2029
World.content:
‘I love the club, the fans and the city,’ says the Ballon d’Or ‌winner after extending his stay with German champions.

Ballon d’Or ‌winner Harry Kane has signed a contract extension with Bayern Munich until June ⁠2029, the ⁠Bundesliga club has announced.

“I feel right at home at FC Bayern,” Kane said in a statement announcing his extention with Bayern Munich on Thursday.

The England captain joined Bayern from Tottenham Hotspur in 2023 and has since helped the German side win two Bundesliga titles, ⁠the German Cup and two German Super Cups.

The 33-year-old striker has scored 156 goals in 161 appearances in all competitions for Bayern and capped his prolific spell in Munich ⁠by winning the Ballon d’Or last week.

He was the first Englishman to win the prestigious award since Michael Owen in 2001.

“I love the club, the fans and the city of Munich. We have a fantastic ‌team and, in Vincent Kompany, a fantastic manager,” the star forward went on to add.

“It makes me very proud to be part of this club. My whole family is very happy here. I was keen to stay. I’m now looking forward to the future and I want to win many more titles with this great club.”

Kane has frequently been linked with a move back to England, where he remains 47 goals shy of Alan Shearer’s Premier League record ⁠of 260 goals.

However, the striker said in August that the Premier ⁠League no longer holds the same appeal for him as he is focused on his career in Germany.

“Since joining us in 2023, he has achieved extraordinary things with his goals, his influence on the game and ⁠as a role model both on and off the pitch,” Bayern CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen said.



“His contract extension is a commitment to FC ⁠Bayern and to a story that is far from ⁠over.”

Bayern did not disclose financial details of the agreement. However, German media reported that the extension is the most lucrative contract in the club’s history and part of a long-term commitment to the England captain.

Kane has finished as ‌the Bundesliga’s top scorer in each of his seasons with Bayern and was named Germany’s Footballer of the Year in 2026.

He has also won the European Golden Shoe twice, awarded ‌to ‌Europe’s leading league goalscorer, and captained England to a third-place finish at this year’s World Cup.

World.title: A month after Yemen government offensive began, war of attrition takes hold
World.content:
The Houthis suffer losses but also inflict pain on government forces and Saudi Arabia. And there are no signs that either side is easing up, analysts say.

Sanaa, Yemen – When news broke on October 5 that Yemen’s internationally recognised government was launching a major new offensive to take control of territories held by Houthi fighters, Mohammed Ahmed began to prepare for the worst.

Sanaa has been under Houthi control since late 2014 after the Houthis seized the capital city in the initial phase of a civil war that has ebbed and flowed for more than a decade.

But when it announced Operation Dawn of Yemen, the new offensive, last month, Yemeni government forces, backed by a Saudi Arabia-led coalition, declared they would aim to retake control of all parts of the country held by the Houthis, including Sanaa.

“A state of worry and uncertainty overwhelmed my family and me,” Ahmed, a 40-year-old resident of Sanaa, said.

Ahmed was not concerned about which side would emerge victorious. Instead, he feared the consequences of hostilities near or inside Yemen’s most densely populated city.

A month after the operation began, Ahmed’s anxiety has eased as Sanaa remains largely calm, apart from recurring air strikes.

Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have scored territorial gains in other provinces, including Taiz and Lahij in southern Yemen, where fighting has not ceased.

But while Yemenis such as Ahmed said the initial momentum surrounding Dawn of Yemen has faded, experts and researchers view the operation as marking a new phase in a war of attrition that shows no signs of easing.



Striking the pillars of Houthi strategy

Turki al-Goblan, head of the Saudi Daimumah Center for Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Houthis have survived in previous years by adapting to strikes and leveraging complex geography, clandestine supply and concealment networks, and the use of civilians as human shields.

That survival strategy is now under stress. The Dawn of Yemen offensive has “dealt a blow to the three pillars of this strategy”, al-Goblan said.

The first pillar, according to him, is the fuel and supply system, which keeps Houthi combat vehicles moving, transports ammunition and delivers reinforcements. Second, the operation has hit the Houthis in the maritime areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the western coast, which serve as outlets through which alternative external supply routes pass. Bab al-Mandeb connects the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea and is a major waterway through which Saudi Arabia exports its oil and Asian economies, such as China, ship commodities to Europe.

Third, some of the tribes surrounding Sanaa have begun declaring mobilisation in support of the internationally recognised Yemeni government, undermining the Iran-backed Houthis’ reliance on them.

“When these three pillars are targeted simultaneously, the question shifts from the scale of losses to the ability to replenish them,” al-Goblan added.

He argued that the pace of attrition has exceeded the Houthis’ ability to recover.

“Attrition ceases to be the opposite of a decisive victory and becomes the means of achieving it as repeated losses translate into an accumulating inability to sustain the fight. This is the scenario I consider more likely.”

Since seizing Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis have taken control of much of northern and western Yemen. Since then, the conflict has remained unresolved.

Abdulsalam Mohammed, chairman of the Yemeni Abaad Studies and Research Center, said the Dawn of Yemen pushed the Houthis to move their forces and their military capabilities, exposing the group to deadly attacks.

“Many of the Houthi field commanders and hundreds of fighters have been killed in air strikes, especially in Taiz and Yemen’s western coast. While the killing of these fighters has not stopped Houthi territorial gains, these gains can be short-lived if the government airpower and ground fighters keep launching coordinated military attacks,” Mohammed said.

Last month, the Yemeni government said its forces killed or wounded 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours. Late last week, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5. The Houthis have not confirmed a death toll and have in the meantime been firing missiles and drones daily into Saudi Arabia too, hitting multiple airports and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.



A war of attrition

Yazeed al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the course of the conflict increasingly appears to be moving towards a prolonged war of attrition as the government offensive has not shifted the balance of power over the past 30 days.

“The conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics inside Yemen; it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the war involving Iran,” he said.

Iran sees the Houthis as a source of strategic leverage, al-Jeddawy noted. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia seeks to curb the group’s military capabilities and prevent it from threatening vital maritime routes, particularly Bab al-Mandeb.

“The growing intensity of the fighting, the scale of the losses they are prepared to absorb and their willingness to climb the escalation ladder suggest an increasingly zero-sum approach,” al-Jeddawy added.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the total number of attacks by the Saudi-led coalition, including air strikes, in Yemen has reached 3,939 since the latest escalation began.

On Monday, the country’s Presidential Leadership Council reaffirmed its commitment to the Dawn of Yemen and its objectives, namely ending the Houthi “coup”, restoring state institutions and extending the state’s authority over its entire territory.

Colonel Wadah al-Dubaish, spokesperson for the government-aligned Joint Forces on Yemen’s West Coast, told Al Jazeera the Houthis have lately expanded their military gains in Taiz; however, the price of such a move is extremely high.

“The group’s expansion has been a big adventure. What the Houthis have lost over the past month is more than their losses over the past years combined.”

Yemeni government forces said they had reclaimed control of the Taiz governorate’s Dhubab district and key positions near Bab al-Mandeb.

Al-Dubaish indicated that the Houthis capitalised on ceasefires over the past decade that offered the group more time to prepare and mobilise for war.

“The lesson is clear: The group threatens all factions in Yemen, and efforts should be united to confront this threat,” he said.

Yemen’s government said on Sunday that its forces recaptured military positions and strategic heights east of al-Hazm, the capital of the northern governorate of al-Jawf.

The Houthis’ resilient missile capability

Since the start of the Dawn of Yemen, neither Yemen’s government-controlled territories nor Saudi Arabia has been safe from Houthi missile attacks.

The group has repeatedly launched missiles, occasionally causing damage, deaths and injuries. One of its latest missile attacks killed at least 70 government security recruits in Shabwah.

Al-Jeddawy said the continued attacks showed that the Houthis retain a functioning and resilient missile capability.

“But the more important question is not simply how many missiles they still possess; it is the scale and nature of the external support they continue to receive – whether in intelligence, targeting assistance, components, technical expertise or weapons replenishment,” he said.



The timing and volume of the attacks, together with the precision and damage achieved in some strikes, point to a wider support system that goes beyond the Houthis’ capabilities in isolation, according to al-Jeddawy.

Al-Goblan, however, interpreted the Houthis’ continued missile and drone attacks differently, arguing that they do not necessarily demonstrate military strength or a coherent operational strategy as the Dawn of Yemen continues.

“Rather, it may represent an attempt to compensate for declining ground manoeuvrability through long-range firepower. It may also be an effort to preserve cohesion across fronts and create a political impact and an illusion of maintaining the initiative,” al- Goblan said.

World.title: US sanctions Indian and Turkish firms accused of helping Iran
World.content:
US Treasury says Indian couple faked ship registries for countries including Guyana and Laos to help Iranian tankers.

Share US sanctions Indian and Turkish firms accused of helping Iran on social media

The United States has imposed sanctions on companies and individuals in India and Turkiye that it accuses of helping Iran get around restrictions on its oil exports and its airlines.

The US Department of the Treasury said on Wednesday that the measures target a “vast criminal network” run by Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, who are based in the northern Indian city of Chandigarh.

Two other Indian nationals who head the couple’s businesses and nine entities linked to Sharma were also sanctioned.

According to the Treasury, the couple falsely claimed to represent the maritime authorities of countries including Guyana, Eswatini and Laos. It said they issued fake flags and certifications that allowed sanctioned tankers carrying Iranian oil to continue operating, including vessels working for the Iranian military and its allied groups.

The department said the scheme dated back to at least 2014 and relied on websites built to resemble official national ship registries.

The Treasury also sanctioned Turkiye-based Fugo Ground Services. It said the company provided ground handling and other services to several US-sanctioned Iranian airlines that still fly to Turkiye, including Iran Air Tour and Saha Airlines.

The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control also warned shipping companies about the sanctions risks of dealing with vessels sailing under false flags.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington would continue to pursue anyone who supports Tehran.



The sanctions freeze any US assets held by those targeted and generally bar Americans from dealing with them.

The measures are part of the Trump administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast”, which aims to cut off oil revenue Iran uses to fund its war effort. The Treasury said last week that its campaign had pushed Iran’s currency, the rial, to new lows and driven inflation to about 90 percent.

The sanctions were announced a day after Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in US midterm elections.

World.title: Israel extends detention of Palestinian journalist Abed Abou Shhadeh
World.content:
Rights group says the journalist’s arrest over an interview with Azmi Bishara is a bid to silence Palestinians.

An Israeli court has extended the detention of Palestinian journalist and political activist Abed Abou Shhadeh who was arrested this week.

Abou Shhadeh was detained after Israeli security forces raided his home in Jaffa overnight on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Tel Aviv Magistrate’s Court ruled that he will remain in custody until Sunday, November 8.

Abou Shhadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, hosts the al-Midan podcast for the Arab48 website and appeared as an analyst on Al Jazeera during coverage of the recent Israeli election.

Police had requested an eight-day extension to his detention on suspicion of “contact with a foreign agent”. The legal rights group Adalah, which is part of his defence team, said it would appeal.

Speaking on Al Jazeera, Adalah founder Hassan Jabareen said Abou Shhadeh had been charged with receiving money from foreign agents in order to support Arab-Israeli voters. Jabareen dismissed the charges as fabricated.

“There is no evidence that [Abou Shhadeh] received money from anyone,” he told Al Jazeera. “They searched his house and found nothing.”

About 15 security officers, some of them masked, had raided Abou Shhadeh’s home overnight on Tuesday, confiscating electronic devices and books in front of his two children.

Arab48 reported that police initially refused to tell his family where he was being held. His lawyer later discovered he was detained at a Shin Bet intelligence facility in Petah Tikva.

“All of this story [is] part of the campaign by the head of [the Shin Bet] and [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu who want to show that Arab voters in Israel are not kosher, are illegal,” Jabareen said.



No party emerged as the winner in Israel’s election last week, with Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, now needing to form a coalition with smaller parties to be able to govern. Arab-led parties made record gains this year, making their collective alliance a candidate for coalition partner.

“The motive behind all of this is the election,” Jabareen told Al Jazeera. “It’s to show that Arab voters and political parties are illegal, so they can’t make a coalition with Eisonkot.”

Israeli media reported that Abou Shhadeh was arrested after taking part in an interview in Qatar with the Palestinian intellectual Azmi Bishara. Abou Shhadeh’s lawyers say his interrogation focused solely on the interview he conducted with the former Knesset member.

“This is not a criminal investigation, it is a campaign to silence Palestinian journalists and political activists,” Adalah lawyer Hadeel Abu Salih said in a statement.

“The police are sending a message to the entire Palestinian public in Israel: Even a public conversation with a political figure can land you in a detention cell.”

According to Adalah, police raised no allegations against Abou Shhadeh other than the interview, which covered the Israeli election campaign and Palestinians, and remains publicly available.

At the hearing, the defence argued that Bishara, a former head of the Arab-Israei party Balad, is not a “foreign agent” and that interviewing him cannot give rise to suspicion of a criminal offence.

According to the Israeli daily Israel Hayom, lawyers also told the court that Abou Shhadeh had worked as a journalist for about six years and conducted the interview as part of the work. They said it was “not a secret meeting” and that investigators already held Abou Shhadeh phone and computer, so there was no real risk of him obstructing the investigation.

Dozens of Palestinian and Jewish activists protested outside the court on Wednesday to demand his release.

Rights advocates have described the arrest as part of a campaign of intimidation against Palestinian citizens of Israel following the election.

David Zini, chief of the Shin Bet, Israel’s security agency, has reportedly sought to question Arab party leaders Mansour Abbas, Ahmad Tibi and Sami Abu Shehadeh, the Balad leader and a relative of the detained journalist.

World.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
World.content:
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.

In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.

But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.

World.title: What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress
World.content:
Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will set in.

They had a reason to be giddy on Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress after a blowout victory.

"Today begins the great American comeback," an ecstatic Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader, declared.

After months of promises on the campaign trail â to investigate corruption; lower the costs of healthcare, groceries and petrol; and curtail the Iran war â they will now begin the much tougher process of putting plans into action.

A shift in the balance of power in Washington doesn't necessarily mean Democrats will immediately get to start checking items off their legislative wish list. Democrats have Congress, but Republican President Donald Trump still has the power to reject legislation.

The Democrats should not consider what just happened "a mandate," US Senator Chris Coons told the BBC, warning that the party was still "deeply unpopular".

"We need to prove we can get stuff done, actually deliver answers to their concerns and questions about low wages and rising costs in particular."

World.title: France gears up for strikes and protests as unions promise national mobilisation
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators are expected to take part in marches across France as five unions join strikes and protests in a national day of action.

The protests began in September with high school students complaining about poor conditions and resources in education, but have spread to include the so-called "yellow-vest" movement and workers.

Authorities expect 500,000 to 700,000 demonstrators to join marches, with tens of thousands more in Paris alone, in a day billed by one union leader as "a great day of convergence".

The five unions have combined forces across the public and private sector, with demands for higher wages to combat the cost of living and protected public services.

Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez has said that 70,000 police and gendarmes are being deployed, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.

More than 250 separate actions are planned for 5 November, with some disruption reported in schools, hospitals and public transport.

Workers have also been asked to halt production at oil refineries, and France is expected to import more electricity than it produces on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.

A coalition of unions has urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic, which is currently â¬12.31 (Â£10) an hour.

World.title: Ronaldo retires from Portugal duty
World.content:
Portugal legend Cristiano Ronaldo says he is retiring from international football.

The 41-year-old forward has scored 146 goals and won 234 caps for his country - both world records - since making his debut in 2003.

He walked out of the Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start the Nations League match against Denmark.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team," Ronaldo said in an Instagram video., external

"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

"Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision, because some decisions are not made with the mind alone - they are also made with the heart.

"A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end."

On Friday Portugal are set to announce their squad for November's Nations League fixtures - against Denmark at home and Wales away.

The Portugal Football Federation said it refuses to "let this farewell take place without due tribute".

A statement read: "It is our firm and immense desire to organise, plan, participate and actively collaborate in what will always be a fitting tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo's immense career, in which fans and the country can applaud and celebrate, once again, the player who has given us so much."

Ronaldo's great rival and Argentina legend Lionel Messi retired from international football in October.

World.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
World.content:
Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.

On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.

He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.

A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.

Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, which he has pleaded guilty to earlier in September.

Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.

Prosecutors said that Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing.

These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.

Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party.

On Thursday, Hong Kong's chief executive John Lee said Wong and Law were "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability".

Their actions "not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society," Lee said in a statement issued after the ruling.

Beijing's foreign ministry said China "firmly supports [Hong Kong] in safeguarding national security in accordance with the law". It also called on "relevant parties" to "earnestly respect China's sovereignty and Hong Kong's legal system".

World.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
World.content:
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.

A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El NiÃ±o weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.

In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.

Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.

El NiÃ±o is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.

It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El NiÃ±o, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.

In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.

World.title: Pope Leo hosts Bob Dylan at official residence in Rome
World.content:
The visit happened ahead of Dylan's scheduled performance on Thursday at the Palazzo dello Sport, one of several Italian stops on his Rough and Rowdy Ways tour.

Leo has previously referenced Dylan in his own work, quoting Dylan's unreleased anti-nuclear song, Go Away You Bomb, in the preface to a book titled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.

"I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled," was the line quoted in the book's warning to the world against rearmament.

The song was written in 1963 amid the Cold War, but was never recorded. The typewritten lyrics were unpublished until 2013 when they were discovered and put up for auction, according to the New York Times.

It was the second time Dylan had met a pope. In 1997 Dylan was invited to perform in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young people for the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna.

Dylan played four songs including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, and reportedly climbed the stage mid-set to greet John Paul with a handshake and exchange a few words.

The then-Pope quoted Dylan's hit Blowin' in the Wind in his sermon to the crowd.

World.title: India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
World.content:
India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.

Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.

One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.

Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.

Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka.

Played by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).

The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG, which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.

The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.

But the response so far has been mixed.

Saibal Chatterjee of NDTV channel gave it, external three out of five stars, saying its visual spectacle often overshadowed the story. Its enormous scale, he wrote, "remains, for the most part, the only thing that stands out", while the acting remains "wildly inconsistent".

World.title: British national tests positive for Ebola in DRC
World.content:
A British national has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the UK government has confirmed.

According to the BBC, the British man tested positive for the virus while in the DRC. Reuters subsequently reported that he would be medically evacuated to the UK for specialist treatment. However, the exact time of the evacuation was not immediately known.

This marks the first confirmed case of a British national contracting the virus during the ongoing outbreak in the DRC, which has claimed more than 5,000 lives.

Ebola is a viral disease that can cause severe illness and spreads mainly through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person.

Symptoms include fever, headache, vomiting, muscle pain, weakness, and diarrhoea.

“The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated,” a UK government spokesperson was quoted as saying.

“Further information will be shared in due course as appropriate. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ebola outbreak

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a species of Ebola virus, and was first declared in DRC in May 2026.

According to the latest figures from the United States Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the outbreak had recorded 10,563 confirmed cases and 5,130 deaths across five countries as of 1 November 2026.

The DRC accounts for the majority of the cases, with 10,532 confirmed cases and 5,126 deaths. The outbreak has affected eight provinces in the country.

Kenya has recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths, while Uganda has recorded 20 confirmed cases and two deaths, alongside one probable case and one probable death.

Nigeria confirmed its first case on 20 October after a traveller with a history of travel to Uganda tested positive for the virus. The patient was subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.

According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), 62 contacts linked to the Nigerian case had been identified and were under follow-up as of 29 October.

Symptoms and transmission

The World Health Organisation (WHO) has explained that Ebola survivors may transmit the virus through sexual intercourse if it persists in their semen after recovery.

However, survivors who have met the criteria for discharge from treatment are not expected to transmit the virus through sweat or saliva, as the virus is cleared from their blood.

World.title: At 45th convention, ANA tackles financial mismanagement, writers’ rights
World.content:
The Association of Nigerian Authors (ANA) has intensified efforts to strengthen financial accountability within its chapters and equip members to protect their intellectual property in an increasingly digital publishing environment.

These issues dominated five workshops held during the association’s 45th International Convention at the Mamman Jiya Vatsa Writers Village in Mpape, Abuja, from 28 to 31 October.

The sessions covered image building and marketing, financial modelling, the creation of a national writers’ directory, authors’ reproduction rights and the management of copyright in digital spaces.

ANA said the workshops formed part of reforms introduced after years of internal disputes, weak financial documentation and difficulties funding its annual conventions.

The association experienced a major leadership crisis following its 2018 convention in Enugu, resulting in rival factions. It also faced concerns over the management of convention funds and the repeated inability of some state chapters to host the annual gathering without financial support from the national body.

ANA National President, Usman Oladipo Akanbi, said the current leadership was working to restore members’ understanding of the association’s founding purpose and rebuild confidence in its operations.

“One of the main quests of sanitising the association is to reorient our members so that they understand why we are here,” Mr Akanbi said. “ANA is a non-governmental organisation, not a parastatal. It remains the foremost literary body in Nigeria and Africa.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Financial reforms

Among the measures introduced by the association are stricter enforcement of annual dues, standardised financial records for state chapters and the use of formal memoranda to document transactions and institutional decisions.

ANA has also strengthened its auditing procedures to make its financial statements more credible to local and international funding organisations.

According to the association, revenue from annual dues increased from about ₦3 million in the 2023/2024 period to ₦8 million in 2026 following the implementation of the reforms.

The new system is expected to make it easier to track income and expenditure across the association while preserving financial records for future administrations.

ANA is also working with Bold Scholars, a digital bookstore and publishing platform, to develop a national directory of Nigerian writers. The database is intended to improve documentation within the literary community and make information about Nigerian authors and their works more accessible.

Protecting writers’ earnings

The convention also addressed the difficulty Nigerian authors face in monitoring the reproduction of their works and receiving payment when their books or other publications are copied.

Representatives of the Reproduction Rights Society of Nigeria (REPRONIG) and the Nigerian Copyright Commission (NCC) trained participants on copyright protection, secondary rights and available enforcement mechanisms.

REPRONIG manages secondary rights on behalf of registered writers. These rights allow authors to earn additional income when their works are photocopied or reproduced by institutions.

Under its Digital Rights Management System, REPRONIG offers blanket licences to universities and other institutions where published materials are frequently reproduced. The licensing arrangement permits authorised copying while providing a means of distributing royalties to affected authors.

The organisation retains 30 per cent of the money collected as an administrative charge, while the remainder is distributed to rights holders based on declarations provided by participating institutions.

REPRONIG’s Acting Executive Director, Tosin Akeredolu, encouraged writers to register and upload details of their works to the organisation’s digital platform.

“It is difficult to track any work. There is no tracker on paperback books,” Mr Akeredolu said. “That is why we do blanket licensing for institutions to ensure that whatever copying activities carried out on their premises are done lawfully.”

Authors urged to protect their work

The NCC also reminded writers that copyright protection begins with the owners of creative works.

The commission’s Deputy Director and Head of Regulatory and Compliance, Mr Olatunji, said authors must take proactive steps to secure their manuscripts rather than depend entirely on regulators after an infringement has occurred.

He acknowledged that monitoring copyright violations across the country remained difficult because of the number of possible entry points at seaports, airports and land borders compared with the commission’s workforce.

“Copyright is a private right. You are the first policeman of your rights. You must ensure your rights are protected,” he said.

Mr Olatunji advised authors to submit their manuscripts to the NCC’s digital repository for safekeeping. The deposited copy can subsequently be updated after publication and used as supporting evidence in disputes involving theft, unauthorised reproduction or ownership.

It can also serve as a backup if an author loses the original manuscript.

Tackling online piracy

The NCC representative also explained the commission’s response to digital piracy through its Special Taskforce Against Online Piracy.

The initiative brings copyright owners, regulators, online platforms and relevant government agencies together to address the unauthorised distribution of creative works.

According to Mr Olatunji, the commission may act on a complaint from a rights holder or initiate an investigation independently when it discovers a possible infringement.

“You or the commission might initiate the case of copyright infringement,” he said. “First, we issue the usual notices for takedown. If it is not complied with, we explore our strategic engagement with sister agencies to step in. If it proceeds beyond that point, then we go into full investigation and possibly prosecution.”

ANA said the training was intended to help its members move beyond writing and publishing to understanding the financial, legal and technological systems that determine how creative work is distributed and monetised.

The association expects the reforms to improve accountability across its chapters while ensuring that Nigerian writers are better prepared to protect their work and earn from its use.

World.title: The war on survival: How Tinubu’s elite economy is suffocating Nigeria’s majority, By Ayodele Adio
World.content:
Whom, then, does this Tinubu economy serve? Macro-economic numbers may look clean on press releases emanating from Aso Rock, but they serve only political officeholders, government contractors, and financial gatekeepers. For the teacher in Ibadan, the trader in Onitsha, the commercial driver in Kano, and the young graduate in Lagos, Nigeria has become a daily endurance test with no finish line.

There is a quiet, now-usual, heavy dread settling into homes and marketplaces across Nigeria. It is no longer just the familiar irritation of rising prices; it has hardened into a creeping, collective premonition. Every time a struggling Nigerian calculates his daily commute, a parent stares at an overdue fee payment notice, and a young worker realises their entire salary cannot buy a single bag of rice, the exact same thought crosses their mind: Nigeria will happen to me.

We have to be clear: this is not a temporary rough patch or an unavoidable storm. It is a deliberate economic design. The Nigerian state currently operates an engine built strictly for the political elite and for those whose stock in trade is proximity to power. How do we begin to reckon unchecked borrowing that runs into tens of billions of dollars, while the middle class evaporates and the working poor are shoved off a fiscal cliff? As Tinubu’s administration approaches the National Assembly to seek approval for a staggering $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion external borrowing plan, the gap between official extravagance and public starvation has never been more glaring.

This is the central point of Atiku Abubakar’s economic diagnosis: government now exists primarily to protect the interests of those in power, while ordinary people are left struggling to afford the basic necessities of life.

The numbers tell a story that official press statements cannot spin. The PiggyVest Savings Report 2025 reveals a country operating at the absolute limit of human endurance. Three in ten Nigerian adults earn below ₦100,000 monthly, while more than fifty per cent step into every new month with zero certainty of how they will cover their basic food and utilities. Only six per cent of the entire population reports feeling financially secure. Food alone now devours seventy-two per cent of household income. Meanwhile, data from the EFInA Access to Financial Services Survey shows that while fifty-three per cent of Nigeria’s poorest have zero access to basic financial safety nets, about 80 per cent are experiencing some form of financial strain.

As nominal wages crawl or sits dead still, inflation burns through purchasing power, handing workers money that melts in their hands before they can even reach the market.

Atiku has consistently argued that no economy can protect its working class without aggressively anchoring five fundamental public pillars: transportation, education, health, food and housing. Under the current administration, every single one of these pillars has been turned into a tool of financial punishment.

When petrol subsidies were abruptly yanked away on Day One of this administration, the government promised 1,000 Compressed Natural Gas buses to cushion the impact. That promise dissolved into thin air. The Presidential CNG Initiative has largely stalled out, leaving millions of workers to bleed out their daily wages on extortionate transport fares just to keep low-paying jobs. In contrast, Atiku proposes an industrial subsidy programme to lower energy costs and state-backed investments in public mass transit fleets to immediately collapse commute costs for urban workers.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In public education, rather than funding universities and vocational centres, tuition fees across public institutions were hiked beyond reach. The state’s answer was NELFUND, which has forced vulnerable young Nigerians into institutional debt before they even earn their first paycheck. Atiku advocates replacing these predatory students loan traps with direct university funding grants and debt-forgiveness provisions to ensure education remains a driver of social mobility, rather than lifelong debt.

Public healthcare remains a wrecking ball aimed at family stability. Out-of-pocket medical expenses mean that a single emergency, a single surgery, or one serious diagnosis is all it takes to wipe out lifetime savings and plunge a middle-class family into structural poverty. Atiku’s plan focuses on expanding universal health insurance coverage alongside strengthening primary care centres to shield vulnerable households from crippling catastrophic medical expenses.

Housing delivery is perhaps the most glaring betrayal. Construction is universally recognised as the single most labour-intensive engine for rapid job creation and wealth distribution, yet public housing in Nigeria remains an elite real estate game. Look at what serious governance achieves when the political will exists: between 2020 and 2024, Algeria built and distributed over 1.7 million public housing units through its state-backed AADL programme. That single initiative put roofs over millions of working families while generating massive domestic employment. In Nigeria, state-backed housing is virtually invisible for the poor, built instead for speculative investors in Abuja and Lagos, while everyday workers sleep in slums or pay extortionate rents. This administration promised 100,000 housing units and has delivered less than a thousand, even though it claims about 10,000 units are under construction. In contrast, Atiku’s blueprint calls for massive state-backed investments in affordable, low-cost social housing that will generate widespread economic activity while restoring human dignity to the working class.

At the epicentre of this devastation sits the food crisis. Agricultural output is dropping off a cliff because farmers are caught in a deadly vise of rural insecurity, unpayable diesel costs, and zero federal input support. When farmers cannot access their fields without risking their lives, families in the cities cannot afford to eat. When a basic basket of tomatoes or a tuber of yam becomes so expensive to buy, then the state has surrendered its most primary obligation to its citizens. To turn the tide, Atiku proposes direct input subsidies, security coverage for farming corridors, and targeted incentives for rural agricultural producers to stabilise food supplies and lower market prices. His plan also signals a strategic shift from an over-reliance on subsistence farming to providing the financial and fiscal environment to encourage mechanised farming.

Whom, then, does this Tinubu economy serve? Macro-economic numbers may look clean on press releases emanating from Aso Rock, but they serve only political officeholders, government contractors, and financial gatekeepers. For the teacher in Ibadan, the trader in Onitsha, the commercial driver in Kano, and the young graduate in Lagos, Nigeria has become a daily endurance test with no finish line.

Atiku Abubakar’s warning remains explicit and urgent: you cannot borrow your way into national prosperity while pricing your own people out of bread, transit, and shelter. Until governance shifts its focus from elite privilege to protecting the purchasing power of the poor, that terrifying premonition of “Nigeria could happen to me” will remain the lived reality of an entire generation.

Ayodele Adio writes from Eti Osa 2, Lagos.

World.title: “Ba A Gudu Ba A Bar Gida”: Fifth Chukker, photography, cultural memory, and the responsibility of belonging, By Mudi Yahaya
World.content:
The “Ba A Gudu Ba A Bar Gida” exhibition locates the responsibility of belonging within this relationship. Nina Fischer-Stephan’s photographs offer evidence of lives whose significance exceeds both the photographer’s original intentions and our present interpretations. Encountering them in Kaduna allows memory, research and lived knowledge to question one another. The exhibition asks us to carry that questioning into the present: to preserve what we can, examine what we inherit and leave future generations the means to understand us more fully. Home endures, in part, through the care with which we make such understanding possible.

The significance of the “Ba A Guda Ba A Bar Gida” archival photography exhibition at the Fifth Chukker Polo and Country Club Resort, Kangimi, Kaduna, takes on a particularly deep relevance at a time when Northern Nigeria is facing political unpredictability, economic hardship, societal disintegration, instability, and displacement in the run-up to the 2027 general elections. The main premise of the exhibition relates to the shared moral obligation to comprehend, defend, and critically analyse what makes up a society. The Hausa proverb from which the exhibition takes its title — understood here as “One does not flee and abandon one’s home” — carries an ethical challenge. In this instance, “home” survives through more than the continued existence of buildings, streets and familiar landscapes.

Home in this instance also depends on the knowledge through which people recognise themselves, understand their relationships and imagine a shared future. When this knowledge becomes inaccessible, a society can become estranged from itself, even while its people remain on the land. This is at the heart of the “Ba A Gudu Ba A Bar Gida” exhibition.

Nina Fischer-Stephan was born in Munich in 1922 and moved to Ibadan, Nigeria, in 1959, with her husband Klaus Stephan, then the Africa correspondent for German television. For more than eleven years, her husband’s press passes afforded her rare access to the royal courts, prominent figures, and architectural heritage of Northern Nigeria.
