Drawing on Nina Fischer-Stephan’s photographs of Northern Nigeria around the early years of independence, the exhibition asks what it means to remain responsible for a place, its people and historical inheritance, through periods of profound uncertainty.

In a region confronting insecurity, displacement, economic hardship and political apprehension, belonging cannot be reduced to residence. Nor does the theme proverb become a judgement against people who leave in search of safety. A family may lose its house without surrendering its identity; a dispersed community may continue to sustain its language, memories and obligations. The question is how the responsibility of belonging survives departure, adversity and change. Understood in this way, home includes what we carry, what we protect, and what we remain willing to rebuild. The exhibition’s title asks whether a society under pressure can preserve the resources through which it understands itself and renews its obligations to others. Historical memory becomes part of that task. Without sustained attention to the lives, institutions and knowledge that have shaped a community, proposals for its future risk resting on an impoverished account of what it has been.

Nina Fischer-Stephan’s photographs offer a compelling starting point, as they allow the viewer to approach historical transformation through everyday life. A country’s independence is often narrated through constitutional milestones, political leaders, and the emergence of national institutions. Yet people also experience historical change through their homes, work, clothing, streets, and encounters with one another. Political transformation enters the ordinary arrangements of existence, sometimes dramatically and sometimes almost imperceptibly.

These photographs invite us to examine that quieter history. Their significance does not require the claim that Northern Nigeria entered photographic history through a European camera. Such a claim would obscure Nigerian photographers, local practices of image-making, and the communities whose participation made the photographs possible. Neither should the photographer’s nationality automatically determine our assessment of her work. What matters is the particular encounter each image records, the perspective it brings to view, and the questions it permits us to ask. Nina Fischer- Stephan’s archive is valuable as a situated record whose meanings can develop through research, comparison, and renewed engagement with the people connected to its subjects.

The Northern Nigeria encountered in the “Ba A Guda Ba A Bar Gida” exhibition was already a complex social world. Its architecture, commerce, scholarship, religious life, craftsmanship, and political institutions did not begin with independence. This “infrastructure” entered a new post-colonial national framework while continuing to change and metamorphose as it reacted to the changes that independence brought. That instance in time in Northern Nigeria therefore invites the viewer to reconsider the assumption that inherited cultural forms and modernity must be opposed. A courtyard, market, or mode of dress, may embody adaptation, practical intelligence, and historical movement, even when an unfamiliar viewer sees only “tradition.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Looking closely means asking about the knowledge that made visible life possible. A building may reveal decisions about climate, privacy, materials, and relations between households. A market may suggest networks of production, exchange, and trust extending far beyond the frame. Clothing may carry distinctions of occupation, occasion, taste, and affiliation that require local knowledge to interpret. These possibilities remain questions for investigation rather than conclusions supplied by appearance alone. The photograph preserves traces of social intelligence; understanding that intelligence requires further work.

This attention gives ordinary people their proper place within history. Those who build, teach, trade, farm, care for families and maintain communal life do more than inhabit the background of political events. Their decisions sustain the worlds in which those events acquire meaning. To attend to everyday life is to recognise forms of historical agency that official commemoration frequently overlooks. The dignity of the ordinary becomes a serious subject of inquiry.

Such inquiry also changes our understanding of photography. A photograph’s meaning does not end when the shutter closes. It continues through the circumstances of its preservation, the captions attached to it, the institutions that circulate it, and the audiences who encounter it. Ariella Aïsha Azoulay’s work on photography, including Potential History, helps frame this continuing relationship between images, power and responsibility. Applied to this exhibition, that approach asks us to consider what obligations arise when we inherit the representations of other people’s lives.

The setting at Fifth Chukker Polo and Country Club resort also becomes part of this discussion. A contemporary institution associated with sports, hospitality and international encounters provides a vantage point from which to consider earlier forms of social organisation. The relationship raises questions about how prestige, private initiative, and public cultural responsibility intersect. An exhibition concerned with collective memory gains substance when the institution hosting it helps people participate in that memory’s interpretation.

All archives are selective; one has to be cautious about how a group of photographs are read and interpreted. Some people become visible because of their statuses, accessibility, or significance to the photographer; others remain unnamed or outside the frame. Saidiya Hartman’s writing on archival silence, developed in the distinct historical context of Atlantic slavery, offers a methodological caution here: surviving records cannot be mistaken for the fullness of the lives they reference. Her work encourages attention to the conditions under which people enter an archive and to the limits of what can be recovered. It does not authorise us to fill gaps with convenient certainty.

Responsible historical imagination acknowledges possibility while keeping speculation distinguishable from evidence. That distinction is essential because seeing can produce a misleading sense of understanding. An authentic photograph can support an inaccurate account of the society it depicts. An orderly street does not establish social harmony; an imposing palace does not demonstrate general prosperity; a market portrait cannot stand for the experience of every woman in a region. The fragment becomes misleading when it is made to carry more historical meaning than the evidence can sustain.

There is a related danger in applying familiar categories too readily. Descriptions such as “backward,” “progressive,” “traditional,” or “modern” may tell us more about our assumptions than about how the people photographed understood their circumstances. Historical interpretation requires us to let evidence unsettle those assumptions. It also requires attention to inequality, exclusion and conflict. Admiration of an image’s elegance should not become an assertion that the world beyond its frame was just.

This is why the “Ba A Guda Ba A Bar Gida” exhibition cannot rest on nostalgia. Beauty may invite attention, but it cannot substitute for historical explanation. The past contains achievements worth sustaining and arrangements that deserve criticism. A mature relationship with cultural memory allows both to be examined. The purpose of preservation is to give future generations the evidence with which to reach informed judgements of their own.

Presenting these photographs in an exhibition in Kaduna creates an opportunity for that examination to become a conversation. Viewers with connections to the places and practices represented may recognise details that other audiences overlook: a building’s former use, the significance of an object, the character of a gathering or the history concealed within a familiar street. Such knowledge can correct inherited descriptions and generate new lines of research. An archive becomes more useful when stored evidence meets living memory.

At this critical time, the choice of location for an exhibition like “Ba A Guda Ba A Bar Gida” is noteworthy and important. Kaduna is the most historically relevant northern town in this regard, as it is a place where different northern experiences can enter the sort of conversation that the “Ba A Guda Ba A Bar Gida” triggers. Kaduna’s connections with administration, education, migration, trade and cultural exchange make it a productive setting for thinking about continuity and transformation. Yet proximity alone does not guarantee accuracy. Local memories can disagree, and identification requires corroboration. The aim is to broaden interpretive authority while maintaining the discipline of inquiry. Community testimony should be treated seriously enough to be recorded, examined and preserved.

The setting at Fifth Chukker Polo and Country Club resort also becomes part of this discussion. A contemporary institution associated with sports, hospitality and international encounters provides a vantage point from which to consider earlier forms of social organisation. The relationship raises questions about how prestige, private initiative, and public cultural responsibility intersect. An exhibition concerned with collective memory gains substance when the institution hosting it helps people participate in that memory’s interpretation.

By extension, the role of the facilitator of this sort of exhibition also matters. Adamu Atta’s role as commissioner therefore matters beyond the provision of a venue or financial support. It raises the question of what patronage can make possible for a wider public. Influence acquires cultural value when it supports access, sustained inquiry and institutions capable of outlasting individual initiative. The exhibition’s open-access intention is particularly significant here. Students, teachers, artists, photographers, craftspeople, and people connected to the photographed communities should have meaningful opportunities to encounter the archive and contribute to its interpretation, especially in a part of Nigeria where there is little or no functional visual art ecosystem of galleries and museums. The irony is even that where a semblance of spaces for aesthetic contemplation in northern Nigeria exists, such places are seen as elitist and out of bounds to the everyday person.

Offering access to spaces where the public have a tradition of visiting to watch and follow popular sports like polo then presents a unique opportunity. Public relevance would now depend on how that welcome is realised.

The Islamic concept of amanah, or entrusted responsibility, offers a meaningful ethical framework for this work. Surah An-Nisa 4:58 connects the rendering of trust with just judgement. Applied to cultural stewardship, its principle encourages us to understand custody as an obligation towards people beyond the institution itself. A photograph may matter deeply to a family, a community or future researchers, regardless of its market value.

There was an intentional curatorial decision to omit detailed scholarly captions from the immediate display. This was done to encourage viewers to look, remember and converse before receiving an authoritative explanation. However, that openness creates a responsibility to distinguish personal recognition from established historical knowledge. The accompanying research record should retain available dates, locations, provenance, and uncertainty, while any new identification should be documented and checked. An invitation to interpretation becomes most valuable when it also provides a route through which knowledge can be tested and added to the archive.

These considerations extend to museums, curators, and cultural institutions more broadly. To preserve photographs of other people’s lives is to accept responsibility for how their humanity will be remembered. Decisions about selection, naming, sequence, and omission influence public understanding. A caption can turn an individual into a stereotype; an unsupported attribution can circulate until repetition gives it the appearance of fact. Institutions must make clear what an image establishes, what research supports, and what remains unknown.

Inherited captions also require scrutiny. A description supplied by a visitor or colonial official may reveal important information about the observer while misidentifying the subject. Preserving that description as part of the archive’s history need not mean endorsing it. A responsible catalogue can retain the original wording, explain its limitations and record subsequent corrections. Historical integrity includes the ability to show how knowledge has changed.

In Nigeria, these sorts of obligations have profound educational consequences. For instance, the Nigerian federal government’s September 2025 curriculum announcement placed renewed emphasis on Nigerian history in basic education.

Such a policy, however, must be supported by teachers, reliable learning materials, and access to primary sources. Museums and archives can help students move beyond memorising names and dates towards evaluating evidence and recognising competing interpretations. Historical consciousness grows when people can ask how an account was produced and whose experience it leaves out.

These policy concerns lead to the question of preservation, which itself requires continuing material commitment. Photographic negatives deteriorate; documents lose research value when their origins become uncertain; digital files become inaccessible without maintenance. Oral knowledge disappears when those who possess it die without being recorded. A collection may survive physically while remaining unavailable in practice because it has not been catalogued or made accessible. The loss reaches beyond scholarship. When evidence disappears, a society has fewer means of questioning the stories told about it.

The Islamic concept of amanah, or entrusted responsibility, offers a meaningful ethical framework for this work. Surah An-Nisa 4:58 connects the rendering of trust with just judgement. Applied to cultural stewardship, its principle encourages us to understand custody as an obligation towards people beyond the institution itself. A photograph may matter deeply to a family, a community or future researchers, regardless of its market value.

This application is an ethical reading, rather than a claim that the verse directly addresses museums or photography. Such a framework should also acknowledge the diversity of Northern Nigeria and the differences within Muslim thought about images. One must first and foremost acknowledge that in many Muslim communities in Northern Nigeria, objections to depicting living beings have created uncertainty about portraiture and the public display of photographs. Interpretations differ amongst scholars, families, generations, contexts, and settings; thus, responding to situations like this requires Islamic theological referencing.

When we encounter the archival photography of our societies, particularly those taken during periods of tremendous historical transformation, we are not only looking at people and places that no longer exist. We are encountering evidence of lives whose meanings were never fully exhausted by the conditions in which they were recorded.

A photograph taken in Kano, Zaria, Kaduna, Maiduguri, Katsina, or Sokoto during the early years of Nigerian independence may appear to offer a simple historical proposition: this is how a specific place looked, how people dressed, how a community lived, and how a society presented itself at a given time.

The “Ba A Gudu Ba A Bar Gida” exhibition consequently turns the viewer’s attention towards the records being created now. Whose daily work receives recognition? Which communities appear only when disaster strikes? Are we preserving enough context for future viewers to understand what they see? The proliferation of digital images does not answer these questions. Abundance can coexist with poor description, fragile storage and a narrow concentration of attention.

However, the deeper relevance of such photos does not always stem from what they disclose about the past. It is in what they reveal about the limits of our current understanding. The photograph becomes a conflict between what we think we know and what history gently urges us to reassess. We may find sophistication where current narratives have led us to assume backwardness. We may find dignity in places where political discourse has conditioned us to expect hardship. We can recognise social cohesion in communities that are currently portrayed predominantly through conflict-related language. We may observe architectural wisdom, cultural assurance, restraint, elegance, and collective belonging that are nearly undetectable under our current notions of development. This does not imply that the past was necessarily superior.

Archival photography should not be used to romanticise historical societies, as its photos can conceal inequality, misery, and injustice just as easily as they reveal beauty. Rather, the photos remind us of something very important: the past was never as easy as our current representations of it, and our present is unlikely to be as thorough as the records we are creating about it.

This realisation elevates vintage photography from a nostalgic activity to one of philosophical and moral investigation. And it begs an extraordinary question: if people who chronicled our society decades ago could not have predicted how future generations would interpret their photographs, how much responsibility do we have now for the images, narratives, and silences we leave behind? Islamic philosophy and Qur’anic teachings provide a particularly rich foundation for approaching this subject. They see humans not only as historical spectators but also as moral agents entrusted with knowledge, testimony, justice, and accountability. From this perspective, documenting a civilisation entails more than just creating a record of its existence. It is to bear responsibility for the way that society will be remembered in the future. An exhibition cannot settle theological debates about representation. It can, however, approach questions of dignity, privacy, intention and accountability with seriousness.

Respectful documentation requires attention to the consequences of making a person’s likeness available to consequences of making a person’s likeness available to strangers across time and place. The desire to preserve history does not remove the need for consent, discretion and care. Surah Al-Isra 17:36 cautions against pursuing what one lacks knowledge of and associate’s perception with accountability.

Read in relation to archival practice, this provides a strong reason for interpretive humility. An image does not disclose everything about the motives, beliefs or inner life of the person depicted. The viewer, photographer and curator each have a responsibility to recognise that limit. Acknowledging uncertainty can protect the integrity of a person’s history more electively than an elaborate unsupported explanation. For younger Northern Nigerians, the stakes are especially substantial. A generation repeatedly encountering its region through accounts of violence, deprivation and political failure may struggle to recognise the extent of its inheritance. These crises demand documentation and action, but they cannot explain the totality of a people’s existence. Photographs can open further questions about scholarship, enterprise, aesthetic judgement, domestic life and the practical knowledge through which communities have sustained themselves.

That encounter need not produce uncritical pride. Its greater value is to enlarge the range of futures that young people can imagine. What knowledge has been neglected? Which practices remain useful? What forms of exclusion require change? What can be learnt from the ambitions of earlier generations without accepting all their assumptions? Historical evidence provides resources for asking these questions with greater independence.

The “Ba A Gudu Ba A Bar Gida” exhibition consequently turns the viewer’s attention towards the records being created now. Whose daily work receives recognition? Which communities appear only when disaster strikes? Are we preserving enough context for future viewers to understand what they see? The proliferation of digital images does not answer these questions. Abundance can coexist with poor description, fragile storage and a narrow concentration of attention. A society may photograph itself constantly while leaving essential aspects of its life undocumented.

To document responsibly is to recognise historical significance before disappearance makes it obvious. It means recording the artisan’s process, the teacher’s experience, the family’s account, and the changing life of a neighborhood while people can still explain their meanings. It also means allowing those represented to challenge descriptions and contribute knowledge. Preservation becomes a continuing relationship. rather than a single act of collecting.

The “Ba A Gudu Ba A Bar Gida” exhibition locates the responsibility of belonging within this relationship. Nina Fischer-Stephan’s photographs offer evidence of lives whose significance exceeds both the photographer’s original intentions and our present interpretations. Encountering them in Kaduna allows memory, research and lived knowledge to question one another. The exhibition asks us to carry that questioning into the present: to preserve what we can, examine what we inherit and leave future generations the means to understand us more fully. Home endures, in part, through the care with which we make such understanding possible.

Mudi Yahaya, a documentary photographer and film-maker, is also an art historian.

World.title: Nigerian Law School denies barring hijab-wearing candidates from Bar exams
World.content:
The Nigerian Law School has denied allegations that female Muslim candidates wearing hijab were harassed or prevented from entering examination halls during the Bar Final Examinations held on 31 October.

In a statement posted on its Facebook page on Wednesday by the Secretary to the Council and Director of Administration, Aderonke Osho, the school described the allegations as false, insisting that it had no policy or institutional practice of religious discrimination.

“The school categorically states that it has no policy or institutional practice of religious discrimination,” the statement said.

The institution explained that its examination rules were designed to ensure proper identification, prevent malpractice, and protect the integrity of the examinations.

Why hijab-wearing student was apprehended

It disclosed that a female student wearing a hijab was apprehended during the Bar Part I examinations on 29 October after she was allegedly found with an earpiece hidden in her hijab and a mobile phone strapped to her thigh.

The school said it was still investigating the incident in line with its examination rules and relevant regulations.

It maintained that examination security measures were applied fairly, without discrimination, and cited Sections 38 and 42 of the Nigerian constitution, which guarantee freedom of religion and prohibit discrimination.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The controversy comes against the backdrop of a 2022 Supreme Court judgement affirming the right of female Muslim students in Lagos State public schools to wear hijab over their school uniforms.

In the case involving the Lagos State Government and Asiyat AbdulKareem and others, the apex court upheld the students’ right to manifest their religious beliefs.

Although the judgement concerned public schools rather than the Nigerian Law School, it remains relevant to discussions about religious freedom in educational institutions.

The Muslim Rights Concern (MURIC) had also criticised an alleged restriction on hijab-wearing candidates during the recent Bar examinations.

The organisation argued that candidates should not be subjected to collective punishment over the alleged examination misconduct of an individual student.

The law school urged the public to avoid premature conclusions and allow its investigation to establish the facts.

It is mandatory for law graudates to pass through a one-year education and pass Bar examinations organised by the Nigerian Law School to be called to the Nigerian Bar.

The school is governed and managed by the Council of Legal Education.

Successful candidates are called to the Bar by the Body of Benchers, which is the highest body of distinction in the Nigerian legal profession.

World.title: NJC rejects exclusion of Imo acting chief judge from shortlist for substantive appointment
World.content:
The National Judicial Council (NJC) has rejected the exclusion of acting Chief Judge of Imo State, Ijeoma Agugua, from the list of nominees submitted by the state’s judicial service commission for appointment as the state’s substantive chief judge.

The council said in a statement on Wednesday that it ordered the Imo State Judicial Service Commission, the body with statutory authority to initiate the process of appointing judicial officers in the state, to include Ms Agugua on its shortlist.

NJC’s Deputy Director (Information) Kemi Babalola-Ogedengbe said in a statement on Wednesday that the council gave the directive at its 112th meeting held on 3 November.

During the meeting, the council, chaired by Chief Justice of Nigeria Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, recommended 28 candidates for various judicial appointments and reached decisions on several disciplinary matters.

“Council also directed the Imo State Judicial Service Commission to include the name of the most senior Judge of the State High Court, the Acting Chief Judge, Hon. Justice Ijeoma Agugua, in the list of candidates for appointment as substantive Chief Judge of the State,” the statement stated.

The statement did not list the names or the number of nominees on the judicial service commission’s initial shortlist.

Persistent crisis

The attempt to fill the Imo chief judge position has been a major bone of contention between the NJC and Imo State authorities since former Chief Judge T. E. Chukwuemeka Chikeka was compulsorily retired over age falsification two years ago in November 2024.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The NJC’s latest decision on the matter signalled the state government’s persistent disapproval of Ms Agugua for the position.

Despite Ms Agugua being the most senior High Court judge, the state authorities passed over her to pick a lower ranking judge to act as the chief judge.

The controversial decision, which paralysed the state High Court for months, was criticised by the Nigerian Bar Association and rejected by the NJC for disregarding seniority principle.

In April 2025, the NJC roundly rejected the appointment of Theophilus Nzeukwu, who was the number four on the hierarchy of judges of the state, as acting chief judge.

The NJC said Mr Nzeukwu’s appointment violated Section 271(4) of the Nigerian constitution which mandates the governor to “appoint the most senior judge of the High Court” to temporarily perform the functions of the chief judge whenever the office becomes vacant.

It also ordered that Mr Nzeukwu should be issued a query for accepting appointment by Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma as the acting chief judge in violation of the constitution.

In June, about two months after rejecting Mr Nzeukwu’s appointment and issuing him a query, the NJC sent him on a compulsory retirement for accepting to be sworn in for the acting chief judge role.

The council also restated its stance, directing Governor Uzodimma to comply with its directive to swear in the state’s most senior judge.

The governor had justified picking Mr Nzeukwu, which he said was based on “credible reports available to him at the time.”

He said in a statement that reports submitted to him indicated Mr Nzeukwu was the “most senior judicial officer not encumbered by unresolved issues.”

But the NJC stressed that the constitutional provision on acting appointments of state chief judges did not leave room for discretion.

Mr Uzodimma subsequently agreed to comply with the directives of the NJC.

But while the state government bowed to NJC’s directive, it remained resolute to only allow Ms Agugua to occupy the office in acting capacity.

Why NJC took latest decision on Imo chief judge position

The NJC said it directed the Imo State Judicial Commission to include Ms Agugua’s name in the list of nominees for appointment as the substantive chief judge in the state, following the consideration of a petition dated 11 June by Bob Kay Njemanze.

It said Mr Njemanze’s petition challenged the exclusion of Ms Agugua from the shortlist submitted by the judicial service commission.

The NJC’s statement did not give the names or number of nominees sent by the judicial service commission.

The council, the body with preeminent roles in the appointment of judges across Nigeria’s superior courts of record, asserted its power to issue such a directive to the judicial service commission to include Ms Agugua’s name in the list of nominees for the substantive chief judge.

“In considering the petition, Council noted that although the State Judicial Service Commission has the constitutional responsibility to advise the NJC on suitable candidates for appointment as Chief Judge, the Council retains the authority to determine the suitability of persons presented to it. It consequently directed its Secretariat to formally request the Imo State JSC to include the name of Hon. Justice I. O. Agugua in the shortlist,” the NJC’s statement stated.

Imo judiciary at the centre of attention

The Imo State judiciary has been at the centre of attention for the wrong reasons for two years.

In November 2024, its then chief judge, Mr Chikeka, was sent on a compulsory retirement over age falsification, setting off the leadership crisis that has dogged the state judiciary since then.

In June last year, the NJC recommended Mr Nzeukwu on a compulsory retirement for making himself available to be sworn in as the acting chief judge “knowing fully well that he was number four in the hierarchy of Judges of the Imo State Judiciary and contrary to Section 271 (4)” of the Nigerian constitution.”

At the same meeting, the council recommended the compulsory retirement of a set of nine judges of the Imo State High Court found to be culpable of age falsifications,

But the council absolved the President of the Customary Court of Appeal, Imo State, V. U. Okorie, who chaired the commission that nominated Mr Nzeukwu as the acting chief judge.

World.title: U17 WWC: Busari hails Flamingos’ bravery as Nigeria eye historic title
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos delivered a statement performance against Brazil to book their place in the final of the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup, with head coach Akeem Busari praising his players for their courage, discipline and determination.

The Nigerian youngsters were comfortably the better side on Wednesday night, producing an impressive attacking display that left their South American opponents struggling to cope. The Flamingos registered 35 attempts on goal, compared to Brazil’s seven, underlining their dominance throughout the contest.

Brazil managed just one shot on target, which came through Greise Kelly’s 89th-minute consolation goal, as Nigeria secured a deserved 3-1 victory to move within one step of a historic title.

For Busari, reaching the final represents a significant achievement not only for the players but also for Nigerian and African football.

Speaking after the encounter, the Nigerian coach expressed his delight at the result while acknowledging the technical quality of the Brazilian side.

“It’s an awesome thing, it’s a great achievement,” Busari said. “Reaching the final is a plus for our country, it’s a plus for our football. We are happy, the class are happy.

“It was a key contest and it wasn’t an easy one. Brazil really showed the stuff they have technically, but we tried to really block the view of their passing line, so we had to show character. [We played] really, really bravely. We appreciate the class because they are young, we could only encourage them and tell them what they need to do to make the final.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Flamingos’ journey to the final has also carried a familiar World Cup storyline, with Nigeria drawing inspiration from Argentina’s remarkable comeback at the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar.

Argentina suffered defeat in their opening match against Saudi Arabia before recovering to lift the trophy, becoming only the second nation to achieve the feat after Spain in 2010. Four years later, Nigeria have followed a similar path at the U-17 Women’s World Cup, responding to their opening-day loss to Poland with a remarkable run that has taken them to the final.

Queen Joseph, who opened the scoring against Brazil, revealed that Argentina’s triumph had provided the team with the belief that an early setback did not have to define their campaign.

“We took the Argentina spirit from the [2022] World Cup after losing our first game,” an overjoyed Joseph told FIFA. “They came back and won the trophy, so we are hoping to God Almighty that we are going to win the trophy.

“I feel very happy. Playing in the final is a big privilege, representing my country in the final is a big privilege for me. I’m super proud of myself and my team because we made history. We are not here just representing Nigeria; we are here representing Africa as a whole.”

While the entire squad deserves credit for Nigeria’s impressive campaign, Awawu Bashiru emerged as one of the biggest talking points against Brazil.

The forward had not started any of the Flamingos’ previous six matches and had accumulated just 73 minutes of playing time before Wednesday’s semi-final. However, handed her first start of the tournament, she repaid Busari’s faith in spectacular fashion by scoring twice to help Nigeria secure their place in the final.

Her performance also earned her the Player of the Match award, with the youngster visibly delighted as she reflected on a memorable night.

“Today was my first start, so I’m so happy, I’m so excited,” Bashiru said, clutching her award. “I’m so proud of myself, my team-mates, my coach and the teamwork. We did it, and it was not an easy task. I thank God. I’m grateful.”

With Brazil now behind them, Nigeria will turn their attention to Japan as they prepare for the country’s first-ever appearance in a FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup final.

The challenge will be another demanding one, but the Flamingos can take confidence from their earlier victory over fellow Asian powerhouse DPR Korea, whom they defeated 3-1 during the group stage.

Busari believes that encounter could provide a useful reference point as Nigeria prepare for the decisive showdown, particularly given the similarities in the footballing philosophies of Japan and DPR Korea.

The coach expects his players to reproduce the same discipline, bravery and tactical commitment that carried them past the North Koreans and Brazil.

“It’s just about showing the same character and playing the same way we played with North Korea, because they play with the same philosophy,” Busari stated. “They want to build the ball, they look at the high line of passes, they want their full-backs to support, so we really want to look at all that.

“I’m excited and I’m happy and the class were happy, but we just really want to pick up the trophy. That would be the icing on the cake.”

Nigeria have already secured a place in history by reaching their first final at the competition. However, with Japan standing between them and the ultimate prize, Busari and his players now have an opportunity to turn a remarkable campaign into a golden chapter for Nigerian and African women’s football.

World.title: Osun govt warns Oluwo over alleged ‘inflammatory’ remarks, fears religious, communal conflicts
World.content:
The Osun State Government has cautioned the Oluwo of Iwo, Abdulrasheed Akanbi, over what it described as inflammatory public statements capable of triggering religious and inter-town conflicts.

In a letter dated November but with no particular day stated and addressed to the monarch, the Ministry of Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs warned that his alleged conduct could undermine communal peace and peaceful coexistence among people of different faiths.

The letter, signed by the ministry’s Permanent Secretary, Wale Alli­yu, said the government had observed with “worries and anxieties” recent inflammatory statements and pronouncements attributed to the monarch.

“The persistence of such crisis-inciting activities and likely disruptive conduct against peaceful interfaith cohabitation has reached a level this administration can no longer ignore,” the letter partly read..

The government reminded the Oluwo, a high-raniking traditional ruling in the state, that the Nigerian constitution guarantees every citizen the right to freedom of religious association, adding that traditional rulers were expected to respect the rights of their subjects.

“You cannot and you must not conduct yourself in any way that can foment religious crisis through serial attacks on people of other faiths,” the letter warned.

It also cautioned the monarch against using his traditional position to promote religious conflict or undermine the cultural values and traditions of the people he governs.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It noted that pursuing a reform with potential to create community violence and conflict is a development its administration will not tolerate.

“Your activities are raising communal tension, sowing seeds of communal and religious discord and increasingly discrediting the traditional values of your people and Yoruba Society of which your domain is a major part of,” it stated.

The government, therefore, outlined six directives to the monarch, including an instruction to stop any further attacks on people of other faiths and refrain from making statements or engaging in conduct that could provoke confrontation with other traditional rulers.

It also urged him to preserve the culture and traditions represented by his throne and conduct himself in accordance with the norms and regulations stipulated in the state’s chieftaincy laws and resolutions of the State Council of Obas.

The ministry said it would monitor the monarch’s compliance with the directives, while the State Council of Obas was also directed to “watch and act on recent developments within Iwo land.”

The Oluwo’s spokesperson, Alli Ibrahim, confirmed to PREMIUM TIMES via a phone call on Thursday that the monarch had received the government’s letter.

Mr Ibrahim said the Oluwo would “respond to that appropriately.”

Oluwo’s controversial views

The letter, however, did not identify the specific public statements or incidents that prompted the government’s warning.

Over the past years, the traditional ruler has repeatedly criticised Yoruba traditional religious practices and other monarchs who retain traditional deities in their palaces.

His controversial stance has pitted him against devotees of traditional religious practices.

He has maintained that those traditional religious practices were not part of true Yoruba culture and traditions.

In late July, the Oluwo reportedly declared that palaces without idols were greater than mosques, churches and shrines.

“Palaces, most especially Yoruba palaces without idols, are greater than Mosque, Church and Shrine.”

He also described kings who promote idols in their palaces as ignorant of their position and urged traditional rulers to remove deities from their palaces and relocate them to shrines or museums.

“It is sad that most Yoruba kings are ignorant of their position.”

On 1 July, the monarch also described traditional rites for newly installed monarchs as a route to idolatry. He described the practices as avenues through which new monarchs could be drawn into idolatry.

On October 10, the mornach also dismissed the significance of ancient Yoruba crowns. In a video shared on his Facebook page, the monarch challenged the cultural significance attached to ancient Yoruba crowns.

“Don’t be deceived, there is nothing like ancient crown. Once a king dies, his children will pack all the crowns he left behind.”

He further argued that a new monarch should make his own crown rather than retain the crown of his predecessor.

World.title: Kane becomes highest-paid footballer in Europe after new deal
World.content:
England captain Harry Kane has signed a record-breaking contract extension with Bayern Munich that will keep him at the German club until June 2029, in a deal reportedly making him the highest-paid player in Europe by basic salary.

According to David Ornstein of The Athletic, the three-year extension is the most lucrative contract in Bayern Munich’s history, although some European players could still earn more than the striker when performance-related bonuses are included.

The 33-year-old’s previous contract was due to expire next summer, but both Kane and the Bundesliga champions were keen to continue their partnership.

Bayern reportedly do not consider the new agreement his final contract, with the club keen to retain the England international for the foreseeable future.

Speaking after signing the extension, Kane expressed his satisfaction with life in Munich, describing his relationship with the club, supporters and city as a special one.

“I feel right at home at FC Bayern. I love the club, the fans and the city of Munich,” he said.

“We have a fantastic team and, in Vincent Kompany, a fantastic manager. It makes me very proud to be part of this club. My whole family is very happy here. I was keen to stay.

“I’m now looking forward to the future and I want to win many more titles with this great club.”

The contract extension comes after a remarkable period for the striker, who won the Ballon d’Or in late October, becoming the first English player to receive the prestigious award since 2001.

He is also expected to become England’s most-capped player during the November international break.

Since joining Bayern from Tottenham Hotspur three years ago, Kane has scored 156 goals in 161 appearances, establishing himself as one of the club’s most influential players.

During his time in Germany, he has won two Bundesliga titles, the DFB-Pokal and two Supercups.

However, winning the UEFA Champions League remains a major ambition for the England captain as he looks to add Europe’s biggest club competition to his collection of honours.

His decision to extend his stay in Germany also appears to have dealt a significant blow to hopes of him returning to the Premier League to challenge Alan Shearer’s all-time scoring record.

With his Bayern future secured until 2029, Kane looks increasingly likely to prioritise further success in Germany over a return to English football.

World.title: 5 takeaways from Ronaldo’s retirement speech to Portugal
World.content:
Portugal’s forward #07 Cristiano Ronaldo reacts after losing the 2026 World Cup round of 16 football match between Portugal and Spain at the Dallas Stadium in Arlington on July 6, 2026. (Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP)

Cristiano Ronaldo has announced the end of his 23-year journey with the Portugal national team, reflecting on his achievements, sacrifices and enduring connection with the country.

In an emotional farewell message addressed to the Portuguese people, the five-time Ballon d’Or winner described representing his country as the greatest honour of his career, while expressing gratitude to his teammates, coaches, family and supporters.

Here are five key takeaways from Ronaldo’s retirement speech.

1. Ronaldo brings his 23-year Portugal career to an end

Ronaldo confirmed that his journey with the Portugal national team, which began in August 2003, had come to an end.

The 41-year-old said it was time to hand over the national team shirt and captain’s armband to the next generation after 23 years of representing his country.

He described the decision as difficult, saying it was one guided not only by his head but also by his heart.

2. He considers representing Portugal his greatest achievement

Despite spending much of his career pursuing individual records and becoming the best player in the world, Ronaldo said his greatest victory was earning the honour of representing Portugal.

Reflecting on his journey, he said: “I spent my life working to become the best player in the world. Today, I realize that my greatest victory was earning the honor of representing the best country in the world.”

3. He acknowledged his failures and sacrifices

Ronaldo admitted that his international career was not without disappointments, recalling defeats, difficult moments and occasions when he could not deliver the results Portuguese supporters wanted.

However, he maintained that he never gave up or stopped feeling proud of representing his country.

He also acknowledged the sacrifices made by his family, teammates and the support staff who contributed to his 23-year journey.

4. He urged Portugal’s next generation to keep dreaming

The former Portugal captain called on young players to continue believing in their abilities and push the country’s footballing ambitions further.

He stressed the importance of producing new heroes and inspiring future generations to achieve what previous generations could not.

“Portugal will always need young people who dream, players who never give up, and new generations who believe it is possible to reach places no one has reached before,” he said.

5. He promised to continue supporting Portugal after retirement

Although his playing career with the national team has ended, Ronaldo said his emotional connection with Portugal would remain unchanged.

He recalled the powerful feeling of standing alongside teammates and supporters during the national anthem, describing it as a moment when differences in social class, profession, opinions and football allegiance disappear.

He concluded by assuring Portuguese supporters that he would continue to celebrate the country’s victories and support the national team.

“The number 7 shirt remains, but the pride of having worn it will be mine forever,” Ronaldo said.

World.title: Wike distances self from court ruling favouring Okorocha over Uzodimma
World.content:
Nyesom Wike

The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, has dismissed claims that he influenced the court judgment which recognised former Imo State Governor Rochas Okorocha as the All Progressives Congress candidate for Imo West Senatorial District in the 2027 elections.

Wike spoke during a live media chat on Thursday in Port Harcourt, where he described the allegations as mischievous, stressing that he neither filed the suit nor had any involvement in the legal proceedings.

“First of all, anybody calling my name is being mischievous. I didn’t go to court. I’m not in APC. I don’t know what the issue is,” he said.

Wike also reacted to reports that Governor Hope Uzodimma had warned, a day before the judgment, that he would seize the vehicles of anyone promoting the proposed Rainbow Coalition in Imo State.

Describing the reported warning as uncivilised, the minister said: “They were saying that because a day before that judgment was given, he had openly warned people that, ‘No Rainbow Coalition here. If I see… I’ll collect the vehicle for you.’ Very, very uncivilised.”

He also clarified a video circulating online showing him dancing with Okorocha, saying it was recorded when he hosted the former governor while he was still in office.

“Now they showed the video where Rochas and I danced when I hosted him when he was governor. So that was that dance,” Wike said.

The controversy followed a Federal High Court judgment in Abuja directing the Independent National Electoral Commission to recognise Okorocha as the APC candidate for Imo West Senatorial District in the 2027 general election.

Justice Obiora Egwuatu ruled that Okorocha emerged winner of the party’s senatorial primary held on May 18, 2026, rather than Uzodimma, and ordered INEC to substitute the governor’s name with that of the former governor.

The case was instituted by Okorocha, who challenged INEC’s recognition of Uzodimma as the winner of the primary. The court held that the evidence presented showed that Okorocha secured the majority of valid votes cast.

The ruling has been contested by the Imo State chapter of the APC, while Uzodimma has indicated plans to appeal.

World.title: Breaking: Ronaldo retires from international football
World.content:
(FILES) This file photo taken on July 11, 2016 shows Portugal’s forward Cristiano Ronaldo smiling while posing with the trophy after Portugal won the Euro 2016 final football match between Portugal and France at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis, north of Paris. / AFP PHOTO / FRANCISCO LEONG

Portuguese football legend Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday that he was retiring from international football.

The 41-year-old, who has played 234 times for Portugal and scored 146 goals, fell out with national coach Jorge Jesus last month after he refused to use him in a Nations League match. Ronaldo immediately left the team camp.

“To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team,” Ronaldo said in a video on his Instagram account.

“I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world,” he continued.

World.title: Zelensky says hopes US election means more support for Ukraine
World.content:
This image grab from a video filmed on December 23, 2025 and provided by the Ukrainian Presidential Office shows Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky addressing in Kyiv. Volodymyr Zelensky said on December 24, 2025 the latest version of a plan to end the Russian invasion would freeze the front line, but still pave the way for Ukrainian withdrawals and the creation of demilitarised zones. (Photo by Handout / UKRAINIAN PRESIDENTIAL OFFICE / AFP) / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE – MANDATORY CREDIT “AFP PHOTO / – / HANDOUT /UKRAINIAN PRESIDENTIAL OFFICE ” – NO MARKETING NO ADVERTISING CAMPAIGNS – DISTRIBUTED AS A SERVICE TO CLIENTS

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has said he hoped the Democrat triumph in the US midterm elections would boost support for Kyiv and help end the war with Russia.

Ukraine and its European allies had been worried about the United States getting closer to Russia since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year.

Ties between Trump and Zelensky have been turbulent, with tensions rising in recent weeks as the US leader criticised Kyiv and made a deal with President Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions in return for the release of Russian diesel.

“There is hope now that there is this balance of power, and that we will be supported more,” Zelensky told German broadcaster ZDF in an interview broadcast late Wednesday.

Zelensky said that if the US Congress “starts talking about strong financial support or military support” it would “influence Putin.”

“And Putin will be thinking about whether it makes sense to keep fighting if the support will only grow. Logically, this will (lead) us to possible negotiations and a possible peace,” he said.

US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks are to be held next week in Abu Dhabi. The talks had been frozen since the Middle East war erupted in February.

Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner have been leading the negotiations amid criticism over their attitude to Russia.

World.title: Breaking: Court sacks Mark-led ADC exco, voids Atiku’s candidacy
World.content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri, Abuja

The Federal High Court in Abuja has sacked the Senator David Mark-led executives of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and invalidated all actions they took on behalf of the party.

The actions included the nomination of a former vice president, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, as the party’s presidential candidate for the 2027 general elections.

Atiku, whose name was earlier published by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) as a candidate for the presidential poll, has since chosen a former governor of Rivers State, Rotimi Amaechi, as his running mate.

However, in a judgment delivered on Thursday by Justice Peter Lifu, the court declared illegal the Senator Mark-led Caretaker Committee of the ADC, which organised the primary election that produced Atiku as the party’s presidential flag bearer.

The court found merit in a suit brought before it by the aggrieved former National Deputy Chairman (North-East) of the party, Nafiu Bala Gombe.

Gombe had approached the court to query the process through which the Senator Mark-led Committee took over the reins of leadership of the party.

He maintained that, with the resignation of the former National Chairman, Chief Ralph Nwosu, he (Gombe) was qualified to assume the party’s leadership.

Consequently, he, among other things, prayed the court to nullify all actions taken on behalf of the party by the Senator Mark-led leadership.

Listed as defendants in the suit, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025, were the ADC, INEC, Senator Mark, Ogbeni Rauf Aregbesola and Chief Ralph Nwosu.

The plaintiff further urged the court to restrain Senator Mark and Aregbesola from parading themselves as National Chairman and Secretary, respectively, of the ADC, insisting that their emergence violated the party’s constitution and the provisions of the Electoral Act.

The court upheld the plaintiff’s claim and granted his reliefs, a verdict that could spark a chain of reactions in the polity, with the presidential election scheduled for January 16, 2027.

Already, the ADC has vowed to appeal the judgment.

Reacting to the outcome of the case, the National Welfare Secretary of the ADC, Mr. Nkemakolam Ukandu, who was later joined as an interested party in the matter, said the verdict would be challenged at the appellate court.

The development comes barely 24 hours after the party’s candidate, Atiku, held a massive rally in Sokoto State as part of his campaign for the 2027 presidential election.

World.title: Youth Confab: FG demands action, not talk from delegates
World.content:
Minister of Youth Development, Ayodele Olawande

By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja

The Federal Government has challenged delegates to the 2026 National Youth Conference to move beyond discussions and produce concrete recommendations that will shape government policies and address challenges confronting young Nigerians.

The government wants the conference to translate ideas gathered during virtual consultations into practical action plans on jobs, education, skills development, security and other critical issues affecting young people.

The Minister of Youth Development, Ayodele Olawande, made the call in Abuja at the opening of the conference’s physical phase, urging delegates to focus on solutions rather than discussions alone.

“Our responsibility now is to carefully examine the issues raised and the proposals received during the virtual consultations. We must identify the most serious challenges, review the solutions already proposed, and develop clear, practical and achievable action plans that can guide government decisions,” he said.

Olawande said the virtual consultations involved young Nigerians from all states and covered governance, employment, education, technology, climate change, peace and security, and national unity.

He said the conference was designed to give young people a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their lives, beyond government interventions in education, skills training, business support and job creation.

“We are not here just to speak to ourselves. We are here to help shape decisions that will affect millions of young Nigerians who are not in this room. That is a duty we must take seriously,” he said.

He urged delegates to respect divergent views and work towards recommendations that would translate into practical interventions for young Nigerians.

World.title: Netanyahu loses religious party’s support as rival tipped to form government
World.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during a press conference in Jerusalem on March 19, 2026. (Photo by Ronen Zvulun / POOL / AFP) /

An ultra-Orthodox Jewish party long aligned with Benjamin Netanyahu declined on Thursday to recommend him to stay as Israel’s prime minister, as signs grew that rival Gadi Eisenkot will have the first chance to form a government.

President Isaac Herzog was holding a second day of consultations with political parties after the October 27 election, in which neither Netanyahu — a polarising right-winger who has led Israel through three years of war — nor Eisenkot secured enough votes for a majority.

United Torah Judaism, which backed Netanyahu after the previous five elections, in its meeting with Herzog declined to recommend Netanyahu again as prime minister, although it also did not side with Eisenkot.

The party informed Herzog “that it has decided not to recommend any member of Knesset to form a government,” the president’s office said in a statement, referring to the 120-member parliament in which United Torah Judaism has won seven seats.

The party, which represents ultra-Orthodox Jews of Ashkenazi origin, who mostly hail from or have roots in Europe, as well as Shas, which represents the same community but of Sephardic, or mostly Middle Eastern and North African descent, have both been backed by Netanyahu as they push to maintain the exemption from military service for religious students.

Netanyahu has preserved the exemption but stopped short of enshrining it in law, in the face of major resentment from many other Israelis as reservists serve multiple tours due to the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

“In whatever government is next formed, our immediate item is sorting out the status of Torah students,” United Torah Judaism lawmaker Isaac Pindrus said.

Eisenkot, a former military chief seeking to unite the centre and centre-right, has been adamant about closing exemptions to military service, with some of his opposition allies harshly criticising the ultra-Orthodox as self-serving.

Observers say United Torah Judaism’s approach may be aimed more at punishing Netanyahu and showing that their votes cannot be taken for granted, while they could still serve in a government if he were to form one.

Herzog will meet representatives of the major parties later on Thursday before tasking one lawmaker with forming a government. He generally bases his decision on which person receives the most party recommendations, making it likely he will ask Eisenkot.

Once Herzog gives the mandate, that lawmaker will have 28 days to form a government, with a potential 14-day extension. If the lawmaker fails, Herzog will then task someone else.

Netanyahu’s bloc — including United Torah Judaism — has 53 seats in the new parliament, as opposed to 48 for Eisenkot’s bloc.

Israeli-Arab parties soared in strength on the back of anger over Netanyahu’s hard-right government, winning 19 seats.

Eisenkot could form a government with the Arab parties but would risk losing support from some in the opposition.

World.title: Otu Decries Obi Convoy’s Attack, Calls on Security Agencies to Fish Out Perpetrators
World.content:
Bassey Inyang in Calabar

Cross River State Governor, Senator Bassey Otu, has condemned in strong terms the attack on the convoy of the Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, Mr. Peter Obi, by suspected political thugs Wednesday in the state capital, Calabar.

In a statement by the governor’s Chief Press Secretary, Mr Linus Obogo, on Thursday, Otu expressed deep sadness and concern over the attack, extending his warm empathy to the visiting presidential candidate and his entourage.



“I extend my deepest, most heartfelt sympathies to Mr. Peter Obi and his team over the deeply disturbing incident that occurred yesterday during his campaign visit to our state capital,” the governor declared, emphasizing that Cross River State stands in firm solidarity with all political actors seeking to engage peacefully with the electorate.

Otu said that Cross River State remains an enclave of civil harmony and hospitality, making the ugly occurrence an unacceptable anomaly.



“As a government and as a people, our hearts go out to him, and we stand in firm solidarity against any act designed to instill fear or disrupt the peaceful exercise of political rights.



“Cross River has long been cherished as the cradle of hospitality, warmth, and civil decorum in Nigeria; our culture is rooted in peace, harmony, and mutual respect for all people, regardless of political affiliation,” Otu said.

​Describing the emotional toll the incident might have had on the leadership and residents of the state, the governor lamented that such hostility contradicts everything the state holds dear.



“To witness such hostility within our dear state breaks our hearts, and we extend our unreserved comfort to Mr. Obi as he continues his engagement with the Nigerian electorate,” Otu added, and offered reassurance directly to the campaign team.

​Lashing out at the perpetrators, the governor spared no words in calling out the hostility for what it truly is.



“We unequivocally condemn this reckless assault and deprecate the action as entirely unwholesome, barbaric, and completely alien to our identity as Cross Riverians,” he asserted, reaffirming that lawlessness will not be normalized under his leadership.

​Emphasizing the true nature of the state, Otu said criminal aggression is contrary to the ethos of the people of Cross River.

“This disgraceful display of lawlessness does not reflect who we are, nor does it represent the cherished values of our peaceful state,” he noted, reassuring political parties that the state remains open and safe for constitutional political activities.

​Sending a stern warning to the perpetrators, Otu reaffirmed his administration’s uncompromising stance on law and order. “Let it be made unmistakably clear: our administration maintains a zero-tolerance stance against political violence and criminality in any form,” the hovernor firmly warned.

​Calling on security agencies to fish out the criminals, Governor Otu pledged that those behind the violence will face swift justice.

“I have directed our security agencies to leave no stone unturned, until every single perpetrator of this shameful act is brought to book to face the full weight of the law,” Otu declared.

World.title: Access Holdings’ 9 Months 2026 Results: Building Stronger Foundation for Sustainable Shareholder Returns
World.content:
Kayode Tokede

Access Holdings Plc’s unaudited results for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 has provided encouraging evidence of a business increasingly focused on the quality of the earnings generated from its considerable scale.

Profit before tax increased by 8.3 per cent to N667.4 billion, from N616.2 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. Profit after tax rose by 5.9 per cent to N474.2 billion, compared with N447.5 billion a year earlier.

Those headline numbers are positive. The more revealing feature of the performance, however, lies in the composition of earnings and the significantly stronger result after impairment.

Significant Improvement After Impairment

Interest income increased by 6.9per cent to N3.1 trillion, while interest expense rose by 10.1per cent to N1.8 trillion. Net interest income consequently increased by 2.7per cent to N1.3 trillion.

The much stronger movement came after impairment. Impairment charges declined by 73.5per cent, from N350.0 billion in the corresponding period of 2025 to N92.9 billion. Net interest income after impairment increased by 32.1per cent, from N08.0 billion to approximately N1.2 trillion.

This is one of the clearest features of the nine-month results. The difference between the 2.7 per cent increase in net interest income and the 32.1 per cent increase after impairment highlights the significance of the reduction in impairment charges to the overall earnings performance.

Fee and commission income increased by 8.4 per cent to N650.9 billion, while fee and commission expense declined by 6.9 per cent to N115.9 billion. Net fee and commission income consequently increased by 12.4per cent to N534.9 billion.

Together, these movements contributed to core operating income of N1.83 trillion, representing growth of 5.4 per cent from N1.73 trillion in the comparable period.

The result therefore shows improvement in two important areas: income generated after impairment and net fee and commission income. Both are encouraging developments, although the sustainability of the improvement will depend on continued revenue growth, credit performance and operating-cost discipline.

The Operating Picture Remains Mixed

The nine-month performance is not uniformly positive, and the results are transparent about the areas requiring continued management attention.

Operating expenses increased by 11.8 per cent to N1.3 trillion. At the same time, total other operating income declined by 40.8 per cent to N234.5 billion. The combined effect was a 3.2 per cent decline in total operating income, from N2.13 trillion to N2.06 trillion.

These figures provide important context for the increase in profitability. The results show stronger income after impairment and higher net fee and commission income, but they also show pressure from rising operating expenses and lower other operating income.

This helps explain why operating efficiency features prominently in the Group’s Scale-to-Value agenda. The results identify stronger cost discipline and greater efficiency from the Group’s infrastructure and capabilities as priorities.

The significance of the Group’s strategic response is that these pressure points are explicitly recognised. Despite them, profit before tax still increased by 8.3 per cent, supported by substantially lower impairments and growth in core income.

A Substantial Balance Sheet

The balance sheet provides another important dimension to the results.

Total assets stood at N52.6 trillion at September 30, 2026, an increase of 1.7per cent from N51.7 trillion at December 31, 2025.

Customer deposits grew by 6.6 per cent to N36.9 trillion, while loans and advances to customers increased by 7.4 per cent to N14.3 trillion. Shareholders’ funds remained broadly stable at N4.5 trillion, compared with N4.5 trillion at the end of 2025.

The size of the balance sheet gives meaning to the strategic language the Group has adopted.

Access Holdings described Scale-to-Value as a progression from building scale to improving the quality and productivity of that scale.

The strategic focus articulated in the results is not simply on further expansion. It is on extracting greater quality and productivity from the scale already assembled, with sustainable shareholder returns identified as the ultimate objective.

Geographic Diversification Has Become Significant

The geographic composition of earnings is another notable aspect of the nine-month performance. The banking group remained the principal contributor to Access Holdings’ earnings, accounting for 96 per cent of the Group’s unaudited profit before tax during the period.

Within the banking Group, operations outside Nigeria accounted for 82.2 per cent of Profit Before Tax. International banking subsidiaries contributed 43.7 per cent, Rest of Africa contributed 38.5 per cent, while Nigeria accounted for 17.8 per cent.

The figures demonstrate the extent to which banking group earnings are now distributed across markets outside Nigeria. The Group said it is leveraging this geographic footprint to deepen customer relationships and increase activity across trade finance, transaction banking, payments and treasury services.

The combination of geographic reach and increasingly diversified earnings provides a substantial platform from which the Group can pursue stronger earnings quality and capital productivity.

The issue presented by the results is therefore no longer simply the breadth of the franchise. Management’s stated focus is on converting that scale into sustainable shareholder returns through stronger execution, robust risk governance and regulatory compliance, effective capital allocation and greater operating efficiency

Scale-to-Value Moves Closer to the Numbers

The nine-month results provide a clearer definition of what Scale-to-Value means for Access Holdings. Execution capacity is described in terms of strengthening accountability and the Group’s ability to translate strategic priorities into measurable outcomes.

Risk governance and regulatory compliance centre on maintaining robust risk and control disciplines and sustained compliance with applicable regulatory requirements across the Group.

Capital discipline places greater emphasis on productivity and risk-adjusted returns, while operating efficiency focuses on cost discipline and more productive use of the Group’s infrastructure and capabilities.

Earnings quality completes the framework, with an emphasis on deepening recurring income streams and strengthening earnings resilience.

Several elements of the strategy connect directly with developments visible in the reported numbers: the significant decline in impairment charges, growth in fee income, the increase in operating expenses and the increasingly diversified contribution from the banking group’s geographic operations.

The results therefore provide a useful financial context for understanding how Access Holdings intends to translate scale into stronger shareholder outcomes.

Risk Governance and Regulatory Compliance Remain Central

The emphasis on regulatory compliance is particularly relevant given the progress Access Holdings has reported towards resolving its position under Section 19(8)(c) of the Banks and Other Financial Institutios Act (BOFIA).

The Group has identified capital recalls from six banking subsidiaries which, when completed, are expected to bring Access Bank’s investment-in-subsidiaries ratio within the statutory 10 per cent threshold.

According to management, the recall process has already been completed in one subsidiary, while shareholder approvals have been obtained in four of the remaining five subsidiaries. Regulatory approvals and other required processes are being progressed across the remaining subsidiaries.

The Group expects to complete the programme within the CBN’s prescribed compliance timeline, subject to the necessary approvals.

This represents an important development for shareholders. The regulatory issue has constrained the Group’s dividend-paying capacity, and completing the programme would remove a significant obstacle to future distributions.

Any dividend decision would, however, remain subject to the Group’s financial position, distributable reserves, capital requirements and the necessary approvals.

Beyond dividends, the programme also demonstrates how more disciplined capital management can improve financial flexibility across the Group. It provides a practical example of the link between regulatory compliance, capital productivity and sustainable shareholder returns.

Stronger Foundation for Sustainable Shareholder Returns

Taken together, the nine-month results show a business beginning to translate its considerable scale into stronger earnings quality.

Profit before tax increased by 8.3 per cent to N667.4 billion and profit after tax rose by 5.9 per cent to N474.2 billion. More importantly, impairment charges declined by 73.5 per cent, lifting net interest income after impairment by 32.1 per cent to approximately N1.2 trillion. Net fee and commission income also increased by 12.4 per cent to N534.9 billion.

These are significant movements because they provide evidence of stronger earnings after credit costs and a larger contribution from fee-generating activities.

There are still areas requiring attention. Operating expenses increased by 11.8 per cent, other operating income declined by 40.8 per cent, and total operating income was 3.2 per cent lower. The significance of the Scale-to-Value agenda is that these areas are not peripheral to the strategy. Operating efficiency, execution capacity and capital productivity are explicitly identified as priorities.

The broader foundation, however, is substantial. At September 30, 2026, Access Holdings had total assets of N52.6 trillion and customer deposits of N36.9 trillion. Within the banking group, operations outside Nigeria generated 82.2 per cent of profit before tax, with international banking subsidiaries contributing 43.7 per cent and Rest of Africa 38.5 per cent.

That combination of balance-sheet scale, deposit strength and geographically diversified earnings gives Access Holdings a broad platform from which to pursue the next phase of its development.

What makes the nine-month results particularly relevant is that the Group’s strategic emphasis is becoming more closely aligned with the requirements of that next phase. Scale-to-Value is centred on stronger execution capacity, robust risk governance and regulatory compliance, disciplined capital allocation, greater operating efficiency and improved capital.

World.title: Breaking: Court Sacks David Mark-led ADC Leadership, Recognises Nafiu Bala Gombe as Party Leader
World.content:
Alex Enumah in Abuja

The leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) under Senator David Mark has been sacked by a Federal High Court in Abuja, in a judgment that could jeopardise the party’s participation in the 2027 general elections.

Justice Peter Lifu, in a judgment delivered on Thursday, held that the emergence of Mark as the national chairman of the ADC, alongside other members of his executive, violated the party’s constitution and established guidelines.

The court consequently nullified all actions taken by the Mark-led leadership, ruling that following the resignation of other party members, the plaintiff, Nafiu Bala Gombe, was the authentic leader of the party.

The judgment has significant implications for the ADC’s preparations for the 2027 general elections, as the party’s leadership structure and the validity of decisions taken under Mark’s administration have been thrown into question.
