World.title: Funding: EFInA CEO Tasks SMEs to Look beyond Conventional Loans
World.content:
Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Enhancing Financial Inclusion and Advancement (EFInA), Foyinsolami Akinjayeju, has tasked small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to rethink their approach to financing, urging them to look beyond conventional loans and identify capital that aligns with their operational needs, growth ambitions and repayment capacity.

Akinjayeju made this call during a panel discussion titled “Access to Capital Beyond Loans: What SMEs Need to Know in 2026” at the ninth edition of the Caladium Lagos SME (CLSME) Bootcamp, held in Lagos.

Drawing on EFInA’s A2F 2026 insights, Akinjayeju noted that only about10 per cent of Nigerians had accessed formal credit, highlighting the need to improve access to appropriate financing while helping entrepreneurs make informed borrowing decisions.

She cautioned that debt could accelerate business failure if repayment obligations exceed a business’s capacity to generate cash flow. Rather than treating borrowing as the default response to a funding need, she encouraged entrepreneurs to assess their productive capacity, identify operational bottlenecks, and determine what type of financing would address their specific challenges.

“Before seeking capital, business owners need to understand their productive capacity, identify the constraints holding their businesses back and determine what financing is appropriate for their needs. The question is not simply how to get money, but how to get the right kind of capital for the right purpose,” she said.

Akinjayeju outlined three considerations for SMEs seeking capital: purpose, proof and partners. Purpose requires business owners to establish exactly what the funding will achieve and how it will address a specific business need. Proof involves demonstrating the ability to execute through reliable financial records, cash flow evidence, repeat customer orders, and a track record of fulfilling commitments. Partners refer to relationships with customers, suppliers, investors and other business associates who may provide financing or facilitate access to it.

She encouraged business owners to look beyond conventional loans, introducing them to the mnemonic capital as a framework for understanding seven alternative financing pathways. These include: customer advances and deposit-backed pre-orders; asset leasing, which allows businesses to access productive machinery and equipment without paying the full purchase price upfront; payables and supplier credit, through negotiated payment terms that free up working capital; invoice financing to enable businesses to obtain early payment against qualifying unpaid invoices; third-party equity investments, through which businesses raise capital in exchange for ownership; awards and grants that can provide non-repayable funding for eligible programmes; and leveraged group financing in the form of savings and credit within cooperatives.

Akinjayeju emphasised that the right financing option is not necessarily the easiest to obtain, and that not all seven pathways will suit every business.

“Entrepreneurs must assess which option best aligns with their business stage, funding purpose, cash flow and growth ambitions, while carefully considering the obligations and trade-offs associated with each source of capital,” she said,

Furthermore, Akinjayeju noted the need for business owners to build relationships before they need financing.

“ A history of trust, reliable delivery and sound business practices can strengthen their ability to secure support when funding opportunities arise,” she explained.

The panel conversation addressed a persistent challenge in the SME ecosystem: entrepreneurs often identify lack of capital as their primary obstacle, while funders need evidence that businesses can use financing effectively and meet their obligations. Speaking on the importance of the discussion, convener of the CLSME Bootcamp, Ayo Bankole Akintujoye, noted that capital is frequently cited as the biggest obstacle to business growth, even when entrepreneurs may need to address other constraints first. He explained that the panel was designed to help business owners examine their financing needs more carefully and understand the range of options available to them.

The CLSME Bootcamp is a non-profit initiative dedicated to equipping entrepreneurs with management, leadership and execution capabilities. Across its first eight editions, the platform directly impacted more than 10,000 SMEs. The ninth edition brought together more than 1,500 participants on-site, with an additional 2,000 expected to join virtually from across Africa.

The discussion also featured Feyisayo Alayande, Executive Secretary of the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund (LSETF), and Ikechi Onyeneke, Head of Business Development, Enterprise Banking, Stanbic IBTC Bank. Moderated by the Caladium Lagos SME Bootcamp Convener, Ayo Bankole Akintujoye, the session examined financing options available to SMEs, funding readiness and the factors that influence financing decisions.

EFInA continues to advance financial inclusion by supporting the development of an inclusive financial system that expands access to quality financial services and creates opportunities for individuals and businesses across Nigeria.

World.title: 2027: I’ll Pick Competence over Politics in Cabinet Formation, Says Donald Duke Declares
World.content:
Ayodeji Ake



The presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), Donald Duke, has said he would prioritise competence over political considerations in appointing members of his cabinet if elected president in 2027.

Duke, who spoke in an interview yesterday in Abuja, said Nigeria’s numerous challenges required a government driven by expertise, capacity and performance rather than political patronage or the need to compensate individuals and groups for electoral support.

“If I am going to pick a cabinet, you may not find any politician in that cabinet,” he said.

The former Cross River State governor argued that forming a cabinet around political interests could distract an administration from governance, as appointees might become more concerned about securing political support for another election than delivering on their responsibilities.

“I’m going for the broke. When you start putting politicians in your cabinet, you are looking at the next election. You are thinking about the people who will support you. For me, I want the people to support me. If you perform, the people will support you,” he said.

Duke maintained that the 2027 presidential election should be about the capacity of candidates to address Nigeria’s economic difficulties, insecurity, unemployment, poor education, healthcare challenges and weaknesses in the justice system, rather than political personalities and party structures.

Reflecting on his experience as the governor of Cross River State between 1999 and 2007, he said his administration’s performance during his first term significantly reduced the need for extensive political mobilisation when he sought re-election.

According to him, his first election was challenging because he had to introduce himself to the electorate, but his record in office helped establish public confidence ahead of his second-term bid.

“My first election in Cross River State was really tough. I was basically introducing myself to the people, and politicians were running around everywhere.

“But by my second election, I hardly needed to go to rallies. You could feel the mood. People would tell me, ‘Don’t worry yourself; you have proved your mettle,’” he said.

Duke argued that the performance of an incumbent should serve as the foundation for seeking another mandate, rather than relying on fresh promises and political campaigns.

“When you prove your mettle, much of the politics disappears. People trust you because they have seen what you can do.

“When you are contesting for the first time, people hold on to your words because that is what you offered them. But when you are seeking a second term, they should hold on to your work. Your work should speak for you,” he added.

World.title: Benue, Oyo, Abia, Other States Yet to Approve State Police Bill as Senate Sets Nov 15 Deadline
World.content:
. 30 assemblies endorse constitutional amendment

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja



The Senate has given the six state Houses of Assembly yet to communicate their positions on the proposed constitutional amendment establishing the State Police until November 15 to do so, warning that failure to respond by the deadline could be deemed as withholding approval.

The Senate Leader, Opeyemi Bamidele, disclosed this during plenary yesterday while updating lawmakers on the progress of consultations with the 36 state legislatures on the proposed amendment.

The outstanding states are Benue, Oyo, Cross River, Niger, Abia and Kano.

The Deputy President of the Senate, Jibrin Barau, has, however, informed the red chamber that the Kano State House of Assembly would transmit its approval to the National Assembly before the November 15 deadline.

The Senate Leader nevertheless said 30 states had already approved the bill, exceeding the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of 24 states needed to advance the amendment.

The outstanding six states are expected to communicate their decisions before November 15, when the National Assembly intends to forward the proposed constitutional amendment to President Bola Tinubu for assent.

Bamidele explained that the National Assembly had completed its responsibility by passing the bill and transmitting it to all 36 state Houses of Assembly for consideration and approval.

He said the constitution prescribed three distinct stages for constitutional amendments: passage by the National Assembly, approval by at least two-thirds of the state Houses of Assembly and presidential assent.

He said: “Three key words are used in the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, as amended. The first is passage, the second is approval, and the third is assent.

“The passage of the bill was the responsibility of the National Assembly, and that has been completed. Approval is required from at least two-thirds of the 36 state Houses of Assembly in the country, while assent must subsequently be given by the President to complete the constitutional amendment process.”

The Senate Leader explained that the constitutional requirements were deliberately designed to ensure that amendments to the nation’s supreme law enjoyed the participation and agreement of critical stakeholders across the different levels of government.

He listed the 30 states that had approved the proposed amendment as Adamawa, Akwa Ibom, Anambra, Bauchi, Bayelsa, Borno, Delta, Ebonyi, Edo, Ekiti, Enugu, Gombe, Imo, Jigawa, Kaduna, Katsina, Kebbi, Kogi, Kwara, Lagos, Nasarawa, Ogun, Ondo, Osun, Plateau, Rivers, Sokoto, Taraba, Yobe and Zamfara.

Bamidele said the 30 approvals represented more than the constitutionally stipulated threshold of 24 states, expressing optimism that the remaining six would communicate their decisions before the expiration of the deadline.

He said: “Two important points need to be emphasised. Firstly, we needed the approval of at least two-thirds of the states for this constitutional amendment to proceed.

“Two-thirds of the 36 states amount to 24. We have already secured approval from 30 states, demonstrating the popularity of this bill among Nigerians through their elected representatives in the various state Houses of Assembly.”

However, the Senate President, Senator Godswill Akpabio, urged the Senate Leader to give the outstanding states a specific timeframe to communicate their decisions, stressing that the National Assembly needed to establish whether they supported or rejected the proposed constitutional alteration.

Akpabio said the establishment of State Police is a significant constitutional development that required broad consultation across the country before the amendment could be transmitted to the president for assent.

Akpabio said: “What I would like you to do is to give a specific timeframe within which the remaining six states should communicate their decisions to us.

“The reason is that we need to know whether they concur with or reject the proposed alteration of the Constitution to allow for the creation of State Police.

“This is an important constitutional amendment, and we must ensure that the entire country is consulted on such an epoch-making bill and piece of legislation before it is eventually assented to by the President.”

Akpabio consequently suggested that the outstanding states should be given another week to communicate their positions.

Responding, Bamidele clarified that the National Assembly had already provided a 30-day window for all the state legislatures to consider the proposed amendment and communicate their resolutions.

He said the Clerk of the National Assembly had on October 15, 2026, formally conveyed a letter to the 36 state Houses of Assembly, indicating November 15 as the deadline for their responses.

“Well, Mr. President, let me clarify that the letter written on our behalf and signed by the Clerk of the National Assembly was conveyed to the 36 State Houses of Assembly on October 15, 2026.

“In that letter, the Clerk indicated on our behalf that the state Houses of Assembly had until November 15 to consider the bill and communicate their decisions. This provides a clear 30-day period to allow them sufficient time to sit, deliberate and take the necessary decisions,” he said.

The Senate Leader explained that the November 15 deadline was necessary because the National Assembly intended to transmit the bill to President Tinubu from that date.

He warned that any state House of Assembly that failed to communicate its position by then would be deemed to have withheld approval, or face whatever constitutional implications might arise from its failure to respond.

“We believe that the remaining six states will use the time available between now and that date to do the needful.

“By that date, any state House of Assembly that has not communicated its position will be deemed to have withheld approval, or whatever constitutional implication may arise from its failure to respond,” Bamidele stated.

He expressed confidence that the outstanding states would take advantage of the remaining period to communicate their decisions, adding that the National Assembly was hopeful that no state would want to be excluded from the proposed constitutional reform.

Meanwhile, the Deputy Senate President, Senator Jibrin Barau Jibrin, informed the Senate that the Kano State House of Assembly had also submitted its response to the proposed amendment.

Barau, who disclosed this during the proceedings, said he had just been informed that the Kano State legislature’s communication was being conveyed to the National Assembly.

“Mr President, I have just been informed that the Kano State House of Assembly has sent its response, and it is being communicated to us.

“There was a delay in the process, but the Kano State legislature has done the needful. It is a very outstanding State Assembly,” he said.

Akpabio welcomed the development, expressing satisfaction with the information.

The proposed constitutional amendment is part of ongoing efforts to restructure Nigeria’s policing architecture by providing for the establishment of State Police Services.

The initiative is intended to create the constitutional foundation for decentralised policing, amid continuing national discussions on how to strengthen security arrangements and improve responses to security challenges across the country.

Although the 30 approvals already secured have surpassed the constitutional threshold, the Senate’s November 15 deadline provides the remaining state legislatures an opportunity to formally communicate their positions before the amendment is forwarded to the president for the next stage of the constitutional process.

World.title: Press Week:  Abia Correspondents Chapel Trains 50 Journalists
World.content:
Boniface Okoro in Umuahia



The Correspondents Chapel of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Abia State, will today (November 4, 2026) kick off a three-day training for over 50 journalists and media professionals ahead of the 2027 general election.

Sponsored by the Chapel, the training programme will run till November 6 at Bishop Anthony Nwedo Pastoral Centre, BCA Road, Umuahia, as part of activities to mark the Chapel’s 2026 Press Week.

With the theme: ‘The Future of Journalism in an Era of Disinformation: Preparing Abia Media Practitioners for Democracy and the 2027 Polls’, the retreat is designed to strengthen capacity for credible, ethical and responsible election reporting.

According to a joint statement issued by the Chairman of the Chapel, Deacon Steve Oko; Secretary, Henrietta Ashikodi; Chairman of the Planning Committee, Peter Okor; and Secretary, Leonard Okachie, participants will be exposed to responsible application of AI in reporting, fact-checking and verification of political claims, ethical election coverage, media safety, hate speech, inflammatory political communication, and promotion of peaceful, credible elections.

The retreat is expected to feature distinguished resource persons, including the Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC) in Abia State, Prof. Sylvia Uchenna Agu, Commissioner of Police, Wilfred Afolabi, and the first female Professor of Mass Communication in Nigeria, Prof. Stella Okunna.

Others are veteran journalist and former Secretary to the Abia State Government, Ralph Egbu; Chief Medical Director of Abia State Specialist Hospital, Dr. Chimezie Okwuonu; and digital expert, Chibueze Ukaegbu.

The statement said the keynote address would be delivered by the Rector of Ogbonnaya Onu Polytechnic, Aba, Prof. Christopher Okoro, at the grand finale, while the Deputy Vice Chancellor of Gregory University, Uturu, Prof. Uwaoma Uche, will chair the event.

The grand finale, which will take place on November 6, will feature a political debate and manifesto presentation by National Assembly candidates from various political parties, to provide them with an opportunity to present programmes to the electorate through the Chapel’s platforms, and promote neutrality, equal media access, and issue-based engagement.

The Chapel said the programme was conceived in response to growing demands of election reporting in an era of digital manipulation, misinformation, disinformation, deepfakes, and misuse of Artificial Intelligence, noting that credible elections depend on an informed electorate and a professionally equipped media.

The event will also feature the presentation of awards to distinguished Nigerians, including the Minister of Works, Senator David Umahi; Prof. Nnenna Oti; and Super Eagles international, Samuel Chukwueze, for their contributions to leadership, public service, and sports.

World.title: Hamzat: The Man, His Vision and Agenda for Lagos
World.content:
With a 100-point development blueprint outlining his vision for the Centre of Excellence, the All Progressives Congress’ governorship candidate, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, has placed accountability, continuity and inclusive development at the centre of his campaign, challenging residents to hold him responsible for every unfulfilled promise. Wale Igbintade reports.

The atmosphere at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts, formerly the National Theatre, Iganmu, Lagos, on Friday, October 30, was unmistakably political, cultural and symbolic.

Thousands of party faithful, residents, political stakeholders and invited guests gathered to witness the unveiling of the manifesto of the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat. Others followed the proceedings through live broadcasts, extending the event’s reach beyond the venue.

The colourful cultural performances celebrating Lagos’ rich heritage, coupled with the presence of prominent political leaders, traditional rulers, religious figures and captains of industry, underscored the significance of the occasion.

Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, who attended as special guest of honour with his wife, Dr Ibijoke Sanwo-Olu, was joined by former Governor Babatunde Fashola, members of the National Assembly, Lagos State House of Assembly, the Governance Advisory Council, traditional rulers and other political leaders.

But beyond the impressive gathering, the central attraction was Hamzat’s attempt to define the next chapter of Lagos’ development journey.

His manifesto, titled ‘The Lagos Promise (Ileri Eko)’, is structured around seven pillars and 100 pledges covering healthcare, education, infrastructure, transportation, economic development, employment, security, housing, environmental sustainability and institutional accountability.

Its central philosophy was captured in a simple but weighty declaration: A promise is a debt.

In what emerged as the strongest political statement of the occasion, Hamzat challenged Lagosians to hold him accountable for every commitment contained in the document.

“I stand before you today not simply to ask for your vote, but to earn your trust, to share my vision for Lagos, to explain what I believe that we must do differently, and to demonstrate why I am prepared to serve you,” he declared.

The Man Behind the Mission

Hamzat’s presentation was not restricted to policy proposals. He offered glimpses into the personal experiences and values that, according to him, have shaped his understanding of public service.

He recalled encountering the late sage, Chief Obafemi Awolowo when he was 14 years old and a student at Olivet Baptist High School, Oyo. Awolowo’s campaign procession had passed along the road in front of his school, giving him an opportunity to see the legendary progressive politician at close range.

The experience, he said, left an enduring impression on him, particularly the philosophy that a nation progresses when people of honour and ability choose to serve.

His political consciousness was also shaped by his father, Alhaji Mufutau Olatunji Hamzat, a banker who later became involved in progressive politics. Elected into the Lagos State House of Assembly in 1979, his father subsequently served as Commissioner for Public Transportation under the administration of the late Governor, Alhaji Lateef Jakande.

Hamzat also recalled his childhood in Mushin, where he attended Odu-Abore Memorial Primary School. Those early experiences, he explained, exposed him to the everyday challenges confronting ordinary Lagos residents.

“Mushin taught me many things. I learned what a clear drain means to a street during the rainy season. I learned what steady light means to a trader at four in the afternoon,” he said.

For him, development is not merely about constructing impressive infrastructure or announcing ambitious programmes. It must improve the everyday lives of residents.

He illustrated this with the story of a 10-year-old boy he encountered under a bridge at Oshodi at about 2 a.m. The child, who had reportedly run away from home in another state because his environment was unsafe, had found sleeping under a bridge preferable to returning home.

The experience reinforced Hamzat’s conviction that government must protect vulnerable children through functioning schools, healthcare facilities, social welfare institutions and effective community support.

“If you are a child and you live in Lagos, then you are a child of Lagos. Lagos will know you are here, Lagos will work for you, Lagos will protect you,” he declared.

He said his parents had instilled three principles in him: respect, work and truth. Respect means treating citizens with dignity; work requires delivery before publicity; while truth demands honesty about government performance.

Seven Pillars, 100 Pledges

The manifesto’s seven pillars are People First, Renewal, Opportunity, Machinery of Government, Inclusion, Security and Resilience, and Everyday Excellence.

A notable feature is its classification of the 100 commitments into 87 firm pledges within the powers of the Lagos State Government and 13 aspirations requiring wider consultations, cooperation with the Federal Government or judicial intervention.

To strengthen accountability, Hamzat promised to establish a Lagos State Service Delivery Office through an executive order, with himself as chairman.

An independent Performance Council would assess government performance, while service charters would be introduced across public offices.

Under the proposed arrangement, complaints would be acknowledged within 48 hours, answered within seven days and resolved within 30 days. Annual performance reports and public scorecards would also disclose achievements, outstanding commitments and reasons for any failures.

He promised that the accountability framework would commence within his first 100 days in office.

Healthcare and education occupy prominent positions in the blueprint. Hamzat promised to increase maternal and child centres from 10 to 15 and expand the Ilera Eko health insurance programme from nearly two million beneficiaries to more than three million.

He also pledged to complete the 150-bed Massey Children’s Hospital, the 280-bed Ojo General Hospital and the 150-bed Somolu General Hospital, providing 580 additional beds. Two more general hospitals are proposed for Ogombo and Ibeju-Lekki, alongside the upgrading of 100 primary healthcare centres.

On education, he promised to strengthen public schools through improved teacher training, professional development and better learning outcomes. He highlighted EKOEXCEL and the Eko Learn initiative, which provides 320 lessons online and on television.

He also proposed establishing a University of Medicine and Health Sciences to expand tertiary education opportunities and strengthen the state’s healthcare workforce.

Jobs, Infrastructure and Economic Growth

Recognising the importance of small businesses and entrepreneurship to Lagos’ economy, Hamzat argued that government cannot create all the jobs required by the state’s growing population. Rather, it must provide an environment in which businesses can expand and employ more people.

He cited the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund’s support for businesses through financing, training and mentorship, promising to expand opportunities for entrepreneurs, artisans and young people.

Among his proposals is a single schedule of lawful government charges to eliminate uncertainty for businesses. He also promised to reserve a defined proportion of state procurement opportunities for qualified Lagos businesses.

Under a proposed apprenticeship programme, students would spend between six and 12 months working with employers, with the state paying 40 per cent of their stipends. Artisans would also receive free professional certification based on their existing practical skills.

For young people, he pledged to expand opportunities in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, robotics, blockchain and other emerging technologies.

Transportation, one of Lagos’ most pressing challenges, received considerable attention.

Hamzat promised to increase the public bus fleet from approximately 1,000 to 4,000 buses, with the capacity to transport one million passengers daily.

He also pledged to extend the Blue Line to Okokomaiko, advance the Green Line from Marina to the Lekki Free Trade Zone and improve connections between the existing rail corridors.

Other proposed projects include the Fourth Mainland Bridge, the Regional Road along the Lekki-Epe axis and Phase II of the Opebi-Mende Link Bridge.

On water transportation, he promised to dredge an additional 140 kilometres of waterways, refurbish 25 ferry terminals and jetties, optimise 15 ferry routes and procure 75 additional electric vessels.

Housing is another major component. Hamzat promised to complete ongoing housing projects, expand Lagos HOMS and introduce more accessible mortgage arrangements.

One proposal is a mortgage scheme requiring a 10 per cent deposit, single-digit interest rates and longer repayment periods, potentially improving access to home ownership for middle and lower-income earners.

On security, he pledged to extend the Lagos State Neighbourhood Safety Agency to all wards across the state’s 20 local government areas and 37 Local Council Development Areas.

He also proposed installing streetlights and CCTV cameras in communities and establishing a State Intelligence Fusion Centre to strengthen responses to organised crime, cybercrime and other security threats.

Water supply and environmental sustainability also featured prominently.

Hamzat promised to complete the Adiyan Phase Two water project, designed to produce 70 million gallons daily and provide water to an additional six million Lagos residents.

He also pledged to rehabilitate 24 micro and mini waterworks and achieve 95 per cent waste collection coverage, alongside the completion of waste transfer stations and a waste-to-energy facility.

On inclusion, he promised to strengthen programmes such as Obirin Eko for women, Omo Eko for young people and Iyi Eko for persons with disabilities, maintaining that Lagos must work for everyone, irrespective of ethnic, religious or geographical background.

First 100 Days

Hamzat identified three immediate priorities for his proposed administration.

The first is the establishment of a Child Protection and Nutrition Agency to ensure that every child below 18 is either in school or learning a trade and receives adequate nutrition.

The second is the Lagos State Service Delivery Office, which would monitor government commitments and provide measurable assessments of performance.

The third is the advancement of a State Wealth Fund, with an independent board and published accounts, to preserve Lagos’ wealth for future generations.

Together, the proposals reflect the manifesto’s emphasis on child welfare, institutional accountability and long-term economic sustainability.

Sanwo-Olu’s Endorsement and Politics of Continuity

While Hamzat presented the policy direction, Sanwo-Olu’s address supplied much of the political and emotional weight of the occasion.

In a deeply personal endorsement, the governor recalled how Hamzat had stepped aside for him during the 2018 governorship contest after party leaders intervened and asked him to withdraw from the race.

Sanwo-Olu said Hamzat had considerable experience and every reason to pursue his ambition, having served in public office for years. However, he accepted the party’s decision and subsequently agreed to become his running mate.

“I did not come here to be polite. I came here to testify,” the governor declared.

He said his endorsement was based on seven years of working closely with Hamzat, particularly during challenging periods such as the COVID-19 pandemic, the October 2020 crisis and the execution of major infrastructure projects.

He described his deputy as a dependable partner who was involved in the technical discussions, planning and negotiations behind government projects.

Sanwo-Olu’s strongest argument for Hamzat’s candidacy was built around the metaphor of a relay race.

He described Lagos governance as a continuous journey in which successive administrations must prepare to receive the baton before the outgoing government completes its tenure.

According to him, President Bola Tinubu ran the first leg, passing the baton to Fashola in 2007. Fashola handed it to Akinwunmi Ambode in 2015, while Sanwo-Olu received it in 2019.

Hamzat, he argued, had been running alongside the administration since 2019 and was therefore well positioned to continue the journey.

“Lagosians have never before been offered a man who ran this long, this close, beside the governor he hopes to succeed,” he said.

The governor also recalled Hamzat’s earlier service as Commissioner for Science and Technology under Tinubu and Commissioner for Works and Infrastructure under Fashola.

He argued that these experiences gave the APC candidate an understanding of the state’s administrative machinery and development priorities.

Acknowledging criticism that Lagos had consistently produced governors from within the same political establishment, Sanwo-Olu defended the state’s succession model.

“Lagos trains its people. There is a difference,” he said.

He maintained that continuity was necessary to complete major projects, including the Fourth Mainland Bridge, the proposed Lekki-Epe International Airport and ongoing rail expansions.

But he was careful to distinguish continuity from complacency.

“Continuity does not mean repeating ourselves. It means finishing what was started, fixing what is not working, and starting what comes next, in that order, with a plan,” he declared.

In an emotional reflection on the approaching transition, Sanwo-Olu said his greatest achievement might be Lagos changing governors without a political quarrel.

“Lagos is going to change governors without a quarrel,” he said.

His endorsement effectively presented Hamzat’s candidacy as an opportunity to consolidate the political and developmental tradition established by successive administrations.

The Test Beyond the Manifesto

For all its ambition, the ultimate significance of Hamzat’s manifesto will not be determined by the grandeur of its presentation or the applause that greeted its unveiling. It will be measured by implementation.

Increasing the bus fleet to 4,000, extending potable water to six million additional residents, expanding health insurance, constructing hospitals and improving affordable housing will require substantial financial resources, administrative discipline and effective coordination.

The proposed single-digit mortgage arrangement will depend on sustainable financing structures, while the expansion of public transportation will require efficient maintenance and integration of road, rail and water networks.

The proposed State Wealth Fund will equally require transparent governance and safeguards against political interference.

More importantly, the promised accountability framework will only be meaningful if the government is prepared to publish unfavourable performance assessments when it falls short of its commitments.

For ordinary Lagosians, the real test will be whether commuting becomes easier, healthcare more accessible, public schools more effective, businesses face fewer obstacles and children enjoy greater protection.

The trader at Alaba, the artisan in Ebute Metta, the commuter travelling from Badagry to Lagos Island, the office worker commuting daily from Berger to Tafawa Balewa Square (TBS), and the family struggling to secure affordable accommodation will ultimately judge the proposed administration by the difference it makes to their everyday lives.

As the October 30 gathering drew to a close, Hamzat’s message was unmistakable: public service must be anchored on respect, work and truth, while political promises must carry the weight of obligation.

His personal journey, administrative experience and Sanwo-Olu’s endorsement formed the foundation of the argument for continuity. But the electorate will have the final say..

The manifesto has placed an ambitious development blueprint before Lagosians and offered a proposed mechanism through which they can monitor its implementation.

Whether those promises become measurable achievements will depend on the electoral process and, ultimately, the performance of the next administration.

For Hamzat, the challenge is to prove that the promise presented at the historic Wole Soyinka Centre can withstand the demands of governing one of Africa’s most complex megacities.

Lagos has heard the promise. The next test is delivery.

World.title: The eye-watering price of a private Table Mountain cable car ride
World.content:
Table Mountain visitors can hire an entire cable car for a private trip up the mountain. Image: canva

Ever wondered what it would cost to have a Table Mountain cable car all to yourself?

The Table Mountain Aerial Cableway Company (TMACC) offers an exclusive private service for visitors looking for a more special way to experience one of Cape Town’s biggest attractions.

The package is available to local and international visitors and can accommodate private groups, special occasions, weddings and functions.



SO, how much does a private Table Mountain cable car cost?

The private experience starts with visitors being fast-tracked past the usual queues.

A member of the Cableway team personally escorts the group to its private cable car, which is reserved exclusively for their return journey.

Guests can then enjoy the ride up the mountain, taking in the panoramic views along the way.



The service is designed to offer an additional level of privacy and social distancing, making it an option for private groups and special events.

According to the Cableway Company, the exclusive-use cable car package costs an eye-watering R78 000.

This price is valid from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 and covers a private cable car for up to 60 visitors.



The service will not be available during TMACC’s busy season from 16 December 2026 to 7 January 2027, however.

Private cable car tickets can be purchased online through Webtickets.

How much do normal Table Mountain cable car tickets cost?

For comparison, standard daily tickets are considerably cheaper than hiring a private cable car.



According to the Cableway’s listed prices, an adult return ticket costs R475, while a child return ticket (aged four to 17) costs R230. South African pensioners pay R130 for a return ticket.

Visitors can also buy one-way tickets:

Adult: R300 for a single trip up or down

R300 for a single trip up or down Child: R165 for a single trip up or down

R165 for a single trip up or down South African pensioner: R70 for a single trip up or down

World.title: Pitso Mosimane names final Bafana squad to face Kenya
World.content:
Bafana Bafana head coach Pitso Mosimane has announced his final squad for the upcoming 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers against Kenya.

South Africa will face Kenya twice in the space of four days, with the first encounter scheduled for Friday, 13 November, at Orlando Stadium before travelling away for the return fixture on Tuesday, 17 November.

Bafana have made a perfect start to their qualifying campaign, collecting six points from their opening two matches against Guinea and Eritrea.



They currently sit at the top of their group and will be looking to strengthen their position with back-to-back victories over Kenya.

One of the talking points from Mosimane’s Bafana squad announcement was the inclusion of Siyanda Ndlovu.

The Bafana coach explained that Ndlovu’s selection is part of the national team’s long-term vision, stressing the importance of recognising and encouraging players who have made significant contributions.

“We acknowledge what your contributions are. We need to encourage him. We are not saying you are going to be part of the team. We have a Vision 2030,” Mosimane explained.

World.content:
Bafana Bafana’s Afcon 2027 dream continues against Kenya on 13 and 17 November. Pitso Mosimane‘s side travel to the East African nation on Friday 13 November.

The return leg will grace the Orlando Amstel Arena on Tuesday 17 November. Both games will kick-off at 18:00.

SOUTH AFRICA START WELL

Pitso Mosimane has enjoyed an ideal start. Under Mosimane, Bafana Bafana’s AFCON 2027 qualifiers began with two straight wins. A 2-1 victory over Guinea and the 5-0 bashing of Eritrea.



The 1996 champions top the group with six points, while Guinea lurk in second spot with three points. With Kenya to qualify as hosts, only the group winner will book a spot at Afcon 2027.

The 2027 Africa Cup of Nations will make history from June 19 to July 17, 2027, as it is jointly hosted by Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. This 36th edition marks the tournament’s historic return to East Africa for the first time since 1976. The competition will maintain its competitive 24-team format, bringing the finest squads on the continent together for a month of elite football.

The qualification race is already intense across 12 groups, with the final lineup set to be decided by late March 2027.

World.title: Orlando Pirates reward two players
World.content:
Orlando Pirates team vs Kruger United in the Betway Premiership. Image: Orlando Pirates

Orlando Pirates have celebrated their bright start to the season by honouring two of the best contributors. The Sea Robbers have named Ghampani Lungu and Thapelo Mokobodi as the latest winners.

GAMPHANI LUNGU MAKES IMMEDIATE PIRATES IMPACT

Zambian star Ghampani Lungu has been awarded the August award, thanks to his immediate impact following his arrival from Siwelele FC.

Lungu sparked Orlando Pirates’ attack during August, the Zambian international played no less than six times, which taliied to close to 400 minutes. He directly contributed to four goals, scoring three times and providing one assist, while creating eight scoring opportunities for his teammates.



One of Lungu’s standout moments came in the MTN8 quarterfinals against Durban City, where he produced a dramatic 91st-minute extra-time volley.

The strike secured the Suzuki Goal of the Month award and further underlined his early influence at the Soweto giants.

THAPELO MOKOBODI TAKES CONTROL OF PIRATES MIDFIELD

Mokobodi, who signed from Stellenbosch FC, has scooped the September honour for his influence in the middle of the park.

The Johannesburg-born star has moved like the best signing of the season so far. The 23-year-old has adapted quickly to Ouaddou’s tactical demands, showcasing his vision, composure and work rate.

Mokobodi played a crucial role in the Buccaneers’ domestic campaign, helping dictate the tempo and maintain their pursuit of silverware.

He also made his mark in the MTN8, opening the scoring in a decisive 3-0 victory over Sekhukhune United in the semi-finals.



Later in September, he delivered a Man of the Match performance against Marumo Gallants, providing two assists.

The midfielder’s tactical flexibility and control have made him an important figure in the Pirates setup, with the September award recognising his growing influence.

With Lungu and Mokobodi collecting the monthly honours, Orlando Pirates will be hoping the duo can sustain their impressive form as the season gathers momentum.

World.title: There’s a new face in latest Bafana Bafana squad
World.content:
Siyanda Ndlovu gets his first Bafana Bafana call-up. Image: @Masandawana/X

Bafana Bafana coach Pitso Mosimane has named his 27-man squad for the two Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers against Kenya.

South Africa will host Kenya at Orlando Stadium on Friday, 13 November before visiting the same opponents on Tuesday, 17 November.

Should Bafana Bafana collect six points in those two matches, they would have all but secured their place in next year’s AFCON in East Africa.



Now, Mosimane has trimmed the team to just 27 from the preliminary squad he announced two weeks ago.

BAFANA BAFANA have a new face in Siyanda NDLOVU

Mosimane has kept the core of the team that he previously selected for his first three matches in charges of Bafana Bafana.

He has, however, brought back Mbekezeli Mbokazi to tighten that defence after months on the sidelines due to a thigh injury.



Mbokazi’s return meant one central defender had to be sacrificed, and it is none other Orlando Pirates captain Nkosinathi Sibisi.

Furthermore, Mosimane has roped in Mamelodi Sundowns winger Siyanda Ndlovu who earns his first Bafana Bafana call-up.

Ndlovu had been knocking on the Bafana Bafana door since his days at Golden Arrows but it is at Sundowns where he has really been flourishing.



And Mosimane could not overlook him give how he has performed since joining the Brazilians at the start of the season.

The 23-year-old speedy attacker has scored three goals and provided three assists in 15 matches across all competitions for Sundowns.
