World.title: SASSA announces ALL payment dates for December 2026
World.content:
The South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) has confirmed the social grant payment dates for December 2026. Payments return to the regular schedule after November’s once-off adjustment.

In a media statement issued on 28 October 2026, SASSA said the payment dates for December 2026 through to March 2027 “will remain as initially announced.”

SASSA will pay grants on the following dates:



Older Persons Grants: Wednesday, 2 December 2026

Disability Grants: Thursday, 3 December 2026

Children’s Grants: Friday, 4 December 2026

The agency reminded grant recipients that the special November dates were necessary because of the Local Government Elections. Under that arrangement, SASSA paid Older Persons Grants on 30 October, Disability Grants on 2 November and Children’s Grants on 3 November.

SASSA said “these adjustments apply only to November 2026 and should not be interpreted as a permanent change to the social grant payment schedule.”

Because December payments arrive early in the month, grant recipients face a longer wait over the festive season. The January 2027 payment cycle begins on 5 January with Older Persons Grants, followed by Disability Grants on 6 January and Children’s Grants on 7 January.



HOW MUCH GRANT RECIPIENTS WILL RECEIVE

Grant amounts remain at the levels that took effect in April 2026, following the Minister of Finance’s Budget Speech:

Older Persons, Disability and Care Dependency Grants: R2 400

War Veterans Grant: R2 420

Foster Child Grant: R1 290

Child Support Grant and Grant-in-Aid: R580

SASSA urged grant recipients who do not receive their money on the specified dates to visit their nearest SASSA local office for assistance.

SASSA WARNS AGAINST IGNORING REVIEW NOTICES

SASSA also called on grant recipients who receive review notifications not to ignore them. The agency said failure to respond to a review notice may result in the suspension of grant payments.



Grant recipients can check whether their grants are under review by sending “Hi” on WhatsApp to 082 601 0111. The service also offers eLife Certification and grant applications.

SASSA further reminded grant recipients to update their details whenever their circumstances change, including their marital status, financial situation, address and cellphone number. The agency warned that outdated contact details could cause people to miss important notifications.

SASSA urged South Africans to rely only on official SASSA channels for payment information and to avoid unverified messages about changes to payment dates.



Win R2 000 in the South African SASSA grant survey

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: Yellow Level 4 warning issued for severe storms in Gauteng and Mpumalanga
World.content:
Severe thunderstorms could bring flooding, hail and strong winds to Gauteng and Mpumalanga. Image: Unsplash

SAWS has issued a Yellow Level 4 warning for severe thunderstorms in Gauteng and Mpumalanga.

The warning stated that the storms could bring heavy rain, hail and strong winds, raising the risk of flooding and damage to property.

The South African Weather Service (SAWS) has issued a Yellow Level 4 warning, cautioning that the storms could also disrupt electricity supply and communications in affected areas.



Which other areas are affected?

The warning covers Gauteng and the Mpumalanga Highveld, as well as central and southern parts of Limpopo.

The eastern parts of the Free State and North West, and KwaZulu-Natal, except the extreme north-eastern parts of the province.

According to SAWS, the thunderstorms could produce large amounts of small hail and strong winds.

lncreasing the risk of damage to settlements and property.

The combination of heavy rainfall and thunderstorms could also leave some roads flooded, particularly in areas where drainage systems struggle to cope with sudden downpours.

Residents in low-lying areas should also remain alert to possible flooding.



Strong winds could bring additional problems, including damage to structures and localised interruptions to power supplies and communication networks.

What to watch out for amid severe thunderstorms

Severe thunderstorms can develop quickly, leaving people with little time to react.

Residents should avoid seeking shelter under trees, stay away from windows during intense storms and unplug sensitive electrical appliances where possible.

SAWS advises residents to remain alert to changing weather conditions and follow updates from the weather service and local authorities.

World.title: DA confident MK Party will not secure majority in eThekwini
World.content:
Democratic Alliance (DA) mayoral candidate for eThekwini, Haniff Hoosen, says he is confident that the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party will not secure a 50% majority in the metro.

Hoosen made the remarks at the KwaZulu-Natal Results Operations Centre (ROC) at the Durban International Convention Centre (ICC) as election results began trickling in. So far, the MK Party has taken an early lead in many KwaZulu-Natal municipalities.

DA CONFIDENT MK PARTY WILL NOT SECURE MAJORITY IN ETHEKWINI

Speaking to journalists at the KZN ROC, Hoosen said he was confident that the MK Party would not secure a majority in the hotly contested municipality.



He attributed this to voter turnout and support for the DA’s efforts to prevent the MK Party from taking control of eThekwini.

“I think we’re going to get closer to that picture and I’m really grateful for the support and the turnout in eThekwini,” he said.

“We mustn’t forget that the polls placed the MK Party at 55% majority and the party itself said it would get a two-thirds majority and we succeeded in ensuring that this does not happen.

“I think that’s a great relief for many people in eThekwini. I am absolutely confident that the DA is going to grow and we already got results from a number of wards that we’ve never won before, several of them were ANC wards previously which we were able to now win.

“And I think what is evident in this election thus far is that thousands of people voted for the DA for the very first time and that gives us comfort that we are definitely growing,” he said.

World.title: Elderly voter dies after collapsing at KZN voting station
World.content:
DURBAN - An elderly voter in Shallcross, Ward 72, reportedly collapsed while waiting in the voting queue on Wednesday.

The voter was rushed to hospital but later died.

KwaZulu-Natal IEC Provincial Electoral Officer Ntombifuthi Masinga conveyed her condolences to the voter’s family on Thursday.

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo announces international retirement
World.content:
LISBON - Portuguese football legend Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday that he was retiring from international football.

The 41-year-old, who has played 234 times for Portugal and scored 146 goals, fell out with national coach Jorge Jesus last month after he refused to use him in a Nations League match. Ronaldo immediately left the team camp.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team," Ronaldo said in a video on his Instagram account.

"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world," he continued.

World.title: IEC: 15.9 million voters participated in 2026 elections
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - An estimated 15.9 million voters participated in South Africa’s 2026 local government elections, almost four million more than in the 2021 polls.

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) released the figure in its latest results update.

About 15.9 million of the country’s 29.2 million registered voters cast their ballots, translating into an estimated voter turnout of 54.5%.

World.title: IEC gives parties until Friday to lodge objections
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Political parties have until 5pm on Friday to lodge objections with the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC).

The deadline comes as the Commission deals with more than 800 complaints from political contestants, most relating to allegations that party agents were prevented from observing voting and counting processes.

The IEC says final election results will only be announced once all objections have been considered and disputes resolved.

IEC Deputy CEO Masego Sheburi says most complaints relate to allegations that party agents were prevented from observing voting and counting processes.

Sheburi says the majority of these complaints have been resolved, with approximately 106 still outstanding as of Thursday evening.

He clarified that contestants have a separate opportunity to raise objections that could have a material impact on the declared results.

Sheburi says the IEC will only be able to indicate when it plans to announce the final results once these objections have been considered.

The Commission estimates that 15.9 million South Africans participated in the elections, including those who cast special votes.

World.title: Mokwana joins Chiefs on a free transfer
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Kaizer Chiefs have completed the signing of Bafana Bafana international Elias Mokwana.

The former Sekhukhune United player returns to the country after a spell with North African giants Esperance de Tunis.

After making a name for himself with Babina Noko, Mokwana joined Esperance in 2024.

The 27-year-old won the Tunisian Super Cup in his maiden season and also represented Esperance at the 2025 FIFA Club World Cup.

He spent the 2025/26 campaign on loan at Al Hazem, featuring 24 times in the Saudi Pro League.

Mokwana made his Bafana debut against Andorra two years ago.

World.title: Google turns off AI for schoolchildren by default
World.content:
WASHINGTON - Google has said it will switch off its AI tools for schoolchildren by default, after drawing criticism for pushing artificial intelligence features to students while schools are still debating how the technology should be used in classrooms.

The search engine juggernaut dominates technology in American schools. Its education apps, including Gmail, Docs and the Classroom platform, are used in classrooms across the country, and its low-cost Chromebook laptops are the devices US schools most often issue to students.

Under the changes Google announced in a blog post on Tuesday, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Search will be turned off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators switch them on.

Google told AFP the new controls would be rolled out worldwide, beginning in the United States, but that it had not yet set a date.

The changes also mean schools will not be able to give students Google Search without its AI features.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, told The New York Times that "Search and A.I. are deeply integrated," as AI features are now built into the company's search engine.

If a school bans AI, he said, students "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google on X of "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."

"No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children," he wrote.

More than 150 million students worldwide use Google Classroom, according to a letter Senators Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley sent to the company last month asking why AI features had been made the default on school devices.

In August, Google opened its Gemini chatbot in Classroom to students of all ages.

Students were shown starter prompts tied to their specific class and assignment, offering guided help or study guides, practice quizzes and flashcards built from their course materials.

The feature was switched on by default for students at schools that had already enabled Gemini.

New York and Los Angeles both announced plans in September to restrict access to AI tools on school devices.

"We are reviewing Google's announcement and its potential implications for schools, educators and students," a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Unified School District told AFP.

The spokesperson said the district believes AI can improve teaching and learning if it is introduced carefully and with clear safeguards, and pointed to district principles requiring that technology support rather than replace teachers and protect student privacy.

New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) are seeking more details from Google about the policy change, but the Gemini chatbot and AI mode are already disabled on Chromebooks used by students in NYC, a spokesperson for the district told AFP.

"NYCPS has also made requests to Google to disable the AI Overview displayed in the Google search result for students," the spokesperson said.

In a statement on X, Google said Tuesday's changes give "schools more choice, not less."

"We know there's concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control," Google said.

World.title: 'Dragon Ball Z' composer elected to Texas attorney general
World.content:
DALLAS - Long before Texas Democrat Nathan Johnson was elected to be the state's attorney general, he was a composer for the music on the acclaimed anime series "Dragon Ball Z."

Johnson won the majority of votes in nearly all of the southern state's border districts and major cities in his race against Republican Mayes Middleton to become the Lone Star State's top prosecutor.

"If you grew up watching 'Dragon Ball Z,' you might know me better than you think: I composed the musical scores for 67 episodes and five movies and had a great time doing it," the 58-year-old posted to Facebook.

The popular, long-running Japanese anime follows martial artists as they defend Earth from space invaders, monsters and more.

"I had a one-year-old at the time, and I remember him sitting on my knee and stuff blowing up. He was like 'Oh, Daddy, Goku!'" Johnson said, naming the show's lead character, in the video he posted.

"He just thought it was super cool."

World.title: eNCA Election Projection | DA might take Ekurhuleni
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Democratic Alliance is projected to win the Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Municipality, according to eNCA's MarkData election projection.

Ekurhuleni has historically been an ANC stronghold. However, the projection suggests the party's support could fall from 38% to about 22% in this local government election.

This decline is not driven by significant growth in DA support, but rather by the rising support of ActionSA.

According to the data, the DA's support in the municipality has remained relatively steady, with the party expected to secure about 29% of the vote.

World.title: Death rumours made me stronger, says ODM leader Oburu
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Speakers Moses Wetang’ula and Amason Kingi when they paid a visit to ODM leader Oburu Oginga at his Nairobi residence on November 4, 2026. [Speaker’s Press Unit]

ODM leader and Siaya Senator Oburu Oginga has said rumours about his death while he was admitted to hospital only strengthened his determination to overcome his illness.

Dr Oburu who is recovering after being discharged from hospital, assured his supporters that he was making remarkable improvement and would return to active politics soon.

Speaking at his Nairobi residence on Wednesday when Speakers Moses Wetang’ula and Amason Kingi paid him a visit, the ODM leader said the rumours only strengthened his resolve to come out of the hospital bed.

“Those who wrote me off while I was in hospital by declaring me dead only made me stronger and more determined to fight my sickness. Here I am, recovering and growing stronger by the day,” he said.

He said that his recovery was a testimony to God's protection, saying those who had spread the false reports had been put to shame.

Oburu admitted that the illness had slowed down him down but he was looking forward to returning to the political arena.

“The sickness slowed my political activities. Very soon, I will be back roaring in the best way I know how,” he said.

The senator thanked the National Assembly Speaker Wetang’ula, his Senate counterpart Kingi and other legislators for taking time to visit him following his discharge from hospital.

He said the visit had lifted his spirit and revealed that he missed participating in parliamentary debates and engaging in national political affairs.

“I have no words to explain my feelings after the Speakers of both Houses and fellow legislators created time to come and check on me,” he said.

“I miss being on the floor of the House debating and roaring in the political arena. I urge my supporters to pray for me and be patient because soon I will be back,” he added.

Despite his recent health challenges, Oburu kept his visitors entertained with his trademark humour while expressing confidence that he would soon resume his political duties.

The two Speakers condemned the spread of false information on social media, particularly rumours that the senator had died while undergoing treatment.

Wetang’ula said they were encouraged by the senator's recovery and wished him a full and speedy return to good health.

He, however, cautioned Oburu against rushing back into politics before fully recovering, urging him to give his health priority.

“Prioritise your health and avoid rushing back into political engagements before making a full recovery,” he said.

The National Assembly Speaker also praised the senator for his courage and determination in facing his health challenges.

Kingi said the Senate missed Dr Oburu's contribution to debates, parliamentary proceedings and national politics.

“As the Senate, we miss your contributions to proceedings and debates as well as your guidance in national politics. We pray that you get better and resume your political duties as soon as possible,” he said.

Those who accompanied the two Speakers included Senate Chief Whip David Wakoli, Senate Minority Leader Stewart Madzayo, Senators William Kisang and Daniel Maanzo.

Others were National Assembly Minority Whip Millie Odhiambo, Parliamentary Commissioner Mishi Mboko and MP Eve Obara.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses Uhuru reconciliation calls, says 'we are one team'
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua received at PCEA Kamangu in Kikuyu constituency by former Kiambu governor James Nyoro on November 1, 2026. [George Njunge, Standard]

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed calls for mediation between him and former President Uhuru Kenyatta, insisting that the two leaders remain in contact and have no differences requiring reconciliation.

Gachagua said attempts by Mount Kenya elders to broker peace between them were unnecessary, maintaining that he and the former Head of State continue to communicate, meet and share meals despite perceptions of a political fallout.

He challenged elders calling for reconciliation to instead focus on uniting the Mount Kenya community, warning that internal divisions could weaken the region's political voice and influence.

“On unity, as a community we have to remain united. Our unity is strength. Nimeona some elders in the newspaper wakisema tunataka to reconcile Rigathi Gachagua and Uhuru Kenyatta. How do you reconcile two brothers, who love one another and work together?” he posed.

The former Deputy President maintained that he and Uhuru were still on the same team, dismissing claims that their relationship had deteriorated to a point requiring third-party intervention.

“President Uhuru Kenyatta and I are one team. We work together. Please elders don’t reconcile us because there is no need for reconciliation. We are working together. There is no work there, we are one. We talk the same language, we meet, talk, we agree,” he said.

Gachagua further urged Mount Kenya elders to resist attempts to divide the community along political lines and instead promote dialogue and cohesion among its leaders.

“Our unity is our strength as a community. Please help me to unite Mount Kenya elders and tell people not to accept to be divided,” he added.

His remarks come amid growing calls by sections of Mount Kenya elders for reconciliation among influential political figures from the region following political differences that have emerged since the 2022 General Election.

Uhuru, who served as Kenya's fourth president from 2013 to 2022, remains an influential political figure in the region, while Gachagua has continued to position himself as a key voice in Mount Kenya politics.

World.title: Not so fast! Court blocks Bomas expansion
World.content:
Contractors hired are barred from clearing vegetation, cutting trees, excavating, grading, fencing, constructing routes, and undertaking any works at the disputed site. [File, Standard]

The Environment and Lands Court has blocked the government from continuing with the construction of a car park inside the Nairobi National Park.

Justice Grace Kemei, in her ruling, said that the contractors hired are barred from clearing vegetation, cutting trees, excavating, grading, fencing, constructing routes, and undertaking any works at the disputed site.

World.title: Kikuyu PCEA church loses 2.7-acre illegally acquired land
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Justice Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent. [Courtesy, EACC]

The Presbyterian Church of East Africa (PCEA) has lost its 2.7-acre piece of land to a school.

This is after the Environment and Lands Court at Thika established that the land under the church's Ruguthi Women's Guild was a school playground and was illegally allocated.

Presiding Judge Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property, and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent.

According to her, the land had been reserved for use as a playground by Kanyiha, Lusigetti and Njumbi Primary Schools.

The verdict follows a case filed by the Law Society of Kenya, with the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) participating as an interested party.

In a statement on Monday, EACC's head of Corporate Affairs and Communication Stephen Karuga said the anti-graft agency presented evidence demonstrating that the land had been reserved for public use and therefore, any allocation to third parties was irregular. Justice Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent. [Courtesy, EACC]

"Our investigations established that the land was set aside in 1957 by the former County Council of Kiambu for use as a school playing field," Karuga said, adding, "the investigations further revealed that there was no letter of offer or acceptance, no evidence of payment of rent rates and no proof that the Women's Guild had paid any consideration to the council for the land."

According to Karuga, the judgement safeguards a vital public facility used by more than 1,300 pupils, ensuring that the playground remains available for learning, sports and recreation for the current and future generations.

As a result, the judge said the allocation, transfer and registration of the land LR. NO KARAI/350 and subsequent issuance of a title deed in 2001 was unprocedural, illegal, null and void.

"An order of Mandamus is hereby issued directing the 3rd respondent, the Land Registrar, Kiambu Chief Land Registrar, to forthwith cancel and revoke the Title Deed and all register entries in respect of the land issued to the 1st respondent on Dec 6, 2001, or at any subsequent date," the Judge said.

The judge further ordered that the said parcel of land be handed over to the Board of Management of the two schools and the Education Ministry.

"An order of permanent injunction is hereby issued restraining the 1st respondent, whether by herself, her church officials, agents, servants, assigns or anyone claiming through her, from entering into, taking possession of, fencing, depositing construction materials upon, transferring, charging, developing or in any other manner dealing or interfering with the land," she ordered.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Zain Hisham wins second gold as Egypt’s Dakar 2026 medal tally reaches four
World.content:
Egyptian swimmer Zain Hisham won his second gold medal at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, after taking first place in the men’s 50m butterfly. Hisham had previously won gold in the 100m butterfly, becoming Egypt’s first double gold medallist at the Games.

His latest victory brought Egypt’s medal tally to four, including three golds and one bronze.

Sondos Sonbol won Egypt’s third gold in the women’s wushu gunshu event, while Ali El-Ramly secured bronze in the men’s 81kg judo competition.

Egypt is participating in the Games with 45 athletes competing in 19 sports, under the supervision of Egyptian Olympic Committee President Yasser Idris.

World.title: Egypt expands hydraulic fracturing, horizontal drilling to boost petroleum, gas output
World.content:
Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi said Egypt is expanding the use of hydraulic fracturing and horizontal drilling as key technologies in the petroleum sector’s five-year plan.

During an inspection of hydraulic fracturing operations at the H-18 well in the Western Desert’s Al Abyad field, operated by the Badr Eldin Petroleum Company (BAPETCO), Badawi said the initiative aims to increase production from existing wells, revive declining wells, and access resources that cannot be economically developed using conventional methods.

Operations at the H-18 well aim to raise its daily gas production from 3 million to approximately 12 million cubic feet using multi-stage hydraulic fracturing.

The minister noted that these technologies have delivered successful results internationally, particularly in the United States and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Egypt’s Western Desert.

He added that the ministry is working with international companies to develop investment incentives and economic models to encourage wider adoption.

A preliminary study by oilfield services company NESR suggests that expanding hydraulic fracturing in the Western Desert could add between 50,000 and 100,000 barrels per day to Egypt’s oil production. However, this potential remains subject to further technical and economic assessments.

Meanwhile, 15 horizontal wells have been drilled in the General Petroleum Company’s Sinai fields, with four more currently underway.

Petrobel has also successfully drilled the SIDRI-48 horizontal well, while plans include drilling two additional horizontal wells in the Nes field.

The Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation is coordinating the initiative, reviewing technical data from 38 production companies to identify suitable wells and reservoirs and prioritize projects based on economic feasibility.

The ministry has also commissioned SLB and Halliburton to assess three opportunities in Abu Rawash reservoirs.

Initial study results are expected gradually during the third quarter of the 2026/2027 fiscal year.

World.title: Egypt, US sign first-ever strategic objective agreement
World.content:
CAIRO, Nov 4 (MENA) – Egypt and the US signed first-ever bilateral Strategic Objective Agreement, on Wednesday, to expand economic cooperation in energy, water management, infrastructure, technology and other development sectors.

Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty attended the signing ceremony alongside the ministers of finance, supply and internal trade, and higher education and scientific research.

The Strategic Objectives Framework Agreement was signed by Deputy Foreign Minister for International Cooperation Samar al-Ahdal and US Embassy Chargé d’Affaires Robert Silverman.

The agreement commits $125 million in US funding to expand opportunities for American companies in Egypt and drive private-sector growth in both countries.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Nader Zaki said that the agreement aims to support economic growth, create jobs and improve public services in Egypt through cooperation with the United States.

It includes the use of American technology to develop water and energy systems, infrastructure, education, healthcare and government services.

The agreement also covers cooperation in artificial intelligence and food security, including the use of modern agricultural methods to improve food production. (MENA)

World.title: Egypt, Syria discuss boosting media cooperation
World.content:
Minister of State for Media Diaa Rashwan praised the longstanding historical ties between the Egyptian and Syrian peoples, expressing Egypt’s readiness to strengthen media cooperation with Syria. Rashwan made the remarks during a meeting on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, with Syrian Information Minister Khaled Zaarour, held at the headquarters of the Arab League in Cairo on the sidelines of the 56th session of the Council of Arab Information Ministers.

During the meeting, Rashwan outlined the support provided by Egypt’s political leadership to the media sector to develop its capabilities and enhance its reach and influence both domestically and internationally.

He also explained the role and responsibilities of the Ministry of State for Information in coordinating with all components of the press and media system to advance the sector’s development, while supporting media institutions and their employees in keeping pace with modern developments in media sciences and applications.

For his part, the Syrian information minister praised the standing of Egyptian media, citing its long history and considerable capabilities. He also commended its role in supporting Arab causes and its coverage of current developments in Syria, which is seeking stability, development and cooperation with all Arab countries.

Zaarour also praised Egypt’s comprehensive progress across various sectors, noting that he had visited the New Capital and its major landmarks, which he said had been built in a remarkably short time to high standards in keeping with modern developments.

He described the city as a model of advanced urban development that could offer valuable lessons to countries seeking progress and modernization.

The Syrian minister also thanked Egypt’s leadership and people for hosting Syrian nationals and providing them with opportunities.

World.title: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
World.content:
The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country’s borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of American foreign policy, unsettling allies and adversaries alike. Now, both are watching to see how an electoral setback at home will shape his actions abroad.

For Iran, Israel and Ukraine, the stakes go well beyond who controls Congress. The result could influence whether Trump pursues a deal with Tehran or more war, how much Washington’s longstanding support for Israel erodes, and how hard he pushes Kyiv to accept terms to end Russia’s war.

Democrats will have new tools to challenge Trump. But he still has considerable freedom to act abroad, leaving world leaders with a question: Will defeat make him more willing to compromise, or more determined to get his way?

Here’s how the vote could impact Washington’s most pressing foreign policy concerns:

Iran gloats, but gets no guarantee of peace

Iran is celebrating Trump’s midterm setback, but it is bracing for what comes next: a possible new US strike or a fresh push for a deal.

Trump admitted in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”

After eight months of striking the region’s economic lifelines to turn American voters against the war, Tehran has hailed the Republican loss as a public verdict on it. Trump acknowledged that war-driven price hikes played a role.

“If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led negotiations with the US, wrote on X.

Demonstrators march through central Tehran toward the former US Embassy during a rally marking the 47th anniversary of the 1979 embassy takeover and hostage crisis on Wednesday. Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu/Getty Images

Tehran is not betting on a change of course in Washington. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone who believes the results will shift US policy is “deeply mistaken,” and officials say Iran’s strategy doesn’t hinge on American elections as they prepare for more war while intensifying diplomacy.

The risk of escalation is real. Reports that Trump might order new, more intense strikes are fueling anxiety across the region, and Tehran has warned that its retaliation would be much wider in scope than in earlier rounds. This week, Trump told some journalists he is considering striking Iran hard, and others that he has no immediate plans to escalate.

“The Iran war has become a political albatross around his neck, leaving (Trump) with a stark choice: cut a face-saving deal and declare victory, or double down militarily to reclaim the initiative,” Ali Vaez of International Crisis Group told CNN. “The danger is that a president weakened at the ballot box may seek redemption on the battlefield.”

Diplomacy offers another path. Talks that stagnated over the summer have picked up in the past week, with Tehran sending officials to Qatari mediators who are circulating proposals with Washington. Before the vote, Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Trump agreed to its seven conditions.

Sanam Vakil of Chatham House said Iran’s leadership “might feel vindicated,” but that “does not necessarily solve their problems.” Trump needs a diplomatic victory yet may be reluctant to appear weak, she said, while Tehran could read his setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. She expects intensified diplomacy alongside military threats, with an interim Strait of Hormuz deal “more realistic” than a comprehensive one.

‘End of an era’ for US-Israel relations

Trump looks on as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during a dinner in the Blue Room of the White House on July 7, 2025. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

In Israel, the election day announcement that Trump would abruptly cut off US military aid to the country was the first surprise. The results, with Democrats sweeping both chambers of Congress in what has been called a “blue tsunami,” are a five-alarm fire in Israel.

Bipartisan support for Israel in the US had already been eroding, with Democrats outraged at Israel over the death toll in the Gaza war and a growing number of Republicans believing the US has given it too much support.

“The only bipartisan issue right now is criticism of Israel,” said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to the US. “It’s an organizing principle for the Democratic Party,” he told CNN. “And it’s becoming an organizing principle for much of the Republican Party.”

Oren said the end of US aid is just the beginning of a process that has only started to play out. He said it’s conceivable that the US could end intelligence sharing with Israel and the joint development of critical military systems, such as the vaunted Iron Dome aerial defense system. He also pointed to the United Nations Security Council, where Republican and Democratic presidents have protected Israel with the US veto.

“We are at the end of an era,” he said.

Yaakov Katz, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, warned there is more to come. “What Trump announced about the military aid yesterday is just the tip of the iceberg of what can change – arms sales could be blocked, sanctions will be proposed and joint economic programs defunded,” he said on X.

The anti-Israel sentiment only hardened during the Iran war, with segments of the US electorate viewing the joint US-Israel strikes as a war that Netanyahu sold to Trump. Even now, Netanyahu has been pushing to resume strikes on Iran, which would reignite a war that drove gas prices and the cost of living higher and contributed to Republicans’ devastating midterm performance.

Netanyahu also faces turmoil at home. In elections a week before the midterms, he lost his majority in parliament, but his main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, does not have an outright majority and would likely need to cooperate with Arab parties, who saw record turnout.

Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, warned that Israel “does not have time to waste” in replacing Netanyahu and leading the country away from sanctions and isolation.

Ukraine waits for a post-Trump world

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is berated in the Oval Office of the White House by Trump, and Vice President JD Vance during a meeting on February 28, 2025. Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is hoping the the “blue wave” will bolster American support for its defense against Russia’s war.

“I am also grateful to the Republicans, but the Democrats speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine and providing assistance to Ukraine,” Zelensky said in comments provided in German by broadcaster ZDF, ahead of the telecast of the interview, according to Reuters.

“They speak about renewing the connection between the United States and Europe… Therefore, there is hope that a balance of power will emerge and that we will receive more support.”

He added: “If Congress now speaks of strong financial support or military assistance, as Europe is doing and demonstrating today, then that will be something positive that will have an impact on Putin.”

For weeks, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s relationship with Trump has been in freefall. Trump has demanded Zelensky be replaced; courted energy deals to benefit Russia; and watched as Ukraine’s tech and intel dependencies on the US were inexplicably thwarted. And so Kyiv was forced to take a position early: wait, with urgency, for a post-Trump world.

And when it began to dawn on Wednesday, there was little official comment from Kyiv at first, Zelensky perhaps happy for the memes of him, sat with a beer and popcorn in front of the mid-term TV coverage, to do the job for him.

A deputy in his office, Sergiy Kyslytsia, pledged on Ukrainian TV that the country would continue to “develop genuine, normal and stable relations” with whoever is in office, seek Patriot interceptors, and navigate both a new Congress and the likely flurry of executive orders that may try to obviate it.

But there can be no disguising that a crestfallen Trump, and the slow clock now loudly ticking on his worldview and presidency, is in Kyiv’s favour. He had claimed a peace was easy to fashion, yet proceeded to punish Ukraine for not agreeing to the demands of its invader. He humiliated, scolded, and then occasionally made up with, Zelensky, while massaged by European allies, aghast at the breakdown in decades of security alliances.

There is still a lot that Ukraine needs Trump and the United States to do. Provide arms, money, and a wider assurance it is on their side. But Kyiv has calculated it cannot depend on Washington, after months of hostility.

There is one downside of the ticking clock however: that Russian President Vladimir Putin determines he has likely a year to pursue, at any cost, the best outcome possible in his war of choice, before the 2028 fight drags Republican policy back to the pro-Ukrainian mainstream. Putin has so far failed to use his apparent great ally, Trump, to secure a battlefield win of note. He may seek to change that while the embers of Trump’s authority burn.

World.title: Melania Trump to bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to White House this week
World.content:
First lady Melania Trump will bring representatives from Russia and Ukraine to the White House on Thursday, after announcing a ceasefire in the city of Oleshky last month.

“First lady Melania Trump will personally bring representatives of Russia and Ukraine, two nations actively at war, together at the White House,” the first lady’s office said on Tuesday, touting the limited ceasefire as an “unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American first lady.”

Trump will host Ukraine’s ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, according to Ukrainian and Russian authorities.

Lubinets and Lantratova have met before, most recently during the Oleshky ceasefire last week. Neither has been involved in top-level negotiations with the US delegations before, but they are expected to be accompanied by officials who have.

The Kremlin announced on Wednesday that Lantratova would be accompanied by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who is an experienced negotiator. Ukrainian media reported that the lawmaker and negotiator David Arakhamia would be joining Lubinets for the meeting.

Speaking to CNN while en route to Washington DC, Dmitriev said that a key motivating factor in his work as an interlocutor was his “deep belief in cooperation between the US and Russia.”

“I’m focused on US-Russia relations in general and if there’s a humanitarian situation to solve, I’m always trying to help,” he said.

Most recently, Marc Beckman, senior adviser to the first lady, thanked Dmitriev for his “leadership in establishing and sustaining the ceasefire in Oleshky.” Last month, US special envoy Steve Witkoff introduced Dmitriev to the freed US citizen Stephen Hubbard — classified by the US State Department as “wrongfully detained” — saying that Dmitriev “had a lot to do with [the release] happening.”

Trump, who will also deliver remarks on the limited ceasefire, has kept a much lower profile during her husband’s second term. But while she’s eschewed some of the more traditional roles of the job, she’s engaged behind the scenes in more substantive policy work.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Wednesday that he’d awarded the first lady the Order of Princess Olga, a Ukrainian civil decoration. It celebrates her “significant personal contributions” to humanitarian support for Ukraine, and her “active human rights and charitable work aimed at rescuing Ukrainian children and citizens.”

Trump announced on October 23 that she had secured a localized ceasefire to facilitate the humane evacuation of elderly residents from Oleshky. The limited ceasefire began on October 27 and concluded on Sunday. Hundreds of people were evacuated from Oleshky and returned to Ukraine, including one man who hadn’t seen his wife for 1,711 days.

The humanitarian situation had become so dire in Oleshky that some residents were forced to eat grass and weeds without access to medicine, clean water or electricity, Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, said last month.

Trump’s office said that she worked directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership as the “exclusive intermediary” through channels she previously established while working to reunite children separated from their families during the war.

“The mission was a success, delivering critical aid to the region and enabling the evacuation of nearly 800 people,” Trump posted on X, adding that she hoped Oleshky “serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.”

The first lady’s office said last month that the circumstances of Oleshky came to her attention during a private discussion at the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.

CNN previously reported that Pope Leo discussed the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky on a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier in October while in the hospital recovering from lung cancer surgery, according to the Vatican. The Kremlin said that Putin “supported” the Vatican’s intention to help alleviate the conditions.

World.title: Trump said he’d accept the election results. Netanyahu is challenging the outcome of his.
World.content:
Tel Aviv —

As Republican losses in the US midterm elections came into focus, President Donald Trump said he would accept the results. The same cannot be said of Benjamin Netanyahu, the man Trump endorsed in Israel.

A week after Israel’s October 27 election, Netanyahu, whose bloc lost its majority, is still challenging the officially certified results. He and his Likud party allege, without presenting evidence, that the vote was “stolen” by Israel’s Arab parties and foreign actors.

The post-election dispute deepened this week after the David Zini, chief of the Shin Bet internal security service and a Netanyahu loyalist, pushed to investigate the leaders of the Arab parties. The attorney general, a longtime target of Israel’s right-wing, refused to authorize such an investigation without evidence.

“Likud and Netanyahu are trying to commit a pogrom against democracy and the rule of law,” Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, said Tuesday.

One day later, Netanyahu doubled down on his claims of fraud. “There are serious suspicions that foreign countries have been involved, using enormous sums of money, in an attempt to manipulate the results of the elections in the State of Israel,” he said in a video statement.

The official results show Netanyahu’s bloc plummeted from a commanding 68 to 53 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, or parliament. The opposition, led by Eisenkot, holds 67 seats. But nearly a third of those comes from the two Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam, after a historic turnout that secured 19 seats.

The Arab parties’ support is decisive to any effort to replace Netanyahu. That is why undermining their legitimacy has become the focus of Netanyahu’s post-election strategy.

Since the results came in, Netanyahu and his right-wing allies have been propagating claims that the election was “stolen” by the Arab parties through bribery, foreign funding and fraud.

A day after the vote, Likud submitted hundreds of testimonies to the Central Elections Committee demanding investigations and arrests. Over the weekend, Netanayhu shared a video on social media of a right-wing activist claiming massive forgeries and calling to “simply invalidate the elections.” The committee has rejected claims of widespread fraud as baseless, saying there is no evidentiary basis to allege systematic compromise of the vote.

The committee did, however, ask the Shin Bet last week to examine “serious suspicions” of foreign funding intended to influence the campaign. In a letter leaked to Israeli media, committee chair Justice Noam Sohlberg cautioned that he could not verify the seriousness of the material. But Netanyahu’s Likud party treated the letter as a confirmation of the broader fraud narrative.

A general view of a session at the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, before it dissolves ahead of the 2026 Israeli elections, in Jerusalem, July 16. Ronen Zvulun/Reuters

Sohlberg appeared alongside the Shin Bet chief and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to make an unusual joint statement Sunday in which they assured the public that the elections were conducted properly. They said that even if the foreign funding suspicions were substantiated, it wouldn’t overturn the result or undermine the integrity of the process.

But Zini’s subsequent conduct has escalated the controversy. A retired Israel Defense Forces major general who describes himself as a “proud messianic,” Zini was appointed by Netanyahu last year from outside the Shin Bet ranks. He is now reportedly seeking to question four senior Arab political figures, including several party leaders.

The Shin Bet told the committee Wednesday that its intelligence “seemingly” points to “extensive phenomena” of large sums being funneled into Israel from foreign sources “on a scale exceeding thousands of people and possibly even more,” according to a source briefed on the matter. The agency said further investigation was needed before it could point “with a high level of certainty” to the scope. But the Shin Bet presented no public evidence.

In a rare statement Tuesday, the attorney general’s office said Zini had prevented the Shin Bet from passing any pertinent evidence to her office or to the police. “In a state governed by law, citizens or elected officials cannot be investigated without evidence justification,” it said. “Anyone who needs to be questioned will be, but no one will be investigated without evidentiary grounds.”

The Likud party, in response, accused Baharav-Miara of obstructing the investigation. Netanyahu’s far-right ally, Itamar Ben Gvir, called on Zini to arrest and investigate the Arab leaders even without the attorney general’s approval. The clash feeds into an ongoing conflict: Netanyahu’s outgoing government voted to dismiss Baharav-Miara in August 2025, but the Supreme Court blocked the move. Since then, the government has repeatedly challenged and defied her directives.

The Arab parties rejected the allegations, accusing Zini of participating in the Likud’s campaign to delegitimize the Arab public, their votes and their record political representation.

“Netanyahu is clinging to power and trying to deny the legitimacy of the Arab public which voted en masse and decided against his government. Zini, appointed by Netanyahu, is acting as a political arm in his service,” the Joint List said in a statement. Mansour Abbas, chairman of Raam, called the move an “an unacceptable attempt to tarnish the Arab public.”

Palestinian candidate Mansour Abbas, leader of the Raam party, holds his daughter as he votes in Israel’s national election, in Maghar, Israel, on October 27. Rami Shlush/Reuters Palestinian candidate Yousef Jabareen of the Joint List party reacts to exit polls during Israel’s national election, at the party election headquarters in Nazareth, Israel, October 27. Jamal Awad/Reuters

Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief of staff and Yashar Party leader, greets supporters after Israel’s general election on October 28 in Tel Aviv, Israel. Amir Levy/Getty Images

Opposition leaders, who are now making plans to use their Knesset majority to replace the body’s speaker, accuse Netanyahu and Zini of dragging Israel into a constitutional crisis and eroding trust in the election.

Eisenkot called the moment a test for Israel’s future “as a liberal democratic state.” He urged security and law enforcement officials to remember they “are servants of the kingdom, not the king.”

Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid called it an “attempt to crush democracy and steal the elections with the help of regime loyalists planted in the security system.” Yair Golan, chairman of the left-wing Democrats party, said Zini has turned the Shin Bet into “a political tool in service of Netanyahu’s campaign to undermine the election results.”

The political test will come in the weeks ahead. If Netanyahu persuades right-wing parties and potential individual defectors in the opposition that relying on Arab parties is illegitimate, he may block the only path to his ouster. But his tactics could also push the divided opposition to come together and hasten the outcome he is seeking to prevent.

World.title: Vance tosses Trump under the bus in a bid to keep 2028 hope alive
World.content:
Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday surveyed the wreckage of the MAGA coalition and spilled his thoughts in an extraordinary social media post that launched the 2028 presidential campaign.

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, relished what Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called “a day of celebration.” In his half-built White House ballroom, he watched the last beam rise to the roof like a sports team’s championship banner.

This bizarre contrast marked a turning point in the Trump era.

The president seemed unaware or indifferent that his fixation on a vanity project epitomized the apparent disregard for Americans’ cost-of-living pain that doomed the GOP in midterm elections. Oddly, as he chatted with reporters, he didn’t seem crestfallen over his party’s epic defeat. Instead, he seemed liberated — able to fully devote himself to constructing a physical legacy.

“Envision chandeliers all over here soon. Envision marble floor. Oh, it’s going to be beautiful. This will be the most beautiful building,” the president said.

President Donald Trump watches as the last piece of steel is hoisted for construction of the White House ballroom during an event on Wednesday. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

As Trump pondered yet more gold fittings, Vance was agonizing about a more onerous assignment — how to pull the Republican Party out of the debacle of losing the House and the Senate. The vice president now faces his own construction project: a new electoral coalition that could also salvage his own presidential dreams.

Vance’s frank social media post, which contained multiple not-so-veiled criticisms of his boss’s presidency and second-term strategy, was a remarkable move for a vice president hours just after a devastating White House defeat.

Vance seeks to claim leadership role

Vance’s post came across as an early pitch to be the first among equals of GOP leaders charting a new path. In that sense, it was an act of political calculation. But is it a sound one? It’s been just two weeks since Vance’s wobbly judgment was exposed by his embrace of a vile attack ad that seemed only to backfire on Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.

Vance wrote, with evident understatement, that he shared the view of one GOP pollster that “our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch” — a period when Trump was citing a “golden age” while gasoline and diesel prices soared. He also sought distance from the president on two defining aspects of his term: the Iran war and the aggressive purge of undocumented migrants.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote, adding, “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement —by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance.” Vance sought some political protection on the latter point, setting up a straw man by implying the only alternative would be “amnesty” pushed by “gaslighting” establishment politicians.

The vice president revealed that he’d asked an unnamed pollster, “one of the smartest people I know in politics,” what would convince disaffected Trump/Vance voters to return. He came up with a list:

“1) End the war

2) Focus on cost of living/inflation

3) Put America First

4) Change our relationship to Israel.”

Vance also notably defended Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy’s calls for a diplomatic end to the Iran war. Since Trump is widely reported to be considering new strikes, this also signaled a potential breach with the president.

Vice President JD Vance listens to Jared Kushner as they attend a quadrilateral meeting between the United States, Iran, Pakistan and Qatar in Switzerland on June 21. Nathan Howard/Pool/AFP/Getty Images

Vance was careful to note when he cited the war as the reason for Republican losses that “the president said so last night.” He has not publicly broken with Trump over the conflict, and he led the negotiating team that produced an MOU with Tehran to end it over the summer — which fizzled on contact with reality.

But there is nuance here that suggests Vance and Trump’s positions are not compatible. The president is now talking about the war’s impact on the midterms almost wistfully, portraying himself as a leader who knowingly made a political sacrifice and paid the price, via high gas prices, to do what had to be done. “I would have done nothing different,” he said Wednesday.

Vance’s commentary, however, leaves open an interpretation that the war was a mistake from the start and has exerted a heavy political price. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Trump avoided an appearance of disagreement with his vice president by telling reporters on the tour that Vance was “probably right” about the war’s impact because it “drove the gasoline up a little bit short term.”

The vice president then sought to defuse any sense of a rift by posting video of Trump saying he thought the statement was “good” during his ballroom tour.

DeSantis is also leading the postmortem

Vance’s position on the war has long caused intrigue because it muddles his previously expressed skepticism of foreign military interventions, which was distilled from his Iraq war service. But by including “America First” and the need to change the US-Israel relationship in his four points, he also seemed to be reaching out to the isolationist Tucker Carlson wing of what’s left of the MAGA coalition, which may play an important role in the 2028 Democratic primary.

Whatever Vance’s intentions, it’s questionable after Tuesday’s GOP wipe-out whether anyone associated with the unpopular Iran war — and this includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio — would be able to explain it away on the 2028 campaign trail.

Vance already has to account for several cycles of political reinvention. And even before the Ramaswamy storm last month, his political dexterity was in doubt. After all, he has only run one major political campaign in his own right — for Ohio Senate in 2022. In that race, he greatly benefited from an endorsement by Trump, who forgave the “Hillbilly Elegy” author for his vehement criticisms in the 2016 presidential campaign.

Vance is not alone in beginning maneuvering for 2028.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis waits to greet President Donald Trump as he arrives at Southwest Florida International Airport in Fort Myers, Florida, on October 23. Mark Schiefelbein/AP

Ron DeSantis, who lost in the 2024 GOP primary to Trump, is up with his own straight talk. As is the case with Vance and Rubio, everything the outgoing Florida governor says is now refracted through a 2028 lens. “It’s very unlikely Republicans will recapture the Congress in 2028. Might not have a shot at Senate control until 2032,” DeSantis wrote on X.

And DeSantis told reporters that Tuesday’s losses were “close to an extinction level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years.” He added that the damage could reverberate for the next decade or more. “If the Republican Party doesn’t have Texas as an anchor then we are not going to be viable nationally going forward,” he said.

The Florida governor’s remarks seem to serve the same purpose as Vance’s: as a claim to future GOP leadership. There were made from a red state that mostly repelled the blue Democratic wave on Tuesday night and that DeSantis has long used as a petri dish for a post-Trump Republican Party.

Pundits were joking on Tuesday that the 2028 presidential campaign would start Wednesday morning.

JD Vance just made it a reality.

World.title: Liberia: National Port Authority Admits Freeport Lagging Behind Shipping Demand; Harbor Master Says Dredging Contract Due This Week
World.content:
MONROVIA – The National Port Authority (NPA) has acknowledged that the Freeport of Monrovia, Liberia’s principal seaport, is struggling to keep pace with the size and number of ships now calling on it. Cargo vessels are queuing offshore, and importers are counting the cost.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

In an exclusive interview with FrontPage Africa, Captain Samuel M. Lynch, the NPA’s Harbor Master and head of its Marine Department, said a contract for comprehensive dredging of the entire port basin and navigation channel is expected to be signed this week. Expansion of container yards and berths would follow within three to eight months, he said.



“The discussion now is that the time is now. The need for it is now that it can’t be pushed further down the line,” Lynch said.

Video footage obtained by FrontPage Africa shows at least five cargo vessels anchored off Monrovia’s coastline, waiting to enter the port. The Freeport handles most of the country’s imported food, fuel, construction materials and other essential goods.

Background: A Senator Sounds the Alarm

The congestion reached the National Legislature last month. In an October 25 letter to Senate President Pro-Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence, Gbarpolu County Senator Amara M. Konneh said importers and shipping agents report that Liberia-bound containers spend an average of more than 30 days at sea before berthing in Monrovia. Some vessels, he said, are being routed to or held at ports in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana.

Konneh, a former Minister of Finance and Development Planning, blamed insufficient container yard space and prolonged delays in dredging the port basin and channel, which he said prevent larger vessels from berthing. He also cited “a multiplicity of opaque transaction costs and fees” charged by APM Terminals, MEDTECH Scientific Limited, Global Tracking and Maritime Solutions (GTMS) and others in the supply chain.

The Senator argued that port inefficiencies may explain why consumer prices remain high even though headline inflation has fallen to 4.6 percent and the Liberian dollar has strengthened against the US dollar. He asked the Senate to summon the NPA, APM Terminals, MEDTECH, GTMS, the Liberia Revenue Authority’s Customs Department, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and customs brokers to testify before the full Senate.

Asked about the congestion last week, NPA Managing Director Sekou Dukuly offered a one-line response: “We are working on dredging and expansion.” Lynch’s interview is the most detailed account yet of what that work involves.

The NPA says the problem is more complex than any single cause. It points to a combination of inadequate infrastructure, bigger vessels, limited berths, weather and operational constraints.

Dredging: ‘A Continuous Requirement’

Responding to criticism that successive governments have announced dredging projects without solving the problem, Lynch said dredging at the Freeport is a continuous requirement because of the port’s location and design.

Unlike naturally deep-water ports, the Freeport suffers from sedimentation. Ocean currents carry sand from the river and nearby coastal areas into the port basin, steadily reducing the depth of water available to ships.

“Naturally, the currents bring the sand from the river and from up north, the coastal areas like West Point. All those areas bring it and deposit it inside the basin,” Lynch explained.

Without regular dredging, he said, the draft available to vessels keeps shrinking, limiting the size of ships that can safely enter. Ideally, the port should be dredged every two to three years, and at least every five years, depending on how fast sediment builds up.

The last dredging was carried out in January 2023 by APM Terminals, the port’s container terminal operator, Lynch said. The new campaign will differ because it covers the entire basin rather than selected sections.

“The scope is a bit different than it was in the previous dredge campaigns,” he said.

Bigger Ships, Same Port

Beyond dredging, Lynch named inadequate container yard space and limited berths as the port’s biggest constraints.

He said the APM Terminals concession provided for the development of about 11 hectares, but discussions are under way to use the entire area to handle growing cargo volumes.

The port’s needs, he said, have changed significantly since the concession arrangement was introduced in 2013. Liberia’s population and economy have grown, imports have risen, and global shipping has moved to much larger vessels.

Ships calling on Monrovia between 2011 and 2013 were generally about 295 meters long. Some of the largest vessels in global shipping now reach about 400 meters. Bigger ships bring more containers: a vessel that once required 600 to 800 container-handling moves can now need as many as 1,600. The container yard, Lynch argued, must expand to match.

He said APM Terminals’ concession obligations include developing the terminal to reflect changing shipping requirements and the port’s growing needs.

Lynch disputed Senator

Konneh’s figure of more than 30 days at sea. He said the average waiting time for container ships across the region is about 26 days, while Liberia’s is now about 12 days, up from a low of about six days at one point.

“In all fairness, let’s be realistic. In the whole region here, the average rate, we’re talking about liners now, container ships. The average wait time is 26 days. Ours is not 26. At some point, we were doing six days. We’re now at somewhere around 12,” Lynch said.

He acknowledged, however, that shallow water has contributed to delays. Because of shallow areas in the channel and basin, larger vessels sometimes have to enter at high tide. The NPA has also banned some vessels from moving at night for safety reasons, so ships that finish working late at night must wait until daylight to leave.

Lynch said no single factor explains the delays. He pointed to operational logistics, how quickly containers are cleared from the yard, and the availability of berths.

Rain Slows Bulk Cargo

The Harbor Master drew a distinction between container ships and bulk carriers bringing in rice, wheat, flour and clinker, the main raw material for cement.

These cargoes must be kept dry, so Liberia’s long rainy season frequently halts discharge. Shipping companies, vessel captains and insurers must weigh the risk of cargo damage before allowing work to continue in bad weather.

A bulk carrier with 50,000 to 55,000 metric tons can normally discharge in about 21 days in good weather, Lynch said. In the rains, the same vessel may stay at berth far longer.

“Sometimes they’re taking six weeks. Sometimes they’re taking six to eight weeks,” he said.

Lynch said such delays are caused by the weather, not by port congestion. The NPA is considering additional dedicated berths for bulk carriers so that ships carrying different commodities are not competing for the same limited space.

The Dredging Plan

Lynch said the project will be carried out in two phases. Phase One will deal with shallow areas in the navigation channel and port basin to improve access and restore safer operating conditions. The contract is expected to be signed this week, and dredging equipment could begin arriving within about 10 days, subject to regulatory and administrative arrangements.

Phase Two, expected to begin within three to eight months, will focus on expansion, including additional terminal space and dedicated berths. Lynch said Phase One would bring immediate improvements, while Phase Two would tackle the port’s longer-term limits.

The dredging will cover the area from the China Union and BMC Pier to the Liberia Maritime Corporation (LMC) Pier, the Western Cluster area, APM Terminals’ facility and the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company (LPRC) facility. The fairway from the open sea through the channel and into the breakwater is also included.

The entire basin is to be restored to a depth of 13.5 meters, compared with the 13 meters targeted in previous campaigns. The project will also remove an underwater rock, marked by an isolated danger buoy, that obstructs navigation. Past dredging campaigns avoided it because removing it requires specialized equipment. Lynch said it must now go to give larger vessels enough room to maneuver. The work will require two marine vessels, including one designed to break up underwater rock.

Nine shipwrecks have also been identified in the port basin, two of them in areas used for navigation. Lynch said the NPA intends to remove all nine now, rather than bring specialized equipment back for Phase Two.

He acknowledged that the wider scope will make this campaign more expensive than previous ones, which reportedly cost between US$5 million and US$6 million.

Toward 24-Hour Operations

If the dredging succeeds, Lynch said, the NPA could relax some of the restrictions now placed on ships. Vessels are currently limited to a maximum draft of about 11 meters. Depending on the final depth achieved, that could rise to between 12 and 12.5 meters, allowing larger and more heavily loaded ships to enter.

Deeper water could also allow night-time sailings to resume, so ships can enter and leave around the clock. Under the current rules, a vessel that finishes work at 11 p.m. may have to wait at berth until daylight, keeping the next ship waiting offshore.

But Lynch stressed that dredging alone will not solve the port’s problems without more berths and container-handling facilities.

Seven Berths Against Tema’s 29

Lynch compared the Freeport with its regional rivals. Ghana’s Port of Tema has about 29 berths, he said. The Freeport of Monrovia has seven under the NPA’s management.

APM Terminals’ quay, about 600 meters long, can take about three vessels in good conditions. But ships of different lengths, some about 200 meters and others over 225 meters, make it hard to use every meter of quay space. Some berths are also reserved for particular vessels, such as the LPRC berth for tankers. With so few berths, ships often must wait for others to finish before they can come alongside. Lynch said additional berths, including dedicated bulk berths, would significantly increase capacity and ease congestion.

Who Pays for the Wait

Ships waiting offshore are expensive. Lynch acknowledged that shipping companies keep paying charter fees, fuel, crew wages and food while their vessels sit idle.

He said, however, that the NPA does not set port tariffs on its own, as these are fixed under existing concession and tariff arrangements. The authority’s job, he said, is to use available berths efficiently and bring ships in as quickly as conditions allow.

“We are flexible in terms of using berths for different types of vessels. We move assets around … We try to accommodate as much as possible,” he said.

For importers, especially small businesses with little cash to spare, those costs remain a heavy burden. Senator Konneh argues they are passed directly to consumers.

Questions Over Long-Term Planning

The congestion raises questions about whether Liberia planned for the growth in shipping traffic and the rise of larger vessels.

Asked how the port’s problems reached this stage, Lynch said its requirements had changed considerably since the original studies and concession arrangements were drawn up. Infrastructure considered adequate in 2013, he acknowledged, may no longer meet today’s needs.

Port planning, he argued, should look beyond short-term projections and include regular reviews so that concessions and infrastructure keep up with economic and shipping realities. He said an independent third-party assessment informed the port’s current master plan, which identified the need for expansion, more berths and better operating capacity. The planned dredging, he said, is the first major step toward carrying out those recommendations.

The NPA now says container ships wait about 12 days, not 30. But Senator Konneh’s complaints and the ships visible from Monrovia’s beaches show the need for more openness about port performance, infrastructure limits and the timetable for fixing them.

The first test is whether dredging begins as promised. The second is whether expanded yards and new berths follow. Until then, the Freeport will keep trying to handle growing shipping demand with infrastructure that the NPA itself admits is no longer enough.
