Mugabe's Youngest Son Arrested in Zimbabwe Over Assault and Vehicle Smuggling

Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of Zimbabwe's late former president Robert Mugabe, has been arrested alongside four other men in connection with an assault case in Harare. The arrests follow an investigation into the alleged smuggling of two luxury vehicles into the country, which the Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission has reportedly seized. The suspects face charges of contravening Section 136 of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act, alternatively Section 182 of the Customs and Excise Act. Police said that the alleged assault took place at Brompton Guest Lodge. Bellarmine previously made headlines in South Africa following his arrest in February 2026 after a shooting incident at his Hyde Park residence in Johannesburg, in which a gardener was wounded.

World.title: South Africa: Presidency Condemns Rising Political Killings - South African News Briefs - November 5, 2026
World.content:
press review

Presidency Condemns Rising Political Killings

Phindile Baleni, the Director-General in the Presidency, has condemned political killings and warned that those responsible would be dealt with by the police, reports eNCA. Her remarks come amid growing concerns over political violence, with Natjoints reporting 20 murders involving political representatives, party members and supporters, and seven arrests. Baleni has urged South Africans to express political views through democratic processes rather than violence.

Govt Prepares for Loss of AGOA Benefits

Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau has said that South Africa is preparing to manage the economic impact of the United States' decision to exclude the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) from next year, reports SABC News. Tau said that the government will continue engaging Washington while working directly with affected companies to prepare for the loss of preferential trade benefits.

Singer Makhadzi Returns Home After Botswana Ordeal

South African singer Makhadzi has secured the return of her travel documents after spending three days in Botswana amid a dispute with a local event promoter, reports TimesLIVE. The singer had travelled to the country for a performance but reportedly received no payment and had no signed agreement with the organiser. Diplomatic intervention by the South African and Botswana governments, alongside legal action, helped secure her release to return home in time to vote in South Africa's elections.

More South African news

World.title: Africa: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games - Kenya on Top, Madagascar on Podium, Senegal Looks to Future
World.content:
Dakar — African women's rugby made its mark at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. At the Iba Mar Diop complex, Kenya secured gold after a spectacular final against Australia, while Madagascar took bronze. For Senegal, the host country, this first international experience opens new avenues for the development of the sport among young girls.

African women's rugby has reason to be ambitious. In Dakar, the young Kenyan women delivered one of the standout performances of the Youth Olympic Games' rugby sevens tournament, defeating Australia 17-12 in a final that went to extra time. This victory highlights the growing strength of women's rugby on the continent.

Trailing on the scoreboard, the Kenyan women found the strength to level the score (12-12) at the end of regulation time, before securing the victory with a decisive try in extra time. A hard-fought win, achieved through courage and determination, that rewards the journey of an ambitious team.

"We came here with one goal: to win gold. We came to represent Kenya," said captain Zain Hido, emotional after her team's victory.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Beyond the medal, this victory confirms the ability of young African players to compete with top-level opponents. It also sends an encouraging signal for a sport that seeks to expand its reach and increase its visibility across the continent.

Madagascar confirms its potential

Kenya was not the only African team to distinguish itself. Madagascar also achieved a remarkable performance by winning the bronze medal, confirming the potential of its new generation of players.

The Ladies Makis demonstrated consistency throughout the tournament, conceding only one defeat, against Kenya in the semi-final. This performance rewards their commitment and the efforts they made to reach this level of competition.

"This medal is for us, for our country! It's the first time for us, it's incredible," said Princia Ranaivoson, bursting with joy after this third place.

Behind this result lie weeks of preparation and the sacrifices of young female athletes forced to juggle training, studies and international ambitions.

Their coach, Dina Razafindratsara, praised the commitment of her players, whose journey testifies to the training work undertaken in Madagascar.

This bronze medal represents encouragement for Malagasy women's rugby and underlines the importance of continuing efforts in coaching, training and access to international competitions.

Senegal, a first to prepare the next generation

For Senegal, the tournament ended without a victory, but with important lessons learned. Finishing last in the standings, the Lionesses suffered a defeat against Spain (0-27), highlighting the experience gap that still separates them from some international teams.

But for this young team, the stakes went beyond sporting results. It was primarily about discovering the demands of international competition and gauging the road ahead.

"I'm proud of the girls. Today, the team represented our country well. They fought hard, even though they lacked experience," declared the national coach, Oumar Diop.

This participation is part of a dynamic of development of women's rugby in Senegal, in particular through the Rugby Rising Play program, supported by World Rugby to encourage the practice of this sport among young girls.

According to the coach, several players joined this initiative less than two years ago. Their participation in the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games therefore represented their first experience at the highest international level.

"After the Youth Olympic Games, we will continue the work, keep this team, train it and always try to compete against the best. We still have a lot of work to do," he added.

For Senegalese rugby, the challenge now is to transform this first participation into a real dynamic of development, by multiplying opportunities for competition and consolidating training systems.

An African podium that brings hope for women's rugby

With two African nations on the podium, the Dakar 2026 women's rugby sevens tournament offers an encouraging illustration of the continent's sporting potential.

Close 

Kenya's victory and Madagascar's bronze medal demonstrate the progress made by some federations, while Senegal's participation highlights the challenges still faced by countries where the sport is still developing.

Beyond individual and collective performances, these results highlight the importance of investing in training, technical coaching, and access for young girls to sports infrastructure.

For African federations, the challenge now will be to capitalize on the visibility offered by these Games to strengthen talent identification, support, and competition programs.

In Dakar, young African rugby players will not only have played matches and won medals. They will also have helped to raise the profile of their sport and pave the way for a generation of athletes determined to advance women's rugby on the continent.

The article was translated from French

World.title: Africa: How Many More COPs Before Climate Promises Become Action?
World.content:
A woman wades through floodwaters in Bor, Jonglei State, South Sudan, where communities continue to live with the effects of flooding from previous years as the country prepares for further climate-related shocks.

Every year before COP, the same question surfaces: what is the one thing Africa needs from this summit?

Ahead of COP31, the answer emerging from a World Resources Institute Africa webinar was clear: Africa must move beyond asking what it can receive from global climate negotiations and focus on what it can bring. With geopolitical tensions, energy disruptions and climate shocks exposing vulnerabilities across African economies, speakers argued that the continent must use the summit to advance practical solutions that strengthen energy security, protect food systems and mobilise climate finance.

A reinvented agency

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Olufunso Somorin, Regional Principal Officer for Climate Change and Green Growth at the African Development Bank, said these challenges were interconnected, warning that simultaneous disruptions to energy, food and economic systems could undermine the continent's development gains. He described them as a triangle of reality - when one is hit, the others strain, and when all three are hit, the development gains of recent years are at risk.

"COP of today, it is now a trade forum. It is now a marketplace."

He said that Africa needed to rethink its approach to global climate negotiations and strengthen its position as a partner in shaping climate solutions rather than simply seeking assistance. His answer was what he called a "reinvented agency". Africa, he said, must move "away from this idea of Africa that needs to be helped, to an Africa that needs to be partnered with."

He also questioned the pace of the process itself, asking that after 30 COPs, how many more does it take to get things done?

That means understanding what COP has become. "COP of today, it is now a trade forum. It is now a marketplace. And what you get out of a marketplace is largely based on who you are and what you bring to the marketplace," he said.

Strengthening energy security

Energy security was one of the key issues at COP31, with the prevailing situation of geopolitical tensions and disruptions to the global energy supply underpinning the risks of being dependent on external energy sources. Africa has significant renewable energy potential. However, the challenge remains translating these resources into reliable and affordable electricity that can support economic growth, businesses, and industrial development.

Yasmin Abdulwassie, Senior Manager for Climate in Africa at the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, said high financing costs and limited public budgets remained major obstacles to scaling up renewable energy investments. "The challenge is really translating that potential into affordable, reliable energy that can be replicated and scaled," she said.

She said philanthropy can help by funding project preparation, policy reform and investment pipelines, so that transition pathways are country-led. She pointed to South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership. The initiative, she said, initially announced with $8.5 billion, had grown to more than $14 billion, proof that investors back credible country platforms.

She also highlighted Senegal's Renewable Energy Investment Facility as another emerging example of efforts to attract investment and support the country's energy transition. "So that type of catalytic role that philanthropy plays is not just about unlocking finance, but helping countries turn lasting financing possibilities for economic reform," said Abdulwassie.

Somorin said that achieving universal energy access would require stronger partnerships that connect national ambitions with clear financing strategies. He cited Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million people in sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030, as an example of how shared targets and country-specific strategies can accelerate progress.

He said 37 African countries had developed national energy compacts outlining their strategies for expanding electricity access, helping attract investment from development finance institutions, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and philanthropic organisations. He said the initiative demonstrated the importance of having a collective goal while agreeing on practical steps to achieve it.

"It is a new way of defining partnership where you have a collective goal, but you also have a shared discussion on the how. How do we get there? What do we need to do differently?" he said.

Beyond energy security, COP31 is urged to give greater attention to adaptation, particularly ensuring that climate finance reaches countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change.

Abdulwassie said that the climate summit should move adaptation commitments toward "real, measurable outcomes," particularly in food systems, water and livelihood infrastructure. She set out three priorities. The first is a credible financing pathway. Countries have committed to tripling adaptation finance by 2035, but Abdulwassie said the detail is missing. "How are we going to do it? How will progress be measured?" she asked, adding that these questions need answers at COP31 and at every milestone after it.

The second is better indicators, and here she pointed to the Belém-Addis vision, a two-year process that runs toward COP32 in Ethiopia. Current metrics, she said, tend to count activities, such as how many farmers completed climate-smart agriculture training. She argued the measure should be whether a farmer's livelihood "stays intact or improves despite climate shocks," and that credible results of that kind are what attract further financing.

The third is matching national adaptation plans with investment plans. She cited a Malawi initiative, backed by philanthropy and led by the African Climate Foundation, in which more than 20 of the country's priority adaptation proposals have been matched with potential investors. The aim, she said, is to give adaptation the same investable pipelines that mitigation projects increasingly have.

Closing the adaptation finance gap

The challenge of mobilising climate finance for adaptation was also highlighted by Somorin, who said African countries needed to rethink how adaptation projects are financed and how their economic value is presented to investors.

"Adaptation is very complex," Somorin said, and the sector has made it harder by lumping everything together as "climate action." He said that adaptation remains more difficult to finance than mitigation because projects often lack the clear financial returns that attract private investors.

Put all climate projects in one finance basket, he said, and about nine in ten that emerge would be mitigation projects. They are simply easier to finance and attract capital more readily. Africa also faces a structural handicap. In every other region, he said, private capital drives climate action. Africa is the only place where public money leads.

His first proposed fix is to stop treating the two as separate. "You use mitigation finance to drive adaptation goals," he said. He gave an example of a solar-powered irrigation scheme in a semi-arid region that cuts emissions through clean energy, but it also lets farmers grow and earn all year round, which is an adaptation result. The more deliberately adaptation is built into mitigation projects, he said, the more capital will reach it.

"I argue that you use mitigation finance to drive adaptation goals," he said.

Somorin also called for a change in how investors assess adaptation projects, arguing that their wider economic benefits should be recognised alongside their immediate financial returns.

He said financiers needed to understand the distinction between financial viability and economic viability, particularly where investments generate long-term benefits that may not immediately translate into revenue. Somorin said the task is to help financiers see that the economic value is real and can be monetized, either now or later, as new markets emerge to turn it into financial returns.

Africa has documented 11 financial instruments for mitigation projects but, at best, three for adaptation. Expanding these financing options, he said, would let more resources flow and would bring non-traditional investors into the adaptation space.

Philanthropy can help unlock larger investments

While development finance institutions have a role in mobilising investment for climate action, Abdulwassie said philanthropic capital could help address some of the structural barriers preventing African countries from accessing climate finance. "Philanthropy alone, we know, cannot close that gap," she said. However, she identified three areas where it could have a catalytic impact: strengthening national institutions, developing country-led investment platforms, and building stronger partnerships across the climate finance ecosystem.

The first is institutional capacity. Where African institutions don't exist, or need strengthening, she said, philanthropic money is best spent building them. That leads to country ownership and brings "the local voice, the local agenda" to the table, alongside partners such as the African Development Bank. She pointed again to South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership, where philanthropic partners and multilaterals helped the government negotiate what international financing would look like. She also made a pointed aside: more grants should go directly to countries to help scale such efforts.

The second is building investment platforms with countries rather than for them. Philanthropy can provide technical expertise, convene partners and help design financing mechanisms and instruments. The models must be contextual, she said, because every country's energy pathway, food system and growth path is different.

The third is strengthening the wider ecosystem of African climate leadership. She cited philanthropic support for the first two Africa Climate Summits, the resulting Nairobi and Addis Ababa declarations, and efforts to give African countries a collective voice through the African Union during South Africa's G20 presidency.

The stakes, she said, are high: climate finance flowing into Africa is less than 2% of what is needed, nowhere near the continent's needs. Without African leadership in these rooms, she argued, the finance ambitions cannot be met.

"Bringing in that collective voice because I believe that ensures that African leadership is there to shape African priorities," she said.

Turning country platforms into action

Somorin said his experience working with country platforms at the African Development Bank had shown that strong national leadership was essential to their success.

He outlined three factors that can help these platforms move beyond coordination. First, governments need clearly defined climate goals and realistic objectives that reflect their national capabilities, political circumstances, and development priorities.

"Nothing substitutes for strong leadership," he said. He named the difference it makes by comparing Rwanda with Niger. Clear, well-structured country goals matter, he said, but so does honesty about capability. Countries that are still asking partners to help train their people, when they should be implementing, are not ready to move. Goals also have to fit a country's political and socioeconomic realities. He said, "You cannot ignore" even when they seem unrelated to climate.

Second, countries must understand the strengths of their development partners, including multilateral institutions, philanthropic organisations and NGOs, and bring them together around clearly allocated responsibilities.

Third, governments must demonstrate their own commitment by contributing resources to the initiatives they want partners to support. Somorin said that countries which tell partners they need support for 80% of a project because they will supply 20% make faster progress than those that put in nothing and ask for everything. A government that commits a set share of its budget over five years, and assigns people to learn and deliver, finds it much easier to leverage what others bring.

Building towards an African COP32

Ethiopia is set to host COP32 in 2027. Abdulwassie said African countries should begin preparing now to ensure the summit delivers beyond political commitments. She said that COP32 should not be viewed as an Ethiopian event alone, but as an opportunity for African countries to unite around shared development priorities and strengthen the continent's influence in global climate discussions.

"COP32 is not just an Ethiopian COP, but an African COP," she said.

Abdulwassie outlined three priorities for the road to COP32. First, African leaders must work together to agree on key priorities. She pointed to the African Union summit in February and the pre-COP period as chances to agree on priorities that can outlast political cycles, including the action agenda and the initiatives each presidency will announce.

Second, Africa should use the run-up to COP32 to showcase successful climate initiatives already underway, demonstrate their results and identify which approaches can be adapted or scaled up in other countries.

Third, she called for greater recognition of local voices, particularly those of young people and communities already driving climate action. She said communities' ambitions and practices need to reach leaders and be translated into action. "How do we make sure the voice of youth in particular ... is translated into action?" she asked. She warned that decisions made today would shape the world inherited by future generations.

Close 

Development partners, she said, should engage Africa not in terms of handouts but as true partners, in a relationship where Africans have resources to trade and engage with, at COP32 and beyond.

To make COP31 a success for Africa, Abdulwassie pointed to stronger continental unity, partnerships and visibility in global climate discussions.

She said African countries needed to speak with a stronger collective voice while building momentum around energy, food security and water resilience. She also stressed the importance of having more Africans present at the summit to share their ambitions, experiences and progress.

Somorin said Africa's voice and leadership must be central to global climate discussions, particularly given the continent's limited contribution to climate change and its disproportionate exposure to its impacts. The voice, agency and significance of that continent, he argued, can never be ignored, but the starting point is Africa asserting its own agency, because the global climate equation is incomplete without Africa's development and resilience.

He urged African countries to move away from the perception of a continent waiting to be helped.

"Africa should be recognised not only for its vulnerability but also for its potential to contribute to global solutions," said Somorin. "If there's any region that could play a significant role in the global solution, it is Africa."

Protecting Africa's industrialisation ambitions

Soha Benchekroun, a climate resilience and industrial development policy researcher and adviser, argued that climate negotiations must give greater consideration to Africa's right to industrialise and move up global value chains.

The aim for COP31, and for the "African COP" in Ethiopia a year later, said Benchekroun, is to make sure climate action "does not undermine our industrialization trajectories." Most African countries are only starting to climb global value chains and build manufacturing and processing capacity at home. Many have moved to restrict raw material exports and promote local processing, a trend she called positive.

The threat, she said, comes from unilateral trade measures adopted in the name of climate policy by industrialized countries: carbon border adjustments, carbon pricing and related regulations. She said the negotiated rules should seek to limit the harm of these measures to African and other developing economies. The timing is pressing, she noted, with more carbon border mechanisms on the way, including the UK's, due to start in January 2027.

"Justice and a good outcome is first about doing no harm to our African development and industrial development pathways," she said.

Benchekroun also said that the just transition debate has focused on wider energy access while giving the right to development, and industrial development in particular, only marginal attention. "We do not expect COPs to sort out our energy infrastructure challenges, nor to promote our own industrialization," she said, "but at least a good start would be to not hinder them." What lifts a continent out of poverty, she said, is infrastructure, industrial development, and local value addition, paired with ways to turn them into benefits for society.

World.title: South Africa: Millions Voted and Now South Africa Waits for Results
World.content:
The 2026 Local Government Elections results process continues to advance, with 24% of votes counted nationally. These are the results at 10am SAST on November 5, 2026.

About 12 million South Africans had voted by 5pm on Wednesday, with Gauteng recording the highest turnout as voting stations prepared to close.

The African National Congress faces a major test in local elections as opposition parties fight for control of municipalities across South Africa.

South Africans are waiting to see who will take charge of their towns and cities after millions went to the polls on Wednesday, 4 November.

Voting stations closed at 9pm, with counting now under way across the country.

The Electoral Commission of South Africa said everyone who joined a queue before 9pm would be allowed to vote.



Gauteng led with three million voters, followed by KwaZulu-Natal with 2.5 million, the Western Cape with 1.5 million and the Eastern Cape with 1.4 million.

Limpopo recorded 1.1 million voters, while Mpumalanga had 854,901 and North West 702,133.

The Free State recorded 588,237 voters and the Northern Cape 299,381.

The figures showed a sharp rise from the 3.5 million people who had voted by 10am.

But not everyone rushed to the polls.

Some voting stations in central Durban reported low turnout, raising concerns about people staying away from the elections.

The day also brought tragedy.

A woman in her late 60s died after collapsing while waiting to vote at Shallcross Primary School in Durban.

Previn Vedan, chairperson of the African National Congress Naidu Makhanya Zone, said an ambulance was called, but the woman's family arranged transport and took her to hospital.

The Electoral Commission said it was investigating the circumstances.

Police also investigated the theft of unused ballot papers and a voting stamp from a voting station in eThekwini.

Heavy rain and local protests caused delays at some stations in the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal.

Despite these problems, the commission said voting had gone well across most of the country.

The biggest political test is for the African National Congress.

The party lost its national majority in 2024 and now faces another battle to hold on to councils across South Africa.

Opposition parties are hoping to take control of more municipalities as voters judge how councils have handled water, electricity, roads, rubbish collection and other services.

Former president Jacob Zuma's uMkhonto weSizwe Party is also contesting its first local government elections after winning significant support in KwaZulu-Natal during the 2024 national elections.

A record 29.2 million people registered to vote.

Close 

More than 136,000 candidates competed for 10,526 council seats across 257 municipalities.

Election officials are counting ballots at the stations where voters cast them, with party representatives and observers watching the process.

Officials will check the figures before sending the results for verification and an independent audit.

The final results are expected within seven days.

Attention will now turn to major cities, including Johannesburg, Cape Town, eThekwini and Ekurhuleni, where parties are fighting for control.

The results will decide who runs local councils for the next five years and whether parties will need to work together to govern.

World.title: Ghana: 'I Want Justice for My Son' - Mother of Slain 15-Year-Old Javits Frimpong Leaves Ghana for USA
World.content:
Emotions ran high at the Kotoka International Airport this morning as Madam Doris Adu Gyamfi, mother of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong, departed Ghana for the United States to join her family in mourning her son.

Javits, a young Ghanaian boy, was brutally killed in the Bronx, New York -- a tragedy that has shocked Ghanaians both home and abroad.

Madam Gyamfi was accompanied to the airport by officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a relative, and other family members, who offered her support as she embarked on the painful journey.

According to the Ministry, staff from Ghana's New York Mission are on standby to receive her on arrival and provide her with all the necessary support as the family works together to give the late Javits a befitting burial.

The Ministry expressed sincere appreciation to the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Hon. Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa (MP), for his personal support throughout the process, as well as his Deputy, Hon. James Gyakye Quayson (MP).

They extended special thanks to the Mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani, and the US Embassy in Ghana for their swift intervention in securing her visa.

As she left Ghana, Madam Gyamfi's demand remained clear and emotional: "I want justice for my son."

The Ministry added that it is its fervent hope that the perpetrators of the heinous crime will be apprehended and brought to justice in due course.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Mugabe's Son Bellarmine Chatunga Arrested Over Luxury Car Smuggling, Assault
World.content:
Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the late former Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe.

Late former President Robert Mugabe's son, Bellarmine Chatunga, and four others have been arrested over the alleged smuggling of two luxury vehicles into Zimbabwe, with the cars seized by the Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission (ZACC) as investigations continue.

Bellarmine, Terrence Johannes Chinyemba, Fredson Peter, Solomon Pamire and Munashe Mubhawu are being held at Highlands Police Station following an operation at a property in Newlands, Harare.

Police documents identify the Zimbabwe Revenue Authority (ZIMRA) as the complainant in the case.The suspects face charges of contravening Section 136 of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act, alternatively Section 182 of the Customs and Excise Act.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to police, the Special Operations Unit received intelligence that a black Mercedes-Benz GLE 53, registration number NB 76 MM GP, and a black Lamborghini Urus, registration number TL 00 GP, had been illegally imported into the country.

The vehicles were allegedly concealed at Number 6A Brompton Road, Newlands, for about a month to evade customs duty and detection. Investigators reportedly established that neither vehicle had a Temporary Importation Permit (TIP) or official entry records.

Police said officers verified the intelligence through surveillance and located the vehicles at the property.

However, they were allegedly physically assaulted by suspects during the operation.

"The incident was immediately reported to the Zimbabwe Republic Police at Highlands Police Station under reference RRB684,7340," the police documents state.

The four were subsequently arrested and are awaiting further legal proceedings.Chatunga is alleged to have assaulted a ZACC officer who was investigating the suspected smuggling operation.

His reported arrest adds to his previous brushes with the law.

He was previously arrested in South Africa on attempted murder charges before being deported to Zimbabwe.

More recently, he was arrested in Zimbabwe in a drugs-related case, which was subsequently withdrawn before plea.

World.title: Kamala Harris urges Dems to 'be ruthless' with power after midterms, demands Trump accountability
World.content:

After Democrats swept control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections, former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and former President Bill Clinton offered their views about how the party should use its newfound power.

Harris called for Democrats to ruthlessly leverage their powers to provide "economic relief" and to hold President Donald Trump's "administration accountable for their deep-seated corruption." Hillary Clinton said that "The post-Trump era begins now," while her husband offered a more conciliatory message, and even called for reining in America's national debt.

"On Election Day, the American people spoke loud and clear: they are done with the corruption, incompetence, and callousness coming from the White House and the capitulation of Republican leaders," Harris declared in part of a Wednesday post on X.

KAMALA HARRIS BREAKS WITH LEFT FLANK, WARNS DEMS THAT IMPEACHING TRUMP IS 'NOT A GOOD IDEA'

"Now, the work begins to actually deliver results. The American people have elected Democrats across the country in federal, state, and local races who must be ruthless in using every lever of power to deliver economic relief for working families and hold this administration accountable for their deep-seated corruption," she asserted.

Hillary Clinton declared in a Wednesday post on X, "Last night, Americans made a clear call for accountability and affordability. A body politic cannot recover until its harms have been treated and its wounds have been healed. Crimes against our people and our Constitution must be answered for. The historic abuses of the last two years must be prevented from happening again."

She was the 2016 Democratic presidential candidate who lost to Republican Donald Trump.

DEMOCRATS' HISTORIC WINS IN TEXAS HIGHLIGHT TAKING CONTROL OF CONGRESS IN MIDTERM BLUE WAVE

"American families should be able to thrive, not just survive. Every child should have the chance to live up to his or her full potential. The American Dream must be more than a mirage. I am confident Democrats can deliver both, and much more. The post-Trump era begins now," Clinton wrote.

"The American people have given us clear direction: to put their needs ahead of the chaos and corruption coming out of Washington. HILLARY CLINTON WARNS DEMS MAY SQUANDER MIDTERM VICTORY IF THEY FAIL TO STAY FOCUSED AFTER ELECTION

World.title: 17 years after Fort Hood massacre, victims' families grapple with gunman's looming execution
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Seventeen years have passed since an Army psychiatrist opened fire at Fort Hood killing 13 people in 2009. Since then, families of three of the fallen have learned to navigate life without their loved ones, finding strength in the values and lessons their father, daughter and spouse left behind.

"It builds character, kid," is a phrase Keely Cahill Vanacker remembers her father Michael Cahill saying, always with a playful punch to the arm, throughout her teenage years whenever she was upset.

Cahill served in the Army National Guard for 23 years as an infantryman before earning a bachelor’s degree in psychology and training to become a physician assistant, providing medical care to soldiers.

"My dad really valued people, and he touched a lot of lives," Vanacker said.

TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE

Growing up in a military family, living all across the country, Vanacker saw Cahill demonstrate the value of treating others with humanity and fairness as he practiced medicine.

"If you were somebody living in a rural Texas post and struggling to even pay for your asthma medication, my dad would find places for you to get your medication," she said.

For Cahill, serving people was a calling; and it did not end when he hung up his helmet. After retiring from the military he continued to serve as a civilian PA at Fort Hood.

As for Amy Krueger, her call to serve came in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.

2001 turning point

"I’m going in."

Those are the words Amy told her mother Jeri Krueger on the afternoon of Sept. 11.

At the time, Amy was a student at the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay, Sheboygan Campus.

"Going in?" Krueger recalled asking her daughter.

"I'm joining the Army, mom."

Krueger was skeptical that her daughter could make a difference in the fight against terrorism.

"Oh, Amy, you can't take on bin Laden all by yourself," Krueger told her daughter.

"Watch me," Amy replied.

The next day, Amy sat in a recruiter's office and would go on to become Staff Sgt. Amy Krueger.

"When Amy said she was going to do something, she did it," Krueger said.

After Amy's first deployment to Afghanistan in 2003 at Bagram Airfield, she returned home and continued her education as a mental health specialist in the Army and completed Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) and Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) programs while continuing her education in psychology.

"She wanted to help people get through things," Krueger said. "Psychology was definitely something she would've been great at."

In 2008, Amy volunteered for another tour in Afghanistan. Between deployments, she was welcomed home by friends and family members.

Even while at home her commitment to service was still on the forefront of her mind.

Krueger had been at work when Amy texted her a picture of a new tattoo she had gotten, which took hours to complete.

"I said, ‘I don't like it,’" Krueger recalled.

Amy asked what her mother meant, thinking she was receiving the typical parental disapproval of new ink.

Krueger explained it wasn't necessarily the tattoo itself she disliked, but what it said.

"I feel like it's a bad omen," Krueger had told her daughter.

Amy brushed her mother's worries off with a chuckle.

The tattoo depicted the American flag, draped across her back, alongside a firearm and soldier’s hat. It read: "All gave some. Some gave all. Sacrifice."

Krueger knew her daughter was determined to continue serving. However, after seeing the new tattoo, Krueger said she couldn't shake the ominous feeling it gave her.

"I always thought she had a feeling that she might not come back," Krueger said. "That tattoo kind of says that. I think that she was prepared to fight, to do what she needed to do, and didn't know if she'd be coming back."

By October 2009, Amy was sent to Fort Hood to prepare for a deployment in December, a deployment she never made.

She was not alone in arriving at Fort Hood with plans for a deployment ahead. Staff Sgt. Justin DeCrow was also preparing to deploy, this time to Iraq, when he reported to Fort Hood.

SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’

Justin DeCrow

From an early age, Justin knew he wanted to join the Army, being influenced by his father Daniel J. DeCrow, who served in the Vietnam war. He then went on to become a satellite communication instructor, where he was known for his work ethic and uplifting others.

"His positive attitude, and humor helped others get through tough times," said Justin's wife Marikay DeCrow.

When fellow soldiers struggled, Justin stayed to help, teach, support and encourage them. For him, failure was not an option.

That same warmth carried into his personal life. Justin and Marikay had known each other since childhood, as he was friends with her brother. It wasn’t until she asked him to her senior prom when they solidified feelings for one another and became inseparable.

"From that time on, we were together," said Marikay. "When he would look at me, all I saw was the love he had for me. I couldn't imagine my life without him."

When they had their daughter Kylah, Justin wasn’t able to return home and meet his daughter for the first time until she was six weeks old.

Justin had learned of his daughter Kylah’s birth 24 hours after the fact, when he was finally able to call Marikay at the hospital.

"He was ecstatic to have a daughter," she said. "We had maybe a phone call for five minutes once a day."

The phone calls were a beacon of hope, offering Marikay a few precious moments of connection with Justin while they were apart.

The hardship continued when Justin attended Advanced Individual Training, AIT, in South Carolina. Marikay recounted traveling back and forth every other weekend to keep the family in contact.

"Sometimes we only had a day, sometimes he was allowed to stay the night with us," said Marikay. "Every trip meant so much to him and us. He spent every minute he could holding Kylah. Leaving him each time was incredibly difficult."

As Kylah grew up, he was always there for her. To this day Kylah reflects the values of her father.

"I see so much of Justin in Kylah," said Marikay. "She is witty and funny, and cares so much about those around her."

Neither of them knew then how precious those days would become, the last they’d have before he headed to Fort Hood.

Nov. 5, 2009

It was a Thursday at Fort Hood’s Soldier Readiness Processing Center when U.S. Army Major and psychiatrist Nidal Hasan opened fire, killing 13 people and leaving 31 wounded.

Hasan had been motivated by Islamic extremism and had negative views on America’s involvement in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Among those 13 were Retired Chief Warrant Officer 2 Michael Cahill, Staff Sgt. Krueger and Staff Sgt. Justin DeCrow, three people whose lives were defined by their service, values and families.

For the families, the attack was the start of a new struggle: trying to understand what happened to and how they spent their final moments.

Putting back broken pieces

After the shooting, piecing together the fragments of that day was difficult for Vanacker. Witnesses were hospitalized with injuries or scattered across the country, and many of Cahill’s colleagues had not seen what he did in his final moments.

Vanacker didn’t get a solid first description until a memorial, when she was approached by a soldier who had shared a cubicle with Cahill.

He described it as any other workday until he heard gunfire down the hall.

"And all of a sudden, your dad just got up, and then he was gone," she recalled him saying.

The uncertainty that followed stretched on for nearly a year as she waited to learn what had happened to her father.

"I was just trying to figure out what had happened and if he was shot trying to help somebody," she recalled. "Was it that sort of thing? It leaves things unanswered for a while, and you have this weird waiting game."

When the pretrial proceedings began, she learned that Cahill had emerged from the examination room before picking up a chair by its legs and charging at Hasan, an act of courage that reflected "character," what he'd spent a lifetime instilling in his children.

In August 2013, Hasan was convicted on all 42 counts by a military jury that then unanimously agreed to give Hasan the death penalty. For 13 years, Hasan has been on the military's death row.

In 2015, after Congress expanded eligibility for the Purple Heart, military victims of the massacre received Purple Hearts, while eligible civilian victims, including Cahill, received the Secretary of Defense Medal for the Defense of Freedom.

Hasan's long-awaited fate

On Oct. 2, President Donald Trump approved the sentence of Hasan, and acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directed that the execution be carried out by firing squad on Dec. 3.

Hasan's execution would be the U.S. military's first execution since 1961 and its first by firing squad since 1945.

"When I received the email that President Trump signed the execution order, I felt a kind of relief come over me, all I could do was cry," said Marikay. "I have been waiting for 17 years to hear this."

Although the execution method has been questioned by some, Marikay said the method does not matter as long as Hasan faces his end.

"He deserves the death penalty, this is justice," said Marikay. "This man destroyed our lives. Justin never got to watch Kylah grow up, graduate, walk her down the aisle, hold his beautiful granddaughters...We were supposed to grow old together."

Vanacker and Krueger said they did not need Hasan's execution for closure.

"He was already dead to me, and I did not think about him. So having an execution is not something I personally needed for my own closure," Vanacker said.

Krueger expressed a similar sentiment. "I do not give him any thought ever. He died a long time ago," she said.

Vanacker and Krueger also bring up another point being the execution may be giving into Hasan’s desires.

"He wanted to be a martyr, and that didn't happen," said Krueger. "So when this happens, does that fulfill his desires?"

9/11 SENT THEM TO WAR. 25 YEARS LATER, VETERANS GRAPPLE WITH WHAT FOLLOWED

"He did that shooting, and he did it in a way where he wanted that attention and he wanted to become a martyr, and we have just played right into his hands," said Vanacker.

The debate over Hasan’s execution took a turn when War Secretary Pete Hegseth said the administration planned to livestream the event.

"We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it in public because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things." Hegseth said.

The families said it was the first time hearing of the livestream plan.

"It feels a little bit like a slap in the face, disrespectful," said Krueger. "I'm sure he didn't intend it but…there should have been somebody that said, 'whoa, wait a minute. There are families that are going to be affected by this.'"

Before Trump announced the cancellation of the planned livestream via Truth Social, Vanacker expressed concern that the administration's handling of the execution could have jeopardized it.

"Hegseth's obsession with barbaric optics probably put this execution in danger," Vanacker said. "Our tragedy is not your entertainment."

She called on Congress to ban livestreamed executions in the military using the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

"I hope they put in the NDAA just banning it outright," she said. "That it can never be considered and not an option ever so it never comes up again. Livestreaming an execution should never be an option."

After the planned livestream was canceled, Krueger was relieved.

"I'm so, so grateful that President Trump took it down, so that's a good thing." Krueger said.

Victims’ families are allowed to witness Hasan’s execution and Marikay has no doubt what she will be doing on Dec. 3.

"The date it was announced, I knew I would be heading to Fort Hood one last time, " Marikay said. "This is closure. I'm ready for it to be over."

Grieving together

Nov. 5 remains a personal day to the families. For them, this day goes beyond Hasan, focusing on the ones they lost.

Krueger remembers her daughter as vivacious and strong, someone who had a way of passing that strength on to others. Today, that same strength continues to carry her mother and how she thinks about what happened.

"I hate the idealism that made him do what he did," Krueger said. "But do I hate him? He’s a human being that was swayed by the beliefs of his leaders and had the free will to carry out a devastating, destructive event."

To continue Amy’s legacy, they have an annual event to raise money for the scholarship in her honor at the local high school.

And just like her daughter, they raise money in a fun way: A bar crawl called Krueg’s Crawl.

"It's a bar crawl, and there's prizes, and so it's fun," said Krueger.

Image 1 of 2 next

Image 2 of 2 prev

This year's event took place on Halloween and consisted of a costume contest, keeping the fun alive in her memory.

When Nov. 5 hits, the family remains intimate.

"We typically do the same thing," Krueger said. "We get together, we go to the cemetery, we talk about her, we remember her, and this year we're doing that as well."

Vanacker and her family revisit their traditions by visiting her father.

"We go, and we leave flowers, and we have a remembrance," she said.

What got her through the first anniversary was her father's four-word sentiment, the same words Cahill had comforted her with through childhood: "It builds character, kid."

"I think this year's a little bit different, Vanacker said. "I think with all the other distractions around, it honestly makes it a little harder. There's a lot more emotions pulling this year."

Although the media attention surrounding the case has brought back emotions for families, the tragedy and hardship these families faced has brought them together.

"We've become like a family," Krueger said. "There was one year and there was a 10-year anniversary to see them and to be with them, that's huge for me."

World.title: Paris Jackson demands $600M from father Michael Jackson's estate in legal war with longtime executor
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Paris Jackson accused John Branca, the sole executor of her late father Michael Jackson's multibillion-dollar estate, of financially retaliating against her and her siblings after she challenged his handling of the King of Pop's fortune.

Paris alleged in new court documents obtained by Fox News Digital, that she and her siblings experienced a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments while Branca maintained an "iron grip" over their inheritance.

She asked a Los Angeles court to order a $600 million distribution from her late father's estate into the family trust after accusing Branca of mismanaging the funds.

PARIS JACKSON SAYS DAD MICHAEL'S UNUSAL RULE HELPED PROTECT HER CHILDHOOD

Branca has been the sole executor of Jackson's estate since 2009. The pop star died that year from acute propofol and sedative intoxication leading to cardiac arrest.

Branca's alleged mismanagement of estate funds included non-contractual gifts to colleagues, aggressive litigation, public attacks and a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments to Jackson's children.

"Without belaboring the point, when Paris began challenging the administration of the Estate last year through her objection to Executor Branca’s non-contractual gifts to his colleagues, her challenges were met with scorched earth litigation, public attacks, and a multimillion reduction in monies provided to her and her siblings by the Estate," her legal team wrote. "This course of conduct and administration should not continue."

In a separate filing obtained by Fox News Digital, Paris accused Branca of using estate resources for personal travel on private jets, improperly charging personal expenses to the estate and concealing the spending from beneficiaries.

She claimed Branca acknowledged taking multiple personal trips and reimbursed certain expenses only after she investigated them. Her attorneys characterized the conduct as "outright theft" and a breach of his fiduciary duties.

"Where the travel is of a purely personal nature, or in service of Mr. Branca's other clients or business affairs, it constitutes outright theft," the court filing stated.

Paris also accused Branca of using estate funds for personal gifts, questioned more than $604,000 in credit card charges and reimbursements, and challenged $9.4 million in executor compensation, $1.4 million in payments to his law firm and roughly $835,000 in public relations expenses.

She further alleged that Branca mismanaged more than $440 million in estate cash while pursuing entertainment projects that benefited him financially, including the Michael Jackson biopic, which reportedly required tens of millions of dollars in reshoots and rewrites.

Her legal team urged the court to reject Branca's financial accounting and order him to provide a more detailed breakdown of the estate's spending.

"Once again, Ms. Jackson’s legal team raises the same hollow complaints and fails to acknowledge the unique structure of the Estate, which is operated as a dynamic business, with customary costs and expenses," a representative for the estate told Fox News Digital. "No rhetoric can hide the fact that the Executors have taken an Estate that was $500 million in debt when Michael died and turned it into the most successful Estate in history, producing $3 billion in revenue and the biggest biopic in movie history, with a box office exceeding $1 billion globally."

As for the $600 million distribution, Paris argued that her father's estate plan entitled his children — Prince, Paris and Bigi — to trust income beginning at age 21 and portions of their inheritance beginning at age 30. She claimed the executor had never funded the trust, despite Michael Jackson's death more than 17 years earlier.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"Michael intended for his children to become the caretakers of his legacy," the petition read. "As each child reached certain ages, Executors were to increasingly provide for each child’s independence."

Paris' filing cited more than $2.5 billion in gross estate earnings and approximately $850 million in cash or cash equivalents as of December 2024. She argued that the estate could distribute $600 million while retaining enough money to cover outstanding liabilities.

"Ms. Jackson’s counsel is well aware that the Estate is prevented from fully funding the philanthropic giving and individual trusts for the beneficiaries until several legal hurdles have been removed, including in particular the ongoing IRS litigation where they sought $700 million in taxes and penalties from the Estate," a statement provided to Fox News Digital on behalf of Jackson's estate said. "The Estate was able to secure a ruling to significantly reduce that amount, but the matter has not been settled and could still change."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Further, the claim that the executor has withheld or ‘cut' payments is a complete fabrication," the statement added. "In fact, more than $200 million has already been distributed for the benefit of Paris and the other beneficiaries. Michael Jackson’s will is clear. None of his children receive a distribution until they are in their 30s. The Estate looks forward to the time when all issues are resolved so that their trusts can be fully funded as Michael wanted."

A court hearing on Paris' request to transfer $600 million into the family trust is scheduled for Dec. 4.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Paris previously spoke about her childhood as the daughter of Michael Jackson. Behind the glitz of Jackson’s larger-than-life world, Paris said her father enforced strict rules to protect his children’s sense of normalcy.

The 28-year-old model recalled in an interview on "Call Her Daddy" that her father required his children to finish their homework and chores before enjoying weekend activities, limited their television and movie viewing, and had them wear masks in public to shield their identities from the intense spotlight surrounding his fame.

Paris said she understood that her father was famous. What she didn’t grasp was the sheer magnitude of his celebrity.

"I just didn't know how famous ... There was definitely part of me that, like when I looked out my hotel window, and it was one of the times where, like, the alias didn't work and there's just like a sea of people with signs and stuff — I'm not so naive to think, yeah, everyone experiences this, you know?" Paris said. "I just didn't understand the lengths."

Air traffic control audio and flight tracking data are revealing the doomed Learjet's final minutes, tracing its path from takeoff in Austin, Texas, to its fatal plunge in Greenacres, Florida, where all nine people on board were killed.

Taken together, the records depict a flight crew contending with turbulence and icing before initiating a climb, only to experience an abrupt and violent descent almost immediately afterward, along with an overspeed warning and an in-flight breakup that investigators have yet to fully explain.

FLORIDA PLANE CRASH VICTIMS IDENTIFIED AFTER 9 PEOPLE KILLED IN FIERY WRECK

Timeline of Learjet N722BD (all times in Eastern Time):

10:37 a.m. - Departure:

Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, his wife, Helen Sharp, 40, and their children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, along with the children's nanny, Anita Maria Cetina, and couple Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr departed from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport on a Bombardier Learjet 60.

TEXAS FAMILY OF 4, 20-YEAR-OLD COPILOT AMONG 9 KILLED IN FIERY FLORIDA JET CRASH

11 a.m. - Reaches cruise altitude:

The Learjet reaches cruise altitude at approximately 41,000 feet, according to flight data. No notable events occur for the next hour and a half.

12:31 p.m. - Air Traffic Control spots precipitation:

While the Learjet is around 41,000 feet in the air, an air traffic controller advised the flight crew of moderate precipitation 5 miles away from them, and then said there were options to go to the left or right. The crew was then told to proceed to a waypoint near Naples, Florida.

NTSB FINDS 'NO EVIDENCE' OF MAR-A-LAGO CONNECTION AFTER FLORIDA JET CRASH KILLS NINE PEOPLE

12:32 p.m. - Flight crew asks for a more direct route:

The flight crew asked about proceeding directly toward the Bahamas, which would take them across Florida. Air Traffic Control approved that route, but warned about moderate-to-extreme precipitation along that route and said the turn toward the Bahamas looked poor from a weather standpoint.

12:35 p.m.: Flight crew alters their plan:

The Learjet flight crew altered their plan, and indicated it would turn toward Naples, Florida and then head toward the Bahamas.

FORMER NFL STAR SAYS HE PREVIOUSLY FLEW ON PRIVATE JET THAT CRASHED IN FLORIDA: 'ABSOLUTELY DEVASTATED'

12:36 p.m.: Air Traffic Control instructs descent:

Air Traffic Control instructed the Learjet to descend to 35,000 feet.

12:40 p.m.: Air Traffic Control authorizes deviation:

Air Traffic Control authorized left or right deviations for weather, telling the flight crew they can proceed toward the Bahamas when able to. Tracking indicates the plane headed further north toward Palm Beach County.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

12:47 p.m.: Conditions deteriorate:

The flight crew indicated that weather conditions are deteriorating, reporting to Air Traffic Control that there is icing and turbulence, asking the controller if there's a "better ride" ahead.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

The crew also reported they are beginning to experience precipitation, and asked to climb to 37,000 feet.

'WE THOUGHT WE WOULD DIE': PASSENGERS THROWN INTO CEILING DURING TERRIFYING FLIGHT

12:48 p.m.: Learjet begins climbing, then rapidly descends:

The Learjet climbed to 35,450 feet versus the approved 37,000 feet before rapidly descending. A mayday call was made to Air Traffic Control, as the plane descended at a rate of about 10,000 feet per minute. The descent rate doubled a short period later, increasing to around 20,000 feet per minute.

SEND US A TIP

The controller advised the crew that altitude is at their discretion, and asked what they needed. A short time later, the crew advised Air Traffic Control, "We’re going to crash into the ground."

MAYDAY CALL CAPTURES PILOT'S URGENT WARNING BEFORE AIRCRAFT GOES DOWN OFF COAST

"I'm here with you. Talk to me," the controller said.

12:49 p.m. - The aircraft crashes:

"Holy f–k, we're out of time!" the flight crew could be heard saying before the plane crashed in Greenacres, Florida.

Alan Diehl, a former NTSB investigator, said in an interview with Fox News Digital that once the Learjet lost controlled flight, the pilots likely had almost no meaningful capacity to bring it back under control.

"For all intents and purposes, they were passengers," he said.

The key point here is that they did not have much time…You have literally seconds to respond, and at some point it may have been impossible."

World.title: Alligator sneaks into North Carolina bagel shop, sends owner scrambling in encounter caught on camera
World.content:

A North Carolina bagel shop owner got an unexpected scare when a 3-foot alligator wandered into his business, turning an ordinary afternoon into a wildlife encounter caught on surveillance video.

The reptile entered Bagel Dock Express in Southport on Oct. 29, slipping through an open back door and making its way through the kitchen toward the front counter.

Surveillance video captured owner Jesse Driscoll's startled reaction when he spotted the alligator inside the shop. Driscoll quickly backed away from the animal before calling 911.

BEAR CRASHES COUPLE'S ANNIVERSARY GETAWAY, RUMMAGES THROUGH TENNESSEE TEA SHOP BEFORE JUMPING ON COUNTER

The business was closed to customers at the time, and Driscoll told WWAY News that he had been distracted by workers installing a new oven when the unexpected visitor appeared.

"It's just so far out of the ordinary for a bagel shop," Driscoll told the media outlet.

The shop owner said he was accustomed to seeing familiar faces stop by the business, but an alligator was something he never imagined encountering.

Southport police and Animal Protective Services responded to the business and removed the reptile.

HUGE BULL MOOSE STUCK IN MONTANA SKATE PARK HAD TO BE TRANQUILIZED IN ORDER TO BE RESCUED

The Southport Police Department confirmed the incident in a Facebook post, saying officers worked alongside Animal Protective Services Officer Ward to capture the alligator and relocate it.

Bagel Dock Express also made light of the encounter in a Facebook post, joking that its reputation had apparently reached beyond its usual customers.

FISHERMAN CAPTURES A CRAZY VIDEO OF AN ALLIGATOR CHASING A BEAR ACROSS A FLORIDA RIVER

"Apparently, word of our fresh bagels has made its way into the swamp!" the post's caption began.

"Our surprise visitor was safely escorted out by local law enforcement. No injuries, no drama… just one VERY unusual customer! Fresh bagels. Wild experiences."

In April, officers helped remove a 12-foot alligator from a residential property and another alligator found beneath a car at a bank drive-through.

World.title: HUGH HEWITT: The GOP is wounded, not dead — but recovery has to start now
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The GOP isn’t dead, but it sure does look and feel that way in the harsh light of the day after Tuesday’s walloping.

The myth of Rasputin is that a Russian monk who pretended to mysticism was poisoned, stabbed, shot, beaten and thrown in a river. He somehow climbed out of the drink and survived. He didn’t.

Miraculous recoveries only happen in the movies, as with "Boris the Bullet Dodger" in Guy Ritchie’s beloved "Snatch," which starred Jason Statham, Brad Pitt, Benicio del Toro and Dennis Farina.

CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES

If you are a Republican feeling low after Tuesday night’s nationwide wipeout, "Snatch" is a good viewing choice. If you or your boss lost, you need to have a laugh because there is no crying in baseball or politics. Wipeouts happen, and the GOP isn’t going to suddenly pull itself beaten and bruised out of the Potomac.

But the Republican Party isn’t dead. It’s just beaten badly, and it will take some years to mend. A lesson from the endless rebuild of the Cleveland Browns: There aren’t any shortcuts. You need patience, and you have to build through the draft.

THUNE PLANS TO RUN FOR REPUBLICAN MINORITY LEADER AFTER DEMS' MIDTERM TAKEOVER

The good news: There’s a best player or 10 within every state's political leadership, and it’s up to Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno to cheer up the Senate caucus and get to work recruiting and fielding a team of GOP Senate candidates for 2028. The same must go on within the much smaller House GOP conference.

It’s up to President Trump to make sure the Republican National Committee, in turn, makes sure that the process of selecting his successor nominee is wide-open and robust. Debates between would-be nominees beginning early in 2027 for an Iowa primary in January 2028, with a New Hampshire primary right behind it will be an excellent forum from which many would-be presidents can test messages and themes with the country as a whole.

LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT

President Trump remains the leader of a badly banged-up party, and he’s often been a terrific cheerleader and needs to be so again.

Not like the "Black Knight" in 1975’s "Monty Python and the Holy Grail" — Tuesday night wasn’t a flesh wound. President Trump will study the ugly results carefully. Disasters have their own clarity about them. No need for an autopsy when the cause of death is, well, everything. President Trump’s State of the Union early in 2027 will provide an agenda around which would-be leaders-in-waiting can rally or reject. He and his team should start to work on that immediately. It will matter a great deal.

The greatness of the Republic is its wonderful resilience. The Constitution is terrifically strong, a work of genius that endures. Parties thought dead beyond recovery indeed do come back. That lesson is not ancient history. No need to recall the eclipse of the GOP after Barry Goldwater’s kamikaze presidential run in 1964, which left the GOP with just 32 senators and 140 members in the House. Really.

Republicans under President Reagan lost the Senate majority in 1986 and tumbled to 45 seats. It took eight years to climb back to a majority in the Upper Chamber.

The GOP lost that Senate majority again in 2006, and their hole got deeper during the financial crisis in 2008. When President Obama soared to his landslide and was sworn in in 2009, there were only 41 Republican senators in attendance and 178 GOP House members.

The silver lining — and it is going to need some polishing to gleam — is that the center-right and conservatives have three cycles before the post-2030 Census national redistricting gets underway. If the ongoing counting of election results in the states brings the worst, Democrats will have "trifectas"— where a party controls the governorship and both houses of the legislature— in 21 states, the GOP will have 19, and 10 will enjoy divided government. Expect redrawing of maps in the 40 states with trifectas that have not done so already, and then wait for the mandatory line drawing in 2032 after the Census. American politics is a dance that never ends.

Recovery after a political crash out can be painful, but it’s best undertaken with clear eyes about what ails the GOP body politic. Anyone with a quick remedy or a single villain isn’t comprehending the scale of the rebuke. It isn’t as bad as 2008’s, but that could follow if another Great Recession looms.

The only certainty for President Trump seems to be: Win the battle with Iran and do so quickly and in such a fashion that there are no doubters about who won and how. The Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait must obviously be open to all traffic passing through them unmolested by the remnants of the Iranian terrorist regime. No more ill-conceived MOUs.

President Trump is the only one who matters on the decision about whether or not to win the battle with Iran and win it quickly. If the new Democratic majorities to be seated in January arrive before the battle is over, they will do their best to interfere with President Trump’s constitutional authority as commander in chief.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

So even as he helps his party stand back up, he should pursue the conflict to success. And Republicans smarting from Tuesday night’s beatdown should keep in mind that if you have to choose between running the Congress and having the Presidency, the latter is by far the better choice.

Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting. This column previews the lead story that will drive his radio/ TV show today.
