World.title: Republicans turn on Trump after devastating midterm losses hand Democrats control of Congress
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Seismic political change is coming to Washington, D.C., and as Republicans sift through the wreckage that was Election Night, fingers are pointing in several directions over who’s to blame.

The blue tsunami Tuesday tore the GOP’s coalition asunder, flipping the balance of power in both chambers heading into the final two years of the Trump administration. And as Republicans search for where things went awry, GOP operatives and insiders told Fox News Digital that it starts at the top with President Donald Trump.

"Look, first and foremost, this is a Trump loss," Dan Eberhart, an oil drilling chief executive officer and prominent Republican donor, told Fox News Digital. "He wanted to be — he wanted people to consider him on the ballot. And unfortunately, as a Republican, that's what we got."

LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT

In the Senate, Democrats scored seven pickups on Election Night, with outstanding races in Alaska and Mississippi still waiting to be called. And in the House, Democrats roared back into power with 27 pickups and with several races still outstanding.

The Iran war, ignoring the economic hurt squeezing voters, attacking sitting Republicans and more are on the list of grievances from Republicans reeling in the days after.

The Senate map, in particular, was at one point favorable for Republicans and viewed as an uphill battle for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats to put a dent in the GOP’s thin, 53-seat majority.

But Trump’s decision to go on a "primary revenge tour and antagonizing senators," a GOP aide told Fox News Digital, among several other issues, opened up the field for Democrats to pounce.

Indeed, Trump’s handpicked candidates were pummeled in races that were once safe bets for Republicans.

DEM FLIPS KEY SENATE SEAT IN BATTLEGROUND NORTH CAROLINA AS COOPER DEFEATS TRUMP ALLY

His backing of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., and fight with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., last year that ultimately led to his retirement and created an opening for Democrats in the Tar Heel State, proved fatal for the GOP, coupled with stunning losses in Maine, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa, kneecapped any chances Republicans had of keeping power in the upper chamber.

"Trump ignored affordability completely," another Republican aide told Fox News Digital. "Ousted good members a la Cornyn, Tillis who knew how to win tough races, and poisoned the base’s opinion of our majority with his SAVE Act/filibuster bulls---."

"We had a great map, and he hijacked [it]," they continued.

In the House, where Democrats are on pace to potentially win upward of 250 seats, Fox News Power Rankings projected that Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran were significant drivers for voting blocs leaving the GOP.

TRUMP'S GAMBLE ON KEN PAXTON BACKFIRES AS DEMOCRAT PULLS OFF HISTORIC TEXAS SENATE UPSET

One House Republican complained that GOP leaders were too focused on "bluster" rather than "doing the job," though they did not mention Trump by name.

"All the name changes were so unnecessary — Gulf of America, Lake of America, Department of War," the GOP lawmaker said.

A second House Republican rattled off a lengthy list of shortcomings, including the quality and character of "certain candidates," Trump’s immigration enforcement, tariffs, general affordability issues, historic midterm headwinds, and "departure from traditional conservatism in favor of populism."

Meanwhile, people in Trump’s orbit blamed the candidates themselves.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump outside advisor Alex Bruesewitz posted on X that "most Republican candidates this cycle were uninspiring, lazy, and thoroughly ineffective communicators."

"I’m not all that surprised by some of these outcomes," he said.

Meanwhile, some are expecting a massive shift in Trump’s base of support in Congress as he heads toward a lame duck likely punctuated by investigations and stalled agendas.

"I think Trump being a lame duck starts today," Eberhart said. "You know, if I'm up in the [2028] cycle, I'm waking up today, I'm against the arch. I'm against the ballroom. I want space from Trump."

World.title: Democrats take House and Senate in historic midterm win
World.content: NBC News projects Democrats have won control of the House and Senate in the midterms. NBC News’ Ryan Nobles looks at some of the historic wins in states like Texas and Michigan along with Republican reaction.Nov. 5, 2026

World.title: Democrats won on affordability. Whether they can deliver it is a different story.
World.content:
Democrats won historic electoral victories Tuesday night on a pledge to make life more affordable for Americans, an issue that united voters across political and demographic divides. Now comes the hard part.

An overwhelming majority of midterm voters had a negative view of the economy, with more than 80% saying they were worried about the price of necessities like gas, groceries and healthcare, according to the NBC News Exit Poll. In a reversal from 2024, voters this year said they trusted Democrats on the economy more than they trusted Republicans.

The stunning electoral results on Tuesday night were the culmination of a monthslong effort by Democrats to make the high cost of living a central campaign issue in races across the country up and down the ballot.

From Kansas to South Carolina to Maine, Democratic candidates uniformly seized on and stuck to the topic of inflation, while Republicans sought to redirect voters’ attention to fears of socialism and crime, often laced with Islamophobia.

In the hours after NBC News projected they would capture full control of Congress on Tuesday night, Democrats continued to hammer their affordability message.

In January, Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York is expected to take up the gavel as the first non-white speaker of the House. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty

“We are laser-focused on addressing the affordability crisis that has been crushing everyday Americans,” House Democratic leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Wednesday morning on NBC’s “TODAY” show.

But tackling affordability in Congress is easier said than done.

How it could actually happen

When Democrats take control of both the House and the Senate in January, they have a decent chance of passing legislation that could limit Trump’s tariff authorities or make it more difficult for him to continue to wage war in Iran. They have also discussed legislation to reinstate Republican cuts to healthcare funding.

Any one of these actions, if fully executed, could push down costs for consumers. But that is a big if.

As president, Trump has the authority to veto any legislation passed by Congress. If he does, Democrats don’t have the two-thirds majorities needed in the House and the Senate to override his presidential veto.

Following the Democrats’ wins Tuesday night, however, Trump said he would be willing to work with the opposition party.

The offer was very similar to an olive branch he extended to Democrats during his first term after they won a House majority in 2018.

Ultimately, that failed to produce any meaningful legislation.

This time around, Democrats made a string of economic promises on the campaign trail.

Jeffries, who is considered a front-runner to become the speaker of the House, has said that if Democrats take back the House they will restore Affordable Care Act health insurance tax credits that expired in 2025 and reverse Medicaid cuts and work requirements in Republicans’ 2025 tax bill.

In the Senate, Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said he would like to see the Senate Finance Committee focus on issues like taxes and rising healthcare costs, while investigating banks allegedly involved in Jeffrey Epstein’s sex trafficking crimes.

The optimistic newcomers

“I think we have a mandate to get stuff done,” said Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich. “I ran on getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets and passing ‘Medicare for All.’”

During his campaign, El-Sayed said he would push to make Medicare, the health insurance program for seniors, available for all Americans. He also focused heavily on cost-of-living issues, even as Trump repeatedly attacked his Muslim faith and accused El-Sayed of being a “jihadist.”

Another one of Tuesday night’s big winners, Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, has proposed eliminating tax cuts that benefit the wealthiest households.

He has also proposed lowering costs for middle-class households by offering free pre-K for all 3- and 4-year-olds and expanding a down payment assistance program for first-time homebuyers.

Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton by more than 12 percentage points in Texas. Brandon Bell / Getty Images

Economic inequality, a central message of Talarico’s campaign, was an issue that resonated with midterm voters this cycle.

According to the NBC News Exit Poll, 69% of them believed the U.S. economic system favors the wealthy, while only 31% said it is generally fair.

Other Democratic candidates have proposed pushing to end the war in Iran as a way to help lower gas prices, along with a proposal to suspend the federal gas tax.

Another key Democratic campaign pledge was to limit the construction of new data centers to help curb rising electricity costs.

Talarico said Wednesday that he was open to working with Trump on issues on which they can find common ground, like suspending federal taxes on gas and diesel and cutting red tape to make housing more affordable.

“I agree with the president on the need to legalize marijuana and reform this broken criminal justice system,” Talarico said in a Fox News interview.

“These are just some of the issues that I agree full-heartedly with President Trump, and I look forward to working with him for all 31 million Texans.”

Democrats have pledged to take a different approach to lowering prices than Trump did two years ago when he won the 2024 presidential race.

A cautionary tale

Both Democrats and the president notched their historic victories on the same promise: to bring down the high cost of living.

Trump promised voters cheaper groceries, gas below $2 a gallon and a wave of new manufacturing jobs.

Instead, prices kept rising, wages struggled to keep pace with inflation, and today there are fewer factory workers in America than there were when Trump took office.

While the broader economy has grown at a relatively healthy rate, the gains from that growth have disproportionately flowed to the wealthiest households, leaving most Americans with an increasingly bleak view of their financial situation.

Unemployment has remained low, but there are relatively few new jobs being added outside of a few areas, like healthcare.

Likewise, broader disruptions to global oil markets from the U.S. and Israel’s war on Iran could outlast any temporary pause in active combat.

Diesel fuel costs have climbed by more than 50% this year as President Donald Trump's Iran war has squeezed oil supplies. Graeme Sloan / Bloomberg via Getty

This is not to say that every element of the U.S. economy today is under Trump’s control. The rapid developments in artificial intelligence, for instance, are the result of organic economic forces more than they are of any single policy choice.

But economists are quick to point to Trump’s own policies as primary drivers of the GOP’s current economic quagmire.

The tariffs he campaigned on have pushed up consumer prices, while the uncertainty around them has weighed on the manufacturing sector he pledged to revive.

The U.S. war with Iran has driven up gas prices and reignited fears around inflation, contributing to higher mortgage rates for homebuyers.

Trump did follow through on his promise to cut taxes, which economists see as a bright spot that is helping to fund corporate investments.

Still, some of those tax savings have already been offset by higher prices, according to an analysis by the Washington-based nonprofit Tax Foundation.

While Trump has touted his tax cuts on the midterm campaign trail, he has simultaneously dismissed voters’ concerns about the cost of living.

He has called affordability a “hoax” and blamed high costs on Democrats.

During a rally last month in Georgia, Trump touted the large profits oil companies were making off high gas prices paid by consumers. “We’re making a freaking fortune,” he said.

At another rally in Montana, Trump announced, “We have very little inflation,” before telling supporters that “prices have come way down.”

That speech took place just hours after the Bureau of Labor Statistics had released new data that showed inflation had jumped in September, to 3.7% annually.

World.title: Series of bomb threats cause flight disruptions across Europe
World.content:
LONDON — Bomb and security threats disrupted passenger flights across Europe Thursday, the latest in a series of incidents that have prompted emergency landings and security sweeps this week.

No explosives have so far been found, and it is not clear who or what is behind the calls. But the threats alone have caused disruption to Europe’s airspace and some of its busiest airports.

An Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome carrying more than 150 people was diverted to a French Air Force base earlier Thursday, the airline said.

A bomb squad was at the Évreux-Fauville Air and Space Force base and all 151 passengers and six crew aboard the Aer Lingus flight had been moved to a safe place, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office said in a statement.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki was escorted by Italian Air Force jets to Rome’s Fiumicino Airport “following anonymous reports of a suspected bomb threat,” according to a spokesperson for the city’s airport authority.

“Police bomb disposal experts have initiated security protocols, with safety checks currently underway,” they said.

A ⁠spokesperson for Finnair ​said ​one ⁠of ‌its flights to ‌Rome had ‌landed ⁠as normal after receiving a ‌bomb ​threat.

A second Finnair flight from ⁠Helsinki ⁠landed as ⁠normal in Vienna ​after ⁠receiving a ‌bomb threat, according to a spokesperson for the carrier.

In the Czech Republic, police said they had received threats about improvised explosive devices being place on four planes heading to the country’s capital Prague.

Media outlets in Bulgaria also reported that three aircraft had been forced to make emergency landings due to bomb threats, Reuters reported citing government ministers.

Belgian media also reported that an airliner forced to land at Brussels’ Zaventem airport ⁠belonged to the Polish airline LOT, according to Reuters.

Thursday’s incidents follow days of airline bomb threats that have forced multiple flights to divert and an airport in Poland to briefly close. No explosive devices were found in the earlier incidents, according to authorities in various countries.

A security operation was also launched at the Greek island port ⁠of Syros on Tuesday after a bomb threat ​to an Israel-bound cruise ship. Authorities said an unknown person claimed an explosive device had been attached to ⁠the hull of the Panama-flagged Crown Iris that was due to sail ⁠to Haifa.

Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents and there were no claims of responsibility.

World.title: Muscle health is key to longevity. Here’s how to measure yours.
World.content:
Muscle health is linked to how well we fight off disease and our longevity. But healthy muscles aren’t just about the size of a bicep or how much we weigh.

An international team of kinesiologists and nutrition experts recently urged doctors to pay more attention to skeletal muscle quality and the ratio of muscle to fat as a key to “metabolic regulation, immune function and overall vitality and functioning.”

“Muscle health estimation could be as important as measuring somebody’s blood pressure,” said longevity expert Dr. Nicolaas Deutz, a professor in the Department of Kinesiology and Sport Management at Texas A&M University and a co-author of the expert review. Kinesiology is the study of physical activity and body mechanics.

Healthy muscles not only help you move safely, they’re also the body’s main storage system for blood sugar, which maintains an active metabolism and lowers inflammation in the body.

Muscle health is usually associated with muscle size in younger people, but that relationship becomes less clear as we get older, said Deutz.

In fact, mass is only a part of overall muscle health. For instance, women generally have lower overall muscle mass than men, yet their muscle health is generally comparable to men’s.

A more complete picture of muscle includes strength, balance, physical function, activity levels and the amount of fat stored within the muscle itself, said Dr. Fatima Cody Stanford, an obesity medicine physician-scientist at Mass General Brigham.

How to prevent muscle loss

There’s growing awareness of how muscle health plays a role in longevity and metabolic diseases such as Type 2 diabetes, especially in the wake of the phenomenal popularity of GLP-1 medications. Drugs such as Ozempic and Zepbound have been shown to improve blood sugar, blood pressure and cardiovascular risk, but they’re also linked to loss of both fat and lean mass, including skeletal muscles.

Stanford, who is also associate professor of medicine and pediatrics at Harvard Medical School, said people taking GLP-1s need adequate nutrition to preserve muscle function.

“As a person loses substantial body weight, the body requires less muscle to carry that weight, and reductions in fat within muscle may improve muscle quality and function,” Stanford said. “At the same time, older adults, individuals with frailty or low baseline muscle mass, and people who are losing weight rapidly warrant particularly close attention to strength, function, protein intake and resistance exercise.”

A sufficient amount of high-quality daily protein — including fish, poultry, eggs, dairy, tofu, beans, lentils, nuts and seeds — helps protect against muscle loss, Stanford said.

The U.S. dietary guidelines encourage people to prioritize protein with nutritious, minimally processed foods at every meal, recommending 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight.

Staying active — working in the yard, walking or weight training — strengthens different muscle groups, Deutz said.

If lifting heavy gym weights isn’t appealing, resistance exercises can effectively preserve muscle strength and function, particularly during weight loss.

“Body-weight exercises, resistance bands, machines or supervised strength work can all be appropriate depending on the individual’s mobility, fitness level and medical history,” Stanford said.

How to measure muscle health

Muscle power is the ability to produce force quickly, and handgrip strength is one of the simplest ways to measure it.

“An often-overlooked consideration is muscle power — the ability to produce force quickly, which declines earlier and more rapidly with aging than muscle strength,” said Stephen J. Carter, associate professor in the kinesiology department at the School of Public Health — Bloomington Indiana University. “From a practical perspective, muscle power is more relevant to daily life than simply strength.”

Grip strength measures the force generated when squeezing a handheld tool called a dynamometer.

While “low” strength depends on factors like age and BMI, a large analysis of grip strength of over 20,000 older men and women defined it as less than 57 pounds for men and 35 pounds for women.

Fortunately, targeted resistance training can successfully improve the numbers.

Carter recommended resistance training, such as free weights, weight machines, resistance bands or body-weight exercises like push-ups, two to three times weekly, progressing gradually to a higher intensity to build more muscle.

World.title: Rep. Ro Khanna allies launch a draft campaign for the 2028 presidential race
World.content:
Allies of Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., are launching an effort to lay groundwork for him to run for president, the leaders of a new draft committee told NBC News.

Former Rep. Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y., and progressive strategist Nomiki Konst are co-chairs of the group — “Run Ro” — which can raise money from donors and begin building support for a Khanna candidacy while he continues to weigh a 2028 bid.

The move comes in the immediate aftermath of a midterm election in which voters swept Democrats into power in the House and the Senate, with some high-profile progressives among the big winners. It also comes as the party’s left wing looks for a new champion who can run in the progressive lane that Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., occupied in the 2016 and 2020 presidential nominating contests.

“By launching now, we are trying to ensure that the presidential primary debate is framed from a progressive populist perspective,” Konst said.

The challenges facing a possible Khanna candidacy are immense. Only one person was ever elected to the presidency directly from the House: James Garfield, R-Ohio, in 1880.

Khanna, a fifth-term lawmaker, has made headlines with bipartisan efforts to force the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and to end the war in Iran. He is nonetheless not even the most famous House progressive considering a presidential bid.

That unofficial title belongs to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who hasn’t yet said whether she will seek the presidency, run for a Senate seat in New York or remain in the House.

“She is my sister, and I love her,” Bowman said of Ocasio-Cortez, with whom he shared a close alliance in the House. “Ro Khanna has shown the work ethic, the humility and the vision that we need in this moment.”

Khanna, who was a co-chair of Sanders’ 2020 campaign, is also a favorite of progressives around the country. And he has been traveling to early primary states for months. He makes no effort to hide his presidential ambitions, and many of his colleagues believe he will jump into the race.

He welcomed the draft committee in a statement to NBC News.

“I’m honored that people are encouraging me to run on a platform of Medicare for All, ending foreign wars and taxing the billionaires,” he said. “We need America’s Next New Deal. Whether I run or support someone else is something I will decide with my family after the holidays.”

Konst said the draft committee will allow her and Bowman to organize now so Khanna isn’t late to the game if he does run.

“The centrists organize and strategize early,” she said. “They have their donors, corporate consultants and leaders lined up for years. Building off the lessons of past primaries, our goal is to channel the progressive energy into a vessel for organizing and spreading our winning message early, as we can’t wait for the politics to line up.”

No candidate has yet entered the field for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

World.title: ‘A Watergate-level repudiation’: Ted Cruz weighs in on midterm wave
World.content:
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Wednesday described the historic Democratic sweep in the midterm elections as an “ass-kicking” for Republicans, urging the party to deliver on economic promises in the next cycle.

“It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election, it was a Watergate-level repudiation,” Cruz said on an episode of his podcast, describing the Democratic shift across the country as a “blue tsunami.”

Cruz, who is not up for re-election until 2030, said that “understandably, people were pissed off,” as “Republicans didn’t do enough to address their very real pain.”

He pointed to tariffs’ raising costs and the Iran war’s dragging on for “too long,” adding, “Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high.”

“Too many Republican politicians seem like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care,” he said.

NBC News exit polls found that more than 80% of voters said they were worried about the prices of necessities: gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare.

“We need to listen and respond. We need to champion economic policies that make a real difference in working people’s lives, and we need to deal with the consequences,” Cruz said.

Cruz said he did call his new colleague, Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico, to congratulate him on his victory.

“I will work with Democrats when they’re willing to be reasonable,” he said. “It was a pleasant conversation, and I told him that I looked forward to working with him to try to benefit Texas.”

However, he also said, “Texas will be red again.”

“We have not suddenly become a bunch of tofu-eating, gun-banning, tutu-wearing pinko commie liberals. That ain’t us. Texas is still Texas,” Cruz said. “We will rebuild as a true blue-collar party not by embracing socialism, but by being real free-market conservatives.”

In his own analysis of the elections, Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who lost the GOP Senate primary in May to state Attorney General Ken Paxton, also acknowledged Republicans’ shortcomings on the economy.

In 2024, voters “trusted Mr. Trump and the Republicans over Kamala Harris and the Democrats to protect their pocketbooks,” Cornyn wrote in an op-ed published by The Wall Street Journal.

However, Cornyn also argued that the party “forgot” how to win elections and instead favored “performative politics.”

“When Republicans force voters to choose between policy and personal character, it is unfair to them and suicidal for us,” he wrote. “We know what the American people want because they showed us: a big-tent Republican Party, competent, focused on Americans’ daily concerns, with room for traditional conservatives and MAGA supporters alike.”

Cornyn wrote that “anyone who is willing to turn the page, restore integrity and rebuild our party can count me in.”

Democrats prevailed across the state Tuesday, with Talarico ending 38 years of GOP dominance over the Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa making history as Texas’ first Latina governor and the first Democratic governor in over three decades.

World.title: Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights in a week
World.content:
Paris — At least 15 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act."

British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared over 20 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent.

So far, it remains unclear who, if anyone, is behind any such coordinated action.

An Aer Lingus Airbus A320 plane is seen at Evreux military air base after the flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to France following a bomb threat, Nov. 5, 2026. Gonzalo Fuentes/REUTERS

The flights impacted on Thursday included:

A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. The flight landed safely and all 151 passengers and six crew members deplaned safely, while military bomb defusal teams got to work examining the plane. Flight tracking sites showed that the Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight turning sharply off its trajectory as it approached, and then making several loops before heading toward Evreux.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to the Italian capital by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts, according to Italy's national news agency ANSA. Rome's Leonardo Da Vinci Airport stopped flights for 30 minutes. A second Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by Jettime, landed as normal in Vienna, Reuters reported.

A Wizz Air flight from Milan Malpensa airport to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna after receiving a threat, also according to ANSA. A second Wizz Air flight bound for Bucharest also landed safely after being targeted, Reuters reported Romanian intelligence as saying.

A flight operated by Polish Airlines LOT flying from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels airport following security warnings. According to a statement from the airline, authorities carried out an onboard security check after it landed and "no hazardous or suspicious items were found."

Three other planes, all Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, made emergency landings in Bulgaria Thursday after indications of potential danger on board, according to Bulgarian National Television (BNT). Flights from Madrid and Copenhagen landed at Vasil Levski Airport in the capital, and one from London Stansted diverted to an airport in Plovdiv. Reuters cited the Bulgarian transport ministry as saying no explosives or suspicious items were found on any of the planes.

Officials in Prague said threats were issued against four flights headed to the Czech capital Thursday. Czech police said on X that all four planes landed and were assessed, and no explosives or suspicious devices were discovered.

Italy's national news agency ANSA reported two more flights, scheduled to land Thursday at Milan's Malpensa Airport, landed safely after receiving "bomb alerts." Neither of the flights were diverted. They were Aegean Airlines flight A3552, which departed from Thessaloniki in Greece, and Ryanair flight FR8953, which arrived from Porto, Portugal. Explosives technicians were inspecting the aircraft, ANSA said.

The threats to commercial airliners Thursday came after at least seven other flights across Europe received bomb threats this week that prompted aircraft searches, diversions and in at least one other case an escort by an Italian fighter jet.

Some of the threats have been sent to airlines by email, but the nature of all of the messages has not been confirmed.

Hoaxes, but on an unusual scale

The British government described the incidents in a statement on Tuesday as hoaxes and stressed that the U.K. had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today," according to CBS News' partner network BBC.

Air transport security expert Paul Mason told BBC that threats to passenger planes "don't happen that frequently," making this week's spate of incidents "unusual."

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told the BBC's Radio 5 Live show. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."

"There are a lot of processes" that airline crew members and ground staff go through "to validate the credibility of the threat," he said.

While no individual or group has claimed responsibility for any of this week's threats, and no government or security official has pointed the finger at any, the incidents come amid rising concern in Europe about state actors, chiefly Russia and Iran, orchestrating low-level sabotage operations to undermine security on the continent.

The growing "hybrid warfare" battlefield

In October, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, said security threats facing the U.K. and Europe were evolving, with malicious actors attacking not only things owned and controlled by the government, but also "aiming at people, businesses, communities."

"Russia remains aggressor number one," McCallum said.

"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.

"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."

Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad as the Polish prime minister said suspicious activity was seen on the Russian side, and that the fast security response may have prevented a "serious provocation."

The flight threats also come amid a wave of cyberattacks targeting European grocery store chains' refrigerators and freezers, and even French blood banks. The hacks have forced thousands of pounds of food to be discarded in several countries, but French authorities said security systems prevented the loss of any blood stored in cooling units.

Nobody has claimed responsibility for, or been blamed for the hacks on commercial refrigeration units as of Thursday.

Experts told CBS News earlier this year that Russia and Iran were stepping up efforts to recruit sometimes-unwitting criminals to carry out sabotage attacks, often for small payouts.

MI6 boss McCallum, in his remarks last month, said Iran in particular was "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites" across Europe.

McCallum noted in particular "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but said Iran was also targeting "harder targets, like military sites."

Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.

A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."

Barry Andrews, an Irish Member of the European Parliament, referred to the diverted Aer Lingus flight to Rome on Thursday in a social media post, saying: "This after several hybrid threats and attacks across Europe, and ahead of the major European summit in #Dublin next week. Does anyone still deny Ireland faces serious security threats?"

World.title: Trump's lawyers to argue appeal in "hush money" case
World.content:
More than two years after President Trump was convicted of 34 felonies tied to a 2016 "hush money" payment to an adult film star, his lawyers are set to argue their appeal Thursday in New York.

Mr. Trump's attorneys in the case have changed — one former defense attorney, Todd Blanche, is now U.S. attorney general, and another, Emil Bove III, is a federal judge — but his new team of personal lawyers has continued in filings to echo the arguments he made throughout the trial in 2024.

An Oct. 16 filing by Mr. Trump's attorney Robert Giuffra, the powerful co-chair of the white shoe firm Sullivan & Cromwell, began with a line that Mr. Trump himself frequently said and posted on social media: The case, "should have never been brought."

Lawyers for Mr. Trump and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg will each get 15 minutes to respond to questions from New York's mid-level appeals panel, the Appellate Division, First Department. Each side has indicated that the case is destined for the state's highest court, called the Court of Appeals, and potentially the U.S. Supreme Court.

A unanimous jury convicted Mr. Trump in May 2024 for his part in a scheme to falsify business records related to reimbursements made to Michael Cohen, his attorney at the time. Cohen had paid $130,000 to adult film star Stormy Daniels, days before the 2016 election, in exchange for her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with Mr. Trump years earlier. Mr. Trump has denied the allegations.

The payment, Mr. Trump's attorney argued, should have been subject to federal election laws that they say preempt state prosecutions. They also claim the prosecutors violated presidential immunity and failed to show Mr. Trump had an "intent to defraud."

"The question here is whether the White House statements and strategy introduced at trial in this criminal case—responding to public allegations of personal wrongdoing bearing directly on the President's integrity and fitness for office—were official," Giuffra wrote.

Lawyers for Bragg have characterized the 2016 "hush money" plan as "a conspiracy to defraud the American public and government regulators."

"The criminal charges here arose from [Mr. Trump's] unofficial, non-presidential conduct—as multiple courts have already found," they wrote in a July brief.

The arguments come a week after the death of a judge who was presiding over a yearslong parallel effort by Mr. Trump to move the case from state to criminal court.

The judge, Alvin Hellerstein, repeatedly rejected Mr. Trump's arguments, and was particularly scathing in his response to Mr. Trump's claim that the reimbursements to Cohen were related to his official work as president.

"Reimbursing Cohen for advancing hush money to [Stormy Daniels] cannot be considered the performance of a constitutional duty," Hellerstein wrote. "Falsifying business records to hide such reimbursement, and to transform the reimbursement into a business expense for Trump and income to Cohen, likewise does not relate to a presidential duty."

World.title: Trump library plans on collision course with Democratic Congress
World.content:
As President Trump prepares for the final two years of his presidency, he is expected to devote more attention to his presidential library, which has become a growing destination for money from companies and allies, according to current and former advisers who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"He undoubtedly recognizes that the library development season opens now, and he will go for it," said a senior administration official. A second administration official said that in this lame-duck period Mr. Trump will focus on "all things he can control, which means: Building."

With Democrats taking control of Congress in January after a sweeping victory in the November elections, lawmakers have pledged investigations into the library's finances.

"The donors bankrolling his personal vanity project will have to answer to a new majority in Congress," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, told CBS News.

In March, Mr. Trump shared renderings of a 47-story tower on a donated plot in downtown Miami. It showed golden escalators, a full-size Air Force One and a giant statue of him raising his fist, as he did after surviving an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. But then he told reporters he does not "believe in building libraries or museums" and that the building is "most likely going to be a hotel," a departure from the traditional library his foundation described to the IRS last year.

The Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, a nonprofit, registered in Florida and run by Mr. Trump's son Eric and son-in-law Michael Boulos, will fund the project. The foundation says it expects to raise $950 million by the end of 2027, including $600 million in 2027 alone, according to its October 2025 IRS application, obtained by CBS News. That far outpaces what Mr. Trump's predecessors had raised at this stage.

Tens of millions of dollars have already come from media and tech companies that settled lawsuits with him. The nonprofit is also collecting donations through a payment processing company that has Donald Trump Jr. on its board, according to a fundraising portal page. And Mr. Trump has said the luxury Boeing 747 that Qatar gave the U.S. last year — now in use as Air Force One — would go to the library, though Eric Trump and the White House have since said that plan is not final.

Some of the most recent money has come from people trying to stay in Mr. Trump's good graces. After the president threatened to cut ties with his top political advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair over their consulting work for a pro-Russian party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the two men donated their fees from that work to the library, The New York Post reported.

A week later, The New York Times reported that Mr. Trump had told aides and allies that his former personal lawyer, Alina Habba Mildon, should donate part of a contract worth more than $50 million to his library or another Trump-related entity. Habba Mildon's contract was with a company tied to the family of a Venezuelan businessman Mr. Trump pardoned in January, the outlet reported.

Asked by CBS News whether she planned to donate some of her fees to the library, Habba Mildon responded to the text message with a "haha" reaction. (She removed the reaction seconds later and declined to comment.)

A former Trump adviser, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the library is now where the fundraising action is, with the midterms over and donors already tapped for the America 250 celebrations and the White House ballroom. MAGA Inc., a super PAC run by Mr. Trump's allies, started September with more than $400 million to spend on Republicans in the midterms. Its filing due in December will show how much left it has in cash on hand.

"The library is one of the last few places he can squeeze people for money," the former adviser said. "That's what a businessman does. He just creates opportunities."

Fresh scrutiny of the library is expected after Democrats swept the House and the Senate on Tuesday. Starting in January, Democrats will have the power to subpoena records and compel testimony. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word warning on X to the administration after the election results: "Lawyer up."

"Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," Warren told CBS News, adding that she will be investigating the library "and any wrongdoing will be held accountable."

A rendering of plans for the Trump presidential library. President Trump, via X

The library has already drawn scrutiny over Mr. Trump's stated plan to display the gifted jet. The plane's memorandum of understanding, signed in 2025 by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Qatar's Minister of State for Defense Affairs Soud bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, called it an "unconditional donation." But when questions were raised about the U.S. accepting and using the Qatari plane as Air Force One, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi concluded that the gift could be conditioned on transferring the plane to the library foundation by Jan. 1, 2029, about three weeks before Mr. Trump leaves office.

In August, Eric Trump told NBC News that displaying the plane was "not the plan at the moment," saying a retired Air Force One would be shown instead.

A Qatari official, speaking to CBS News on the condition of anonymity, said what happens to the plane after Mr. Trump leaves office is not Qatar's concern. "This is something the Americans need to deal with," the official said.

The White House referred questions about the library and whether any final decisions have been made about the plane or a hotel to the foundation, which did not respond to requests for comment.

"The Trump Presidential Library will be one of the most magnificent buildings in the world and a living testament to the indelible impact President Trump has made on America and its people," Davis Ingle, a spokesman for the White House, said in a statement.

Tens of millions from companies Mr. Trump sued

There have been two iterations of the library's nonprofit funding structure. The first, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Fund, was incorporated in Florida in December 2024, days after ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward the library to settle a defamation suit over anchor George Stephanopoulos' inaccurate on-air claim that Mr. Trump had been found civilly liable for raping writer E. Jean Carroll. A jury found him liable for sexual abuse.

Other settlements followed. Meta agreed to pay $22 million toward the library over the suspension of Mr. Trump's accounts after the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Elon Musk's X paid $10 million to settle a similar suit by Mr. Trump and other plaintiffs. And Paramount paid $16 million over the editing of a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Paramount reached the settlement before its merger with Skydance Media. The combined company, Skydance, is CBS News' parent company.

By then, the current foundation had been incorporated in Florida in May 2025, listing Eric Trump, Boulos and James Kiley, an attorney who has represented Mr. Trump, as trustees. The original fund was dissolved that September after failing to file a required annual report. Jacob Roth, an attorney who incorporated the first fund, declined to comment.

In March, Sens. Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Rep. Melanie Stansbury asked the four companies for details of their payments. ABC said its $15 million was still in an escrow account held by a law firm representing Mr. Trump, where it had been since December 2024, awaiting release to the foundation. Paramount said it had paid $16 million but did not say to whom. Meta said $22 million had been "designated" for the library but did not say whether or where it was paid, and X, citing confidentiality, did not say how much of its $10 million settlement went there.

Mr. Trump's financial disclosure, filed in June, lists $56.5 million in settlement money from ABC, Meta and Paramount as paid to the foundation. It lists $8 million from X as paid to Mr. Trump himself, without saying whether some funds reached the foundation. The foundation's October 2025 filing with Florida charity regulators, which it labeled a proposed budget, projected $50 million in revenue and about $6 million in spending.

Meta and ABC declined to comment. X did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Skydance referred CBS News to the company's July 2025 statement announcing the settlement, which said the $16 million included the plaintiffs' legal fees and costs and that the remainder would go to Mr. Trump's future presidential library, with nothing paid to him personally.

The settlements are not the only large gifts. SoftBank, the Japanese investment giant, told Congress in July that it gave the foundation $50 million in January to support a library exhibit highlighting U.S.-Japan relations. Two months later, Mr. Trump's Energy Department announced it would lease federal land at a former uranium enrichment plant in Ohio to an affiliate of SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, for a data center campus that the company says will be the world's largest for artificial intelligence.

A spokesperson for the Energy Department said the agency signed its lease agreement with the company on Feb. 26, about a month after SoftBank's donation to the library foundation. They added that a local development group first proposed the project in October 2024, before SoftBank acquired the lease rights in the fall of 2025. SoftBank did not respond to a request for comment.

A library or a hotel?

The library foundation's filings offer few other details about how it operates. When it registered as a charity in Florida, the foundation said its officers did not expect to be paid. But in its application to the IRS, the foundation said it would pay its leaders. It projected spending $400,000 on compensation in 2025, rising to $1.2 million in 2027. The foundation's bylaws say trustees can't be paid, but other roles can come with compensation. Eric Trump is both a trustee and the foundation's president.

The foundation told CBS News it expects to file financial disclosures covering fiscal 2025 by Nov. 15. It did not respond to a question about whether Eric Trump will be paid.

Fundraising for the library is led by Meredith O'Rourke, who has worked with Mr. Trump since 2016.

The foundation also raises money through PSQ Impact, a donation platform run by PublicSquare, a company whose board includes Donald Trump Jr. The foundation's donation page says contributions will "help preserve important archives, promote civic education, and inspire generations to come." Trump Jr. began receiving $42,000 a month in consulting fees from PublicSquare in August 2024, according to Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he was not aware of the fundraising page and had no involvement in it. PublicSquare did not respond to questions about how much has been raised through the donation page or what fee, if any, it is charging for processing.

"This is just one example of many where the Trumps are set to possibly profit off something connected to Donald Trump's presidency," said Zach Everson, a researcher for the progressive consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen.

It remains unclear what form the library will ultimately take. Mr. Trump's suggestion that it could become a hotel is cited in a lawsuit filed in May by Miami residents, a local nonprofit and a Miami Dade College student. They argue that Florida's gift of the 2.63-acre parcel, a former college parking lot, violates a U.S. constitutional provision that bars states from giving the president financial benefits.

The land was appraised at more than $67 million, but the suit cites real estate experts who say its true market value is over $300 million. The plaintiffs note that the state's terms require only that the site include "components of a Presidential library, museum, and/or center" within five years, and do not preclude a hotel.

Other presidential libraries have been built on donated public land. Chicago leased parkland for Mr. Obama's center for $10, and Little Rock used eminent domain to assemble the site for Mr. Clinton's. But Florida conveyed its parcel outright.

The Justice Department has argued that Mr. Trump is immune from the suit. In September, U.S. District Judge Rodolfo Ruiz II, a Trump appointee, halted discovery, writing that the defendants' arguments for dismissal, including presidential immunity, "may prove to be successful." He has not yet ruled on motions to dismiss the case, and a ruling may not come until March, according to Gerald E. Greenberg, a lawyer for the plaintiffs.

If the suit is dismissed, Greenberg said the plaintiffs are likely to appeal.

"This case is really about one of the core anti-corruption provisions," Greenberg told CBS News, saying the founders "understood the dangers of people currying favor with the sovereign by giving him gifts."

"It is extremely disturbing to think of our skyline and our downtown being blighted by this monument to corruption," he added.

World.title: Indiana carries out first of 3 U.S. executions set for Thursday
World.content:
An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two children was executed early Thursday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S.

Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend's house in the Evansville area in 2010.

Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m., according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer.

She said Weisheit's final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words.

Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions Thursday, which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. would be put to death on the same day.

Alabama, Tennessee and Oklahoma conducted executions on Aug. 13.

It would be Florida's 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, matching a record set by the state in 2025, but was the first this year in Indiana.

The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Pike said in a statement dictated to her lawyers and released a month after the botched execution that she's been in pain every moment since she woke up confused in a hospital. "I had not contemplated life beyond that night," she said.

Lawyers wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.

Weisheit's latest objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said it's confident "in our ability to humanely carry out" the execution.

Following the execution, Braun issued a brief statement noting Weisheit's case was reviewed many times by state and federal courts.

"These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence," he said. "Today, Weisheit's sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court."

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said that the execution provided "long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty."

The execution on tap in Florida

In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.

A federal appeals court in 2024 said Guardado, now 64, had received a "full and fair" hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.

Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said that his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.

Alabama's scheduled execution

Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old Taylor with the victims' Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state's third this year.

Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.

"If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today," said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.

The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

World.title: Did Republican efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
World.content:
Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.

But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.

Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:

Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.

As of Wednesday, Republicans had won 24 seats and Democrats had won 14 seats, making Texas a dummymander.

Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Seven Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night, and CBS News estimates another district is likely Democratic. Republicans have only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.

North Carolina

Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of Wednesday, four Democrats had won and CBS News estimated that another five were likely Democratic. Republicans had not yet won any races, with CBS News estimating one race was likely Republican and another four were toss-ups.

If Democrats ultimately win any of the undecided races, North Carolina will be a dummymander.

Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority Black districts that currently have Democratic representatives.

As of Wednesday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates one district is a toss-up and the state's 5th District will be going to a runoff. If Democrats win either of those districts, Louisiana will be a dummymander.

Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled, making Alabama a dummymander.

Tennessee

Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Nashville.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats and Democrats had one. As of Wednesday, Republicans had won six seats and two races were set to go to a runoff, including the newly drawn 9th District in Nashville. If Democrats win one or both districts, Tennessee will be a dummymander.

Florida

Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. As of Wednesday, Republicans had won 16 seats, Democrats had won seven and there were five districts that CBS News estimated were toss-ups. If Democrats win any of the toss-up races, Florida will be a dummymander.

Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew their map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.

Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.

Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held onto their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.

South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Two other races are considered toss-ups.

California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. As of Wednesday, Democrats won in 42 districts, while CBS News estimates another six are likely Democratic. Republicans have won two districts and another two are likely Republican.

Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.

Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.

Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.

Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.

Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won seven seats, Republicans won two and two are considered toss-ups.

Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

World.title: All the House districts that flipped in the midterm elections
World.content:
Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Tuesday by flipping more than two dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep-red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the Northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.

Winners in dozens of races have yet to be projected by CBS News.

Here's a look at the districts that swung from one party to another:

Upsets

In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

Missouri's 2nd District : Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out viewed it as solid-red.

: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps viewed it as solid-red. Indiana's 5th District : Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.

: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024. Kentucky's 6th District : The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.

: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago. Wisconsin's 1st District : Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.

: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September. Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.

Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz of Indiana speaks to reporters outside the speaker's office at the Capitol on April 26, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Rematches

A few Democrats won against Republicans who they'd faced before — in one case, multiple times.

Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria of Virginia speaks as the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol holds its final meeting on Capitol Hill on Dec. 19, 2022. J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Northeastern Battlegrounds

Both parties invested in districts in the Northeast, including seats with a history of swinging from one party to another, and a competitive Pennsylvania seat that was held by an overperforming Republican for a decade.

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania, speaks during a news conference at the Capitol in Washington, D.C. Tierney L. Cross / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Tight Midwestern Districts

A few Midwestern states will have dramatically different congressional delegations starting next year.

Michigan Democrat William Lawrence greets supporters at an election night event on Nov. 3, 2026, in Lansing, Michigan. AP Photo/Kristen Norman

Texas

Republicans in the Lone Star State redrew their House maps last year with the goal of picking up as many as five seats that were held by Democrats. Ultimately, one seat flipped to the GOP, and two red districts were captured by Democrats. The shifts coincided with a slate of statewide Democratic wins in Texas, which elected its first Democratic senator and governor in decades.

Latin Grammy winner and Democratic candidate for Texas' 15th Congressional District, Bobby Pulido, speaks during a joint campaign event in Weslaco, Texas on Oct. 25, 2026. Gabriel V. Cardenas /AFP via Getty Images

California

Voters in California approved their own redistricting plan after Texas redrew its maps, aiming at moving several California seats to the left. Democrats have picked up all five of the seats they had hoped to flip.

Republican Rep. David Valadao of California speaks during the news conference on the Invest to Protect Act on May 12, 2022. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

Other Flips

A handful of other districts changed hands.

World.title: 2 Native American women make history in midterms
World.content:
Two Native American women made history Tuesday night in the 2026 midterm elections, winning a Senate seat and a governorship — both firsts for Native women — as Democrats swept races across the country.

In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.

Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo, was already the first Native American to serve as a Cabinet secretary. She defeated Republican Gregg Hull, former mayor of Rio Rancho, in the race for governor.

Flanagan, an enrolled member of White Earth Nation, defeated Republican Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster and conservative commentator.

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, left, and former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland. Nov. 3, 2026. Getty images

Who are they?

Haaland has notched many firsts. She became the first Native American woman to chair a state political party in 2015 when she was elected to lead the Democratic Party of New Mexico. In 2018, she became one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress, alongside Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas, who was reelected Tuesday. Haaland later served as former President Joe Biden's Interior secretary from 2021 until January 2025.

On the trail, she spoke about raising her daughter alone, selling homemade salsa and relying at times on food stamps.

"My story is a lot like many New Mexicans — humble beginnings," she told a Rio Rancho congregation in October.

Flanagan got her start as an organizer, then served on the Minneapolis School Board and led the Children's Defense Fund Minnesota. She was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives in 2015 and has been lieutenant governor since 2019, where she has helped reshape Minnesota's relationship with the state's 11 tribal nations.

Raised by a single mother in Section 8 housing, Flanagan had childhood asthma that kept her in and out of hospitals. She's been an outspoken supporter of Medicaid, saying that it "saved [her] life."

What do they stand for?

Haaland ran on the cost of living, protecting New Mexico's Universal Child Care program and overhauling its child welfare system. She also blamed President Trump for cuts to federal safety net programs. She has promised to issue an executive order on day one to pause the construction of new large-scale data centers until the state Legislature passes guardrails.

Flanagan drew on her own upbringing to connect with voters who are feeling financially squeezed. She ran as a progressive, backing "Medicare for All" and national paid family and medical leave.

"Minnesota, you just beat Donald Trump again," Flanagan told supporters on Tuesday night at her election watch party in St. Paul, where White Earth leaders played a victory song on a drum.

Why does it matter?

The National Congress of American Indians, the country's oldest and largest association of tribal governments, called the wins historic milestones for Indian Country. Native American women make up approximately 1% of the U.S. population, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, but have long been underrepresented in elected office.

"Long before Native women were welcomed into the halls of government, they were leading our Nations, protecting our families, and shaping the future of Indian Country," NCAI Executive Director Larry Wright Jr. said in a statement to CBS News.

"For young Native girls across Indian Country, these victories send an important message: their voices matter, their leadership is essential, and they belong wherever possibilities are reimagined," said Wright.

He added that he hopes that representation translates into "meaningful progress," in particular, protecting tribal lands and honoring treaty obligations between the U.S. government and tribal nations.

A third Native American woman could soon join Haaland and Flanagan in making history this midterm election. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola, who is Yup'ik, is in a Senate race with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan that remains a toss-up, according to CBS News estimates. The outcome may not be decided until ranked-choice tabulation later this month.

World.title: What comes next as Democrats win House, Senate
World.content: What comes after Democrats' big victory Democrats are set to control both the House and Senate in the new Congress following a series of historic midterm victories. CBS News' Caitlin Huey-Burns reports. More

World.title: Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction
World.content:
Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction

toggle caption i Department of the Interior

This could be a make-or-break week for President Trump's triumphal arch.

For months, the Trump administration has barreled toward his dream of building a 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C.: rubber-stamping and side-stepping various federal reviews, cutting out Congress and announcing imminent construction despite a lack of final approval and an ongoing legal battle.

In May, the entirely Trump-appointed Commission for Fine Arts approved the arch's design — still incomplete at the time. In September, a federal council packed with Trump allies abruptly terminated a historic preservation review that participants had already criticized as rushed.

Sponsor Message

It all comes to a head on Thursday, when the National Capital Planning Commission will meet to consider final approval for the controversial structure. The arch is the only item on the agenda; the meeting will be online-only and is expected to take five hours because of the high volume of public participation.

Nearly 120 concerned citizens have signed up to speak, an unusually high number for such meetings and a symbol of the widespread public opposition. Democratic lawmakers, veterans, historic preservationists and more than 100,000 people have spoken out against the arch in written comments, local protests and previous commission meetings.

Among their many concerns, critics say the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital.

The White House has repeatedly said the arch will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery" and be "one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world."

"It will be one of the great things we've ever done," Trump said from the Reflecting Pool on Monday, giving the arch — alongside several other D.C. construction projects — valuable airtime in his last in-person remarks before the midterm elections.

The planning commission is widely expected to greenlight the arch. It approved preliminary site and building plans over the summer, and its new Trump-appointed chair, Mark Paoletta, expressed his enthusiastic support for the arch in an op-ed published last month. The administration says that after a successful commission vote, all that's needed to break ground is sign-off from its own Department of the Interior.

Sponsor Message

In fact, the government notified a federal judge late last month that, pending those two approvals, "construction could commence as early as" Thursday.

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/Pool/AFP via Getty Images

It filed that notice as part of the ongoing lawsuit brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian who argue the arch is unlawful without approval from Congress. The Trump administration has not sought that, instead citing Congress' century-old authorization of a pair of columns on that traffic circle that were ultimately never built.

The plaintiffs promptly asked District Judge Tanya Chutkan to issue a preliminary injunction before Thursday's meeting to block the administration from "taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction, of any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization" while the case plays out.

A group of advocacy, historic preservation and conservation organizations quickly signed on to a supporting brief. At a hearing last Friday, Chutkan heard from both sides and expressed skepticism about the government's sense of urgency and national security claims. Then, over the weekend, D.C. and Virginia jointly filed their own lawsuit, calling the arch "flagrantly illegal" for a whole host of reasons.

Chutkan has consolidated the two cases, with all eyes on her docket as Thursday's meeting ticks closer.

On Monday, the judge ordered the government to notify the court within one hour of any arch decision by the National Capital Planning Commission, National Park Service and Department of the Interior — and to provide notice within 30 minutes of "any activity related to or in preparation for the construction of an arch on Memorial Circle."

Chutkan's order suggests she may wait to issue a ruling on construction until after the planning commission meeting, which is scheduled to adjourn at 6 p.m. ET.

On Tuesday, the Trump administration asked Chutkan to clarify and to modify her order to require 24 hours' notice instead, explaining that even though its staff is "working diligently (including nights and weekends) on this matter, it takes time for decisions to be communicated through the various chains and then appropriately drafted into a notice suitable for filing with the Court."

Sponsor Message

The plaintiffs responded with their own filings, opposing that request. They compared the situation to that at D.C.'s East Potomac Park, where the government provided the judge in that case less than a full day's notice before cutting down 430 trees during a holiday weekend.

"Indeed, Defendants recently demonstrated just how much they can change the status quo in a matter of 24 hours," the lawyers wrote.

The judge later clarified her wording but kept the timeline the same.
