World.title: Hard truths
World.content:
TUFTON... we must obtain more value from the investments we have already made (Photo: JIS)

THE latest review of Jamaica’s public health sector presents a mixed bag of progress and troubling setbacks, with improvements in infrastructure and staffing overshadowed by soaring medicine costs, weaknesses in primary health care, and persistently high maternal and neonatal deaths.

Most alarming is the finding that complications from non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for nearly four in every five deaths in Jamaica, while too many patients are turning up at hospitals with conditions already at an advanced stage.

The findings are contained in the Jamaica Health Public Expenditure Review, prepared by the World Bank at the request of the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) and the Ministry of Health and Wellness, covering the years 2016 to 2022.

Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton, who presented aspects of the report, along with the Government’s response, to Parliament on Tuesday, did not shy away from the findings, describing the review as “candid” and declaring that the Government accepts its conclusions.

“The review asks how much Jamaica spends on health, how well that money is spent, and what results it buys for our people,” Tufton explained.

He noted that the review measures Jamaica’s progress against the World Bank’s 2017 review, and compares the island’s performance with countries of similar demographic profiles.

He told Parliament that NCDs cause close to 80 per cent of deaths, maternal and neonatal mortality remain too high, and Jamaica’s per capita health expenditure is still below that of comparable countries, including Brazil, Grenada, Guyana, St Lucia, Dominica, Suriname, and Colombia.

Too much of the country’s health care spending, he acknowledged, is also being channelled into expensive late-stage hospital care, while medicine costs have risen rapidly.

“We need more nurses and more doctors in our health centres. And our service level agreements with the regional health authorities are not yet used to their full potential to hold the system accountable,” Tufton acknowledged.

According to the minister, “None of these findings comes as a surprise to the ministry. They validate the internal assessment that the ministry itself undertook, which led to the development of Vision for Health 2030, our 10-year strategic plan.

“That assessment told us that a health system built for acute and infectious disease must be reoriented towards prevention, primary healthcare and the management of chronic illness; that our workforce must grow and be deployed where it is needed most; that our facilities need sustained investment and maintenance; and that we need stronger governance and accountability for results,” said Tufton.

He posited that, working independently, the bank has reached the same conclusions.

“That tells us that we have diagnosed the problem correctly and that we are on the right road,” he said before reminding of the steps the ministry has taken over the past 10 years to address each of the bank’s findings.

“The ministry has not waited. Over the past decade we have acted on each of these fronts,” said Tufton.

On the matter of prevention, he reminded of the ‘Jamaica Moves’ programme launched in 2017 to tackle physical inactivity, poor diet, and the risk factors for NCDs. He also reminded of the ‘Know Your Numbers’ campaign, which encourages Jamaicans to have annual health checks and understand what he values mean for their health status.

On primary care, Tufton said the health and wellness ministry adopted the Primary Health Care Policy and, through the Health Systems Strengthening Programme, with support from the Inter-American Development Bank and the European Union, was upgrading health centres into comprehensive facilities. These include the Greater Portmore Health Centre, and redeveloping Spanish Town Hospital.

“On mothers and children, the Programme for the Reduction of Maternal and Child Mortality strengthened high-dependency and neonatal care in our hospitals; and the Western Child and Adolescent Hospital in Montego Bay, a gift of the People’s Republic of China, will be the first hospital of its kind in the English-speaking Caribbean,” said Tufton.

“On infrastructure, we have rehabilitated the Cornwall Regional Hospital and, following Hurricane Melissa, we are working with the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority to rebuild the Black River, Falmouth, and Noel Holmes hospitals to a more resilient standard,” he added.

Tufton told the Parliament that the National Health Fund (NHF) integrated the NHF Card and the Jamaica Drugs for the Elderly Programme in 2020, simplifying access for patients.

Regarding human resources, he said “The review rightly identifies people as the foundation of any health system.” He said the ministry is focused on training more health care workers, retaining those already employed, and deploying them to primary care and underserved communities.

Tufton argued that the review records real progress, and he asked his fellow lawmakers to note it. He also stressed that Jamaica stands out in the region for the priority it places on health, highlighting that by 2021/22 the ministry’s spending had reached 16 per cent of central government expenditure, a larger share than almost every other Caribbean country.

Tufton also pointed out that the burden on households has fallen as the Government now finances 68 per cent of current health spending, up from below 40 per cent in 2012. He said out-of-pocket payments have fallen to 15 per cent, below the international threshold of 20 per cent.

He also cited investment in health facilities, sharing that capital spending more than doubled in real terms between 2015/16 and 2019/20, while spending on the maintenance and upgrading of facilities rose by 150 per cent.

Additionally, Tufton noted that more Jamaicans were getting their medicines, with NHF prescriptions rising from 1.5 million to 2.7 million, enrolment growing by 86 per cent, and prescription fill rates growing from 85 to 92 per cent.

Tufton said the health workforce has grown, with 1,996 posts for medical officers established since 2016.

“Of note is that there has been a 30 per cent increase in doctors in primary care, in keeping with the reform of primary health care, moving from 338 in 2023 to 432 in 2025.

Arguing that the World Bank’s central message is that money alone is not enough, Tufton said, “We must obtain more value from the investments we have already made”.

Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes latched on to that point, telling Tufton, “As I listened the minister’s presentation, it just drives home the point that we have been making — spending more money on health does not equate to better health care.”

World.title: Utility cables hobble SPARK project
World.content:
President of Greenwood Citizens Association Trevor Burnett, Jr indicates a section of unfinished road in his community.

GREENWOOD, St James — Utility cables have emerged as the latest obstacle delaying the completion of a Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to Our Road Network (SPARK) project in Greenwood, St James.

Contractors have been unable to complete the rehabilitation of just under one-mile of road leading into the community as they await relocation of the underground wires.

“The reason why the Greenwood project has not been completed is that there are some telecommunications cables that are there. We have made requests to the telecommunications company that is responsible for those cables to move them,” minister without portfolio in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Job Creation Robert Morgan, told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

He has responsibility for works.

“We can’t move them because if we move them, then they might get damaged and a large portion of the area would be without telecommunications services,” the minister added.

The Greenwood road is among several in St James earmarked for rehabilitation under the government’s $45-billion SPARK programme. However while other roads — including some on which work began later — have seen varying levels of completion, the Greenwood project remains unfinished.

The incomplete section stretches approximately half-a-kilometre from the community’s entrance off the highway to a section of Greenwood Avenue.

“We are really trying to work with the telecommunications company to remove those cables — I think some of them are fibre-optic cables — so we can finish the road,” Morgan continued.

Work began on the road late last year but the project has been plagued by delays, which the minister acknowledged. While most of the repairs have been done and drainage installed, the last portion has lagged for about six months. China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), the contractor undertaking the project, has completed approximately 90 per cent of the work.

“I know the residents have been challenged. Because initially we had a water line issue where we had to instal new pipes and now that the road is pretty much paved that little section there is a challenge to the residents; so we are working on it,” Morgan assured.

For now, sections of the unfinished road remain open for drainage works, with caution signs placed in the area to alert motorists and pedestrians to potential hazards.

President of the Greenwood Citizens’ Association Trevor Burnett, Jr said he had been given a similar explanation for the delay.

“CHEC came out, I think August 1st, and said they were going to put in a new drain so that we don’t have any more flooding and as they started to dig, Flow cables and fibres underground started to be impacted,” he shared.

“We got Flow involved and so we are waiting on Flow now to complete their leg. They are supposed to move the fibre from underground, temporarily, and put it on poles so that CHEC can get to install the drain,” Burnett, Jr added.

Already concerned about the delay, the association president said he is also worried that there may be additional challenges ahead if the relevant parties fail to properly coordinate their work.

“After they remove the underground cables and put them on the post and CHEC completes their road paving, will Flow have to dig up the road again in order to bury back their fibre?” he asked.

“We need to know if they can work in conjunction with each other. My thought process is that Flow or CHEC would have put in some pipes alongside the drain so that Flow can just insert their fibres inside of it and we have a smooth sailing going forward,” Burnett, Jr explained.

He said he has been seeking answers but had yet to receive any substantial response.

Meanwhile, residents continue to contend with the inconvenience caused by the unfinished project.

“When it rains, it’s horrible, it’s flooded and you can’t get in and out most of the time. Pedestrians have to be using alternative routes, we have to be creating detour roads for pedestrians to go in and out of the community,” Burnett, Jr said.

He said CHEC had placed marl on the road as a temporary measure. However, the recent dry spell has turned the area into a dust bowl for those travelling through the community.

Residents said the situation continued to disrupt their daily lives and urgently needs to be addressed.

“When it rains it’s a problem and when it’s dry, it’s a dust nuisance; every day I have a cold,” complained Madge-Neil Burnett, who owns Greenwood Plaza.

She said the conditions have also affected her business.

“My thing them spoil up. Some of them we clean and sell [but] a lot of it we have to throw them away,” she lamented.

World.title: Bomb threats target at least 12 more European flights
World.content:
According to the BBC, two other flights were diverted Thursday following similar alerts: a Wizz Air plane from Milan to Warsaw, which was diverted to Vienna; and a Ryanair flight from London to Sofia, which was diverted to Plovdiv, Bulgaria.

Finnish carrier Finnair told broadcaster Yle that two of its aircraft — both departing from Helsinki and bound for Rome and Vienna — were subject to police checks after landing following bomb threats. The plane bound for Rome was also escorted by Italian fighter jets.

Another bomb threat affected a flight operated by LOT from Warsaw to Brussels Airport on Thursday morning. Airport spokesperson Ihsane Chioua Lekhli told Belgian newspaper Het Nieuwsblad that police carried out searches and no further security measures were deemed necessary.

Two other Ryanair flights bound for Sofia — one from Copenhagen and the other from Madrid — were also reportedly targeted by bomb threats.

The Czech police said on social media that four flights bound for Prague Airport were also threatened, but officers assessed “the severity of the threats as low.”

Seven passenger aircraft were searched on Monday and Tuesday by authorities in Spain, Poland, Italy and Bulgaria following bomb threats. No explosives were found, but the alerts also led to the temporary closure of Warsaw Chopin Airport.

The risk of someone successfully smuggling a bomb aboard an airplane is low, said Jan-Arwed Richter, CEO of JACDEC, an aviation-safety analysis firm.

“Today there is hardly any thinkable way to get explosives aboard a commercial flight,” he said. “The last real bombing of a flight took place on Oct. 31, 2015 on a flight from Egypt to Russia because of security loopholes and personnel shortcomings that were rectified immediately.”

World.title: ‘Skip the TED talk’: Iran trolls Vance over midterm defeat analysis
World.content:
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf gestures while speaking during a meeting with Iranian and Iraqi business representatives at the Iranian Embassy in Baghdad on August 20, 2026. | Hamed Malekpour/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images

The speaker of Tehran’s parliament jabbed the U.S. vice president for his 614-word missive on X.

A senior Iranian official mocked JD Vance on Thursday for a lengthy social media post in which the U.S. vice president conceded that the American-Israeli war on Iran caused the Republican Party’s midterm election meltdown this week.

“Losing gambler energy, can’t walk away from the table. Boss is prepping the next war phase while America teeters on an Israel-First cliff. Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament, shot back at Vance.

In his screed on X, published less than 24 hours after the Republicans suffered an election wipeout, Vance pointed to four things that needed to happen for voters to return to the party in future ballots.

World.title: ‘Stop using US tech’: EU lawmaker says Starlink service cutoff led to deaths
World.content:
Salla issued her stark warning as a pushback against Brussels’ growing focus on AI adoption over building frontier models in Europe. In her Sept. 16 State of the Union address, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "We do not need to be the ones who develop the frontier technology to be the ones who draw the greatest value from it."

Salla argued that Europe needs frontier models to have "any room in these negotiations," over the direct of artificial development and safety. Leading French frontier lab Mistral has likewise warned that Europe will be shut out from shaping AI without a player leading development of the most advance models.

Salla said building frontier firms also requires capital and a more integrated market. She called for harmonized insolvency and tax rules and cross-border pension-fund investment, citing Danish funds financing weapons development in Romania as an example.

World.title: UN experts warn of Big Tech influence over Ireland’s digital oversight
World.content:
Irish government authorities have long faced criticism for being too lax on tech giants, whose presence is critical to the country's economy. Last year, the appointment of Niamh Sweeney, a former lobbyist for Meta, as Ireland's data protection commissioner reignited criticism from civil society over "the perception and reality of the DPC’s independence."

The privacy regulator and the government have consistently denied any claims of undue influence.

The U.N.'s Special Rapporteur on the Right to Privacy Ana Brian Nougrères and Special Rapporteur on the Independence of Judges and Lawyers Margaret Satterthwaite said the decisions of the Irish DPC "can affect individuals across the European Union," making its independence "particularly important."

"Regulatory authorities must be able to take decisions without undue influence, including from the powerful industries they oversee," they said.

The experts said there are risks associated with having a "revolving door" between regulators and the industries they regulate, and that selection processes to appoint regulators should use "objective, specialized criteria, include impartial selection panels" and "identify potential conflicts of interest before an appointment is made."

“Previous private-sector employment does not automatically compromise independence, but professional relationships, financial interests and continuing obligations require effective scrutiny and, where appropriate, disclosure and recusal safeguards,” the experts said.

World.title: French National Assembly unanimously rejects budget bill
World.content:
A large screen displays the results of a vote during a session of the National Assembly on the first-reading examination of the 2027 draft state budget bill in Paris on November 4, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

The government looks increasingly likely to force through its €43 billion budget squeeze without a parliamentary vote.

PARIS — France's National Assembly unanimously rejected the 2027 state budget bill Wednesday night, in a further sign that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will have a tough time getting through €43 billion in budget savings.

458 lawmakers from both Emmanuel Macron's camp and the opposition voted against the first part of the text that deals with tax income. It had been extensively amended by various groups, resulting in a proposal no one was happy with. The second part of the text, which covers spending, was also struck down as a result. The government's draft budget will now go directly to the Senate where it will be debated from Nov. 20.

The French lower chamber had already rejected the other leg of the 2027 budget, which covers state pensions and the health care system. It will now be discussed in the Senate.

World.title: Farage’s Reform gets serious on defense
World.content:
“We want to come into government with a comprehensive program that we can deliver to the machine, rather than have a flimsy manifesto with a few headline commitments and ask them to work out how to deliver it,” a senior party official told POLITICO. Like others in this article, they were granted anonymity to discuss policy issues.

MacIntyre served in the military for 40 years and retired as a wing commander in the Royal Air Force last week to take up the role.

"Having someone of Angus’ stature and calibre speak for us on defence shows how seriously Reform UK takes protecting the interests of Britain’s military," party leader Nigel Farage said ahead of the announcement.

MacIntyre blamed successive Conservative and Labour governments for underfunding the military.

"Neither can be trusted. Only Reform UK can fix and rebuild our armed forces," he said in the statement.

But the announcement comes more than two years after the last election. Since then, the party surged in opinion polls, leading for many months before recently falling behind Labour after Andy Burnham became prime minister.

World.title: German prosecutors investigate hotel death of Bavarian minister
World.content:
Prosecutors in Germany have opened an investigation into the death of Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria’s deputy prime minister, after his body was found in a Berlin hotel on Wednesday evening.

Authorities in the German capital “have launched a death investigation,” Berlin Police said in a statement. A spokesperson for the Berlin Public Prosecutor’s Office told Bild overnight that there is “currently no initial suspicion of a criminal offense. At this stage, nothing can be ruled out.”

Aiwanger, who was 55 when he died, had served as Bavaria’s deputy minister-president and economy minister since 2018, representing the Free Voters conservative party. He was due to speak at the opening of his party’s new Berlin office. He reportedly told colleagues he felt unwell during the day and stayed in his hotel room.

Aiwanger led the Free Voters party in Bavaria from 2006 and nationally from 2010. Under his leadership, the party, which grew out of local independent voter groups, entered government in Bavaria for the first time in 2018 as the junior partner to the conservative Christian Social Union.

“With Hubert Aiwanger, we lose not only a committed politician and companion, but also a person who had a lasting impact on the political landscape. The Free Voters will continue their work in the spirit of Hubert Aiwanger,” the party said in a statement issued Thursday.

World.title: How to find a job in the age of AI
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping Europe’s job market. The Commission is hoping to do something about that.

Today on the show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Sarah Wheaton discuss the unveiling of Commissioner Roxana Mînzatu’s Education and Skills Package. In it, the EU executive sets out plans to boost vocational education and training for jobs that require physical presence and manual expertise — jobs that AI won’t be as likely to snap up in the future.

Next, the culprit behind this week’s cyberattack on supermarket freezers across Europe remains a mystery. But we explain why cybersecurity experts are looking toward Moscow.

Finally, some MEPs have AI doing their homework — and European Parliament President Roberta Metsola is not happy about it.

World.title: China threatens EU with retaliation as EU mulls “kill-switch” to defend its market
World.content:
China’s ambassador to the EU, Cai Run, threatened on Thursday to retaliate if the EU adopted unilateral measures against Chinese interests.

 

The statement came as the European Commission is working on a new trade defence tool, dubbed a “kill-switch,” that could cut off Chinese access to the EU market in the event of serious market disruption caused by its aggressive trade policies.

“China opposes politicising economic and trade issues, overstretching the concept of security, and resorting to unilateral or maximum pressure,” Cai said.

He added: “If the EU side insists on adopting restrictive and discriminatory measures against China, China will have to take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its interests.”

As the EU faces a record-high trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, Brussels is seeking to protect its market from low-cost Chinese imports, which have surged by 25% over the past year, according to Chinese customs.

Last October, EU leaders tasked the European Commission with developing an instrument that could be rapidly deployed against countries whose political or economic actions have serious repercussions for the EU market.

Franco-German move

EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič told MEPs on Wednesday that the tool should be presented by the end of the year and would allow the EU “to react much faster, even by limiting the exports into the European Union.” He added that it would target “countries which are treating us [the EU] unfairly or which are harming European interests.”

Presented as country-agnostic, the tool would nevertheless directly target Chinese interests, which rely heavily on the EU’s 450 million consumers to sell their excess of production.

France and Germany pushed for such an instrument in early October, as every EU member state now faces a trade deficit with Beijing, with Chinese imports threatening entire sectors of their industries.

The Franco-German move came amid ongoing negotiations between Brussels and Beijing, which had begun the previous June with the aim of rebalancing trade relations. It also came just days before the Commission reached a deal on 9 October to reduce Chinese imports of hybrid cars into the EU.

Since the deal on cars, talks have resumed at a technical level between EU and Chinese officials, with Brussels hoping to replicate such an agreement in other sectors. A new meeting between Šefčovič and China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao is scheduled for March 2027.

Given the urgency of the situation, EU leaders have also asked the Commission to adopt measures, including quotas and tariffs, against Chinese imports in the chemicals and machinery industries, as pressure on the EU market has become unsustainable for European producers.

Šefčovič has repeatedly said that, with thousands of jobs at stake in the EU, the EU-China trade issue had become a political one in Europe, with high expectations among EU citizens.

Despite ongoing talks with China since June, the Commission has continued to impose additional duties on Chinese imports entering the EU following investigations product by product that found Chinese producers were benefiting from unfair pricing or subsidies from China.

This is not the first time China has threatened the EU with countermeasures. It already did so against a bill – the Industrial Accelerator Act - currently under discussion by the EU’s co-legislators seeking to limit access to EU public procurement and impose strict conditions on investments in the EU market, also targeting Beijing without explicitly naming it.

World.title: Leonardo tops €60 billion in orders as defence, drones and space grow
World.content:
Leonardo has received orders exceeding 60 billion euros for the first time, the company said in a statement released on Thursday.

 

"The results for the first nine months of 2026", which also include rising revenues in all the sectors in which the Italian group is active in defence and aerospace, "confirm the soundness of our development path, characterised by financial solidity, a strong commercial proposition, the breadth of our offering and the expansion of our production capacity", said Lorenzo Mariani, Chief Executive Officer and General Manager of Leonardo.

"We are working to further improve our capabilities in order to translate the strength of the order backlog into greater production and delivery capacity", Mariani added, "as required by the current reference scenario".

The 28 per cent increase in orders (compared with the same period last year, to a total of 60.4 billion) and the other results for the first three quarters of this year, approved on Wednesday at a meeting of the Board of Directors, also open up prospects for the immediate future.

"The integration and digitalisation of platforms, the development of industrial partnerships and targeted M&A activity are the foundations of the strategic plan that will make it possible", the head of Leonardo further commented in the company statement (source in Italian), "to play a central role in the new configuration of the international AD&S industry and to strengthen our positioning so we can respond to market developments".

Among the projects pointing in this direction, Mariani explicitly mentioned the one for the new GCAP fighter aircraft, the joint ventures with Rheinmetall and Baykar for new vehicles and drones, the alliance with Airbus and Thales to create a European operator in space and the technological development of the Michelangelo Dome.

The increase in the order backlog was generated in part (by around 6 billion euros) through the acquisition of Iveco Group's Defence division, which Leonardo completed last March.

Leonardo is a listed company in which the Italian state holds a stake through the Ministry of Economy and Finance.

World.title: Poland arrests six suspected of spying for Russia and supplying its military
World.content:
Poland, a key supporter of neighbouring Ukraine in its war against Russia, said on Thursday it had arrested six people suspected of spying for Moscow and supplying its military.

 

Among the detained are five Poles between the ages of 25 and 52, as well as a 37-year-old Russian national, the coordinator of Poland's special services, Tomasz Siemoniak, wrote on X.

Four suspects, including the Russian national, have been charged with espionage and placed in pre-trial detention for three months, Poland's internal security agency (ABW) said.

"The group is believed to have illegally supplied Russia with significant quantities of components for military use, employed in particular in the production of ammunition and weapons systems," they said.

The charges against the group of six also include violations of regulations governing the international trade in goods and technologies of strategic importance for national defence and international security.

A member state of the EU and NATO located on the alliance’s eastern flank, Poland has repeatedly accused Russia of "sabotage" since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Polish territory is the main transit route for Western military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine.

On Tuesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that Poland had foiled a possible provocation during the night at the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Group active since 2023

According to the investigation's findings, the criminal scheme operated from June 2023 until December 2025.

The group's activities extended across Poland, Lithuania and Russia and it was responsible for ordering and purchasing goods, arranging their collection, and transporting them across the border into the Kaliningrad Oblast.

To transport the items, suspects used vehicles equipped with hidden compartments. They then crossed the Polish-Russian border on numerous occasions. However, some of the goods were intercepted by Polish border authorities.

The items traded illegally were ammunition components, including shell casings and projectiles.

According to the prosecutor's office, the total value of the components purchased and transported to Russia exceeded 2 million Polish Złoty (€455,430).

Firefighters walk at the site of a destroyed warehouse after a Russian drone attack in Sofiivska Borshchahivka on the outskirts of Kyiv, 5 November, 2026 AP Photo

Charges for those detained

In addition to the espionage charges, four of the suspects have been charged with acting for the benefit of Russian intelligence against the Republic of Poland.

The Internal Security Agency (ABW) is now conducting further investigation to establish the full extent of the group's activities.

According to Siemoniak, nearly 100 people have been charged as part of espionage and sabotage investigations conducted by the ABW since 1 January 2024.

World.title: Portugal great Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football
World.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he won’t play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men’s all-time international scoring record.

 

It was a sad ending to a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after falling out with coach Jorge Jesus.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team,” the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media.

"I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.”

Portugal plans tribute to 'greatest of all time'

While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina after a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo’s final appearance with Portugal ended up being on 24 September in a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League.

Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn’t plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team’s training camp.

Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo during a Nations League match between Portugal and Wales in Lisbon, 4 September, 2026 AP Photo

Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him.

The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing “deep gratitude and immense admiration” for Ronaldo’s service to the country.

“Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal’s profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!” the federation said.

It said it intends to organise a tribute to Ronaldo “in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much.”

Like Messi, Ronaldo will keep playing at club level, and is expected to finish his club career at the end of this season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

He is in pursuit of his 1,000th career goal and sits on 985. Of those, a record 146 goals came in 234 appearances with Portugal.

World.title: North Korea tells EU to 'mind its own business' after draft UN resolution on human rights
World.content:
North Korea lashed out at the European Union over its draft UN resolution addressing human rights in the country, state media reported on Thursday, telling the bloc to "mind its own business".

 

Pyongyang has long been accused by the United Nations and other critics of widespread rights abuses, including running prison camps and severely restricting freedom of expression and access to information, while little is known about its criminal justice system.

The UN General Assembly has adopted a resolution condemning North Korea's human rights violations every year since 2005.

"The EU submitted again a 'draft resolution' flagrantly distorting the human rights policy and situation of the DPRK," the North's UN mission said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency, referring to the country by the initials of its official name.

The North said the move was a "farce" and a "politically-motivated provocation".

European Union flags flap in the wind outside EU headquarters in Brussels, 4 November, 2026 AP Photo

"Human rights are by no means a monopoly of the West," it said.

"In cities across Europe, from Paris to Brussels where the EU is headquartered, streets are filled with demonstrators from all walks of life demanding such elementary rights as the rights to existence," it added.

"The EU had better mind its own business, instead of hyping up the non-existent 'human rights issues'."

The resolution is expected to be adopted by the UN General Assembly's Third Committee later this month before going to the full assembly for final approval.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights said last year that human rights in North Korea have shown no improvement over the past decade and had in fact worsened in many cases.

World.title: Iran: Flames engulf banner depicting US and Israeli leaders
World.content:
Flames engulfed a huge red banner showing Donald Trump, JD Vance, Benjamin Netanyahu and Steve Witkoff in Tehran's Enghelab Square on Wednesday, as crowds gathered to mark the anniversary of the 1979 US embassy hostage crisis.

 

The four figures were pictured with torn clothes and apparent injuries. Demonstrators marched with portraits of Ali Khamenei and his son Mojtaba, while others displayed caricatures of Trump and Netanyahu, including one depicting the US president as a dog on a leash.

At the former American embassy, crowds chanted "Death to America" and "Death to Israel" and stamped on US and Israeli flags.

The rally followed a Democratic sweep of Congress in the US midterms, although one participant told AP that the election outcome would make little difference to American policy towards Iran.

The annual event commemorates the 1979 hostage crisis, when 52 Americans were detained for 444 days.

World.title: Rheinmetall shares plunge more than 17% after profit warning over order delays
World.content:
Düsseldorf-based Rheinmetall AG saw its shares plunge more than 17% by 10:00 CET on Thursday after the German defence group cut its annual sales and profit margin forecasts.

 

In a statement released on Wednesday evening, the company said it now expects revenue of approximately €13.2bn for 2026, down from its previous forecast of €13.7bn–€14.2bn. The operating margin is expected to reach around 18.5%, down from 19%.

The company said a major German military order under the Arminius project was now unlikely to be placed this year, pushing the associated advance payments and revenue into 2027.

Arminius is Germany’s planned large-scale purchase of Boxer wheeled armoured vehicles, produced by Rheinmetall and fellow defence group KNDS.

Rheinmetall also expects less revenue than planned from newer activities in its weapons and ammunition business, particularly its cooperation with Dutch company Destinus.

Separately, delays in acceptance checks for batches of artillery ammunition will push some revenue into 2027, it said.

The German arms manufacturer still expects positive operating free cash flow for the full year.

This is the second time the defence group has cut its sales forecast this year, following a similar move in August after Germany cancelled the F126 frigate programme. Rheinmetall had expected to secure a major role in the project, and the cancellation reduced its expected annual revenue by €300m. Its operating margin forecast was unchanged in August.

Rheinmetall reports strong quarterly results

For the third quarter, Rheinmetall said it had met expectations, reporting sales up 32% to €3.149bn, compared with €2.308bn in the same quarter a year earlier.

Operating profit in the quarter ended 30 September rose 62% to €553m from €342m, boosting the operating margin to 17.5% from 14.8%.

Order intake stood at €2.893bn, which the company described as a good, although slightly lower, level.

For the first nine months, sales were up 38% to €8.4bn, and operating profit jumped 69% to a record €1.339bn.

The company’s shares have fallen more than 48% since the start of the year, reversing some of the sharp gains of the previous three years.

The wider European defence sector also faced selling pressure on Thursday. At around 10:00 CET, BAE Systems was down more than 4%, Leonardo lost 2.8%%, Thales traded lower by 0.9%, while Babcock and Saab lost 1.3% and 2.7%, respectively.

The falls followed losses on Wednesday amid concerns about tighter scrutiny of US military spending following the Democrats’ election victory. Robert Stallard, an analyst at Vertical Research Partners, predicted greater congressional oversight of defence policy and spending in a note to clients, cited by MarketWatch.

JPMorgan cut its price target for Rheinmetall to €1,150 from €1,350 following the warning, while keeping its “Neutral” rating. Analyst David Perry questioned the longer-term sales outlook for some army products and the targets for joint ventures announced since October 2024. He also warned that the company might have to cut its 2030 targets.

World.title: North Korea tells EU to 'mind its own business' on human rights
World.content:
North Korea's UN mission has lashed out at the European Union over a draft UN resolution. Pyongyang has said the West does not have a monopoly on human rights.

North Korea, responded European Union's draft United Nations resolution on human rights in the country by telling the bloc to "mind its own business," state media reported Thursday.

Pyongyang has long been accused by the UN and human rights advocates of committing human rights violations.

North Korea's UN mission said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency that the move was a "farce" and a "politically motivated provocation."

It said the resolution is "flagrantly distorting it's human rights policy," claiming that human rights are not "a monopoly of the West."

Referring to the protests in Europe, "Streets are filled with demonstrators from all walks of life demanding such elementary rights as the rights to existence," the North Korean mission said.

"The EU had better mind its own business, instead of hyping up the non-existent 'human rights issues,'" it added.

South Korea to co-sponsor the resolution

The UN General Assembly has adopted a resolution condemning North Korea's human rights violations every year since 2005.

According to the South Korean Yonhap News Agency, Seoul has decided to co-sponsor the resolution proposed by the EU.

It is the fifth consecutive year that Seoul has done so, following a break from 2019 to 2021 under the liberal Moon Jae-in government.

The draft text is expected to be adopted by the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly later this month, before being submitted to the UN General Assembly for final approval.

World.title: Poland arrests four over alleged spying for Russia
World.content:
Poland has charged four people with espionage and says they were spying for Moscow. Two more have been accused of shipping military components to Russia.

Polish authorities said Thursday they had arrested six people over alleged military component shipments to Russia, four of whom they charged with espionage.

Investigators said the group illegally supplied Moscow with significant quantities of parts used to manufacture ammunition and weapons systems despite an embargo.

What are the suspects accused of?

Four suspects, including the Russian woman, were charged with espionage and placed in pretrial detention for three months, Poland's Internal Security Agency (ABW) said. The other two are subject to non-custodial restrictions.

All six also face allegations of violating rules governing international trade in goods and technologies of strategic importance to national defense and international security.

"Russia is subject to a strict embargo in this area, and this operation was designed to circumvent it," Siemoniak told reporters.

The suspects are five Poles aged 25 to 52 and a 37-year-old Russian woman, intelligence coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak said.

Why is Poland concerned about Russian operations?

Poland, an EU and NATO member, is a major supporter of Ukraine and the main transit route for Western military and humanitarian aid to the country.

Siemoniak said nearly 100 people had been charged in ABW espionage and sabotage investigations since January 1, 2024.

Warsaw has repeatedly accused Russia of sabotage since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland had foiled a possible provocation at its border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave.

The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Kremlin has consistently denied conducting sabotage operations in NATO countries.

World.title: Finland court jails captain and crew member over Baltic cable sabotage
World.content:
Finland seized the Fitburg freighter last year over the suspected sabotage of cables linking Helsinki and Tallinn. It's one of several incidents of damaged infrastructure in the Baltic since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

A Finnish court on Thursday convicted the Russian captain and a senior crew member of the cargo ship Fitburg for damaging two undersea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland last year.

The Helsinki District Court found the two defendants guilty of "aggravated criminal damage."

It said in a statement that they had intentionally dragged the ship's anchor along the seabed for around 130 kilometers (81 miles).

The captain was sentenced to three and a half years in jail, while the crew member, an Azerbaijani citizen, was sentenced to two years and 10 months.

They were also ordered to jointly pay around €1.9 million ($2.1 million) in damages, the Reuters news agency reported, with the captain to pay about €85,000 more.

The defendants denied any wrongdoing and have challenged Finland's jurisdiction in the case.

What else do we know about the Fitburg freighter?

Finnish authorities seized the vessel on December 31 on suspicion that it had damaged cables linking Finland's capital, Helsinki, and Tallinn, Estonia.

Finnish police at the time said the ship had been dragging its anchor for hours when it was discovered.

The Fitburg and its 14-member crew had been en route to the port of Haifa, Israel, from the Russian city of St. Petersburg when the incident occurred.

Finland has stepped up efforts to protect its undersea infrastructure following a series of incidents involving cables and pipelines in the Baltic Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

World.title: Several European flights receive bomb threats, some divert
World.content:
Several flights across Europe have either diverted or landed with a military escort after bomb or security threats. The first reported case involved a flight from Dublin to Rome landing outside Paris; more soon followed.

Several commercial flights made either unscheduled or high-alert landings in Austria, France, Italy, Belgium, Czechia and Bulgaria, according to authorities in the various countries.

Planes made unscheduled landings in Evreux, France; in Vienna, Austria; and in Bulgaria. A flight from Finland landed in Rome as scheduled but with a military escort, and another landed in Brussels amid a security threat.

The incident in France became public knowledge first, but the other similar reports soon followed.

This follows bomb threats leveled against several European flights earlier this week, prompting a series of similar unscheduled landings.

Tuesday's incidents turned out to be hoaxes, and preliminary information shows no sign of dangerous materials in Thursday's threats has been reported as yet.

What happened in the subsequent alerts across Europe?

Finland's Finnair carrier reported that two planes landed at their scheduled destinations but amid security scares.

One Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome landed with a military escort, according to Italian news agency ANSA. Another plane from the Finnish capital, operated by Jettime, also landed in Vienna as scheduled.

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw made an unscheduled landing in Vienna.

Bulgaria reported three aircraft making emergency landings because of bomb threats.

Three Ryanair flights to Sofia — from Copenhagen, Madrid and London Stansted — also all landed under high alert. Two of them touched down in Sofia as scheduled and one diverted to Plovdiv, the airport's CEO said.

The Bulgarian threats concerned Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, two of which landed in Sofia and one in Plovdiv Image: Stoyan Nenov/REUTERS

Polish carrier LOT also confirmed Belgian reports that one of its planes was landing as scheduled in Brussels after receiving a security alert, but it said cabin crew conducted a routine inspection and had found no sign of a concrete threat.

Police in the Czech Republic later said that they were preparing officials at Prague airport for four landings after threats of improvised explosive devices being on board.

"We assess the relevance of the threats as low," police said. "Nevertheless, we do not underestimate the threat, which is why all necessary security measures have been activated with the least possible impact on passengers and airport operations."

Police said the planes would be swept for dangerous materials on landing.

What do we know about the first incident outside Paris?

An Airbus A320 plane has been diverted to the Evreux airbase to the west of Paris following a bomb threat.

The office of French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced the incident on Thursday, saying it was monitoring the situation "in real time."

The flight was headed from Dublin, Ireland, to the Italian capital of Rome.

Tracking websites showed the plane, part of the Aer Lingus fleet, sharply deviating its course as it was around Paris' airspace and heading towards the more isolated airfield in Evreux.

France's air force said that it dispatched planes "as soon as the incident was reported."

"The aircraft has been diverted and is being escorted to Evreux airfield," it said.

Lecornu's office subsequently confirmed that the plane, part of the Aer Lingus fleet, had landed safely at the airfield.

The Evreux airbase in northeastern France, not far from Paris, is typically used for military purposes not commercial flights [FILE: July 9, 2025] Image: JP Pariente/SIPA/picture alliance

What happened during the earlier disruptions?

The prior threats to commercial flights this week turned out to be hoaxes that nevertheless caused diversions and major security mobilizations.

In one case, the Italian air force escorted a plane to its emergency landing.

The threats targeted airlines including Poland's LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair.

While it's not yet clear if there is a link, these disruptions to commercial aviation also coincided with a series of apparent cyberattacks targeting freezer units in major supermarkets and even French bloodbanks.

All the cases remain nascent, but have the potential hallmarks of so-called hybrid attacks designed to cause maximum disruption with minimal effort and resources.

This is a developing story, more to follow.

World.title: South Korea tests Arctic shipping route amid Russia-West row
World.content:
For South Korean ships, navigating off north coast of Russia dramatically reduces travel time to Europe, but the pro-Ukraine coalition might see it as undermining their efforts to isolate Moscow.

A South Korean container ship completed a voyage to Western Europe through the Arctic Ocean off the northern coast of Russia in October, fueling Seoul's hopes of exploiting the route as a shortcut for trade.

The ship made the round trip from Busan to Rotterdam in just 50 days, saving at least 10 days compared to the fastest travel times along the more commonly used Suez Canal route. The Northern Sea Route (NSR) is not only around 7,000 kilometers (4,350 miles) shorter, it also avoids the geopolitical flashpoint of the Middle East.

But the faster delivery times might not exactly trigger celebrations across western European capitals.

Cargo ship PanStar Acro left from South Korean port hub of Busan in August Image: Jung Yeon-je/AFP

Analysts say the nations arrayed against Russia over its invasion of Ukraine fear that South Korean President Lee Jae-myung is looking to boost Seoul's economic relations with Moscow. This would run contrary to the efforts to cut off Russia made by Kyiv and its Western alies.

One of the reasons for South Korea testing the Arctic route is its undoubtedly large economic potential. But analysts told DW that Seoul also hopes that, by having a working relationship with the Russian regime, they could sway its leader Vladimir Putin against providing more weapons to North Korea.

Lee's government, they suggest, will need to navigate the geopolitical waters extremely carefully.

Climate change opening up NSR

The container vessel PanStar Acro left the South Korean port of Busan on August 22 and navigated around Russia to reach the southern British port of Felixstowe, then continued its journey by sailing to Rotterdam in the Netherlands and Gdansk in Poland, before heading back along the NSR.

PanStar Acro is not an ice breaker, but it has some ice-resistant design features Image: Yonhap News Agency/REUTERS

For decades, the NSR was impassable due to the North Pole ice cover. With the ice in retreat due to climate change, navigation is becoming possible, although commercial ships often need to be accompanied by an ice-breaker vessel at certain times of year.

According to the Arctic Council, an international body which includes the US, Russia, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Iceland, last year saw a record 1,812 vessels operating in the Arctic. That marks an increase of 40% compared to 2013.

The NSR "presents significant economic potential" for South Korea by linking it more closely to the key markets of Europe while bypassing the challenging waters of the northwest Indian Ocean, said Joseph Kristanto, a maritime security analyst at Singapore's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

"In addition to potentially lowering shipping costs and transit times, the route's development could strengthen Busan's position as a regional maritime hub and create opportunities for South Korea's shipbuilding sector."

European Union unveils new Arctic strategy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Lee government has outlined plans for regular commercial services on the NSR by 2030, with the first Korean ship to complete the voyage merely a test of the logistics.

Fears of 'strategic dependency'

The danger, however, is that by developing the NSR as South Korea's favored route to Europe, "it could introduce a new form of strategic dependency on Russia as Moscow exercises considerable control over navigation along its Arctic coastline," said Kristanto.

"From the European perspective, closer economic engagement with Russia risks undermining efforts to isolate Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine."

Kristanto pointed out that Moscow could apply pressure through regulations and "the provision of icebreaker assistance.”

The analyst also said that European diplomats' concerns over Seoul's recent engagement with Moscow go beyond the NSR and include the alleged delivery of around 165,000 tons of fuel — aboard sanctioned Russian tankers — to Russia in August.

All of this is happening as Pyongyang, Seoul's archrival, is sending troops to help Russia in its war against Ukraine.

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Was Seoul's row with Kyiv a calculated move?

"South Korea is very interested in accessing the NSR as climate change means that a route that was previously impossible to use is now accessible and makes perfect economic sense," said Andrei Lankov, a Russian-born professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University.

At the same time, Seoul is "trying to send signals to the Russian government that it is willing to manage relations," he added.

It also coincides with Seoul taking a firmer stance against Ukraine, a position that dates back to September, when President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the UN General Assembly and confirmed that two North Koreans who had been taken prisoner in Ukraine had been moved to South Korea. Seoul reacted angrily and claimed that Zelenskyy had violated an agreement to keep the transfer of the two POWs secret.

Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The dispute degenerated into a major diplomatic spat, with Seoul demanding apologies and ultimately withdrawing a number of its diplomats from Kyiv.

Lankov believes the row may have been somewhat performative on Seoul's part as it allowed Lee's administration to distance itself from Kyiv and resist pressure to provide material help to Ukraine. He said this stance would have been appreciated in Moscow.

"And then Russia could reciprocate by not providing North Korea with advanced and dangerous military technology," Lankov added.

Korea keeps low profile while waiting for Ukraine war to end

"Right now, South Korea wants to fly under the radar, to examine the possibilities and be prepared for when the war is over, and sanctions on Russia are lifted in the future," said Lankov. "That's the economic plan, but they are also hoping that by working with Moscow they can halt the transfer of more weapons to the North."

Kristanto also expects Seoul to "pursue a cautious and incremental approach."

"Seoul is unlikely to abandon the initiative altogether, particularly given growing Chinese interest in Arctic shipping, but it will also seek to avoid unnecessarily antagonizing its Western partners," he said.

"Ultimately, South Korea is not necessarily choosing between Russia and the West, but attempting to preserve a potentially valuable economic opportunity without compromising its more fundamental strategic relationships."

World.title: Germany news: Deportations on the decline
World.content:
11/05/2026 November 5, 2026 Government reaches deal for public ownership of tank manufacturer — report

A German Leopard 2 A6 tank Image: Christoph Hardt/Panama Pictures/picture alliance

Business daily Handelsblatt has reported that the federal government has reached a deal with the KNDS defense firm for a takeover of the German part of the business by the state.

Although headquartered in the Netherlands, KNDS is a holding company for French weapons maker Nexter and the German defense company Krauss-Maffei Wegmann (KMW).

Up until now, KMW, a major tank manufacturer, has been family-owned and controlled.

Handelsblatt said it had received a copy of an agreement, labeled "confidential," which states that the German government will now have a 50% stake in the business.

The deal has long been in the works, but this was the first confirmation that negotiations were finished.

World.title: France braces for fresh protests as unions strike over higher wages
World.content:
Unions representing the education sector, rail employees, public hospitals and postal services called the strike. Authorities have deployed some 70,000 police and security officers across the country.

Hundreds of thousands of people were expected to march in French cities on Thursday, as public workers staged a strike alongside protesting students.

The mobilization, called by trade unions seeking higher wages, comes after demonstrations over education and the rising cost of living on October 17 triggered some of the worst rioting France has seen in years.

Police were out in force for Thursday's protests, with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announcing around 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country.

Unions said that around 260 rallies were planned nationwide. Authorities estimated some 500,000 to 700,000 people would take part in the demonstrations, including about 80,000 in the capital, Paris.

As part of Thursday's demonstrations, French high school students staged a sit-in in front of the Lycee Henri IV high school in Paris Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

Protests in Marseille, Lyon, Paris

Demonstrations kicked off in the southern cities of Marseille and Lyon, and Nantes in the west, on Thursday morning. Reuters reported police had fired tear gas at protesters in Lyon.

Meanwhile, authorities in the western region of Brittany said "masked individuals" had tried to block roads in the city of Rennes.

The main protest in Paris was scheduled to begin at 2 p.m. local time (1300 GMT).

Reuters reported that high school students and other protesters had already faced off against riot police in the French capital on Thursday morning after they blocked a street with rubbish bins.

Who is striking on Thursday?

Public and private education unions have called for staff to walk off the job, as well as unions representing rail workers, public hospitals and postal services.

They are demanding an increase in the minimum wage, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people.

The Education Ministry said 17.5% of ​primary school teachers were expected to strike. French power unions were also to join the action, state-owned utility EDF said.

Media reports said state railway operator SNCF expected only minor disruptions to long-distance services. It was not immediately clear to what extent a strike called by air traffic controllers could disrupt air traffic.

France has seen frequent nationwide protests over the cost of living in recent weeks Image: Christophe Archambault/AFP

Among those joining Thursday's marches are students who have been protesting for weeks over deteriorating learning conditions. Those demonstrations have grown to include widespread anger over high living costs and inequality.

Although the recent student-led protests have largely been peaceful, some saw clashes with police, with officers using tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds, as well as rioting and looting.
