World.title: Polish journalist held at Ukraine border and handed three-year entry ban
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A prominent Polish journalist and commentator, Łukasz Warzecha, has been prevented from entering Ukraine and handed a three-year ban on crossing into the country. Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”. Polish journalist Łukasz Warzecha was travelling to Kyiv on a study visit jointly organised by Poland’s @MieroszewskiPL Centre and the Ukrainian Institute @UA_Institute an institution affiliated with Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. According to head of @MieroszewskiPL Dr Łukasz… https://t.co/Tawp2hEJ5u — Sławomir Dębski (@SlawomirDebski) November 2, 2026 Warzecha had been due to join a study visit to Ukraine for Polish journalists organised by the Mieroszewski Centre, a Polish state institution, and the Ukraine Institute, a Ukrainian public body affiliated with the foreign ministry. The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection. However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years. Proszę państwa, oto miś. Miś jest bardzo grzeczny dziś. pic.twitter.com/aVEUnkGhM7 — Łukasz Warzecha (@lkwarzecha) November 3, 2026 Adamski revealed that his organisation had sought to intervene with the foreign ministries of both countries, but to no avail. Warzecha said on social media that he had been told the decision, which was issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), was made due to “security reasons”. Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”. At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha. In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream. Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively. However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians. OKŁADKA "Do Rzeczy" nr 35: Ukrainizacja Polski. Raport "Do Rzeczy" o groźnym procesie pic.twitter.com/SUYy1GhIat — DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) August 25, 2024 Speaking to Do Rzeczy after the ban against him was issued, Warzecha said he had “wanted to confront my own views with open-minded politicians and opinion leaders in Ukraine. Unfortunately I was not given the opportunity to do so”. Ukraine’s decision was criticised by Andrzej Śliwka, an MP from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. He asked if Warzecha had been banned “because he dared to criticise Ukrainian corruption, the confrontational policy toward Poland, and the distortion of history”. “One can agree with editor Warzecha or not, but such a decision demands explanations and a firm response from Polish authorities,” wrote Śliwka. At the time of writing, Poland’s government had not commented on the case. Polski dziennikarz, red. Łukasz Warzecha, otrzymuje od ukraińskich służb trzyletni zakaz wjazdu na Ukrainę. Dlaczego? Czy dlatego, że odważył się krytykować ukraińską korupcję, konfrontacyjną politykę wobec Polski i zakłamywanie historii? Można zgadzać się z red. Warzechą albo… https://t.co/JvuhLL9O8F — Andrzej Śliwka 🇵🇱 (@SliwkaAndrzej) November 2, 2026 Adamski said that the visit to Ukraine had been arranged specifically with the aim of “representing diverse editorial perspectives”. The Mieroszewski Centre last month arranged a similar visit for Ukrainian journalists to Poland. The aim was “to enable Polish journalists to gain direct knowledge of the situation in Ukraine, engage in conversations with representatives of various communities, and achieve a better understanding of the challenges facing Ukrainian society”, wrote Adamski. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, there have also been regular tensions between the two countries, in particular over their difficult shared histories. This year has seen the two sides clash over the unresolved issue of large-scale massacres during World War Two. World.title: Polish ambassador to UN becomes third envoy to resign amid crisis over constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw. All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS. Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation. All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 2, 2026 On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021. Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively. While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK. Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau. Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022. On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS. Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”. The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court. It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government. Święczkowski has also been supported by Nawrocki, who dramatically entered the court in the early hours of Saturday morning, clashing physically and verbally with the self-proclaimed acting head of the court, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own. The current government, a broad coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, does not recognise the TK due to those illegitimate judges and has ignored its rulings since replacing PiS in power in December 2023. This year, Tusk’s coalition began appointing judges to fill vacancies on the court. It has condemned Nawrocki and Święczkowski for refusing to accept those judges, saying that their actions are unlawful. Given those circumstances, Tusk and his government have argued that tough action is necessary to restore the legitimacy of the TK. On Saturday evening, Tusk gave an address to the nation declaring that there can be “no compromise” over the rule of law. "On some issues, there can be no compromise," declared Prime Minister @donaldtusk in an address to the nation on the crisis around the constitutional court. He condemned the actions of President Karol Nawrocki, accusing him of "intimidating judges" https://t.co/RPyt87mcFO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 However, a number of legal experts – including many who were highly critical of PiS’s policies towards the TK and other courts – have expressed doubts over the manner in which Korwin-Piotrowska and her colleagues have sought to take control of the tribunal. Further developments are expected on Tuesday, when Korwin-Piotrowska has called a general assembly of the tribunal. However, it is uncertain that she will obtain the necessary quorum of 10 judges normally required for the assembly to be valid. While the eight judges appointed by the ruling coalition this year are all expected to attend, those appointed under the PiS government appear likely not to. World.title: Poland launches operation along Russian border in response to reports of planned sabotage
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish police have launched a special operation to secure the area along the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. The operation – which has involved sending additional officers, including counter-terrorism forces, to the northeastern Podlasie and Warmia-Masuria provinces – was first reported by broadcaster RMF and confirmed by the national police chief, Marek Boroń. “Police are putting security measures in place around the Kaliningrad region in anticipation of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage,” he told RMF. “This is based on information we also have from external security services.” “We are responsible for ensuring the safety of the citizens living there, as well as for facilities and any situations that may pose a threat to society,” he added, noting that the police were coordinating their operation with the army, border guard and security services. RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups. In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”. That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region. A spokeswoman for the police headquarters, Katarzyna Nowak, told broadcaster TVN that they were unable to provide any further information on the nature of the operation as the details are confidential. W Komendzie Głównej Policji powstał sztab operacji specjalnej prowadzonej w Warmińsko-Mazurskiem i na Podlasiu przez policję przy współpracy wojska, straży granicznej i służb specjalnych – mówi dziennikarzowi RMF FM Krzysztofowi Zasadzie szef KGP Marek Boroń. Chodzi o działania… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) November 2, 2026 On Thursday last week, the deputy police commander, Tomasz Michułka, issued an order for officers to be on “full readiness” between 2 and 8 November due to the “operational situation across the country”. Some had interpreted that order as related to the situation around the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw, where riot police were called in on Friday to secure the court amid protests against an attempt by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the TK. However, on Friday night, the police issued a statement “emphatically denying” that the order had anything to do with the situation at the TK. They said that it was, in fact, “related to the current threats regarding acts of sabotage and subversion”. The following day, Boroń himself wrote to police officers confirming that Thursday’s order had been issued in response to “attempts to destabilise our country by foreign intelligence services from the east”. List Komendanta Głównego Policji do funkcjonariuszy pic.twitter.com/3jTMdme1bz — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) November 1, 2026 Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism identified Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Those operations have included an arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and an attempt to derail a train. In September this year, a Russian military helicopter crossed the border from Kaliningrad and remained in Polish airspace for around 42 seconds before returning. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace from Ukraine before landing in a field in eastern Poland. The Polish government has regularly warned in recent months that Moscow is planning further provocations against eastern NATO member states, including potential border violations. World.title: American Man Suspected of Racist Assault at Prague’s Želivského Stop
World.content:
Police are investigating an alleged racist assault at the Želivského tram and metro stop in Prague’s Vinohrady district after an English-speaking man reportedly attacked a passerby and damaged his phone.

The suspect has since been identified, although police have not confirmed reports linking him to an American previously detained in Russia.

The incident took place on the morning of November 4 on Vinohradská Street, close to the Želivského stop.



According to the victim, an Arab man who has lived in the Czech Republic for several years, the confrontation began when a stranger started shouting racist remarks in public.

The man allegedly called for the deaths of Black people, Jews and Arabs.

The victim challenged the statements, telling the stranger that racist abuse and threats against people because of their background were unacceptable.

He then began recording the encounter on his mobile phone, fearing that the situation could turn violent.

“I started recording in case I was attacked—and, unfortunately, that is exactly what happened,” he later wrote in the Facebook group Vinohradská parta.

Footage of the confrontation shows the alleged attacker directing insults at the victim. At one point, he raises his phone and says, “Hello, Trump?” He also appears to threaten the other man with death before the confrontation turns physical.

The suspect then allegedly grabbed the victim’s mobile phone and threw it into the road. According to the victim, the device was struck by a passing truck. Although he managed to recover it, the phone was damaged.

The victim said he had reported the incident to the police and called on local residents to help identify the alleged attacker.

“I am dealing with this through the police, but the perpetrator has vanished. Let’s find him and show that violence and racism have no place in Vinohrady,” he wrote.

The original Facebook post containing the video was subsequently removed. The victim suggested that its disappearance might have been connected to the ongoing police investigation.

Police later confirmed that they were dealing with the case as a suspected criminal offence.

“We are handling the matter as a suspected criminal offense, and we have identified the suspect,” police spokesperson Eva Kropáčová told Czech tabloid Blesk.

Suspect reportedly linked to Russia

The investigation has also raised questions about the man’s identity.

The suspect could be an American citizen who previously faced criminal proceedings in Russia and was ordered by a Russian court to undergo compulsory psychiatric treatment.

The man was reportedly accused of assaulting a female police officer in Russia. Media reports have also suggested that he holds Czech citizenship and travelled from Russia to Prague, where he is currently staying.

However, Czech police have not confirmed whether the individual identified in connection with the Želivského incident is the same American mentioned in the Russian case.

World.title: Fake Apartments and Rental Scams Target Students in Prague, Police Warns
World.content:
Prague Police are warning about a growing number of rental fraud cases, with international students among the groups most vulnerable to fake apartment listings.

Leaving everything you know behind is the beginning of a new chapter. A new city. A new home. A new life.

After weeks of searching, you finally have the keys to your apartment in Prague. You climb the stairs of an old building, find the right door and put the key in the lock.

But it will not turn.

You try again. You check the address, look at the contract and reread your messages with the supposed landlord. Everything appears to be in order, except for one crucial detail: the apartment was never yours.

The address exists. The building is real. But the home you thought you had rented does not belong to you.



A Key That Opens No Doors

Rental scams are an increasingly common problem in Prague’s housing market, with international students among the most vulnerable targets.

Many arrive in the Czech capital without knowing the local rental system or having the opportunity to view an apartment in person. The pressure to secure accommodation before the start of the academic year can also make students more vulnerable to convincing-looking fraudulent listings.

In 2024, Czechia ranked ninth among Erasmus+ programme countries for incoming higher education mobility, with approximately 17,000 arrivals, according to Dům zahraniční spolupráce.

The growing number of international students in Prague has also increased the demand for accommodation.

Charles University, one of the city’s largest universities, has repeatedly warned prospective international students about rental fraud. According to its 2024 annual report, the university had 11,455 international students from 139 countries, out of a total student population of more than 54,000.

The university advises students to watch out for several warning signs, including requests for deposits or other payments before a contract has been signed, pressure to finalise an agreement unusually quickly, and landlords who claim to be living abroad.

Offers that appear too good to be true should also raise suspicion.

Three Cases, Nearly CZK 150,000 in Losses

Prague Police have also warned about an increasing number of rental fraud cases involving apartments.

In mid-January, three cases were reported within a single week, resulting in combined losses of nearly CZK 150,000, or approximately €6,000.

One increasingly common method involves collecting deposits from prospective tenants for apartments that are never actually rented out. In some cases, fraudsters advertise properties they do not own or have no right to rent.

Police have not ruled out the possibility that the suspect involved in the January cases may be connected to other similar incidents, meaning the number of victims could be higher.

For international students, the consequences can be particularly severe.

Police and universities therefore advise prospective tenants to verify listings carefully, avoid sending money before signing a contract and viewing the property, and remain cautious of unusually cheap offers or landlords who create pressure to pay quickly.

World.title: Frank Sinatra & Friends Live Show Brings Las Vegas Classics to Prague
World.content:
Fans of Frank Sinatra and the golden age of Las Vegas entertainment will have a chance to relive the era this Christmas.

The Frank Sinatra & Friends Live Show will arrive in Prague on December 29, bringing its tribute to the legendary Rat Pack to O2 Universum.



Originally created to mark the 100th anniversary of Frank Sinatra’s birth, the international production features Stephen Triffitt, George Daniel Long and Mark Adams, three performers known for their portrayals of Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and Sammy Davis Jr.

All three previously starred in the acclaimed The Rat Pack Live from Las Vegas, performing for nearly a decade in London’s West End. Their careers have also taken them to stages alongside prestigious orchestras, including the BBC Concert Orchestra, the London Symphony Orchestra and the Amsterdam Metropole Orchestra.

The trio has since taken the show around the world, recreating the music, humour and spontaneous stage chemistry that made the original Rat Pack one of the most celebrated entertainment acts of its time.

The Prague performance will feature more than just the three leading artists. They will be joined by the Golddiggers, a trio of singers and dancers whose costumes and choreography add a classic Las Vegas revue atmosphere to the production. The show will also feature a special appearance by Nancy Sinatra.

The programme includes classics such as Fly Me to the Moon, My Way, New York, New York, Strangers in the Night and more.

Combining live music, comedy and theatrical performances, the production aims to recreate the atmosphere of the Las Vegas stages that defined an era of popular entertainment.

World.title: Beyond the Usual Order: 7 Prague Restaurants to Try on Bolt Food
World.content:
We all have one. The order you place without thinking. Same app, same five restaurants, same Thursday night. It is comfortable, it is reliable, and if we are honest, it is getting a little boring.

Prague’s food scene runs far deeper than the places that sit at the top of your feed. Tucked into Nusle side streets, Dejvice corners and the quieter end of Libeň are small kitchens with loyal regulars, big personalities and dishes worth crossing the river for.

The good news? You don’t have to cross the river. They deliver.

So as the evenings get darker and the sofa gets more convincing, we asked Bolt Food to point us towards the city’s hidden gems. Here are seven places worth adding to your rotation, from an Aussie pub in Vinohrady to a half-metre pizza you will want to share (or not).

1. The Down Under, Vinohrady

For when you miss home (or just miss a proper pie).

On Vinohradská street sits what bills itself as Prague’s only Australian restaurant. The menu reads like a trip home: a whole section of beef, chicken and vegetarian pies, a chicken parmy, a proper schnitty, fish and chips and, for the curious, a bag of “Skippy’s” kangaroo jerky. Wash it down with something from the Aussie bottled beer list.

Can’t make it in? The pub classics travel well. A pie with a side of gravy and the match on your own TV is a very respectable Sunday.

What to order: the Melbourne Pie, the most popular pie on the menu, with gravy on the side. Or the chicken parmy if you’re properly hungry.

2. Pizza Bici, Dejvice

For when you want a pizza with a story

During lockdown, half of Prague learned to bake sourdough bread. Pavel Petřík went for sourdough pizza instead. A few years, many pop-ups and one very customised electric cargo bike later (yes, it carries a pizza oven that runs hotter than 500°C), Pizza Bici has a permanent home on Na Hutích in Dejvice.

The shop is decorated with vintage bike parts, and the sourdough dough is the star. The menu is short and built for takeaway, with picks like the Marinara Sprint, a Mortadella & Pistachio and the spicy Diavola Express.

What to order: the Mortadella & Pistachio for something different, the Diavola Express if you like heat.

3. Pizza Napoletana, Podolí

For flatmate nights and office Fridays

Yes, a second pizza place. But this one comes with a measuring tape. Near the Žluté lázně riverside, Pizza Napoletana bakes proper Neapolitan pies with San Marzano tomatoes and Sabelli mozzarella, plus its party trick: pizza by the half metre.

The mezzo metro pizzas are built for sharing (in theory). The Margherita D.O.P. comes with buffalo mozzarella, the Parma version with cured ham and rocket, and the Carciofara is a little wild, with artichoke cream, salsiccia, pistachios and crispy potato. Prefer your own pizza? The classic 32 cm range covers everything from marinara to quattro formaggi.

What to order: one half-metre pizza for the table, and a slice of torta caprese for whoever wins the last piece.

4. Alambre, Nusle

For when Tex-Mex just won’t cut it

If you have ever lived somewhere with a serious taco scene, you know the difference between Mexican food and “Mexican-style” food. Alambre, on náměstí Bratří Synků in Nusle, is firmly in the first camp: modern, casual and easy to love.

The menu leans into the dishes taco lovers actually crave: tacos al pastor, loaded nachos, quesadillas and the house namesake, Alambre Camarón. The real headliner, though, is the birria de res quesadilla.

What to order: birria quesadilla, no debate. Add tacos al pastor if you are feeding two.

5. Tahini, Nusle

For the hummus purists

Supermarket hummus is fine. Then you try the real thing and there is no going back. Tahini on Nuselská street calls itself the home of legendary hummus, with Israeli roots and, lately, an Indian twist on the menu too.

Start with the classic hummus plates, topped with anything from falafel and chicken shawarma to sabich or a full shakshuka. Feeling adventurous? Check the daily specials, which have included mezze spreads and hummus with lamb kebab.

What to order: Hummus & Sabich, or Hummus & Shakshuka on a slow weekend morning.

6. Hadog Burgers, Libeň

For proper American-style burgers

Out on Sokolovská, far from the burger joints of the centre, Hadog has quietly built a loyal following. Expect 200 g beef patties, melted cheese and sauces with a kick, like the Chipotle burger with smoked cheese, bacon, BBQ sauce and chipotle mayo.

Smash fans should head straight for the Smash Juicy Lucy, one of the most popular picks on the menu. Any burger can come in a gluten-free bun or with a Beyond Meat patty, so nobody gets left out of burger night.

What to order: the Smash Juicy Lucy, or the Chipotle burger if you like it smoky.

7. Bento Café & Bistro, Holešovice

For when you can’t decide which Asian cuisine you’re craving

Small room, fresh flowers on the tables, big portions. Bento Café & Bistro in Holešovice is the kind of neighbourhood spot locals tend to keep to themselves.

The menu hops across Asia, from Vietnamese bun nem to udon noodles and a red curry ramen that regulars rave about.

It is exactly what you want on a grey November evening: something warm, something fresh and a little bit of everything. Don’t skip the homemade passion fruit lemonade.

What to order: red curry ramen on a cold night, bun nem when you want something lighter.

Your new rotation, sorted

An Aussie pie in Vinohrady, sourdough from a cargo-bike pizzaiolo, birria in Nusle and ramen in Holešovice. Prague tastes a lot more interesting once you look past the usual suspects.

All seven are available on Bolt Food, so the only thing you need to explore is the app. Open Bolt Food, search for any of the names above and try something new this week. Your Thursday-night order will forgive you.

Ordering more than once a week? Then Bolt Plus is worth a look. Members get free delivery from Bolt Food partner restaurants marked with a “+” in the app, on orders over 170 CZK (delivery discount up to 45 CZK), with no promo codes to type in.

The membership covers your rides too, with cashback on every trip and up to three free cancellations a month. And the first month is free, so you can test it on your new hidden gems before deciding.

World.title: Your Next Weekend Away: A Renovated Neoclassical Spa Hotel in Františkovy Lázně
World.content:
The hotel, housed in a 1918 Neoclassical building, has renovated its rooms, restaurant and wellness facilities.

Františkovy Lázně, one of the Czech Republic’s best-known spa towns, is offering visitors a renovated accommodation option following an extensive refurbishment of the five-star Harvey Spa Hotel.



Located in the town’s park zone in western Bohemia, the hotel occupies a Neoclassical building dating back to 1918. The recent renovation covered all 105 rooms, as well as the lobby, corridors and restaurant, updating the interiors while retaining the building’s historic character.

The hotel is situated next to the town’s central park, within walking distance of its main colonnades and mineral springs. Glauber I Spring, one of the town’s traditional drinking cure springs, is located in the nearby park by Swan Lake.

Spa treatments and wellness facilities

The hotel offers a range of spa treatments, massages and wellness services, alongside a relaxation pool, sauna and fitness centre. Guests can combine traditional spa procedures with recreational facilities during both short stays and longer wellness programmes.

The property also features a restaurant and BAR 222, which has been renovated as part of the wider refurbishment.

Františkovy Lázně has a long history as a European spa destination, attracting visitors with its mineral springs and therapeutic treatments for more than 200 years. In 2021, the town became part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing Great Spa Towns of Europe, together with ten other historic spa towns across seven countries.

Its compact centre, historic colonnades and landscaped parks make it suitable for visitors looking to explore the town on foot. The surrounding region also offers opportunities for walking and excursions beyond the spa centre.

Staying at Harvey Spa Hotel

The hotel has 105 air-conditioned rooms, all refurbished as part of the renovation. You can book your room directly here.

Its location directly beside the central park also means guests can reach the town’s main spa attractions on foot, while the hotel’s five-star facilities make it possible to combine accommodation with spa treatments and wellness services during the same stay.

World.title: Christmas Charity Market Brings Gifts and Flavours from 50 Countries to Prague
World.content:
One of Prague’s best-known international Christmas events will return this November, bringing gifts, food and traditions from nearly 50 countries under one roof.

The DSA International Christmas Charity Market 2026 will take place on Saturday, November 21, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the Hilton Prague Atrium.



Organised by the Diplomatic Spouses Association (DSA) together with Prague’s international diplomatic community, the annual event allows visitors to shop for Christmas gifts while supporting Czech charities.

Stalls representing almost 50 countries will offer a wide range of products, including traditional sweets and spices, gourmet food, handicrafts, toys, glassware, porcelain, cosmetics, fashion accessories and Christmas gifts.

The market is held under the patronage of First Lady Eva Pavlová and regularly attracts thousands of visitors.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by DSA Prague (@dsa_prague)

Shopping for a Good Cause

The event also serves as one of the DSA’s main fundraising initiatives. Money raised through the market, together with donations and sponsorship, is distributed to Czech charitable organisations.

Earlier this year, the association awarded a total of CZK 1.32 million to 16 Czech charities during its Grant Award Ceremony in June.

According to Jana Muranska, President of the Diplomatic Spouses Association, the event is intended to bring together Prague’s international community while supporting organisations working across the Czech Republic.

“The Christmas Charity Market is about much more than Christmas shopping,” Muranska said. “It brings together people from across the world in a spirit of friendship, generosity and solidarity.”

World.title: “The Art of James Cameron” to Open at Prague’s Municipal House in April 2027
World.content:
An exhibition dedicated to filmmaker James Cameron will open at Prague’s Municipal House (Obecní dům) on April 29, 2027, bringing more than 300 items from the director’s archive to the Czech capital.

Titled The Art of James Cameron, the exhibition will run until October 3, presenting original drawings, paintings, film props, costumes and photographs connected to the Canadian director’s career.



Visitors will also see examples of 3D technologies developed or adapted for his films, alongside multimedia installations and audio commentary in which Cameron discusses his artistic development.

The collection will cover several decades of his work, from early sketches and storyboards to the technical innovations behind some of Hollywood’s biggest productions, including The Terminator, Aliens, Titanic and the Avatar films.

Although Cameron is widely recognised for pushing the technical boundaries of cinema, the exhibition will focus on his work as an artist and illustrator.

His creative process often began with pencil and paper, with early sketchbooks filled with imaginary creatures, futuristic machines and visions of distant worlds.

The exhibition will also explore recurring themes in his films, including the threat of nuclear catastrophe and the risks posed by rapid advances in artificial intelligence.

Cameron made his feature-film debut in 1981 with the action horror film Piranha II. His breakthrough came three years later with The Terminator, followed by Aliens in 1986. He continued to explore science fiction with The Abyss (1989), which follows a team investigating an underwater encounter with an unknown form of life.

His biggest success at the time came with Titanic (1997). The film won 11 Academy Awards and became one of the highest-grossing productions in cinema history, earning approximately $1.85 billion worldwide.

World.title: Prague Music Week Brings Czech and International Music Names to Prague
World.content:
From November 4 to 6, Výstaviště Praha will become a hub for musicians, industry professionals, and fans interested in everything happening both on and off the stage.

The fourth edition of Prague Music Week—themed “Women Shaping the Industry”—will feature keynote interviews with Aneta Langerová and Jana Kirschner, as well as discussions with local artists such as Lenny, Jiří Burian, Eva Saija Burešová, Klára Vytisková, and Ventolin.



A newly confirmed guest is singer Ben Cristovao, who will join a panel addressing the surge of AI-generated music.

International guests include renowned PR expert Fiona Bloom, Sziget Festival Operations Director Ádám Kiss, diversity, equity, and inclusion specialist Brechje Merckx, and representatives from Spotify.

Will also join: Finnish music industry professional Maija Talvisto; Christine Osazuwa—founder of Measure of Music and an expert in music data and analytics; Vasja Veber, co-founder of the leading analytics platform Viberate; Kristina Janušauskaitė, Executive Director of the IFPI European Office.

The event will offer practical workshops, speed-meeting sessions, opportunities to receive feedback on one’s own work, a technology expo, industry awards, informal gatherings, and space for forging new collaborations.

Tickets for the festival portion of the program are available for purchase via the GoOut and NFCtron networks.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Prague Music Week (@praguemusicweek)

Conference tickets can be obtained via a voluntary contribution through the NFCtron platform. More information is available at www.praguemusicweek.cz.

Prague Music Week will feature an Expo spanning 2,000 m², showcasing companies and products that are driving the music industry forward.

Throughout the day, attendees can combine conference sessions with exploring new innovations, participating in hands-on activities, and connecting with exhibitors.

The Expo will also include an “Experience Lab,” where visitors can try out new skills and discover the technologies used in producing music events.

World.title: Hungary’s former central bank governor Matolcsy to remain in detention amid concerns about destroying evidence
World.content:
Hungary’s former central bank governor, György Matolcsy, will remain in custody after a Budapest court upheld his pre-trial detention in a major investigation linked to the National Bank of Hungary (MNB) scandal.

The court cited concerns over potential flight, interference with evidence and the risk of further criminal activity, while also pointing to Matolcsy’s extensive personal and business connections.

Matolcsy’s connections and his son’s disappearance

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court rejected appeals against the detention of Matolcsy and two other suspects, confirming the initial ruling that ordered their imprisonment until 23 November 2026. In its decision, the court highlighted the suspects’ financial resources, international mobility and alleged close family, economic and personal relationships as factors increasing the risk of them becoming unreachable by authorities.

The concerns are further heightened by the whereabouts of two alleged members of the suspected group, who are currently abroad at unknown locations. They are identified as Ádám Matolcsy, the former central bank governor’s son, and György Stofa. International arrest warrants have reportedly been issued for both individuals. The court argued that the extensive network of relationships surrounding the suspects could facilitate their escape or allow them to influence the investigation indirectly.

Evidence destruction fears deepen the investigation

The court also expressed serious concerns about potential interference with evidence in the ongoing MNB investigation. According to its statement, investigators are still analysing substantial quantities of seized electronic data and documents, identifying additional individuals and conducting witness interviews. Further questioning of existing suspects may also be necessary.

The court said concrete circumstances supported the risk of evidence being compromised. Investigators reportedly discovered documents connected to the criminal proceedings within the interests of one suspect, while circumstances suggesting the possible destruction of evidence had also emerged. The investigation has additionally uncovered documentary evidence, witness statements, audio recordings and transcripts, as well as IT data concerning the creation and alleged backdating of documents.

Why Hungary’s court rejected the bail

The court ruled that neither bail nor house arrest with electronic monitoring would sufficiently protect the investigation. According to the judges, restricting a suspect’s physical movements would not prevent indirect communication, electronic contact or attempts to influence witnesses and evidence through other individuals. A contact ban was also deemed insufficient, given that the full circle of people potentially involved in the proceedings remains unknown.

Matolcsy’s former position as central bank governor and his previously unblemished criminal record were not considered sufficient to eliminate the risk of reoffending. The court pointed to his suspected informal leadership role within an organised group, alongside long-established economic and personal relationships, as grounds for maintaining detention.

The ruling does not constitute a finding of guilt. The investigation into the MNB scandal remains ongoing, with authorities continuing to examine the alleged financial misconduct and the potential involvement of further individuals.

World.title: Hungary’s Magyar government ends Orbán-era subsidy programme for Republika Srpska
World.content:
Hungary’s new government has stopped a 2026 agricultural machinery spubsidy programme reserved exclusively for Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Serb-majority entity, Republika Srpska. The scheme was part of a EUR 100 million support package announced by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Milorad Dodik in 2022, but its future – and the fate of the remaining funds – remains unclear.

Subsidy programme that Viktor Orbán started ends now

According to Radio Free Europe’s Balkan Service, the Progressus Foundation, which administered the programme in Republika Srpska, announced on 16 October that it was suspending the latest grant call after the new Hungarian government halted its funding.

The call, launched on 13 March 2026, was open for only five days due to exceptionally high interest. A total of 1,025 applications were submitted from Republika Srpska and the Brčko District. Farmers could have received grants ranging from EUR 2,500 to EUR 25,000, but applicants will now be informed that the call has been cancelled.

Neither the Hungarian government nor the Central European Economic Development Network (CED), which managed the programme on Hungary’s behalf, had explained the decision or clarified whether the funding could resume by the time Radio Free Europe published its report.

More than EUR 28 million already spent

The programme was announced in 2022 by then Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Milorad Dodik, at the time the president of Republika Srpska. Although the wider package was worth EUR 100 million, at least EUR 28 million had been spent on agricultural machinery, equipment and tools by the end of the first two rounds in 2022 and 2023.

Farmers in Republika Srpska contributed an additional EUR 12.9 million of their own money, bringing the total value of purchases to more than EUR 39 million. In total, 1,959 projects were approved.

The scheme did not provide farmers with cash grants directly. Instead, they could apply for support to purchase machinery and equipment manufactured exclusively in Hungary, provided they covered at least 30% of the investment themselves. They also had to pay Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 17% import VAT.

Farmers left disappointed as questions remain

Some farmers had already set aside their own money for the latest round. Slaviša Simojlović, a farmer from Bijeljina, told Radio Free Europe that he had secured around EUR 8,000 for new machinery and expected the foundation to return the money he had invested if the programme was cancelled.

The president of Republika Srpska’s Association of Agricultural Producers, Stojan Marinković, said farmers were disappointed, particularly after benefiting from the first two rounds.

However, the programme’s economic purpose has also been questioned. Admir Čavalić, a professor at the Faculty of Economics in Tuzla, told Radio Free Europe that the scheme was not a conventional development grant, as farmers could only buy Hungarian-made products and had to contribute their own money. He argued that it could also be viewed as a way of promoting Hungarian exports.

The end of an Orbán-Dodik partnership?

The programme was part of broader economic and political cooperation between Orbán and Dodik, which included a EUR 126 million loan from Hungary’s state-owned EXIM Bank to Republika Srpska in 2022, as well as planned energy and infrastructure investments.

Dodik left the entity’s presidency in 2025 after a final court ruling sentenced him to one year in prison and barred him from holding public office for six years.

The cancellation of the 2026 agricultural programme marks another change in Hungary’s relationship with Republika Srpska following the change of government in Budapest. However, it remains unknown what will happen to the unspent portion of the original EUR 100 million package or whether any of the other planned projects will continue.

World.title: Hungary could face extra costs for quitting Russian gas and oil early, Russian analyst warns
World.content:
Hungary’s plans to move away from Russian oil and gas could come with a hefty price tag, according to a Russian energy analyst. While the country is exploring alternative supplies, Igor Yushkov warns that ending long-term contracts ahead of schedule could expose Hungarian companies to financial penalties on top of the higher cost of replacement energy.

The warning follows Foreign Minister Anita Orbán’s announcement that Hungary intends to end its dependence on Russian energy supplies earlier than the European Union’s deadlines. As previously reported, Hungary’s target for becoming independent of Russian gas is October 2027.

In an article published by Russian outlet V Fokuse Mail, Igor Yushkov, an expert at Russia’s Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation and the National Energy Security Fund, warned that Hungary could face both higher energy costs and contractual penalties if it ends its Russian gas supplies before the EU ban takes effect.

Could Hungary still have to pay Gazprom?

One of the biggest risks identified by Yushkov concerns existing long-term gas supply contracts. He argues that if Hungary stops purchasing Russian gas voluntarily, Gazprom could demand compensation for terminating the agreements early.

The situation could be different if deliveries were interrupted because of sanctions. In that case, Hungarian companies might be able to invoke force majeure provisions. However, if they decide to end the contracts themselves, they could face contractual penalties, according to the analyst.

This could leave Hungary paying twice: first for potentially more expensive alternative gas supplies and then for compensation related to the cancelled Russian contracts.

The exact financial consequences would depend on the terms of the agreements and how any early termination was handled. No specific penalty amount has been established.

Replacing Russian oil will also cost more

The transition could prove challenging for oil supplies as well. Anita Orbán has said that MOL is examining the possibility of sourcing crude oil from non-Russian suppliers and transporting it to Hungarian refineries through Croatia’s JANAF pipeline system.

Yushkov argues that replacing Russian crude is technically possible, but would require more expensive purchases and transportation. Refineries could also need to blend different types of crude to maintain production.

The analyst believes these additional costs could eventually feed through into fuel prices.

Another immediate complication concerns US sanctions. A temporary exemption allowing purchases of oil from Russian companies Lukoil and Rosneft is due to expire on 21 November.

Meanwhile, negotiations are under way over the potential purchase of the Russian-owned stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company. Orbán has said MOL, as well as the Russian and Serbian sides, are interested in completing the transaction in time.

Higher energy prices could affect households

The potential consequences would not be limited to the oil market. Yushkov also warns that more expensive natural gas could push up the cost of electricity, heating and hot water.

However, his assessment represents the view of a Russian energy analyst, rather than a confirmed forecast of what Hungarian households will pay. The actual impact will depend on alternative supply prices, infrastructure capacity, contractual arrangements and the government’s energy policies.

Yushkov also pointed to Hungary and Slovakia’s legal challenge against the EU’s planned ban on Russian gas imports. The two countries previously argued that such restrictions should require unanimous approval by member states. The EU, however, treated the measure as an internal market decision that could be adopted by qualified majority voting.

The case has not yet been withdrawn. Yushkov believes Hungary’s closer alignment with Brussels under its new political leadership could eventually lead to the legal challenge being dropped, potentially putting pressure on Slovakia to follow suit.

World.title: Budapest makes mobile ticket validation easier – But fare-dodging could cost you more
World.content:
Validating digital tickets on Budapest’s public transport has become easier, as new QR-code stickers are now available inside vehicles across the city. Passengers using the BudapestGO app and other mobile ticket apps can scan their tickets after boarding, while several fines for travelling without a valid ticket have also increased.

The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) began installing the new stickers in the second half of October, and the rollout has now taken effect. Previously, passengers generally had to scan a QR code outside the vehicle before boarding. With the new system, they can also validate their digital tickets once they are on board.

The change is particularly useful for passengers who reach a bus, tram or trolleybus just before it departs and do not have time to validate their ticket at the stop.

Where can you find the new QR codes?

The stickers have been placed in different locations depending on the type of vehicle:

Buses and trolleybuses: on the ticket validation devices inside the vehicles.

on the ticket validation devices inside the vehicles. Trams: next to every pair of doors. The existing stickers near the driver’s cab will remain available, too.

next to every pair of doors. The existing stickers near the driver’s cab will remain available, too. HÉV suburban railway services: next to the ticket validation devices at every pair of doors.

The new option is designed to make digital ticket validation quicker and more convenient, but it does not mean passengers can wait until a ticket inspector appears before validating their journey.

Validate your ticket immediately after boarding

Passengers must still validate their digital tickets before starting their journey. If they cannot do so before boarding, they must scan the QR code inside the vehicle immediately after getting on.

There is also an important restriction: the QR codes inside vehicles are temporarily unavailable while ticket inspections are taking place. BudapestGO and other mobile ticket apps notify users when this happens.

In other words, the new system is intended to make life easier for passengers who have a valid ticket but need a little extra time to validate it. It is not a way to avoid paying for public transport or to validate a ticket only when an inspector appears.

Budapest raises several public transport fines

Alongside the QR-code rollout, several penalty fares increased on 2 November. The penalty for travelling without a valid ticket or pass, when paid on the spot or within two working days, has risen from HUF 12,000 to HUF 15,000 (approximately EUR 41).

Passengers who pay within 30 days now face a penalty of HUF 30,000 (approximately EUR 83) instead of HUF 25,000. The reduced penalty for passengers who buy a monthly pass on the day they are caught and present it within two working days has also increased, from HUF 6,000 to HUF 7,500 (approximately EUR 21).

The BKK reminds passengers to have a valid ticket or pass before starting their journey and to follow the relevant validation rules when using digital tickets.

World.title: Hungarian studio transforms abandoned Zurich railway site into striking timber oasis – PHOTOS
World.content:
Hungarian architecture and design studio HELLO WOOD has completed a major new project in the heart of Zurich, turning a former railway site into a three-storey, year-round destination for dining, entertainment and relaxation. Covering 2,500 square metres, Remise Rosa combines experimental timber architecture with a permanent community space – and took just five months to build.

The project marks an important milestone for HELLO WOOD, whose work has grown from architectural summer schools and temporary installations into permanent, large-scale developments. Created in collaboration with Swiss client Miteinander AG, Remise Rosa brings together a restaurant, beer garden, terraces, entertainment areas and spaces for relaxation in one complex.

Designed to operate throughout all four seasons, the development combines indoor and outdoor areas, offering visitors a place to meet and spend time in the city regardless of the weather.

Photo: György Palkó

From temporary installations to permanent architecture

Remise Rosa builds on the experimental design approach that has defined HELLO WOOD‘s work for years. The studio has become known for its educational architecture camps and creative pop-up structures, and the Zurich project translates this playful visual language into a permanent, high-quality setting.

According to lead architect Balázs Szelecsényi, the aim was to create a place where visitors feel special and can rediscover their inner child. He said the project demonstrates how ambitious architecture can strengthen communities while also supporting a successful business.

The result is intended to be more than just a restaurant or beer garden: its different functions and spaces are designed to come together as a lively urban meeting point.

Photo: György Palkó

How the timber structure was built in just five months

Although the complex has a playful appearance, its construction relied on advanced technology and precise planning.

The main structure uses cross-laminated timber (CLT), a material made from layers of wood bonded together. HELLO WOOD selected it for its durability, renewable origins and sustainability credentials.

The building elements were manufactured in advance using computer-controlled CNC technology, which allowed each component to be produced with millimetre precision before being transported to the site. This prefabrication approach helped the team complete construction in just five months.

It also made the assembly process faster and quieter, reducing disruption to the surrounding neighbourhood in Zurich.

HELLO WOOD’s growing presence in Switzerland

Zurich has been an important market for HELLO WOOD since 2016. The studio has previously worked on projects including Urban Surf, June & Julie and Fraulein Holle, and sees Remise Rosa as another significant step in its Swiss journey.

The project was delivered through HELLO WOOD’s integrated Design & Build model, meaning the studio managed the process from the initial architectural concepts through to construction on site. According to the company, this approach helped keep the development on budget and on schedule while meeting the client’s operational and design requirements.

Photo: György Palkó

HELLO WOOD CEO András Huszár said Switzerland had been a key market for the studio for years, adding that Remise Rosa represents the culmination of its work there and demonstrates what can be achieved when timber architecture meets an ambitious business concept.

With its combination of dining, outdoor spaces and distinctive timber design, the completed development gives Zurich a new year-round meeting place – and offers a striking example of Hungarian architectural expertise making its mark abroad.

World.title: Could Democrats’ US midterm victory make it cheaper for Hungary to borrow?
World.content:
The Democrats’ victory in the US midterm elections has triggered a shift in global financial markets, weakening the dollar and pushing bond yields lower. The changes could also benefit Hungary by making it cheaper for the state to borrow money and supporting the forint, although analysts warn that the impact may be temporary.

The Democrats secured majorities in both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Wednesday’s midterm elections, dealing a significant political setback to President Donald Trump. Investors responded by reassessing the outlook for American government spending, economic policy and the technology sector.

The forint strengthens as the dollar weakens

The US dollar lost ground against several major currencies following the result, including the euro, pound and Japanese yen. The forint also strengthened against the dollar.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Hungarian currency briefly traded below HUF 363 to the euro, a level last seen on 19 October. Against the dollar, it strengthened to around HUF 322, compared with approximately HUF 324 earlier in the day.

Government bond yields also declined. The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds fell by around five basis points to 4.91%, while the yield on German 10-year bonds dropped by three basis points to 3.3%.

US stock markets initially opened weaker but recovered during the day. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 of the largest publicly listed US companies, recorded its biggest intraday gain in three months, according to G7.

Don’t miss this: London analysts share when Hungary could join the eurozone

Why could the result benefit Hungary?

One reason for the market reaction is that a Democrat-controlled Congress could make it harder for Trump to push through additional spending measures and expand the federal budget deficit.

For example, the president’s promised USD 5,000 payment to every American adult is now unlikely to go ahead. Investors may also expect greater scrutiny of other government spending, potentially easing concerns about US borrowing and putting downward pressure on bond yields.

This matters beyond the United States. When US Treasury yields fall, European bond yields can also come under pressure, potentially lowering borrowing costs for countries such as Hungary.

There may also be an indirect benefit for the forint. A more divided political landscape in Washington could reduce uncertainty and market volatility, encouraging investors to take greater risks and invest in emerging-market currencies.

András Nagy, an analyst at Erste, told Világgazdaság that this could increase demand for the forint and other emerging-market currencies.

Analysts warn the impact may not last

However, the positive effects are far from guaranteed. Péter Aradványi, chief analyst at Equilor, told Világgazdaság that the direct impact of the election on Hungarian assets was likely to be limited. He expects domestic economic factors to remain more important in determining the forint’s exchange rate and Hungarian bond yields.

There are also potential risks in the United States. Political disagreements over the federal debt ceiling could intensify again, potentially putting upward pressure on yields, particularly for shorter-term government bonds.

Meanwhile, tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and restrictions on data-centre investments could affect US economic growth. A renewed trade conflict between the United States and Europe would also create risks for the wider market.

For now, Erste expects the euro to remain in the HUF 360–370 range over the coming months. The US election result may offer Hungary a more favourable international financial environment, but it is unlikely to determine the country’s borrowing costs or currency performance on its own.

World.title: International train tickets from Hungary now on sale, announces transport minister
World.content:
Tickets for most international daytime trains departing from Hungary are now available for the winter timetable, which begins on 13 December 2026. The announcement brings good news for travellers planning Christmas market visits, festive trips abroad or journeys home for the holidays.

Budapest-Vienna trains to run hourly

Dávid Vitézy, Hungary’s Minister for Transport and Investment, announced the launch of ticket sales in a Facebook post on Wednesday, highlighting the growing popularity of international rail travel. The winter timetable will maintain hourly international train departures between Budapest and Vienna, providing regular connections between the Hungarian and Austrian capitals throughout the season.

Tickets are also available for several other popular destinations, including Košice in Slovakia, Ljubljana in Slovenia and Zagreb in Croatia. Travellers can additionally book journeys to numerous destinations in Transylvania and Western Europe. For those seeking a winter getaway, the High Tatras in Slovakia will also remain accessible by rail. Vitézy recommended the EUR 60 Tatra Excursion Ticket, which can be purchased at railway ticket offices.

The minister noted that the Budapest-Belgrade railway line is already included in the new timetable. However, the precise launch date for passenger services has not yet been confirmed, as the final quality assurance and certification reports are still being prepared. Consequently, tickets for the route are not currently available through Hungarian, Serbian or Austrian sales systems. Ticket availability will be updated once the opening date is officially confirmed.

International rail travel continues to grow

Recent figures indicate that international railway travel is becoming increasingly popular among passengers departing from Hungary. According to sales data from MÁV and its foreign railway partners, international passenger traffic approached 2.68 million travellers during the first eight months of 2026.

MÁV’s own sales figures show that nearly 985,000 passengers purchased international train tickets between January and September, representing a 9 per cent increase compared with the same period last year. More than 65 per cent of international tickets are now purchased online or through mobile applications, reflecting the growing importance of digital booking services.

World.title: Ancient Roman treasure lost in WWII found hiding in Hungarian museum collection after 80 years
World.content:
An ancient bronze of Apollo that vanished during the Second World War and was feared lost forever went back on display at the Hungarian National Museum on Wednesday, 80 years after it was last seen.

The statue’s return to public view is a detective story in itself. It resurfaced recently in the museum’s modern-age mixed collection, where it had been entered in the 1961 inventory book as a “pharmacy figurine” of unknown origin from the mid-19th century. It took the museum’s conservators and archaeologists to establish its true identity — that of the Apollo bronze believed lost in the war, the museum told MTI on Wednesday.

The work is one of the museum’s earliest pieces, acquired before 1825. Its first scholarly publication appeared in 1894, tracing it probably to Pecs, the site of the Roman town of Sopianae. Before the war it was a fixture and highlight of the archaeological exhibitions; amid the post-war disorder of the museum’s collections it slipped into the modern-age holdings, where its age and origin went unidentified for decades.

The 56-centimetre figure depicts a naked youth in a pose invoking contrapposto, the compositional principle of mature classical sculpture. Its striking eyes were covered in silver sheet, and they still seem to glow against the dark bronze of the face. Its eye modelling, stockier proportions and deeply grooved hair point to a date in the second half of the 2nd century AD, the Antonine period.

The hollow, thin-walled casting was made by ancient bronzesmiths using the indirect lost-wax process — body parts cast separately, then joined by soldering. Curiously, while the front has suffered aggressive pitting corrosion, the back survived the centuries in almost pristine condition.

In Greek mythology, Apollo is the most complex of gods, embodying order, radiant intellect and moral purity. This figure follows the Apollo Citharoedus type, the kithara-singing Apollo popular since the Hellenistic age: the raised left arm once held the instrument, the lowered right hand the plectrum. Apollo’s stringed instrument stood for mathematical precision and the triumph of civilisation over untamed Dionysian wildness.

Medium-sized bronzes are rarities, their production prohibitively expensive in antiquity. The newly identified work once graced a representative space — perhaps a garden or a fountain — of a Roman town house or country villa.

The Apollo can be seen for a month from Nov 4 in Room 6 of the museum’s permanent archaeological exhibition “On the Border of East and West“, as part of the Treasure of the Month series of small exhibitions.
