World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Takaichi to skip U.N. climate summit in Turkey
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has no plans to attend a two-day leaders meeting of a U.N. climate summit set to start in Turkey on Wednesday, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Thursday.

Environment Minister Hiroyoshi Sasagawa will attend ministerial meetings of the summit, officially known as the 31st meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, or COP31, which starts Monday.

It will mark the third consecutive year that a Japanese prime minister has not attended a U.N. climate summit.

Takaichi will be absent for scheduling reasons, Kihara said at a news conference. The government does not think the absence will undermine Japan’s presence in climate diplomacy because Sasagawa will convey the country’s stance on climate change, he said.

World.title: NTT Docomo faces network glitches
World.content:
NTT Docomo on Thursday said that some customers across Japan are having trouble accessing the internet on their mobile phones and making calls.

The network glitches started around 11:20 a.m., the Japanese mobile phone carrier said, adding that it is investigating the cause.

Affected are customers who use NTT Docomo’s 5G Standalone high-speed, high-capacity telecommunications network service. The emergency call function is working, the company said.

The company separately said that it has suspended online services, as its servers may have experienced unauthorized access.

World.title: Nintendo’s net profit drops in Q2 as Switch 2 unit sales slow
World.content:
Nintendo reported a drop in quarterly net profit on Thursday as unit sales slowed for its Switch 2 console, but the Japanese gaming giant is maintaining its annual forecasts.

A remake of 1990s action-adventure classic “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time,” which comes out Thursday, has sparked nostalgic fan excitement.

But market analysts will be watching to see how much the title can boost sales of the Switch 2, which became the world’s fastest-selling games console on its 2025 release.

World.title: Japan’s seemingly unchanging ancient sport of sumo may already be at peak optimization
World.content:
The Chicago Bears carving up the vaunted Seattle Seahawks defense on Monday Night Football this week was a reminder of just how vital technical innovation is in team sports.

Head coach Ben Johnson reached deep into his bag to pull out formations and plays that put Seahawks’ defense in a blender, with experienced players constantly caught out of position.

It was a scene that starkly contrasted with how things normally play out in individual sports.

World.title: Nigeria’s ‘godfathers’ pull the strings ahead of elections
World.content:
As Nigeria heads toward elections in just over two months, political battles will be waged over the airwaves and at rallies — and, perhaps more importantly, behind the scenes, by the country’s “godfathers.”

The Nigerian political scene is dominated by a caste of competing kingmakers stretching all the way to the very top — with President Bola Tinubu, who is seeking reelection, known as the “godfather of Lagos.”

Nigeria’s distinct brand of patronage, where politicians owe loyalty to the unelected figures who backed their rise, has bred a culture which, critics say, leads the government to prioritize elite hobnobbing and backstabbing over making ordinary people’s lives better.

World.title: Japan denies seeking Myanmar’s removal from blacklist
World.content:
Japan’s Ministry of Finance has denied pushing for Myanmar to be removed from a global financial watchdog’s blacklist after a report said last week that it was among countries supporting the removal.

Myanmar was added to the Financial Action Task Force’s (FATF) blacklist in 2022 as the country was plunged into turmoil and widespread civil war following a military coup. The blacklist requires countries to apply enhanced screening to financial transactions with Myanmar to avoid money laundering and terrorist financing.

“There is no fact that the Japanese government sought to have Myanmar removed from the FATF blacklist,“ the ministry said in a statement to reporters. “Japan hopes that Myanmar will make the necessary improvements to strengthen its measures against money laundering and related illicit activities.”

Myanmar remained on the blacklist following a closed-door meeting of the 40-member global body in Paris on Oct. 30. Japan did not state at the Paris meeting that it wanted Myanmar removed, the ministry said in its statement.

It was reported on Oct. 30 that Japan was pushing for Myanmar’s removal, according to a senior Japanese government official and another person familiar with the matter. One of the people, reached on Thursday, said they stood by their comments, while the other could not be immediately reached for comment.

A spokesperson for Myanmar’s military-backed government said in a message on Saturday that various “friendly countries” were supporting its efforts to be removed from the list.

“The United States, China, Japan, India, South Korea and Indonesia recognize Myanmar’s efforts. We are grateful to all of them for acknowledging Myanmar’s current progress,” the spokesperson added, without elaborating.

South Korea’s foreign ministry said it was “encouraging Myanmar to abide by FATF duties, and closely coordinating with FATF member countries on the issue.”

The government “is making efforts to strengthen the capabilities of countries that have not fully implemented FATF standards to combat money laundering and terrorist financing,” the ministry said.

All the other countries named by the spokesperson either declined to comment or did not respond to a request for comment.

Myanmar’s military-backed government did not immediately have comment on Japan’s denial that it was pushing to have Myanmar removed from the list.

World.title: New Zealand leaders make final appeals as election remains tight
World.content:
New Zealand’s party leaders made final appeals to voters on Thursday, three days before a general election that polls show is too close to call as discontent around an ailing economy continues to swell.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told reporters while campaigning in Hawke’s Bay that the election would likely go down to the wire.

“The message is pretty simple — it’s going to be tight and close,” he told reporters, “we want to encourage everybody to get out and party vote National,” urging voters to give National another three years to “complete the job.”

Polls released this week showed no clear majority for either bloc of parties, with the centrist Opportunity Party positioned as a potential kingmaker. Political commentators expect it could take weeks for New Zealand to form a government with support growing for smaller parties as voters lose confidence in the two largest ones.

Opposition leader Chris Hipkins said Labour hoped to form a Labour-led government before Christmas.

“The best way to ensure there is a change in government, and most New Zealanders are indicating to us they want a change in government, is to give your party vote to Labour so we are the biggest party,” he said.

Early voting began on Oct. 26 and, by Tuesday, 1,250,057 votes had been cast, compared with 1,007,928 at the same point in 2023, according to Electoral Commission data.

The election is largely a verdict on the government’s handling of the economy. Inflation has eased from earlier peaks, but petrol and other everyday costs have renewed pressure on households.

An Ipsos survey published this week found inflation and the cost of living remained voters’ biggest concern. Healthcare and hospitals followed at 45%, while petrol prices and fuel rose to third place at 31%, ahead of the economy at 30% and unemployment at 19%.

New Zealand has emerged only slowly from a prolonged downturn, with growth subdued, household budgets strained and unemployment rising to 5.7% in the third quarter, its highest level in 11 years.

“This was very much an election about the economy, so mostly cost of living,” said Mona Krewel, a senior political science lecturer at Victoria University of Wellington. “This is the one issue that unites all voters. No matter if people are young or old, it’s actually where they come together.”

She said Labour had run a strong campaign on the cost of living, while National and other center-right parties had focused more broadly on the economy.

Krewel said ACT and New Zealand First had sought to elevate immigration as a campaign issue but had struggled to dislodge economic concerns.

World.title: AI skills are make or break in U.K.’s brutal youth jobs market
World.content:
Artificial intelligence skills are no longer optional for the hundreds of thousands of young Britons seeking their first job, according to data from recruitment platforms that show how the technology is deciding who gets a foothold in the toughest labor market in decades.

Entry-level postings mentioning AI have almost tripled since the start of last year, figures provided by job-search website Adzuna show. The surge largely reflects employers adding AI skill requirements to established roles such as sales representatives, software engineers or assistants.

Separate data from Indeed shows one in six vacancies for entry-level roles in banking, legal, software development and other highly exposed occupations now mentions AI, double a year ago. Research for the British Chambers of Commerce meanwhile warned of the “very real threat” of a two-tier labor market emerging.

World.content:
Warning: graphic content follows.

Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung could have been struck on the head seven times with a hammer when she was allegedly murdered three years ago, a court has heard.

Forensic pathologist Dr Kwok Ka-ki said on Thursday that Choi was fatally struck on the head with a blunt object, leaving a large hole on the right side of her head and causing extensive bleeding in her brain and skull.

World.title: Mainland Chinese firm, director admit fraud in HK$52.9m Hong Kong bottled water scandal
World.content:
A mainland Chinese company and its director have pleaded guilty to fraud after submitting falsified certificates to win a HK$52.9 million (US$6.78 million) contract to supply drinking water to civil servants in Hong Kong.

The high-profile procurement scandal came to light in August last year after civil servants raised concerns about the quality of products supplied by Xin Ding Xin Trade, which held a three-year contract to provide XinLe-brand bottled water to government offices on Hong Kong Island and some outlying islands.

At a hearing on Thursday, company director Lui Tsz-chung pleaded guilty to seven charges, admitting that between May and August last year he submitted altered documents to the Government Logistics Department, deceiving it into believing that his products had been vetted and produced by Robust (Guangdong) Drinking Water, a prominent food and drink company on the mainland that manufactures purified and mineral bottled water.

World.title: Cathay Pacific Airways to give eligible Hong Kong staff bonus worth a month’s pay
World.content:
Cathay Pacific Airways will award eligible Hong Kong-based employees a discretionary bonus equivalent to one month’s pay for 2026, marking the fourth consecutive year it has offered the payout.

The bonus will be paid on January 7 next year, according to an internal staff announcement seen by the South China Morning Post. The airline credited employees for helping it achieve successive years of solid financial performance.

“You are at the heart of Cathay’s success, and we remain committed to recognising your contributions through competitive rewards, including the discretionary bonus and profit share scheme,” the announcement read.

World.title: Hong Kong working carers shun family-friendly measures amid stigma fears: study
World.content:
More than half of working carers in Hong Kong have never used the family-friendly measures offered by their companies, a study has found, sparking calls from experts to change workplace cultures to prevent carers being stigmatised.

The findings came even as the study, released on Thursday, also showed carers benefited from measures such as flexible working hours and working from home, which led to fewer symptoms of depression and reduced the burden of caregiving.

Bobo Lau Hi-po, a professor at the School of Arts and Humanities of Tung Wah College, who led the study, said some carers inevitably worried how colleagues viewed them when they took leave repeatedly for caregiving matters, pointing to “a certain degree of labelling”.

World.title: Hong Kong needs ‘forward-looking’ plans amid changes in industrial chains: John Lee
World.content:
Hong Kong should proactively plan and implement forward-looking strategies amid rapid changes in global industrial chains and the rapid development of technology and artificial intelligence, the city’s leader has said at an economic forum.

Speaking at the Hongqiao International Economic Forum in Shanghai, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Thursday that the government’s GoGlobal task force had helped more than 360 mainland Chinese firms establish or expand their businesses in Hong Kong since it was established last year, with about a third of them setting up regional or international headquarters.

“Faced with the severe, rapidly changing restructuring of the global industrial chain, and the high-speed development of technology and artificial intelligence, Hong Kong must proactively plan and implement forward-looking strategic layouts,” Lee said at the forum, which is taking place alongside the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai.

World.title: US asset manager Federated Hermes opens Hong Kong office to tap China’s tech rise
World.content:
US asset manager Federated Hermes has opened its office in Hong Kong, after two years of preparation, joining a wave of international financial giants competing for growth in the Asia-Pacific region.

The company, which managed US$884 billion worth of assets as of September, considered a Hong Kong office two years ago and its board approved a plan a year later. Its office in the Nexxus Building in Central adds to its Asia-Pacific footprint in Singapore, Tokyo and Sydney.

“Hong Kong is a premier wealth and asset-management hub,” said Jim Roland, head of business development in Asia-Pacific and Australia for Federated Hermes, on Wednesday. “Opening our Hong Kong office helps deepen our relationships with private banks, family offices, wealth intermediaries and institutional investors and is an important step in our long-term regional growth strategy.”

World.title: Hong Kong government doctor found guilty of misconduct over driving conviction
World.content:
A senior government doctor has been found guilty of professional misconduct over a dangerous driving conviction and his failure to report it promptly to Hong Kong’s medical watchdog.

The Medical Council ordered that a warning letter be issued to Dr Edmond Ma Siu-keung, head of the infection control branch at the Department of Health’s Centre for Health Protection, following a disciplinary inquiry on Thursday.

The inquiry heard that Ma was convicted of dangerous driving at Sha Tin Court on December 5, 2024, after running a red light and turning right at the T-junction of Tate’s Cairn Highway and Siu Lek Yuen Road.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.title: China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.content:
Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang pledged to share China’s market with the rest of the world and promote balanced international economic development at the opening ceremony of the 2026 China International Import Expo (CIIE) on Thursday.

“Mutual benefit is at the heart of trade and economic cooperation,” Ding said in his opening address. “Open and connected markets are fundamental for such partnerships.”

Ding also called for deeper investment cooperation, greater collaboration in technological innovation, and stronger dialogue to remove trade barriers.

This year’s CIIE, the ninth annual event and the largest edition to date, welcomes a record 4,142 overseas companies from 162 countries, regions, and international organizations to Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center. The event’s total exhibition area is also its largest, exceeding 440,000 square meters.

The event, which runs Nov. 5 to 10, welcomed more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and global leading enterprises, with 2,000 companies participating for the first time. A record more than 480 products will either make their global, Asia, or China debut at the expo, including a laparoscopic surgery robot by Johnson & Johnson, a cochlear implant capable of 360-degree sound coverage by Swiss hearing care firm Advanced Bionics, and a 6G terminal prototype by U.S. tech company Qualcomm.

This year’s exhibition comprises six main sections covering technical equipment, consumer goods, food and agricultural products, automobiles and smart mobility, medical devices and health care, and trade in services. It also offers a dedicated “innovation incubation zone” for tech startups.

CIIE has also expanded efforts to support African countries, with free exhibition booth space for the “least developed” countries up 17% from last year’s exhibition. The expansion comes as China introduced zero tariffs on imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations in May.

Launched in 2018, CIIE is the world’s first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports. The expo underlines China’s continued efforts to promote inclusive economic globalization and build an open world economy.

In the first nine months of 2026, China’s imports of foreign goods reached 16.7 trillion yuan ($2.5 trillion), up 22.3% year on year, the fastest growth since 2021, according to official data.

(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo’s exhibition center in Shanghai, Nov. 5, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.title: Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.content:
Applications aimed at preventing impulse purchases have soared in popularity during this year’s Double Eleven, the world’s largest shopping festival. The apps involve users listing the items they want, along with their prices, then sharing them with friends and strangers who vote on whether they should buy them.

Dozens of such mini-programs have sprung up across major platforms including WeChat and Alipay following the August success of the WeChat mini-program “Still Want to Buy?” (Hai Mai Me in Chinese), domestic media reported last week. Related hashtags have garnered tens of millions of views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Thursday.

Domestic e-commerce giant Alibaba launched Double Eleven, also known as Singles’ Day, on Nov. 11, 2009, as a 24-hour shopping event. The festival has since grown to a monthlong event across all e-commerce platforms and begins around mid-October.

The trend comes as young Chinese consumers become increasingly money-conscious. According to a May report by Ireland-based consulting firm Accenture, 82% of the country’s Gen Z — more than 230 million people — have started saving money or cutting back on non-essential spending.

The rise in anti-impulse-buy apps dates back to the release of Still Want to Buy? in August. Created by a 29-year-old developer under the pseudonym Qiancheng, the app gained more than 75,000 daily active users within three days of its launch, and total registered users exceeded 500,000 as of mid-September. More than 85% of users are females under 24, Qiancheng told local media.

He said the tool came about after his girlfriend suggested using automated office purchase approval systems — which employees must go through to obtain authorization for work-related purchases — to govern shopping decisions. He added that he often personally feels regret after making impulse purchases.

“It’s difficult to make money nowadays, so I think it’s worth letting people we trust help us make better spending decisions,” Qiancheng said.

However, Still Want to Buy? was taken down on Oct. 31, reportedly due to targeted reporting from online trolls. Qiancheng told local media he is applying to have the mini-program relisted and is developing an independent app to expand the program’s function.

WeChat mini-program “Wait Up, Wallet” also offers similar features to Still Want to Buy?, but it allows users to seek advice from total strangers.

This October, Lin Yinjie, a 20-year-old college student from the eastern Fujian province, vibe-coded a similar app, the Alipay mini-program “Hold On a Sec.” The app lets users log items and prices and set a cooling-off period, during which friends help them decide whether to buy. So far, the program is mainly used by Lin and her friends and does not have a wide audience.

Lin told Sixth Tone that she used to place orders mindlessly while scrolling shopping apps and social media. “As a student on a tight budget, I know how easily the desire to buy things can quietly drain my wallet,” she said.

“A 9.9-yuan ($1.50) purchase seems insignificant, but before you know it, you’ve spent hundreds of yuan,” she said, adding that, “A lot of things I think I really want turn out to be things I no longer care about after a few days.”

Over the past week, Lin says her tool has helped her save over 80 yuan, which she used to buy a camera memory card instead. “It’s like trading ‘unnecessary spending’ for something I actually need,” she said.

Public reactions to the apps have been mixed. While many users report receiving practical advice through the mini-programs, others note an unfortunate side effect. “When I review other people’s requests, I end up wanting to buy the items myself,” one user noted on Douyin. “It’s turned into a product recommendation feed.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.title: Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.content:
For nearly 27 years, Starbucks coffeehouses in China have been a haven for non-paying patrons attracted by its comfortable seating, ample power outlets, air conditioning, and free restrooms.

This stemmed from the American company’s foundational brand concept of making its outlets “third places” — safe, accessible spaces between home and work to relax and connect with friends, whether you intend to spend or not.

Now, it seems, spending is mandatory.

In late October, Starbucks China introduced a nationwide purchase-required seating policy, pledging to be “clear in its rules but warm in its execution,” with staff encouraged to politely stop non-paying customers from hogging tables and chairs. At the same time, it unveiled plans to invest more than 300 million yuan ($45 million) in reshaping the in-store atmosphere.

As the company undergoes major corporate restructuring while continuing to expand, does it risk losing its “third place” image in China?

Stirred up

The first Starbucks on the Chinese mainland opened in Beijing’s World Trade Building in 1999. Today there are about 8,000 outlets across 1,100 counties in the mainland.

Li Kele regularly visits her local store in the southwestern Sichuan province. After walking in and sitting down on Oct. 21, taking a moment to browse various online platforms for discounts, Li was soon approached by a barista brandishing a menu and asking if she needed any help. “The store never used to push customers to place an order,” she says.

Starbucks outlets have been attracting non-paying patrons since the 1980s, and the company officially adopted a worldwide open-door policy in 2018.

However, concerns over disruptive behaviors, alongside the company’s desire to prioritize paying customers and staff’s experience, prompted the global headquarters to reverse the policy in January last year.

The change began at its North American stores, where a new code of conduct stated that Starbucks coffee shops, patios, restrooms, and other facilities were for employees and customers only.

Anecdotal evidence suggests baristas in China began nudging seated patrons to make purchases in early 2026.

One customer shares that in January they observed employees at a Starbucks branch in Beijing’s central Xidan shopping district walking around the store offering table service to people without drinks, which is not typically available, and promoting discount coupons. Sometimes they’d subtly point out that the store was crowded and seating was scarce.

On Oct. 19, social media users in several cities began posting about signs spotted at Starbucks stores that stated customers should “make a purchase before taking a seat.”

When a domestic media outlet contacted Starbucks China for a response that same day, a spokesperson denied any plan to introduce a purchase-required seating policy. But within 48 hours, the company made a complete U-turn, announcing that such a policy would take effect on Oct. 22.

The move has sparked much debate online. Yet in real terms, implementation has so far been limited to advisory measures, such as signage.

“The latest wording is that they (head office) encourage us to ask people to leave,” says Zhang Yi, a part-time Starbucks barista. “They want us front-line staff to persuade non-paying customers to give up their seats in whatever way we consider peaceful.”

However, because the practice isn’t tied to their performance review, employees might be reluctant to enforce the new rules, Zhang adds. “If I’m on shift, I won’t do it. I’ll just work the way I always have.”

In the grind

Starbucks built its “third place” branding concept based on the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg’s 1989 book, “The Great Good Place,” in which he describes the human need for communal, welcoming social environments separate from home (the “first place”) and work (the “second place”).

This positioning requires providing space for relaxed socializing. But when revenues don’t keep pace with increases in rent and operating costs, it becomes a potential pain point.

When Brian Niccol was appointed CEO of Starbucks in September 2024, same-store sales — a metric that measures revenue growth from established locations — were on the slide in the U.S. market.

To reverse the trend, he launched “Back to Starbucks,” a plan aimed at “rediscovering the power of third places” by improving the in-store experience, such as reintroducing old-school ceramic mugs and handwritten names on cups, as well as more comfortable seating. He then scrapped the 2018 open-door policy.

Investor data suggests the changes have already had an effect in North America, where same-store sales were up by 8.1% year on year in the third quarter of fiscal 2026 (Sept. 29, 2025, to Sept. 27, 2026) and same-store transactions grew by 4.5% over the same period.

In China, recent growth in same-store sales has been powered more by product innovation, deliveries, and price adjustments, according to Cathy R. Smith, Starbucks’ chief financial officer.

As online take-out orders increase and in-store spending declines, running a brick-and-mortar “third place” becomes more expensive. In this case, seat-hogging shifts from being a tolerable service issue to an operational problem.

Pressing issue

In April this year, Starbucks completed a $4 billion joint-venture transaction with Boyu Capital, a China-focused alternative asset management and private equity firm based in Hong Kong. The deal gives Boyu a 60% share in Starbucks’ China retail business and transitions all 8,000 coffeehouses into licensed operations.

The U.S. coffee giant says it expects the transaction proceeds, along with the value of its retained 40% stake and licensing agreement, to account for more than $13 billion over the next decade. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, Starbucks’ international segment operating margin increased to 19.1%, up from 13.6% a year earlier.

However, while the deal benefits global headquarters, Starbucks China still faces pressure to expand. At a partner forum in April, CEO Molly Liu confirmed the company is already two-thirds of the way to its goal of opening stores in more than 1,500 counties over the next three years.

With this in mind, the purchase-required seating policy looks more like an efficiency drive, as the company attempts to cut costs.

This also comes amid a major restructuring of Starbucks China’s workforce. As all staff are now part of the joint venture, they can no longer hold Starbucks shares, which trade on New York’s Nasdaq exchange. This means the end of the Bean Stock program in China, which since 1991 has awarded full- and part-time employees shares after a certain tenure.

Liu said at April’s partner forum that benefits would continue through fiscal 2026, with a new long-term incentive plan to be introduced in the fourth quarter. As of Nov. 4, there had been no further announcements.

As social insurance contributions are mandatory only for permanent staff in China, barista Zhang believes the company prefers to hire part-time workers. Jiemian News reported in January that Starbucks China’s official recruitment channels were promoting vacancies in 269 areas, with full-time positions making up just over 20%.

Behind its new seating policy is a contradiction Starbucks China cannot easily escape: the “third place” concept justifies the brand’s premium, yet recent growth has come from deliveries and discounts, bringing sales without a customer ever sitting down.

The joint venture and its target to grow to “as many as 20,000 locations over time” sharpen that contradiction. Smaller markets and leaner per-store costs make it hard to build to the original standard.

Therefore, tightening seating rules, restructuring its workforce, and expansion look less like separate decisions than part of one cost logic.

(Due to privacy concerns, Li Kele and Zhang Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Zhan Fangge.

A version of this article originally appeared in Baobian News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A sign asks customers to make a purchase before taking a seat at a Starbucks. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.content:
A Chinese app designed to report hotels that allegedly have bedbugs and other pests has been updated and re-released following controversy over the validity of the claims. The app attracted more than 300,000 users at its peak, flagging over 600 hotels nationwide, according to its creator.

In a Sunday post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, the creator of the app, a WeChat mini-program called “Bedbug Map,” announced that he alone would now review bedbug reports — previously, evidence was approved if a majority of users verified it. He also clarified that users are required to upload photographic evidence of bedbugs. The next day, he also posted a review of nearly 300 rejected bedbug reports, explaining why each had been declined.

Released Sept. 16, the mini-program lets users report hotels with bedbugs, cockroaches, or other pests, resulting in a bug or question mark icon over the hotel’s location. Tapping it reveals the number of user reports.

Controversy arose after reports that multiple hotels were asked by customers for refunds after they reported having found bedbugs via the app after their stay. One hotel was allegedly asked to refund 3,000 yuan ($450) in room charges after a report citing “two bumps” on a guest’s body was posted on the map and approved by users. According to the report, the hotel later asked a third party to inspect the premises, but found no traces of bedbugs.

The creator, a 26-year-old manufacturing industry worker who asked to remain anonymous, told Sixth Tone that in the past few days he had personally reviewed more than 700 pieces of photo evidence submitted over the previous two months.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone revealed that 232 hotels are now marked on the mini-program’s map, down from the more than 600 reported before Monday. The mini-program currently lists 36 hotels as having successfully appealed reports after submitting third-party evidence.

The app has also been taken down twice, most recently in late October, by WeChat parent company Tencent, citing its restrictions on applications run by and registered to individuals.

The creator told Sixth Tone that Bedbug Map was created with the help of AI in under two weeks. He said he got the idea after searching online for bedbug information after he and his girlfriend developed bites following a move, discovering most bedbug posts involved hotels.

On the day of its release, the mini-program attracted over 100,000 users, according to the creator. Under his release announcement on Xiaohongshu, many commented asking him to expand the function to public transportation, which he then added to the app. However, the function was removed in subsequent updates.

“I guess the reason the app was well-received is that it addresses a key pain point for the average traveler: the lack of cleanliness and the resurgence of bedbugs.”

The mini-program previously allowed users to submit reports without photo evidence. However, after users raised concerns about the potential for people to maliciously target hotels without evidence, the program was updated in late September to allow users to upload photographic evidence. Photos can be either uploaded or taken directly via the mini-program — in the latter case, the app automatically adds a watermark showing the time and location.

“I’m simply the initiator,” he said. “The goal is to get everyone involved in managing the mini-program’s data and reviews.”

Hotels can also appeal bedbug reports — indicated on the map by blue semicircular icons above such locations — as well as upload disinfection records, business licenses, and photos of pest-control operations.

The creator said he even recruited volunteers at one point to inspect the hygiene of hotels that filed appeals. However, the function was soon taken down because of concerns about volunteers’ safety, among other issues.

He said that managing the mini-program alone has “brought pressure and criticism,” adding that he hopes the government will “provide professional guidance to improve (the app’s) credibility.”

In an interview with domestic media, Lin Feiran, a lawyer at Beijing King & Capital Law Firm, suggested the company bring in professionals to identify insects reported at different locations.

State media outlet CNR News wrote in a Monday commentary that “a map pieced together by internet users being used to fill the gap in hygiene information shows that formal (reporting) channels are lacking,” encouraging hotel booking platforms to display bedbug records publicly.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Weibo and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.title: Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.content:
A few weeks ago, I served as a judge on a food program in China, where I met many chefs and got a close look at how they develop new dishes. I was particularly impressed by one dish: a steamed egg custard topped with a rich crab paste made from crab roe and fat. It was a combination I had never considered before. The crab paste had a delicate aroma and a rich, oily texture, while the steamed egg custard was soft and silky, perfectly balancing its richness.

I was struck by the dish’s ingenuity, but it also raised a question: Would people be willing to pay for the recipe and instructions on how to make it?

I put this question to one of the chefs on the program. He smiled at me as though I were a child and asked why anyone would pay for a recipe. He then let me in on an industry secret: When a restaurant discovers that a competitor has introduced a new dish, it will order it and have its own chefs taste it, analyze its ingredients, cooking techniques, and seasonings, and work out how it was made. In most cases, they can reproduce it. The chef told me he had recreated other people’s dishes and had his own copied by others.

It all sounded rather cutthroat. The person who bears the cost of innovation often reaps little of the reward.

In Chinese cuisine, creating a new dish is not nearly as simple as diners might imagine. Chefs must find the right ingredients, adjust proportions, experiment with different cooking temperatures, refine textures, and continually adjust based on customer feedback. Developing a successful dish can involve dozens or even hundreds of failed attempts before it is ready to serve.

The time, ingredients, and labor costs of this trial-and-error process are all borne by the original creator. Yet as soon as the dish reaches the table, anyone can observe, taste, analyze, and even reproduce it. For a competitor, learning most of the techniques needed to make a dish may cost little more than the price of a meal.

Even more frustrating, many of these innovators lack the resources to promote their creations. A small restaurant might be the first to develop a dish but lack the advertising budget, media exposure, or network of locations to popularize it. Meanwhile, a larger restaurant can simply copy the dish and quickly introduce it to a wider audience. Since more people encounter it there first, they may assume the larger restaurant came up with it.

This suggests that the first-mover advantage does not necessarily apply in the restaurant business. Being first matters only if consumers know who created the dish and the original creator has the resources and business acumen to turn that innovation into a brand and a source of revenue. Otherwise, the creator is essentially providing free research and development while introducing consumers to a dish that benefits the entire market.

The challenge of protecting intellectual property is not unique to Chinese cuisine. It affects chefs around the world. Business schools often hold up KFC’s fried chicken recipe as a classic example of a trade secret, but the company’s real competitive advantage lies in its supply chains, restaurant network, and brand value. The law does not prohibit you from reverse-engineering KFC’s fried chicken and making it yourself, or even selling it to your neighbors, provided you don’t market it as “KFC Original Recipe Chicken.” For smaller restaurants, therefore, protecting a recipe may matter less than building the brand and reputation that give it lasting commercial value.

The celebrated 18th-century Chinese food writer Yuan Mei associated dishes with particular names as a way of preserving their origins. For example, in his influential cookbook “Suiyuan Shidan” (“Recipes from the Garden of Contentment”), he included dishes called “Prefect Wang’s eight-treasure tofu” and “Governor Yang’s tofu.” In this way, no matter how often later generations copied these dishes, their names remained tied to their origins.

However, this naming convention has its limitations. Prefect Wang, Governor Yang, and the better-known Kung Pao (of Kung Pao chicken fame) all refer to the chefs’ employers rather than the people who actually did the cooking. Only in his “Biography of Chef Wang Xiaoyu” did Yuan Mei praise a chef, elevating an obscure kitchen worker to a culinary figure remembered by later generations.

Similarly, General Tso’s chicken is familiar to almost everyone in the United States, yet few know the name Peng Chang-kuei, the chef credited with creating the dish and introducing it to America. Diners know the name of General Tso, but not the person behind the dish.

One way to recognize innovative chefs would be to give them explicit credit for their creations. For example, instead of simply labeling a dish “Chef’s Recommendation,” menus could identify the chef or team of chefs who developed it, along with the restaurant and year it first appeared. This would acknowledge the contributions of both the creators and the restaurants that invested in their work.

Chefs could also license their original recipes to restaurants and large chains. Another possibility would be to establish an industry-wide registry of original dishes, where chefs and restaurants could record development dates, launch locations, photographs, and successive versions of their recipes. That way, even if other restaurants later copied a dish and achieved greater commercial success, its creator’s contribution would not simply be forgotten.

Of course, implementing such measures would not be easy. The greatest resistance might not even come from imitators, but from within the restaurants where new dishes are developed.

For restaurant owners, naming a dish after its creator also poses risks. Chefs tend to move between jobs, and when one leaves, dishes bearing their name could become an awkward legacy, potentially even requiring a restaurant to overhaul its menu. At the same time, chefs have traditionally enjoyed relatively low social status. Within restaurants, they often have little say in day-to-day operations and limited bargaining power to protect their own interests, making it difficult to secure adequate recognition for their contributions.

These two problems are closely related. When chefs receive little recognition for their work and feel little ownership over the dishes they create or the restaurants where they work, they may be more inclined to leave. This, in turn, gives restaurants even less incentive to credit individual chefs. It may help explain why, in the rare cases in which a dish bears its creator’s name — such as Fei Da Chu’s chili stir-fried pork, sold in cities across China — the chef behind it is also the restaurant’s owner.

Protecting and rewarding the creators of original dishes, whether through naming rights or other institutional and technological mechanisms, could help raise chefs’ social status, strengthen their bargaining power, and create a more equitable relationship between chefs and restaurant owners. Restaurants, in turn, could attract diners who appreciate the work of individual chefs and are willing to pay for originality. The result could be a positive cycle of culinary innovation, recognition, and consumption.

A dish may be replicated almost perfectly, but the experience, creativity, and reputation behind it cannot. The chef who conceived the idea, the sous chefs who tested the recipe, the team members who continually refined it, and the restaurant that provided the resources and space for experimentation all contributed to the story behind the dish. Recognizing their contributions is about more than giving credit where it is due. It is also about respecting the generations of chefs who have shaped Chinese cuisine and ensuring that their knowledge, skills, and traditions continue to be valued.

(Header image: The illustration in the center depicts Yuan Mei, a Qing Dynasty poet, scholar, and artist, in a 19th-century painting by Chinese artist Ye Yanlan. Images from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.title: China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.content:
China has approved its first domestically developed amino acid-based nutritional powder, designed to give patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) — a rare genetic disorder that affects metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine — greater freedom in what they eat. Treatment of PKU requires lifelong dietary restrictions to prevent developmental disorders and brain damage.

The new formula officially entered the Chinese market on Oct. 30 and was jointly developed by Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research, and dairy producer Bright Dairy.

PKU affects about one in every 11,000 newborns in China, with an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 registered patients nationwide.

Due to a genetic defect, people with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. The resulting buildup can damage brain cells, requiring patients to follow a low-phenylalanine diet by cutting out meat and eating low-protein grains, while relying on milk powder-like formulas to supplement the other amino acids they need.

Earlier formulas contained 30% to 60% amino acids, with the rest composed of fats, carbohydrates, and other nutrients.

“As patients grow older, they need more protein. That means consuming more of these formulas, which also means taking in more fats and carbohydrates, increasing the risk of obesity,” Cai Wei, director of the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research and leader of the research team, told domestic media.

In contrast, the new formula contains 95% amino acids, allowing patients to meet their amino acid needs without consuming as much fat or as many carbohydrates, and giving them more freedom to enjoy other normal low-protein foods.

Zhuang Yingying, a 33-year-old PKU patient, told domestic media that patients previously relied heavily on imported products, and overseas supply disruptions were common. Special low-protein foods such as rice and noodles cost five to 10 times as much as regular varieties.

The formula, designed for PKU patients aged 1 and older, could save some families more than 1,000 yuan ($140) a month, according to domestic media.

Domestic PKU formulas have existed for decades, but long faced hurdles in gaining regulatory approval in China, partly because of gaps in national standards for food-grade amino acids, according to a 2020 report by domestic media outlet China Times. High registration costs and the small patient population have also discouraged manufacturers from entering the market.

China approved its first PKU medical formula in 2018, an imported product, while the first domestically produced formula received regulatory approval in 2025.

Since 2018, some parts of China, including Shanghai and neighboring Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, have introduced public health insurance coverage for foods formulated for PKU patients. In Shanghai, annual coverage ranges from 8,000 yuan for infants under 1 to 12,000 yuan for patients over 10.

Development of the new formula began in 2024 and received regulatory approval in September 2026. The research team has also worked with companies to develop everyday foods for PKU patients, including noodles, steamed buns, cookies, and mochi.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: From the Shanghai Morning Post)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.title: Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.content:
At her desk in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai, a county in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, Chai Fenfen has hung a large print of a 100-yuan banknote.

“I came here to make money,” she says. “That’s what keeps me motivated.”

After jobs selling insurance and real estate, Chai joined the workshop in 2024. Making nails offers steady earnings and the flexibility to take her children to and from school. Workers there are paid by the piece, typically earning 3,000 to 4,000 yuan a month ($450 to $600).

But for the businesses supplying that work, the early boom has given way to fierce competition over price.

Once known for its crystal trade, Donghai used its existing e-commerce networks to build an industry around press-on nails — ready-made artificial nails that customers attach themselves. By 2024, the county had nearly 25,000 businesses in the trade, according to its press-on nail industry association.

Chai’s employer, wholesaler Li Zhifu, entered the business in 2021, and now has around 2,000 workers across his production sites and more than 20 storefronts in the county.

In the beginning, Li says, almost anything sold, regardless of color or design. Competition has since squeezed profits. He estimates that six or seven out of every 10 people who entered the trade have gone out of business.

Some businesses are competing on design, selling elaborate, handmade sets for hundreds of yuan. Others are expanding overseas sales through TikTok Shop.

As overseas orders grow, Li is experimenting with machines to make nails his workers currently produce by hand.

“For large overseas orders, consistency is key. Everything, from colors and designs to rhinestone placement, has to match,” he says. He expects machine-made nails to eventually dominate that market.

(Header image: Craftswomen work in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai County, Jiangsu province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.title: China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.content:
China’s latest viral reality show is about broken friendships — rather than failing romance — between celebrities.

“I Miss You” surpassed 100 million views within two days of its Oct. 22 debut, and topped the real-time TV popularity chart on Chinese review platform Douban since last Thursday. Topics related to the show have repeatedly trended on the microblogging platform Weibo since airing.

Produced by streaming platform Mango TV, the show brings together four pairs of celebrities who have reportedly fallen out for an 18-day trip through the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region.

The show is widely seen as a riff on China’s popular relationship reality shows and follows a similar format to “See You Again,” whose fifth season aired in late 2025, which takes celebrity couples in troubled marriages on an 18-day trip before they decide whether to divorce.

In “I Miss You,” guests discuss their former friendships as a group and one-on-one with their ex-friends, play games, and share their feelings with the production team. A panel of celebrities, a psychologist, and a journalist comment on their interactions.

The most discussed pair on “I Miss You” so far has been Xu Fei and Li Na, two contestants from the 2006 season of “Super Girl,” a popular televised singing competition regarded as a cornerstone of China’s fan culture.

The two were close friends during the competition 20 years ago, but their friendship later collapsed after Li came to believe that Xu had reported her to their management company for taking outside jobs in violation of her contract. Li said the company subsequently stopped arranging work for her, which she sees as having dealt a major blow to her career. Xu denied the accusation, instead blaming a third person.

As the two revisited their past on the show, their memories of their friendship moved many viewers, with one highly upvoted comment describing their relationship as “an epic saga of love and hate.”

Xu said in tears that she had loved “wasting time together,” and noted that her current preferred snacks are the “ones Li loved back then.” Li also recalled how, even when the two appeared to be bitter enemies, they would sometimes end up crying in each other’s arms after getting drunk at gatherings.

Yet the two remained at odds over the past accusation. During an interview with the production team, Li said she had hated Xu “for a long time,” at one point shouting, “What about the money I lost?”

The other three pairs of celebrities include an actor who cut ties with a longtime producer friend after feeling pressured to accept a role, an actress and a writer who fell out when the latter grew closer to a third person, and former professional esports teammates who fought over training strategies, eventually leading one to leave the team.

“‘I Miss You’ feels so much more pure than ‘See You Again,’” read a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that received almost 3,700 likes. “In a marriage, you have to argue about more than feelings. There’s property, children, parents, and so much else. With friendship, we can sit down and focus on just one thing: how we feel about each other.”

Fu, a 21-year-old viewer from the southern Guangdong province, told Sixth Tone that she found the show’s focus on friendship “refreshing” given how rarely such relationships take center stage on screen.

“We’re so used to understanding intimate relationships through the lens of romance, but rarely give serious thought to the love, possessiveness, jealousy, dependence, disappointment, and reconciliation that exist in friendships,” she said.

Another 21-year-old viewer based in Shanghai, surnamed You, added that the show’s appeal lies in friendship’s lack of definition.

“Friendship can be as intense and possessive as romance, full of love and resentment, or it can be something much more casual,” You said. “People can have very different ideas of what friendship means, and that alone can create tension.”

Contributions: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “I Miss You.” From Douban)

World.title: World No. 1 pickleball star Anna Leigh Waters sets December Manila showcase
World.content:
For the second time in three months, world No. 1 pickleball player Anna Leigh Waters returns to Manila for another exhibition showcase, this time at the famed Araneta Coliseum

MANILA, Philippines – World No. 1 pickleball player Anna Leigh Waters makes a quick return to the Philippines.

Following a well-received debut tour in Manila last October, Waters will next grace the legendary Araneta Coliseum on December 9 with a series of world-class exhibitions and other activities, while organizers have also promised musical performances with celebrity guests.

“The moment Anna Leigh Waters stepped onto Philippine soil last October, the clamor from fans and players was electric,” organizers shared in an official statement on Thursday, November 5. “We quickly realized that an ordinary venue simply wouldn’t suffice.

“Moving this showcase to the Smart Araneta Coliseum was an easy decision driven entirely by the overwhelming public demand. We want to ensure that as many fans as possible have the opportunity to witness the world’s greatest pickleball player in action, live.”

General ticket sales for the event presented by wellness brand IAM Worldwide begin on Monday, November 9, following a limited exclusive sale period this Thursday, November 5.

“Pickleball is more than just a game to me. It’s speed, focus, and endurance, all in one. That’s why I am more than willing to support a community that values performance and wellness together,” the 19-year-old American sensation said in a video release.

“Let’s celebrate sports, health, and the power of staying strong together,” added the teenage prodigy, who has been the all-time women’s pickleball pro title record holder since October 2022 at age 15.

Waters has also been the undisputed pickleball pro title record holder since November 2025, after eclipsing doubles partner and men’s world No. 1 Ben Johns, and has since won an unprecedented 200th career title at the 2026 PPA Veolia Chicago Cup last October.

Passionate Filipino fans arrived in droves to meet the global face of pickleball in her last foray on Manila soil, as Waters joined packed crowds in various Taguig and Makati sports apparel stores last October 13 to 15.

Already part of TIME100’s Most Influential People in Sports, the young Waters also gamely shared her life success story to fans and media, and encouraged Filipino players to fully enjoy and embrace the process of the rising sport. – Rappler.com

World.title: How communities in Cebu marked Tino’s first anniversary
World.content:
YEAR AFTER. Residents of Liloan and Compostela, Cebu, mark the first anniversary of Typhoon Tino with a penitential walk from Cotcot Gymnasium to Tiltilon Elementary School, followed by a solemn Mass, early morning on November 4, 2026.

Through the Padayon Cebu chatroom on Muni, Cebuanos revisit the devastation of Typhoon Tino, share updates on affected communities, and call for lasting solutions a year after

MANILA, Philippines – A year after Typhoon Tino devastated communities across Cebu, residents are still grappling with flooding, unsafe living conditions, and questions over flood-control efforts.

These concerns took center stage in the Padayon Cebu chat room on Muni in the Rappler app, where survivors shared stories, discussed conditions in affected communities, and highlighted activities that marked the first anniversary of Typhoon Tino on Wednesday, November 4.

Leading up to the anniversary, Cebuanos in the chat room initiated a discussion titled “Isang taon matapos ang Tino, kamusta na ang Cebu?” (How is Cebu a year after Typhoon Tino?). They reflected on the devastation of the disaster, and discussed the challenges that affected communities continue to face a year later.

Cebu-based Mover Jerome Valdez shared the story of Alma Quingco, 46, from Barangay Maslog, Danao City, who was on duty at the University of the Philippines Cebu when Tino struck. When she returned home, floodwaters had made their house inaccessible, and many of their belongings had been swept away.

“Despite the help, the experience left a lasting impact. Alma shared that there are still fears and trauma associated with what happened. Even now, the memory of how quickly the floodwaters rose remains with her,” Valdez shared in the chat room.

The discussion also brought attention to villages in Tambisan, where severe flooding continues even during ordinary rainfall, and families who remain without safe, permanent relocation a year after their homes were destroyed.

Violy Musngi of La Paloma Village, during Rappler’s #MoveCebu roadshow in October, recalled how residents were caught off guard by Typhoon Tino, with floodwaters reaching waist-deep levels in her area and rising above head level in Tambisan.

“We were surprised by the waist-deep flooding, which persisted even after Typhoon Tino. Residents in Tambisan are also suffering from leptospirosis. After Tino, there’s flooding after flooding. Even light rains now cause flooding almost immediately,” Musngi said during the forum.

Reymarr Hijara of the Movement for a Livable Cebu (MLC) also joined the online discussion. MLC is a civic group in Cebu, advocating for safer and more sustainable flood management.

In November 2025, they proposed a petition for urgent flood-management measures, including the creation of a Cebu Floodwater Management Office, relocation of families from high-risk areas, protection of watersheds, and a review of flood-control structures. The group also called for no-build zones in areas inundated during Tino.

But even a year later, according to Hijara, implementing the six proposed flood-management actions remained largely unfinished or unverified a year after Tino.

The most concrete development, he said, was MLC’s invitation to join the Provincial Flood Control and Drainage Task Force, created under Executive Order 74 after the November 2025 flooding. However, Hijara stressed that the task force’s formation and MLC’s participation did not amount to implementation of the group’s proposed measures.

“A task force is not yet implementation,” Hijara said in the chat room.

The discussions in Padayon Cebu also highlighted two activities around the November 4 anniversary: a multi-stakeholder dialogue on flood-control accountability and a sustainability walk through downtown Cebu.

Commemoration through a community walk

To examine urban vulnerabilities, University of the Philippines (UP) Cebu’s College of Communication, Art, and Design (CCAD), together with participants from the University of the Philippines Open University and Japan’s Meiji University, held a walk through downtown Cebu.

The guided walk passed through areas including San Nicolas, Pasil, Taboan, Carbon Market, Plaza Independencia, and Colon, examining Cebu’s built environment, public spaces, transportation systems, and cultural heritage.

According to an announcement by UP Cebu’s CCAD, Tino’s severe flooding served as a point of reflection as participants considered how cities can adapt to flooding and extreme heat while preserving their cultural identity.

The walk also drew comparisons between climate adaptation approaches in the Philippines and Japan, including lessons Cebu could apply to building safer and more livable communities.

Dialogue raises concerns over relocation, flood-control accountability

Aside from a community walk, various groups also organized a dialogue to discuss the pressing concerns among survivors.

The dialogue titled, “Kahinumdom pa mo namo? (Do you still remember us?) A Multi-Stakeholder Dialogue on Flood Control Accountability and the Continuing Concerns on Typhoon Tino Survivors,” was organized by Sugbuanong Pakigbisog Kontra Kurapsyon (SuPaKK) in collaboration with partner organizations.

During the dialogue, John Roy Rigodon of the Sectoral Transparency Alliance on Natural Resource Governance (STANCe) shared findings from visits to communities along major rivers in Cebu, including the Kinalawan River in Toledo City and the Cotcot River in Liloan and Compostela, where he examined the situation of residents living in flood-prone areas a year after Tino.

According to Rigodon, the communities continue to face concerns over their safety when typhoons hit. This includes being at risk to flooding and lack of safe and permanent relocation.

“Will they be safe in the next typhoon?” he asked, pointing to relocation as a major concern among residents.

The dialogue also raised questions about flood-control spending. Organizers cited P17.4 billion in major river flood-control projects from 2016 to 2025, including P11.1 billion for the Butuanon River, and called for transparency and accountability. These figures were also reported in a SunStar Cebu investigation on how Tino’s floods exposed how flood control projects failed in Cebu.

Moreover, Norika Ishikawa of the Cebu Anti-Corruption Coalition and Center for Emergency Aid, Rehabilitation and Development Inc.(CONCERN) questioned how the government would lead rehabilitation efforts for Tino-affected communities amid reported cuts to disaster rehabilitation and housing funds for 2027.

She said recovery must go beyond providing houses, calling for safe and affordable housing with access to livelihoods, utilities, roads, hospitals, and schools.

“Disaster rehabilitation is not an expense. Building back better is a public investment,” Ishikawa said.

Ishikawa said the next steps identified during the dialogue include formulating a relocation agenda with Tino-affected informal settler families and mobilizing for an accountability action on November 30.

“Nakakalungkot ang sharing, nakakagalit ang inaction, but hopeful pa rin (The sharing is saddening, the inaction is infuriating, but there is still hope),” she said.

Typhoon Tino caused widespread devastation in Cebu, affecting nearly 2 million people, displacing over 636,000, and resulting in 96 confirmed deaths with many still missing. It also damaged approximately 262,000 homes (over 24,000 totally destroyed), leaving affected communities struggling to recover a year later.

A year after Tino, affected communities still continue to call for safe relocation, transparent flood-control spending, and rehabilitation that addresses their long-term needs. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who are the Cabinet members of BARMM chief Macacua’s admin?
World.content:
CABINET. BARMM Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua announces on November 5, 2026 the newly constituted Cabinet of his administration, marking what he hailed as a "defining moment" in Bangsamoro history.

The newly constituted Cabinet brings a mix of veteran lawmakers, technocrats, and legal professionals to lead the region's ministries and offices

COTABATO CITY, Philippines – Following the historic inauguration of the region’s first-ever elected parliament, Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua officially announced on Thursday, November 5 the newly constituted Cabinet of his administration, marking what he hailed as a “defining moment” in Bangsamoro history.

The announcement comes on the heels of a vetting and screening process conducted by a special committee, designed to select leaders based on “competence, professional experience, integrity, and a strict commitment to moral governance.”

“To my fellow Bangsamoro, this government is yours,” Macacua declared. “We will pursue a policy of moral governance, integrity, and accountability.”

The newly constituted Cabinet brings a mix of veteran lawmakers, technocrats, and legal professionals to lead the region’s ministries and offices:

Senior Minister: Member of Parliament (MP) Abunawas Maslamama

Member of Parliament (MP) Abunawas Maslamama Cabinet Secretary: Abdullah M. Cusain

Abdullah M. Cusain Bangsamoro Attorney-General’s Office: Judge Duque D. Kadatuan

Judge Duque D. Kadatuan Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education: MP Atty. Naguib G. Sinarimbo

MP Atty. Naguib G. Sinarimbo Ministry of Social Services and Development: Atty. Alirakim Munder







Atty. Alirakim Munder Ministry of Health: MP Atty. Jimael Salam D. Salliman

MP Atty. Jimael Salam D. Salliman Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform: MP Atty. Ishak V. Mastura

MP Atty. Ishak V. Mastura Ministry of Interior and Local Government: Jordan S. Bayam

Jordan S. Bayam Ministry of Public Order and Safety: Datu Jomar U. Midtimbang

Datu Jomar U. Midtimbang Ministry of Labor and Employment: MP Atty. Kitem D. Kadatuan, Jr.







MP Atty. Kitem D. Kadatuan, Jr. Ministry of Trade and Investment, and Tourism: Atty. Faizal M. Padate

Atty. Faizal M. Padate Ministry of Indigenous People’s Affair: MP Jo Genna Jover

MP Jo Genna Jover Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management: Atty. Ubaida C. Pacasem

Atty. Ubaida C. Pacasem Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, and Energy: MP Akmad Brahim

MP Akmad Brahim Ministry of Science and Technology: MP Hanie Bud







MP Hanie Bud Ministry of Human Settlement and Development: MP Engr. Rashdi T. Adiong

MP Engr. Rashdi T. Adiong Ministry of Transportation and Communication: Termizie G. Masahud

Termizie G. Masahud Ministry of Public Works: Engr. Basir M. Ibrahim

Macacua acknowledged that the governance workload ahead is immense, but emphasized that the regional leadership’s resolve remains even greater. He underscored the administration’s dedication to preserving the hard-won gains of the peace process.

“We commit to sustaining the gains of the peace process and ensuring that the dividends of autonomy are felt in every household and every community,” Macacua said. “Together, with the continued support of our national government, local government units, and our partners, we will write a new chapter of peace, prosperity, and dignity for our people.”

Reflecting on the big tasks ahead, Macacua underscored that the newly formed administration will vigorously pursue moral governance—the foundational policy initiated by former chief minister Al Haj Murad Ebrahim.

“My fellow Bangsamoro, this government is yours,” Macacua stated. “We will pursue and vanish your moral or moral governance that had been initiated by former chief minister Al Haj Murad Ebrahim. Indeed, the work ahead is immense, but our resolve is greater.”

Macacua also committed his administration to sustaining the ongoing peace process and ensuring that the tangible dividends of regional autonomy reach every household and community.

He also expressed gratitude for the continued, collaborative backing of the national government, inter-governmental units, and international and local partners in cultivating peace, prosperity, and dignity for the Bangsamoro land and its people. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who’s next for Maharlika Fund after Joel Consing?
World.content:
'Whatever we have achieved can only grow from here,' says Maharlika Investment Corporation's top boss, Joel Consing, who's set to step down on November 23

Rafael “Joel” Consing Jr. knows exactly when his time at the Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC) ends.

November 23. Five o’clock sharp.

But who will take over the country’s still-young sovereign wealth fund? That part we don’t yet know.

“It’s been reported my term as PCO ends at the end of this month. Any announcement on the transition will come from the Palace,” Consing told reporters on Thursday, November 5.

Play Video

Leaving too is MIC’s chief investment and operating officer Kheed Nielsen Ng, who is co-terminus with Consing.

Though MIC’s boss has kept mum on who might take his place, one name making the rounds is Finance Undersecretary Ma. Angela “Angel” Ignacio, who oversees the Department of Finance’s (DOF) Government Corporations and Investments Group.

Ignacio joined the DOF in February 2026, but she is no stranger to Finance Secretary Frederick Go or Consing himself. All three previously worked at the now-defunct Office of the Special Assistant to the President for Investment and Economic Affairs, which Go headed before taking over the DOF. Ignacio served as an undersecretary, while Consing was its executive director before taking the helm at Maharlika.

When asked about it, Consing offered no confirmation. The appointment, he said, remains the call of the President.

So after three years at the helm, does Consing have any parting instructions?

“I don’t give instructions to my successors,” Consing said. “No instructions, just a suggested path forward.”

What he is leaving behind, however, is paperwork. Lots of it. MIC departments are assembling year-end reports. For his part, Consing is preparing a compendium of his research papers, which he intends to share with his successor and the Land Bank of the Philippines.

“All the stuff that we’re doing actually came as a result of my research background. And I’ve written much more than what we’ve done. I’m turning over all of those to my successor,” he said.

There is also the matter of preserving the institutional culture, arguably just as important a matter, especially for a fledgling sovereign wealth fund that found its inception marred by governance concerns.

“One of the messages that I’ve always told them, and I continue to tell them, and which I will tell them on the 23rd when I leave is: They are the legacy of MIC, apart from what it aims to achieve. And they’re also my continuation, my transition. So hence, whatever we have achieved can only grow from here,” he said.

As for his own next act, Consing said he is leaving government, though he did not rule out returning someday.

Before joining the government in 2023, he was the chief financial officer of Enrique Razon Jr.’s International Container Terminal Services Inc. and managing director at HSBC.

For now, he says he is occupied with making sure MIC is left “very, very strong” and with handing over a “very healthy organization” to his successor. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Rappler Investigates] Who’s taking care of our dead?
World.content:
