“Cybercrime is evolving rapidly, and our response must evolve even faster. No country can meet these challenges alone. Success depends on cooperation among governments, law enforcement and judicial authorities, the private sector, academia, civil society and international organizations,” said Stolpe.

Expanding international legal cooperation

Kazakhstan has expanded its participation in international agreements governing cybercrime investigations and access to electronic evidence.

On Sept. 30, Kazakhstan ratified the Council of Europe’s Convention on Cybercrime, commonly known as the Budapest Convention, which establishes mechanisms for investigating cybercrime and obtaining electronic evidence across borders.

Kazakhstan was also among the first countries to sign the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime in October 2025, with ratification currently underway. Adopted by the UN General Assembly in December 2024, the treaty establishes a global framework for international cooperation in cybercrime investigations.

As of Nov. 4, the convention had 96 signatories, including the European Union, but only three countries – Azerbaijan, Qatar and Vietnam – had ratified it. The agreement requires 40 ratifications to enter into force.

Beyond these legal frameworks, Kazakhstan has stepped up cooperation with foreign law enforcement agencies to dismantle fraudulent call centers, including those operating abroad, investigate the illegal trade in personal data and trace stolen funds.

Authorities have also expanded cooperation with major technology platforms, including Google, Meta and TikTok, to identify online fraud schemes.

According to the ministry, measures taken over the past two years have contributed to a 21% decline in online fraud cases in Kazakhstan. Current prevention efforts focus on detecting scams before financial losses occur, improving digital literacy and protecting people particularly vulnerable to online fraud.

Cybercrime specialists demonstrate new technologies

The conference featured an international hackathon supported by INTERPOL, bringing together 38 specialists from 13 countries and representatives of 20 regional cybercrime units within Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs. Participants demonstrated technical solutions designed to detect cybercrime and assist investigations, while an accompanying exhibition showcased digital security technologies developed in Kazakhstan and abroad for law enforcement agencies and financial institutions.

The conference participants also adopted a joint statement outlining priorities for future cooperation, including faster exchanges of information and electronic evidence, improved investigative methods and specialized training. The statement also identified cybercrime prevention, technology sharing and stronger international partnerships as areas for joint action.

World.title: Beyond Memorandums: How Cyberport and Central Asia Are Building Startup Bridge
World.content:
HONG KONG – Hong Kong’s Cyberport is looking to deepen its ties with Central Asia as technology hubs in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan seek to connect their startup ecosystems with international markets, investors and partners. In two separate interviews with The Astana Times on Nov. 4 as part of Cyberport Venture and Capital Forum, Eric Chan, Cyberport’s chief public mission officer, and Shakhzod Narzullaev, head of product-market fit at IT Park Uzbekistan, outlined complementary approaches: Hong Kong offers an established technology and financial ecosystem, while Central Asian partners can help startups move across neighboring markets and build a wider regional presence.

Wholly owned by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government, Cyberport is home to more than 2,400 companies, including 30 listed companies, 10 unicorns and more than 500 AI and data science startups. Companies in its ecosystem have expanded into 36 markets worldwide.

Chan said the regulatory environment should make room for experimentation, particularly when technology companies work with financial institutions. Rather than simply telling companies what they cannot do, regulators should create controlled environments in which businesses can test new solutions and develop them in cooperation with established financial institutions.

AI is now driving a larger share of the hub’s work. Chan said Cyberport initially supported companies using generative AI to develop and fine-tune large language models, but the focus is increasingly shifting toward redesigning business processes.

“What I can see is that people are getting a lot more serious and the scale of those projects is a lot bigger,” he said, explaining that companies are moving beyond testing individual applications toward integrating AI into their operations.

“It’s not a matter of whether we should do it. It’s a must, it’s an imperative now,” Chan said.

He also stressed that AI adoption cannot be separated from risk management, cybersecurity, governance and ethical considerations, adding that AI should be more accessible beyond the business community. Through its “AI for All” initiative, it plans to reach students, parents, older people and disadvantaged communities.

“AI should be democratized for everyone. It should not be concentrated for just a few who can afford it,” Chan said.

Talent is another part of Hong Kong’s proposition. Chan pointed to the city’s 12 universities and what he described as the “free flow of talent,” funding and data.

“At the end of the day, we are grooming talent for the globe, not just for Hong Kong or any other countries,” he said, noting that international exposure can benefit both companies and specialists who eventually return to their home markets.

Cyberport’s Central Asia strategy: partnerships before offices

Cyberport’s engagement with Central Asia has developed through visits to technology hubs in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Chan said. In June 2026, during Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee’s visit to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Cyberport signed memorandums of understanding with Astana Hub and IT Park Uzbekistan. The agreements cover technology transfer and cooperation in AI, fintech, smart city solutions and Web3, alongside support for overseas expansion and international market access. IT Park Uzbekistan and Cyberport are also discussing exchanges of projects and potentially investments, although a detailed plan has yet to be finalized, according to Narzullaev.

Chan said Cyberport does not intend to establish a permanent office in every market, preferring to build relationships with established local organizations.

“Since we may not be able to afford to have people in every country, every jurisdiction, what we do is we find a good partner, a good strategy partner,” he said.

The model is intended to be reciprocal. Cyberport wants to help Central Asian startups find investors, customers and business partners in Hong Kong, while its partners can support Hong Kong companies entering their markets. He believes international expansion is essential even for companies operating in an established ecosystem such as Hong Kong.

“Anyone has the aspiration to become the next unicorn. Not just the unicorn from Hong Kong, but the unicorn of the world. They have to operate in multiple markets,” he said.

For head of product-market fit at IT Park Uzbekistan Narzullaev, regional cooperation starts with a question of scale. Individual Central Asian countries can compete with one another to attract investment, he said, but presenting themselves separately to global markets can limit their visibility.

“Why can’t we present ourselves as Central Asia when we go to the global market? And why don’t we do it together?” he said.

The Central Asian Innovation Hubs initiative, developed with Kazakhstan, gives the countries a shared brand at international events, where they present startups together rather than compete for visibility. Narzullaev said Tajikistan was now joining the initiative. The partners have also developed a shared hub in China where founders can work, hold meetings and connect with local businesses. For startups entering an unfamiliar market, he said, having a place and a network to turn to can make a significant difference.

Narzullaev also challenged the assumption that Silicon Valley should automatically be the first destination for every startup seeking venture capital. Deep-science projects requiring very large initial investments may need to look to the United States, he said, but companies seeking more modest early-stage funding could find opportunities closer to home.

“If your startup needs $500,000, up to $3 million to $5 million, you can easily find this money in our regions,” he said.

In his assessment, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan currently have more venture capital available than investment-ready projects, making the region an attractive option for founders who are prepared to develop their products and build teams before approaching investors.

He was also refreshingly blunt about the practical value of memorandums. IT Park Uzbekistan has signed about 70 memorandums with organizations in different countries, he said, many of which risk becoming little more than documents and photographs without concrete obligations.

“We want to remove it altogether,” he said, describing the need to move away from symbolic agreements toward partnerships with measurable results.

IT Park Uzbekistan is therefore working on a proposed Global Growth Alliance that would bring technology parks, investors and other startup-support organizations into a functioning international network. He said the initiative could develop into an annual forum, with the first global summit planned in Uzbekistan in May 2027.

Narzullaev described the idea of working with international partners such as Cyberport as creating an “IT embassy of Uzbekistan” in Hong Kong, allowing Uzbek startups to have a local base without requiring IT Park to establish a separate office and maintain its own staff and infrastructure.

“It is not logical to go to all the countries and open an office there. But Hong Kong is an interesting region for us and we can be part of it,” he said.

He said rather than treating Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan as competing destinations, Narzullaev views them as interconnected markets within a wider regional opportunity.

“If Kazakhstan grows, Uzbekistan grows. If Uzbekistan grows, Kazakhstan grows,” he said.

For Narzullaev, that is ultimately the logic behind building partnerships across the region: a startup’s success in one Central Asian market can create opportunities in another, making the region more attractive to international companies and investors as a whole.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry Reviews Plan to Promote President’s Address Abroad
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry held a collegium meeting chaired by Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi to discuss the implementation of priorities outlined in President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state-of-the-nation address, the ministry’s press service reported on Nov.5.

Participants also reviewed a comprehensive plan to promote the address’s key messages internationally and explain its main priorities to foreign audiences.

Opening the meeting, Tileuberdi noted that the address carried particular symbolic significance as it was delivered in the year marking the 35th anniversary of Kazakhstan’s independence.

He said it outlines the country’s main development priorities, strategic goals and objectives.

World.title: Kazakhstan Prepares for High-Level Diplomatic Week with International Leaders
World.content:
ASTANA – King of Jordan Abdullah II Bin Al Hussein will pay an official visit to Kazakhstan on Nov. 5-6 at the invitation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Aibek Smadiyarov, the president’s press secretary, announced on his Telegram channel on Nov. 4.

The two leaders will discuss ways to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, investment, economic relations, culture and humanitarian affairs.



During King Abdullah II’s August 2025 visit to Kazakhstan, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to closer ties and broader cooperation.

Tajik President Emomali Rahmon will also visit Kazakhstan on Nov. 5-7 at Tokayev’s invitation. The leaders are expected to discuss further strengthening their strategic partnership and allied relations.

Meanwhile, Astana will host an Aqaba Process summit on Nov. 6, bringing together several heads of state.

World.title: ‘Factual inaccuracies and misjudgements’ – Georgian Foreign Ministry responds to European Commission report
World.content:
In response to the European Commission’s critical enlargement report, Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said the document contained factual inaccuracies and flawed assessments. It argued that these reinforced anti-Georgian narratives and narrowed the scope for constructive engagement between the European Union and Georgia.

The Foreign Ministry says the report wrongly describes the Georgian authorities’ actions as “state capture”. It argues that governing the country is the duty of a government elected by an overwhelming majority in a democratic society.

“It is concerning that the European Commission’s report, through factual inaccuracies and flawed assessments, reinforces anti-Georgian narratives. This, in turn, narrows the scope for constructive engagement and dialogue between the European Union and Georgia,” the ministry said in a statement.

The ministry claims that the European Union held no meetings with Georgia at any level during the reporting period, despite the Association Agreement providing for them. It says this resulted from the suspension of dialogue with the Georgian side following the European Council’s conclusions of 27 June 2024. According to the ministry, this has limited the European Commission’s ability to assess Georgia’s progress objectively.

The ministry also argues that the report’s selective analysis of legal issues encourages their politicisation, undermines the rule of law and amounts to an attempt to interfere in the country’s internal affairs.

It further says that describing Georgian politicians’ responses to actions targeting Georgia as “hostile rhetoric” infringes on freedom of speech and damages the partnership between Georgia and the European Union.

“Although the enlargement report on Georgia has largely served to voice biased assessments and reinforce political speculation, the Georgian side will examine the European Commission’s report in detail and submit substantiated comments to the Commission,” the statement said.

The Foreign Ministry insists that Georgia’s leadership remains ready to engage in open and constructive dialogue with the European Union, based on mutual respect.

What does the European Commission’s 2026 report say?

According to the European Commission’s 2026 enlargement report, the state of democracy in Georgia has deteriorated further. The document sets out several key criticisms of the country’s government:

● Democratic backsliding and concentration of power: The European Commission says democratic institutions are weakening, political and civil liberties are being restricted, and the government is increasingly concentrating power in its own hands.

● Attempt to ban opposition parties: The Commission believes the proposal to ban five opposition parties threatens the country’s democratic foundations and raises further concerns about the use of the judiciary for political purposes.

● Electoral environment: The authorities have failed to carry out fundamental electoral reform. According to the report, the 2025 municipal elections took place in a polarised and repressive environment, marked by voter intimidation, pressure and legislative changes that gave the ruling party an advantage.

● Restrictions on civil society: The European Commission is concerned about the use of criminal proceedings and charges such as sabotage and assisting hostile activities by foreign organisations against civil society representatives. In the Commission’s assessment, this runs counter to democratic pluralism.

● Judicial independence: For the third consecutive year, the European Commission has recorded a deterioration in the judiciary. According to the report, judicial independence and impartiality have been undermined, while legal changes have increased the risk of state capture of the system. The Commission also criticised the harsh sentences imposed on demonstrators.

● Corruption and de-oligarchisation: The Commission says there has been no progress in tackling corruption. Georgia has had no anti-corruption strategy since 2020, and the authorities have taken no steps towards de-oligarchisation. The report also points to the role of oligarchic influence in facilitating state capture.

● Failure to meet visa-free travel requirements: Georgia has made virtually no progress on the European Commission’s previous recommendations, which concerned the protection of fundamental rights, combating discrimination and fighting corruption. As a result, the Commission has activated the revised visa suspension mechanism.

● Relations with Russia and sanctions: Georgia’s alignment with the EU’s foreign policy has fallen from 40% to 38%. The country has not joined most of the sanctions imposed by the EU on Russia, Belarus and Iran. The report also notes an increase in the number of direct flights to Russia.

● EU financial assistance: In response to democratic backsliding, the EU suspended €121.3 million in bilateral funding for the Georgian government in 2024. Georgia’s participation in new EU programmes under the Association Agreement has also been suspended.

● Anaklia port project: The European Commission notes that the project has become fully state-owned, construction work was suspended for several months, and budget funding for the project fell by 60% during the reporting period.

World.title: Baku says there is “no war” with Armenia, yet allocates 20.8% of its state budget to defence and national security. What will money be spent on?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s defence budget

On 4 November, the Milli Majlis Committee on Economic Policy, Industry and Entrepreneurship discussed Azerbaijan’s draft state budget for 2027. The document allocates 8.816 billion manats (approximately $5.19 billion) to defence and national security, accounting for 20.8% of total budget expenditure.

On 2 October, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev told a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP):

“Today, there is no conflict or war between Azerbaijan and Armenia. The situation along the border is calm.”

However, in the same speech, Aliyev described strengthening the country’s military capabilities as “one of the main tasks”. Azerbaijan and Armenia have yet to sign a peace agreement. Baku has made amendments to Armenia’s constitution a condition for signing one.

We reported on the revenue side of the budget in September. Now we turn to the other side of the equation:

If there is no war, why is one-fifth of the state budget going to defence and national security? And what do we know about its largest spending item?

What do the figures tell us?

In 2023, Azerbaijan spent 5.85 billion manats (approximately $3.45 billion) on defence and national security. The figure rose to 6.56 billion manats (approximately $3.86 billion) in 2024 and reached 8.07 billion manats (approximately $4.75 billion) in 2025. The 2026 budget allocated 8.72 billion manats (approximately $5.13 billion) to these areas, while the 2027 draft budget provides for 8.82 billion manats (approximately $5.19 billion).

Over four years, spending has increased by roughly 50%, although the rate of growth is slowing. In 2025, the increase stood at 23%, while the government forecasts growth of just 1.1% in 2027. Meanwhile, an earlier medium-term government plan projected a reduction in defence and national security spending to 7.97 billion manats (approximately $4.7 billion) by 2030.

Despite the slower growth, spending remains substantial. In 2027, defence and national security will rank as the second-largest item in the state budget, after economic activity. The government plans to allocate 5.1 billion manats (approximately $3 billion) to education and 2.08 billion manats (approximately $1.23 billion) to healthcare. Combined, spending on these two sectors will be 1.6 billion manats (approximately $942 million) lower than the allocation for defence and national security.

Per capita, defence and national security spending will amount to around 858 manats (approximately $505), compared with just 203 manats (approximately $120) for healthcare. Meanwhile, state budget expenditure will exceed revenue by 3.15 billion manats (approximately $1.85 billion).

The same pattern can be seen in 2026. According to the Finance Ministry, the government allocated 5.25 billion manats (approximately $3.09 billion) to defence and national security in January–September, compared with 3.12 billion manats (approximately $1.84 billion) for education and 954 million manats (approximately $562 million) for healthcare.

High military spending is not unique to Azerbaijan. According to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), military expenditure accounted for 6.5% of Azerbaijan’s GDP in 2025 and 6.1% of Armenia’s. The global average stood at 2.5%. Azerbaijan and Armenia ranked sixth and seventh worldwide, respectively, by military spending as a share of GDP. In terms of the increase in this indicator, Azerbaijan ranked second after Ukraine, with a rise of 1.4 percentage points.

Defence spending will rise from 2.99 billion manats (approximately $1.76 billion) in the 2026 budget to 3.37 billion manats (approximately $1.99 billion) in the 2027 draft. At the same time, funding for “special defence projects and measures” will fall from 4.5 billion to 4 billion manats (approximately $2.65 billion to $2.35 billion). Spending on national security will decrease from 520 million to 480 million manats (approximately $306 million to $282 million), while funding for the border service will increase from 540 million to 550 million manats (approximately $318 million to $323 million). Other expenditure will rise from 160 million to 410 million manats.

The largest allocation goes to “special defence projects and measures”. In 2025, Azerbaijan spent 4.58 billion manats (approximately $2.7 billion) on these projects, accounting for 57% of total defence and national security expenditure. For comparison, in 2023, according to Ziyafat Asgarov, chairman of the parliamentary defence committee, spending on this item reached 2.07 billion manats (approximately $1.22 billion), even after the government added another 1 billion manats (approximately $588.3 million) through a budget revision.

In 2027, this item’s share will fall to 45%, as funding for special defence projects decreases while spending on the armed forces rises by 12.7%. However, the government may revise the allocation during the year, as it did in 2023 following budget amendments.

The draft budget describes the purpose of this funding only in general terms: strengthening defence capabilities and providing the armed forces with equipment and supplies. It says the authorities allocate the money “in accordance with the assigned tasks and signed contracts”.

In the Finance Ministry’s 2026 “Budget for Citizens” document, the government classifies funding for these projects as capital expenditure. The allocated 4.5 billion manats exceed the amount earmarked for the reconstruction of Karabakh and Eastern Zangazur (approximately $2.06 billion) by 1.3 times. They also amount to almost ten times the spending on targeted social assistance (approximately $273.5 million).

However, the 2026 budget law provides no detailed breakdown of this spending category. The document does not identify the contracts involved, the suppliers or the types of weapons the government plans to purchase. By comparison, the “Budget for Citizens” separately lists 35 million manats (approximately $20.6 million) for military personnel’s housing and 15.5 million manats (approximately $9.1 million) to compensate them for rental costs. In 2027, the combined allocation for these two items will fall from 50.5 million to 29.7 million manats (approximately $29.7 million to $17.5 million).

Many countries classify details of military procurement as secret. However, media outlets sometimes report on individual contracts. For example, in October, Israeli company Elbit Systems announced a $235 million contract to supply multiple-launch rocket systems, but did not disclose the buyer. Israeli publication Calcalist reported that Azerbaijan had placed the order, although the company did not confirm this information. Media reports put the cost of Azerbaijan’s purchase of JF-17 fighter jets from Pakistan at $1.6 billion.

Thus, almost a tenth of the state budget goes towards a single spending category whose detailed breakdown remains closed to the public.

How do the authorities justify this spending?

In September, Prime Minister Ali Asadov said that defence and national security spending would remain “as always” one of the largest items in the budget. He also noted that 44% of budget expenditure served social purposes.

President Ilham Aliyev cited two reasons why Azerbaijan needs to strengthen its military capabilities. The first concerns Armenia. Despite the initialling of a peace agreement and the start of trade between the two countries, Aliyev referred to historical events and said: “…we must remain vigilant and be ten times stronger than them at all times, every single day.”

The second reason, he said, involves wars and conflicts in neighbouring regions. According to Aliyev, new sources of conflict are emerging “in the North, in the South and in the Middle East”, while no international mechanisms exist to stop them. The president therefore believes Azerbaijan must have enough military power to ensure that “no one would even think of staging any provocation against Azerbaijan”.

Aliyev acknowledged that the country also had “other needs”, including the reconstruction of Karabakh and improving people’s living standards. However, he added: “But if we cannot defend ourselves, then every other project we undertake will lose all meaning.”

Economist Khalid Kerimli shares a similar view: “We cannot expect stability in this area for now. On the contrary, tensions are likely to increase.”

What does “ten times stronger” mean in figures?

Armenia’s draft 2027 budget allocates approximately 616.5 billion drams, or around $1.7 billion, to its Defence Ministry. This represents a 9.5% increase on 2026, when the government cut the defence budget to 563 billion drams. The allocation will therefore almost return to its 2025 level. Azerbaijan, meanwhile, plans to spend 8.8 billion manats, or around $5.2 billion, on defence and national security.

Azerbaijan’s allocation is therefore roughly three times larger than Armenia’s. However, the Azerbaijani figure also includes spending on national security and the border service.

Armenian political analyst Suren Surenyants believes that Baku wants to consolidate the political gains it made through its military superiority, as the current balance of power cannot last indefinitely. At the same time, he says there is not yet sufficient evidence to conclude that Azerbaijan is preparing for another military escalation.

Despite the initialling of a peace agreement, neither country plans to reduce military spending in 2027. Armenia will increase its allocation by 9.5%, while Azerbaijan will raise its spending by 1.1%.

Will signing a peace agreement lead to lower military spending? Aliyev’s words following his statement about the need to be “ten times stronger” suggest the opposite: “It will remain as it is today, tomorrow as well.”

After parliamentary committees review the draft budget, the Milli Majlis will debate it in a plenary session. The 2026 budget law did not provide a detailed breakdown of the 4.5 billion manats allocated to “special defence projects and measures”.

World.title: Georgia must adopt European laws if it wants to join EU – ambassador
World.content:
Georgia’s EU accession

According to EU Ambassador to Georgia Pawel Herczynski, the EU accession process is based not on a candidate country’s own assessment of its progress, but on the European Union’s evaluation. In other words, it is the EU that assesses the progress made by a candidate country, not the other way around.

Herczynski made the remarks in response to a statement by Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, who said at an EU enlargement summit that the Georgian authorities were optimistic about a possible change in the EU’s approach towards Georgia.

“This is a simple truth and the foundation of EU enlargement: the European Commission assesses Georgia, not the other way around. The accession process is based on a voluntary application. By applying for EU membership, a country agrees to be monitored and assessed by the European Commission,” Herczynski said.

According to the ambassador, some candidate countries take EU accession seriously. He named Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova as frontrunners in the accession process.

At the same time, Herczynski said, some countries express an interest in joining the EU but are in fact moving away from the European path and reversing the progress they have made.

“This is extremely regrettable, but it is the sovereign decision of each candidate country,” he stressed.

The EU ambassador also said that if Georgia wanted to join the EU, it should adopt European legislation rather than American, Russian, Chinese or other countries’ laws.

Herczynski was particularly critical of the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence, which he said was incompatible with EU legislation.

According to the ambassador, the EU had warned the Georgian authorities about this as early as 2023. At the time, the ruling party withdrew the repressive law, after which Georgia was granted EU candidate status at the end of the year. However, the authorities soon reintroduced the same legislation in parliament.

“We said loudly and clearly, including myself: ‘Please don’t do this. This law is not compatible with EU legislation.’ And we also said loudly and clearly that there would be consequences. The Georgian government decided to continue down this path. Then came another law, and another law, each one widening the gap between the European Union and Georgia,” Herczynski said.

According to the ambassador, Georgia is free to decide which laws to adopt, but a country seeking to join the European Union must implement EU legislation.

Herczynski also responded to Irakli Kobakhidze’s calls for dialogue, noting that the EU supports dialogue but that Georgia’s ruling party had stripped it of any substance over the past three years.

According to the ambassador, democratic backsliding, pressure on civil society, threats to ban political opposition groups, actions against independent media and a daily campaign to discredit the European Union were preventing the resumption of dialogue.

“The European Union is built on dialogue. Dialogue is part of our DNA. Behind me, you can see the flags of the 27 EU member states. We constantly negotiate and compromise to reach consensus. As the EU, we fully support dialogue. The problem is that over the past three years, the ruling party in Georgia has rendered this dialogue meaningless,” Herczynski said.

He questioned what exactly the EU and the Georgian authorities could discuss when the ruling party was talking about the “deep state” and the “global war party”, as well as drawing parallels between the European Union and the Soviet Union.

“Do you expect serious representatives of EU institutions to start discussing the definition of the ‘deep state’? Do you expect us to engage in dialogue about the ‘global war party’? This smear campaign must stop for dialogue to resume,” he said.

Pawel Herczynski

The EU ambassador also addressed the ongoing proceedings in Georgia’s Constitutional Court concerning a request to ban opposition parties. Herczynski said the European Union was following the process with great concern.

According to him, attempts to ban opposition parties threaten the foundations of democracy in Georgia. He also reiterated the European Commission’s position, expressed several days earlier by EU Commissioner Marta Kos.

Herczynski said that if the authorities attempted to ban opposition parties that had passed the electoral threshold in the last parliamentary elections, it would be an unprecedented case in the history of the Council of Europe.

“I do not want to speculate about something that has not yet happened. We are following the proceedings in Georgia’s Constitutional Court with great concern. Attempts to ban the main opposition parties through a lawsuit in the Constitutional Court threaten the foundations of democracy in the country,” he said.

According to the European Commission’s enlargement report of 4 November 2026, Georgia’s EU integration process remains suspended, while the situation in the country has deteriorated further compared with the previous year.

The European Commission assessed that the Georgian authorities had taken no steps during the reporting period to implement the nine steps set out for the country to advance its EU accession process.

The report highlights the weakening of democratic institutions, restrictions on political and civil liberties, problems with judicial independence, attempts to ban opposition parties and a lack of progress in tackling corruption.

The Commission also points to Georgia’s incomplete alignment with sanctions against Russia, an increase in direct flights to Russia and the presence of Georgian companies on EU sanctions lists.

Consequently, due to continued democratic backsliding, the European Commission is no longer issuing new recommendations on accession negotiation chapters, except in areas relating to fundamental reforms.

World.title: Armenian businessman Samvel Karapetyan detained while under house arrest
World.content:
Samvel Karapetyan detained following search

Prominent Armenian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, founder of the Tashir Group and leader of the opposition Strong Armenia party, has been detained.

A criminal investigation has been launched against Karapetyan and 35 others. They are suspected of:

Causing particularly large-scale financial damage to Electric Networks of Armenia (ENA).

Embezzling entrusted property.

Money laundering on a particularly large scale.

The total damage allegedly caused to Electric Networks of Armenia exceeds 64.585 billion drams (more than $180m).

Armenia’s Investigative Committee said the alleged offences were committed between 2016 and 2024 by a group of individuals led by “S.K.”. Investigators are examining four alleged criminal episodes in the private sector.

The committee said the alleged crimes had been uncovered following extensive investigative work and on the basis of information obtained from the National Security Service, the Interior Ministry and the State Revenue Committee.

Billionaire Samvel Karapetyan was already under house arrest in connection with a separate criminal case. In June 2025, he was charged with publicly calling for the seizure of power and the overthrow of the constitutional order. Several months later, another criminal investigation was launched, and Karapetyan faced additional economic crime charges, including money laundering. In July 2026, criminal proceedings were also initiated against his nephew, Narek Karapetyan. He is accused of coercing people into attending gatherings and money laundering on a particularly large scale. The court imposed bail of 1 billion drams ($281,000) and a ban on leaving the country.

Searches began early in the morning

Armenia’s Investigative Committee began conducting searches early in the morning at the homes of Strong Armenia party leader Samvel Karapetyan and his nephew Narek Karapetyan, who heads the parliamentary faction of the same name.

“Searches are also being carried out at other addresses linked to the Karapetyan family,” party spokeswoman Aghavni Sukiasyan said.

The Investigative Committee later confirmed the information, specifying that simultaneous searches were being conducted at 65 locations. It emerged that the searches were being carried out by the Main Department for the Investigation of Economic Crimes as part of a criminal investigation.

Investigative Committee reveals details of alleged crimes

Several hours after the searches, Armenia’s Investigative Committee released details of the case under investigation:

“Members of a criminal group operating under the leadership of S.K. – including certain members of the Board of Directors of Electric Networks of Armenia CJSC, the company’s general director, his deputy and other senior officials – abused their powers in managing the company’s day-to-day operations with the aim of embezzling company assets on a particularly large scale.”

Investigators found that the individuals concerned had deliberately taken out bank loans exceeding the company’s actual operational needs. The funds were then transferred under the guise of dividend payments to the offshore company Liormand Holdings Limited and Tashir Capital CJSC. Both companies are shareholders in Electric Networks of Armenia (ENA) and belong to the Karapetyan family.

“With the aim of laundering funds obtained through the aforementioned criminal activities, executives of more than ten interconnected organisations, under the leadership and direction of S.K., created the appearance of large-scale financial transactions within the framework of civil-law and corporate relations. They concealed the criminal origin of the embezzled funds, converted them and mixed them with their other income. In doing so, they disguised the true nature and origin of the illegally obtained assets and funds, making them appear legitimate and thereby laundering money and obtaining criminal proceeds,” the Investigative Committee said.

As a result, Electric Networks of Armenia allegedly suffered financial losses on a particularly large scale.

The supervising prosecutor decided to initiate criminal proceedings against 36 individuals, and an investigator ordered their detention. The criminal investigation is ongoing.

Opposition alleges “political pressure”

Strong Armenia parliamentary faction leader Narek Karapetyan linked the morning’s developments to his party’s position on the new Constitution. According to him, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan is trying to pressure the party into a “deal”. He claimed that the prime minister would offer to release Samvel Karapetyan in exchange for the party’s agreement to hold a referendum on the new Constitution.

“They are trying to persuade us to allow the Constitution to be put to a referendum and adopted. Look at what is happening. Whatever they are told in Baku, they come back and start trying to convince us [to agree to it]. We are the obstacle preventing them from pushing through a Constitution that suits Aliyev,” he stressed.

Nikol Pashinyan has said that the draft of Armenia’s new Constitution is ready and that its text will be published in November. For a referendum to be held, two-thirds of parliament’s members must vote in favour of the initiative. However, the ruling party does not have enough seats and expects opposition lawmakers to support the proposal. The prime minister has repeatedly stated that constitutional reform is necessary for Armenia itself. ёThe opposition, however, believes that the government’s initiative is driven by a demand from Azerbaijan. Baku has called for amendments to Armenia’s Constitution as a precondition for signing a peace agreement, arguing that it contains territorial claims. The Constitution itself contains no provisions that could directly give rise to such concerns. However, it refers to the Declaration of Independence, which mentions the unification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. It is already known that this reference will be removed from the new Constitution.

Narek Karapetyan said the Strong Armenia party would not change its position even if hundreds of people were arrested.

He argued that the developments had nothing to do with economic crimes and accused the authorities of attempting to exert political pressure on the opposition.

After law enforcement officers detained his uncle, Narek Karapetyan used stronger language:

“He thinks he can achieve something with his birdbrain. Nothing you have planned has worked, and nothing ever will. You are simply afraid of our enemy,” Karapetyan said, addressing Pashinyan.

World.title: European Commission: Georgia’s EU integration process remains stalled, situation worsens over past year
World.content:
T

EU’s negative assessment of Georgia

The European Commission published its 2026 enlargement report on 4 November. It says Georgia’s EU integration process remains stalled and the situation in the country has deteriorated further over the past year.

According to the Commission, the Georgian authorities took no steps during the reporting period to meet the nine recommendations set for the country as an EU candidate to allow the accession process to move forward.

The recommendations included: Combating disinformation: countering information manipulation targeting the EU and its values. Alignment with EU foreign policy: bringing Georgia’s foreign and security policy closer to the EU’s positions and decisions. Overcoming political polarisation, including ensuring inclusive cooperation between political parties in parliament. Ensuring free and fair elections in line with international standards. Strengthening parliament’s role and oversight of state institutions and ensuring their independence. Carrying out comprehensive judicial reform to guarantee the full independence and impartiality of the courts. Fighting corruption, including strengthening the effectiveness and independence of anti-corruption bodies. De-oligarchisation: ending the excessive influence of private interests over the country’s economic, political and public life. Improving the protection of fundamental rights and the rights of vulnerable groups.

The Commission’s report points to the opposite trends:

Weakening of democratic institutions;

Restrictions on political and civil freedoms;

Problems with judicial independence;

Attempts to ban opposition parties;

No progress in fighting corruption.

The Commission also highlights Georgia’s failure to fully align with EU sanctions against Russia, the growing number of direct flights between Georgia and Russia, and the inclusion of Georgian companies on EU sanctions lists.

Because of the continued democratic backsliding, the European Commission will no longer issue new recommendations on accession negotiation chapters for Georgia, except in areas requiring fundamental reforms.

On 4 November, EU Ambassador to Georgia Pawel Herczynski formally handed over the report to Georgian authorities. It was received by Deputy Foreign Minister Giorgi Zurabashvili, who was appointed in November as the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia.

Attempt to ban opposition parties

One of the strongest criticisms in the European Commission’s report concerns proceedings in the Constitutional Court following a lawsuit filed by the ruling party seeking to ban five opposition parties.

Georgian Dream claims the parties violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties whose aim is to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments cited by the ruling party is the opposition groups’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current government. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government.

The European Commission says the proceedings pose a threat to the foundations of democracy in Georgia. It also expresses serious concern over the possible use of the judicial system for political purposes.

Concerns over October 2025 municipal elections

The European Commission notes that the authorities have failed to carry out fundamental electoral reform, despite recommendations made over several years.

According to the report, the October 2025 municipal elections took place in a highly polarised and repressive environment, significantly undermining the competitiveness and transparency of the electoral process.

The Commission points to legislative changes that favoured the ruling party, a boycott by most opposition parties, the lack of an impartial election administration, and pressure and intimidation of voters.

Neither the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) nor reputable domestic election-monitoring organisations were present to observe the vote.

Prosecution of civil society representatives and concerns over judicial independence

The report also highlights new legislative restrictions on citizens’ participation in political life. The Commission says these changes run counter to international standards of pluralism and democracy.

The European Commission expresses concern over the use of criminal law against civil society representatives.

The report refers to criminal investigations launched on charges including “sabotage”, “assisting foreign organisations in hostile activities”, “financing activities directed against the constitutional order” and “harming state interests”.

The Commission says such actions undermine the principles of democratic pluralism.

The report explicitly states that this approach is incompatible with Georgia’s EU integration process.

According to the report, the independence, impartiality and integrity of the judicial system remain seriously undermined.

The Commission also points to harsh and disproportionate sentences handed down to protesters. It says this raises concerns that the judiciary is being used as an instrument of repression.

Amendments to the legal framework governing the judiciary, introduced in December 2025, further weakened its independence and increased the risk of the judiciary being brought under government control, the report says.

No progress in fighting corruption

According to the European Commission, Georgia had previously reached a certain level of preparedness in the fight against corruption, but made no progress during the reporting period.

The report notes that the country has had neither an anti-corruption strategy nor an action plan since 2020.

The legal framework also makes no provision for an independent advisory body, while whistleblower protection laws need to be brought further into line with EU standards.

The Anti-Corruption Bureau was abolished, with its preventive functions transferred to the State Audit Office. The Commission says the changes failed to take into account recommendations from GRECO and the Venice Commission on the effectiveness of these functions and institutional independence.

The Commission warns that the new model risks making these functions ineffective.

On a positive note, the report says monitoring of asset declarations by public officials was significantly expanded during the reporting period, while the number of corruption-related cases also increased.

However, the European Commission expresses concern over the selective approach to tackling corruption.

Recommendations made over several years on safeguards for the autonomy of the Prosecutor’s Office and judicial independence also remain unimplemented.

De-oligarchisation

According to the report, no steps have been taken towards de-oligarchisation.

The European Commission says a deeply entrenched system of oligarchic influence contributes to state capture and undermines democratic consolidation.

Visa-free travel: recommendations remain unfulfilled

One of the key sections of the European Commission’s report concerns visa-free travel for Georgian citizens.

According to the Commission, Georgia has failed to implement almost all the recommendations made in its previous report under the visa suspension mechanism.

The recommendations focused mainly on protecting fundamental rights and tackling discrimination and corruption.

Following an official assessment in July 2025, the Commission found that the Georgian authorities had failed to take the necessary corrective measures. Instead, they introduced further restrictive laws that run counter to Georgia’s commitments to protecting fundamental freedoms.

In response, the European Commission activated an updated visa suspension mechanism for Georgia, initially for 12 months from 6 March 2026.

The first stage affected holders of diplomatic, service and official passports.

An enhanced dialogue with Georgia was held in June 2026. However, according to the report, it brought no progress on the issues that had prompted the EU’s concerns and led to the activation of the suspension mechanism.

Russia, sanctions and Georgia’s foreign policy

According to the European Commission’s report, Georgia’s alignment rate with EU foreign policy statements and restrictive measures fell from 40% to 38%.

Georgia has not joined most EU sanctions against Russia, Belarus and Iran. The report also highlights a significant increase in direct flights between Georgia and Russia.

Under the EU’s 21st sanctions package, transactions involving the Kulevi oil refinery linked to the trade and processing of Russian oil were banned.

The refinery was granted a six-month transition period to wind down these activities. An exemption may be possible if it switches to alternative oil supplies, subject to appropriate monitoring.

The report notes that Russian crude has become the refinery’s largest source of imported feedstock.

Three cryptocurrency service providers registered in Georgia or recently operating in the country were also added to the EU sanctions list.

EU financial assistance and programmes

The European Union has also reduced financial assistance to Georgia in response to democratic backsliding.

Since 2024, €121.3 million in bilateral funding earmarked directly for the Georgian authorities under the EU’s 2021–2027 Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument has been suspended.

Georgia’s participation in new EU programmes has also been put on hold since 2024.

Georgia has taken part in various EU programmes since 2014. It remains involved in Horizon Europe, Creative Europe, EU4Youth, the Customs programme, Fiscalis and the Interreg Black Sea Basin programme for transnational cooperation.

However, Georgian organisations and individuals can still access certain opportunities under Erasmus+ and the European Solidarity Corps.

Anaklia port: state ownership and funding cuts

The European Commission’s report also addresses the Anaklia deep-sea port project.

According to the document, the project’s development model was changed in July 2026, with the port moving to a so-called landlord port model, which involves full state ownership of the port.

The report notes that construction work was suspended for several months and that state budget funding for the project was cut by 60% during the reporting period.

Georgian authorities respond to European Commission report

Nikoloz Samkharadze, chairman of parliament’s Foreign Relations Committee, said the report was neither realistic nor impartial.

He said the European Commission had no clear understanding of the work being done by the Georgian state or the reforms carried out by government ministries and agencies to bring the country closer to the EU.

Samkharadze attributed this to a lack of proper contacts between the Commission and Georgian government institutions.

Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili said the Georgian authorities had provided the EU with all the information needed to prepare the report, but it was unclear how that information would be reflected in the final document.

Bochorishvili said the lack of dialogue with the EU, including at technical and political levels, made it impossible to properly analyse and assess developments in the country.

How Georgia’s EU accession process came to a halt

Georgia applied to join the European Union in March 2022. In June that year, unlike Ukraine and Moldova, which were granted candidate status, Georgia was given a European perspective. To obtain candidate status, the country was asked to meet 12 priorities, mainly related to democracy, the rule of law and human rights.

In December 2023, Georgia was granted EU candidate status.

However, in June 2024, following the adoption of the “foreign agents” law and other decisions by the authorities, the EU effectively put Georgia’s accession process on hold. On 27 June, the European Council said the actions of the Georgian authorities were jeopardising the country’s European path and had effectively halted the accession process.

The situation deteriorated further on 28 November 2024, when Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the government would not put the opening of EU accession talks on its agenda before the end of 2028 and would refuse EU budget grants.

The announcement triggered mass protests.

The authorities used force and special equipment against demonstrators, and hundreds of people were detained. The use of force against protesters, ill-treatment of detainees and restrictions on the right to peaceful assembly drew criticism from international organisations and human rights groups.

Further legislative changes followed, placing additional restrictions on civic space.

The European Commission’s 2026 report reflects the continuation of these trends: Georgia’s accession process remains stalled, the recommendations have not been implemented, and democratic backsliding, weakening judicial independence and restrictions on fundamental rights continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: ‘Some European leaders don’t want to be photographed with you’ – Georgian PM’s visit to Brussels: what happened
World.content:
Georgia’s Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze took part in the second EU summit, organised by Euronews in Brussels. The summit focused on the prospects for EU enlargement, candidate countries’ integration into the bloc, and the political and economic challenges involved.

At the summit, Kobakhidze invited European Commission representatives to hold open, public debates on democracy, the rule of law, human rights, the economy and transparency.

He said the assessments in the European Commission’s forthcoming report did not reflect reality and described the report as politicised. Kobakhidze said the Georgian government was ready to discuss all contentious issues in public, but claimed that the European side was unwilling to engage in dialogue.

Kobakhidze made these remarks a day before the European Commission published its 2026 annual enlargement report. The report assesses the progress candidate countries have made towards EU membership against criteria including: Democratic institutions and elections;

The rule of law and judicial independence;

Human rights and media freedom;

The fight against corruption;

Economic conditions and reforms;

Progress towards closer integration with the European Union.

What Irakli Kobakhidze said

The prime minister said the Georgian government disagreed with the assessments in the European Commission’s report and believed that issues concerning the country should be open to public debate.

“We criticise European bureaucrats. We are inviting European Commission representatives to take part in a public discussion, a public debate, because we believe that everything in the report does not reflect reality. But let’s debate it. Let’s hold a public debate with European Commission representatives. This is a politicised report,” Kobakhidze said.

He said the European Commission’s report drew on assessments by experts, but the Georgian government disagreed with their conclusions. According to the prime minister, Georgia is one of the most democratic countries among the EU candidates. He also claimed that the country upholds the rule of law and human rights and enjoys high rates of economic growth.

Kobakhidze said the Georgian government was proposing talks with EU representatives, but insisted that they should take place in public rather than behind closed doors. He said the public had a right to know which issues the two sides were discussing and what arguments each was putting forward.

Kobakhidze said the government was confident in its position and believed its decisions served to protect the country’s sovereignty and build a more developed, democratic and transparent state.

Speaking about relations with the European Union, the prime minister said Georgia could not change its behaviour without dialogue. If the European side had concerns about Georgian laws or specific government decisions, he said, it should raise them directly with the Georgian authorities.

“If anyone wants to change Georgia’s behaviour, they should talk to us. But the problem is that they do not talk to us. They are not ready to engage in dialogue,” Kobakhidze said.

The prime minister said Georgia had its own values, which he claimed were in line with those of the European Union. He listed sovereignty, democracy, the rule of law and judicial independence among them.

Kobakhidze also drew a comparison with the Soviet era, saying relations with Europe should not be based on one side giving orders to the other.

“We were part of the Soviet Union for 70 years. I was young at the time, and this is what happened: whatever Moscow said, Georgia had to do. That was not an appropriate approach in a democratic society. Europe needs to adopt a different approach, and we are optimistic that attitudes will change. We are not puppets,” the prime minister said.

Speaking about the attitude of European countries towards Georgia, Kobakhidze also referred to protests in France. He called on EU representatives to apply a consistent and unified approach when assessing Georgia’s laws and government actions.

The prime minister nevertheless expressed optimism that the EU’s attitude towards Georgia would change and that both sides would reconsider the current course of their relations.

At the summit, journalist Maria Tadeo asked Irakli Kobakhidze about the Georgian government’s attempt to ban five opposition parties.

“We have a very good example: Ukraine and Moldova. They have banned political parties and are much further ahead than we are. So we intend to catch up with them,” Kobakhidze replied.

Asked whether this could create problems if he wanted to continue talks with the EU, Kobakhidze said he was inviting “European bureaucrats to provide legal comments”.

“The case is before the Constitutional Court of Georgia. We have asked the court to rule on the constitutionality of certain political parties. This is a legal matter. We are inviting European bureaucrats to provide legal comments. But no one is offering legal comments; they are only making political statements. In doing so, they are interfering with Georgia’s independent judiciary, which goes against European standards,” Kobakhidze retorted.

Maria Tadeo also asked Kobakhidze about his relations with European leaders. In particular, she raised the widely held view that some European leaders would not want to be photographed with him. Kobakhidze replied that he had photographs with all of them.

Comment

According to Rikard Jozwiak, editor of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Europe bureau, the EU’s 2026 enlargement report says the Georgian authorities have taken no steps to improve democracy or protect fundamental rights in the country.

Jozwiak says these problems prompted the European Union to suspend visa-free travel for holders of Georgian diplomatic passports. He warns that this also puts the country’s visa-free regime as a whole at risk.

The report also repeats last year’s assessment that Georgia remains an EU candidate “in name only” and continues to turn down the benefits that come with candidate status and the pre-accession process.

What is the Euronews EU Enlargement Summit?

The Euronews EU Enlargement Summit is an international political event organised by the European media outlet Euronews in Brussels. It was first held in 2025.

Its main purpose is to discuss the prospects for EU enlargement: how the process of admitting new member states should move forward and what political, economic and democratic reforms this requires.

The summit brings together representatives of EU institutions, leaders of EU member states, presidents and prime ministers of candidate countries, members of the European Parliament, and political and economic experts.

Discussions cover candidate countries’ progress, EU enlargement policy, security, democracy and economic cooperation. The event is broadcast on television and digital platforms.

However, this is not an official EU summit or a formal negotiating format organised by EU institutions. Rather, it is a high-level international forum for discussion.

Euronews EU Enlargement Summit

World.title: Foreigners face higher costs and stricter requirements to obtain residency in Armenia
World.content:
Armenia’s new residency application rules

From 1 November, foreigners in Armenia have had to apply for residency permits entirely online. The government has also increased the state fees applicants must pay.

A temporary residence permit now costs 150,000 drams ($418), up from 105,000 drams ($293). A permanent residence permit now costs 250,000 drams ($698), compared with 135,000 drams ($377) previously. Applicants will not receive a refund if the authorities reject their application.

The Migration and Citizenship Service says the number of people seeking residence permits in Armenia has recently increased.

For example, Armenia granted residence permits to 10,561 foreigners in the first half of 2026, compared with 6,656 during the same period in 2025. That represents a 59% increase. Russian citizens make up the largest group among those who received temporary or permanent residence permits.

Analyst Artem Yerkanyan believes that Armenia is regulating the inflow of foreign nationals in line with its own interests.

He explains that making it harder to obtain residency clearly shows that the country is shifting its priorities from quantity to quality.

However, he sees no reason to believe that Armenia will stop attracting people relocating from abroad, particularly from Russia.

“For the overwhelming majority of Russian relocants, this reform will not be a life-changing ordeal. They will be able to adapt easily to the new conditions,” Yerkanyan said, pointing to the rules that apply within the Eurasian Economic Union.

Russia leads the EAEU, whose members include Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia. The union operates a customs framework that guarantees the free movement of labour, goods, services and capital.

Foreign nationals can obtain temporary residency if they have grounds to stay in Armenia for at least one year. These include studying, employment, family circumstances, business activities, Armenian ancestry or other grounds recognised by law.

Foreigners can qualify for permanent residency if they are married to an Armenian citizen, have a close relative who holds Armenian citizenship or have a close relative with special residency status. However, applicants must also have accommodation and sufficient means of subsistence, and must have lived in Armenia for at least three years. Applicants of Armenian ancestry or those who run a business in the country can also qualify for permanent residency.

Special residency status will no longer be granted: what is changing?

The changes, which took effect on 1 November, affect not only state fees but also the eligibility criteria for residency and the procedures for processing applications.

The Interior Ministry says temporary residence permits will now be valid for up to one year, while permanent residence permits will last five years.

The grounds for obtaining permanent residency include:

Armenian ethnicity;

making investments in Armenia;

providing exceptional services to the country;

having family ties or running a business in Armenia, subject to additional legal requirements.

From now on, Armenia will have only two types of residency status: temporary and permanent.

The authorities will no longer grant special residency status. However, those who already hold it will retain all their rights and obligations until their status expires.

Until 1 November 2026, Armenia also granted a special residency status valid for 10 years. The prime minister awarded it to foreign nationals of Armenian descent, as well as foreigners engaged in economic or cultural activities in Armenia. They received a special Armenian passport that allowed them to enter and live in Armenia without an entry visa. People with special residency status enjoyed the same rights and freedoms as Armenian citizens and had the same obligations. The only exception was that they could not vote. They were also exempt from compulsory military service in the Armenian Armed Forces.

Applicants must now submit residence permit applications through a single online platform. The authorities will make decisions within 30 days.

“EAEU regulations will remain in force” – deputy interior minister

Armenia’s Deputy Interior Minister Armen Ghazaryan said that citizens of Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states remain subject to special rules. These reflect the union’s principle of free movement of labour.

As a result, EAEU citizens do not need special permits to work in another member state.

“This provision remains in force. Throughout their employment in Armenia, citizens of EAEU member states – for example, Russia or Kyrgyzstan – are considered to be legally residing in the country.”

According to Ghazaryan, once EAEU citizens obtain a document confirming the legality of their stay in Armenia, they enjoy the same rights as other foreign nationals legally residing in the country.

The document confirming their legal stay costs 30,000 drams ($83).

The deputy minister stressed the importance of digitising procedures for granting residency on the basis of employment or education. He noted that study ranks second among the reasons foreign nationals apply for residency in Armenia. Employment accounts for the largest number of applications.

He also said the government plans to introduce a new type of visa – a work visa – to make it easier for people to enter Armenia. It will complement the existing visa categories: visitor, official, diplomatic and transit visas.

Comment

Analyst Artem Yerkanyan notes that the changes which took effect on 1 November will primarily affect foreigners engaged in economic activities in Armenia.

He points out that, previously, a foreign national could obtain residency by registering as an individual entrepreneur and paying minimal tax. Under the new rules, applicants will have to:

“Invest a more substantial amount in their business – either maintain a bank account balance of at least 1 million drams ($2,793) or provide proof of turnover over the previous 60 days;

In addition, if a foreign national is a co-founder of a limited liability company, its registered capital must amount to at least 2 million drams ($5,586).”

As for Russian citizens, the expert noted that they will continue to benefit from the privileges available to citizens of EAEU member states. In particular, Russians can stay in Armenia for 180 days a year without restrictions.

“Moreover, if they take up employment in Armenia under an employment contract, they will no longer need additional permits. They will only have to pay the fees and taxes required by law,” he added.

Yerkanyan believes that Russian relocants will be able to adapt to the new rules after the necessary consultations.

“They should approach these changes with understanding, as they reflect Armenia’s national interests. Armenia is not the only country reforming its legislation. Kazakhstan, for example, has taken a similar path, and its rules are considerably stricter.”

According to Yerkanyan, the changes to the residency application process reflect both Armenia’s transition to biometric passports and its efforts to liberalise the visa regime with the European Union. In other words, the EU has driven these changes through its requirements.

He believes countries around the world are now seeking to attract migrants who are “law-abiding, economically active, competent and well-educated”:

“In this respect, Armenia is in a fairly advantageous position, because the migrants arriving here – Russians, as well as Indians and Iranians – are not ‘problematic’ migrants.”

In his view, Europe, by contrast, faces serious threats from the arrival of “problematic” migrants. However, he stresses that Armenia should also approach migration with greater caution.

“Until recently, the Russians arriving in Armenia were self-sufficient IT specialists. But if Russia does announce mobilisation, less affluent people may try to move to Armenia. They are more likely to create additional problems for the country than to contribute to the state budget.”

World.title: Georgia’s new amendments to Election Code: how will they affect right to challenge election results?
World.content:
The Georgian government is proposing amendments to the Election Code that would significantly affect the procedures for counting votes and challenging election results, the powers of the election administration, and the registration rules for local and international election observer organisations.

The bill was introduced in parliament on 28 October.

What will change

Election results will no longer be compiled at district level

Until now, Georgia has had three tiers of election commissions:

Precinct commissions , which operate at polling stations and count the votes cast at each station separately;

, which operate at polling stations and count the votes cast at each station separately; District commissions , which collect and consolidate data from the precinct commissions in their respective districts;

, which collect and consolidate data from the precinct commissions in their respective districts; The Central Election Commission (CEC), which compiles the overall results based on data from the district commissions.

Under the proposed changes, polling station protocols will go directly to the CEC, which will compile the results itself.

The final results protocol can only be challenged on specific grounds

Under the amendments, a challenge to the results protocol will only be admissible if:

It omits or incorrectly records data from precinct election commissions;

It omits, incompletely records or incorrectly reflects the results of final court rulings concerning violations of election law.

The amendments also specify that “a claim filed with a court in violation of the requirements of this paragraph will not be admitted for consideration”.

If a court does accept a claim, it will only be able to examine the specific circumstances defined by law.

District commissions will no longer have to conduct random recounts after elections

Until now, district commissions had to randomly select five polling stations and recount their votes within six days of the end of an election.

The amendments abolish this requirement.

The bill’s authors argue that, at polling stations equipped with electronic voting machines, officials count the votes after printing out the results. At stations without such machines, they digitise ballot papers within two days and publish them online. They say this makes additional random recounts unnecessary.

The deadline for finalising election results will be cut from 26 days to 15

Previously, the CEC had 26 days to finalise the results of parliamentary elections, Tbilisi City Council elections and the Tbilisi mayoral election. It had 15 days to finalise the results of local government elections and mayoral races in other municipalities.

Under the new rules, the CEC will have to finalise the results of all elections within two weeks of election day – no later than the 15th day.

Any court proceedings challenging election protocols must also conclude within this period.

The explanatory note accompanying the bill says that 14 days are sufficient to challenge results before district commissions and in court.

“Accordingly, by the 15th day, final protocols that have entered into force will already be in place, while the additional 11 days only prolong the process,” it says.

Winners will have less time to submit campaign spending reports to the Audit Office

An electoral subject – a party or bloc – that preliminary results show has secured the legally required number of votes will have to submit a full report on its election spending to the Audit Office within five days.

Previously, parties had 12 days to submit these reports.

If a party that wins an election fails to submit its report on time or violates the law, the Audit Office will issue a written warning and demand that it rectify the problem. If the violation is serious and could have affected the election results, the CEC will be able, on the Audit Office’s recommendation, to apply to the court and finalise the results without counting the votes cast for that party.

Broadcasters will no longer be able to reallocate unused political advertising slots to other parties

Under the new bill, the final second of every political television  must display the name and number of the electoral subject. Broadcasters will not be allowed to air political s that fail to meet this requirement.

Previously, broadcasters and publications could reallocate advertising time or space to another electoral subject if a party or bloc declined to use its allocated slot.

The amendments will prohibit this practice.

The bill’s explanatory note says the change will help prevent broadcasters from allocating political advertising time beyond the limits set by law.

“This effectively removes the right to challenge election results”

Nona Kurdovanidze, director of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), believes the amendments would effectively remove the possibility of challenging election results.

The lawyer points in particular to the new rules governing challenges to the CEC’s final results protocol. She says that, had these rules applied during the 2024 parliamentary elections, it would not even have been formally possible to challenge violations of ballot secrecy. Consequently, the Tetritskaro court precedent would never have been established.

The Tetritskaro precedent concerns events during Georgia’s parliamentary elections on 26 October 2024.

Voters marked a circle next to their preferred party’s number on the ballot paper. They then placed the ballot inside a special frame envelope and fed it into an electronic vote-counting machine. The ballot papers were printed on thin paper, so the marker ink showed through on the reverse side. As a result, anyone could see how a voter had cast their ballot when they inserted it into the machine.

GYLA subsequently launched legal proceedings over the breach of ballot secrecy, seeking to annul the results at every polling station that used electronic voting technology.

On 4 November, Vladimir Khuchua, a judge at the Tetritskaro District Court (Tetritskaro is a town in southern Georgia), upheld GYLA’s claim and annulled the results at 30 polling stations in two electoral districts. This was the first time a court had confirmed a breach of ballot secrecy during the 2024 elections. However, on 7 November, the Tbilisi Court of Appeal overturned the ruling.

Amendments to Georgia’s Election Code

World.title: Azerbaijani media discuss Patriotic War coverage at round table (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. A round table on the topic "The Chronicle of the Patriotic War in Azerbaijani Media" was held at the Media and Broadcasting Council.

This was reported by the Media and Broadcasting Council.

According to the report, the head of the Department for Work with Media Entities and Journalists at the Media and Broadcasting Council, Natig Mammadli, who moderated the round table, stated that the historic Victory marked a significant milestone in the development of the Azerbaijani media. He noted that solidarity and civic responsibility within the national information space held particular importance during the Patriotic War (Second Karabakh). He also emphasized that the addresses made to the nation by the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, as well as his interviews with international media outlets during that period, played a crucial role in conveying the country’s position to the global community.

Ilham Tumas, a participant of both the First Karabakh War and the Patriotic War, and an author of non-fiction books on the subject of war, highlighted the efforts of journalists in delivering prompt and accurate information from the front lines to the public, countering the disinformation spread by Armenia, and presenting the realities of the war to the international community.

Mail Asgarov, a participant in the Second Karabakh War and a department head at ARB TV, noted that the professionalism, patriotic stance, and sense of responsibility regarding information demonstrated by journalists during the war played a vital role in communicating the realities of Azerbaijan to the world. He emphasized the importance of passing this experience on to young journalists and ensuring they are well-prepared to meet the challenges of the modern information environment.

Bahruz Mammadzade, a member of the Board of the Press Council of Azerbaijan who served in the Special Forces of the Azerbaijani Army, highlighted the significance of an ideological victory in war. He noted that the Patriotic War was defined not only by military operations but also by the struggle waged in the information and ideological spheres.

Maghrur Aliyev, a participant of the Patriotic War and a veteran-journalist, spoke about the bravery of the young people who made history in Karabakh. He stressed the importance of conveying the examples of heroism and self-sacrifice demonstrated by those who contributed to the restoration of the country's territorial integrity to future generations.

Fardin Isazade, a participant of the Second Karabakh War and a military journalist for Baku TV, along with Araz Khan, a staff member at Public Television, underscored the necessity of delivering information to the public accurately, promptly, and objectively during wartime.

At the round table, the speeches of other journalists who operated during the war and in combat zones were also heard; participants exchanged views regarding their work during the Patriotic War, the events they witnessed, and the professional experience they gained. Additionally, a video was presented during the event, showcasing the course of the Patriotic War, the path leading to the historic Victory, and significant moments experienced during that period.

World.title: Azerbaijan approves partially revised Radio Regulations
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. President Ilham Aliyev signed a law approving the “Partially Revised Radio Regulations and Their Annexes.”

The text of the document has been published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.
