World.title: Uzbekistan plans to double uranium output to 15,000 tons by 2030
World.content:
Photo: the telegram channel of the press secretary of the Uzbek president

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Uzbekistan plans to increase annual uranium production to 15,000 metric tons by 2030, up from 7,500 tons in 2026, while targeting more than $2.7 billion in output from 16 types of critical raw materials, as President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reviewed plans to expand the country's mining and processing industries on Thursday.

According to the presidential pres service, the targets were presented during a review of the 2026 priorities and longer-term development plans of state-owned uranium producer Navoiuran and the Uzbek Technological Metals Plant.

The presentation highlighted growing global demand for critical minerals and metals. While demand for traditional metals is increasing by an average of 1% annually, the market for critical minerals is expanding by approximately 10% per year, according to the information presented.

At the Uzbek Technological Metals Plant, the main priority is to establish a complete production chain covering geological exploration, mining, mineral processing, advanced refining and the manufacture of finished products.

The company plans to launch 12 investment projects by the end of 2026, expand its range of localized products and increase production of high-purity selenium and tellurium.

Mirziyoyev instructed officials to accelerate projects involving critical minerals and expand the range of products manufactured in the country. In addition to five types of products already being produced — tungsten, molybdenum, selenium, tellurium and rhenium — Uzbekistan plans to develop production of additional critical minerals, including nickel, cobalt, graphite, antimony, tin, manganese, platinum, vanadium, mercury and copper.

Under the country's plans, annual output across 16 types of critical raw materials is expected to exceed $2.7 billion by 2030.

Particular attention was given to tungsten processing projects, for which Uzbekistan plans to attract $1.1 billion in investment and increase production to nearly $2.2 billion by 2030. The presentation also covered the development of deposits containing rare and rare-earth elements, expanding the plant's resource base and accelerating investment projects.

Additionally, the president reviewed Navoiuran's production performance and development plans amid growing global demand for uranium. According to the presentation, demand for uranium raw materials has increased by 15%–20% in recent years and is expected to rise by a further 28% by 2030.

To increase production, the company plans to expand geological exploration and technological drilling, develop production infrastructure, commission additional sorption units and create 250 new jobs in 2026.

Moreover, the presentation addressed the supply of chemical reagents required for uranium production. Measures are being considered to strengthen cooperation with domestic industrial companies and increase supplies of technical sulfur, sulfuric acid and nitric acid.

Mirziyoyev emphasized the need to introduce alternative technologies into production. By 2030, the share of reagents that can replace sulfuric acid is expected to reach 40%.

Through these measures and the commissioning of additional production facilities, Navoiuran aims to increase annual uranium output from 7,500 tons in 2026 to 15,000 tons by 2030. The company also plans to expand its explored uranium reserves to 200,000 tons.

Following the presentation, Mirziyoyev instructed officials to ensure the timely implementation of investment projects, strengthen the companies' mineral resource bases, commission new technological facilities, increase the production of higher-value-added goods and expand exports.

World.title: November 8 marks Azerbaijani people's national will triumph - analyst
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. November 8 is a day in the history of Azerbaijan that embodies the national will of the people, the strength of the army, and the state’s commitment to its strategic goals, political analyst Azer Garayev told Trend.

“The liberation of Shusha on November 8, 2020, marked a decisive turning point in the Patriotic War and rendered Armenia’s defeat inevitable. This historic event was the logical outcome of years of state-building, military reforms, consistent diplomatic efforts, and the unity between the people and the army. The significance of November 8 is linked to an entire era in Azerbaijan’s modern history. Having overcome the severe political, economic, and military challenges faced during the early years of its independence, the country eventually transformed into one of the region’s powerful states. At the foundation of this journey lies the statehood strategy of Heydar Aliyev, followed by the policy of development and strengthening implemented by President Ilham Aliyev,” the analyst said.

According to him, the origins of Azerbaijan's current successes are to be found in the state-building process carried out during the early years of independence.

“In the early 1990s, Azerbaijan found itself in an extremely complex situation. As a result of Armenia’s military aggression, 20 percent of our territories were occupied, and hundreds of thousands of our compatriots were displaced from their native lands. The country faced political instability, economic decline, and serious challenges within its defense system. Under these circumstances, safeguarding the state’s independence and ensuring its future development became the primary objective.

With the return of Heydar Aliyev to power in 1993, significant steps were taken to restore political stability and strengthen state institutions in Azerbaijan. Necessary conditions were established to develop the country’s economic and political potential, expand international relations, and build a national army. The development priorities defined during those years laid the foundation for Azerbaijan’s future strength.

Following the election of Ilham Aliyev as President in 2003, this strategy entered a new phase. The diversification of the economy, the development of the energy sector, the expansion of transport infrastructure, and the implementation of social projects became the key directions of state policy. The efficient management of oil revenues expanded the country's financial capabilities. These resources were directed toward strengthening defense capabilities, procuring modern weaponry, upgrading military infrastructure, and training professional military personnel.

President Ilham Aliyev repeatedly stated that Azerbaijan's territorial integrity must be restored and that the country would mobilize all its resources to achieve this goal. This stance defined the primary direction of the state's long-term strategy," the analyst noted.

Garayev pointed out that, in parallel with the enhancement of its military potential, Azerbaijan was also strengthening its international standing.

"By pursuing a balanced and pragmatic foreign policy, Azerbaijan developed cooperative relations with various power centers. Its strategic partnership with Turkey, energy and economic cooperation with European nations, and the maintenance of relations with Russia and other neighboring states expanded the country's regional and international reach.

Through active participation in the UN, the Non-Aligned Movement, the Council of Europe, and other international platforms, Azerbaijan brought the consequences of Armenia's policy of occupation to the attention of the global community. UN Security Council resolutions and the fundamental principles of international law supported Azerbaijan's territorial integrity. By sustaining a diplomatic struggle over many years, Baku established a legal and international foundation for future political decisions," he emphasized.

According to the analyst, the 2020 Patriotic War demonstrated the results of the policy Azerbaijan had pursued for many years. Following further military provocations by the Armenian armed forces on September 27, 2020, the Azerbaijani Army launched counter-offensive operations. Throughout the 44-day war, our Armed Forces demonstrated a high level of combat readiness, proficiency in utilizing modern technology, and great professionalism.

The operations conducted by the Azerbaijani Army highlighted the advantages of modern warfare tactics. The deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles, the integration of reconnaissance and strike capabilities, and seamless coordination between units dealt a severe blow to the enemy's defense system. The heroism of our soldiers and officers, the public's support for the army, and the resolute stance of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief were the key factors behind the victory.

The liberation of Shusha on November 8 proved to be the decisive turning point of the war. The city’s complex geographical terrain and strategic importance made the operation exceptionally challenging. Thanks to the valor and professionalism displayed by Azerbaijani military personnel in this mountainous region, Shusha was freed from enemy occupation. This news sparked a profound sense of joy and pride throughout the entire country.

The historic address in which President Ilham Aliyev announced the liberation of Shusha took a special place in the memory of the people. The loss of Shusha shook Armenia’s military-political positions, and the war concluded with the signing of a trilateral statement on November 10, 2020. Azerbaijan achieved a historic milestone toward the restoration of its territorial integrity," Garayev noted.

Garayev remarked that employees of the State Security Service (SSS) also made significant contributions to the achievement of this victory.

"During the Patriotic War, they played a significant role in preventing the enemy's acts of sabotage and subversion, ensuring information and cyber security, and providing the Azerbaijani Army with operational and counter-intelligence data. This service has also been highly valued by the state: according to official information from the State Security Service (SSS), for their bravery during military operations and subsequent activities, 7 members of the Service were awarded the 'Zafar' Order, and 14 were awarded the 'Karabakh' Order, while many others received various other orders and medals," he recalled.

He added that the victory of 2020 defined new tasks for Azerbaijan regarding the full restoration of its sovereignty and the future development of the liberated territories.

"Following the Patriotic War, Azerbaijan began to play a key role in shaping new political realities in the region. Nevertheless, the presence of separatist forces in Karabakh and the continued presence of Armenian armed units on Azerbaijani territory kept security issues at the forefront.

On September 19, 2023, the Azerbaijani Army launched localized anti-terror measures. As a result of the operation, which lasted less than 24 hours, separatist armed units were disarmed, and an agreement on their surrender was reached on September 20. Thus, state sovereignty was fully restored across the entire territory of Azerbaijan. The leaders of the separatist regime were detained and held accountable.

This event marks a significant milestone in the history of Azerbaijan's modern statehood. The country ensured the restoration of its constitutional order within its sovereign territory. The military victory achieved in 2020 was brought to completion in 2023 with the full restoration of sovereignty," the analyst emphasized.

According to Garayev, one of the main directions of state policy thereafter became the restoration of the liberated territories and ensuring the return of former internally displaced persons to their native lands.

"Today, large-scale construction and development projects are being carried out in Karabakh and East Zangezur. New highways, airports, energy infrastructure, residential complexes, schools, and medical facilities are being built. Within the framework of the Great Return program, the phased return of former internally displaced persons to their homes is being facilitated.

The work underway in Shusha, Fuzuli, Zangilan, Jabrayil, Lachin, and Aghdam constitutes an integral part of the state's long-term development plans. Modern urban planning principles, alternative energy sources, and smart infrastructure solutions are enhancing the future economic potential of these territories. Karabakh and East Zangezur also hold a significant place in Azerbaijan's green energy agenda.

Furthermore, Baku is promoting an agenda for regional peace and cooperation. Azerbaijan is engaged in negotiations, based on specific principles, aimed at normalizing relations with Armenia and securing long-term peace. According to Azerbaijan's position, a sustainable peace must be built upon respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, as well as the inviolability of international borders," he pointed out.

The analyst also characterized the meeting held in Washington in August 2025, attended by the leaders of Azerbaijan, Armenia, and the US, as a significant event for the future of the region.

"The agreements reached in Washington created new opportunities for advancing the peace process in the South Caucasus. During the meeting, which involved President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, Prime Minister of Armenia Nikol Pashinyan, and US President Donald Trump, the text of a peace treaty was initialed. This marked a crucial step toward a political and diplomatic resolution to a conflict that had persisted for many years.

As a result of Azerbaijan’s principled stance and consistent diplomatic efforts, new prospects for regional cooperation have emerged. The restoration of transport links, the expansion of economic relations, and the opening of communication channels are of vital importance for the future development of the South Caucasus. The Washington agreements represent a significant achievement in terms of garnering international support for Azerbaijan’s peace agenda," Garayev said.

According to the analyst, the historical significance of November 8 will hold a special place in the national memory of future generations.

"November 8 demonstrated that the Azerbaijani people stand tall in the face of adversity and possess the resolve to engage in a long-term struggle to achieve their national objectives. This victory showcased the strength of the state, the professionalism of the army, and the unity of society.

Today, Azerbaijan faces even greater development goals. The revitalization of Karabakh, the return of the population to their native lands, the expansion of economic opportunities, and the establishment of lasting peace in the region form the core of these objectives. Azerbaijan is now building its future as a victorious state and strengthening its proactive role in regional processes.

November 8 showed us that when national will, strong statehood, and well-defined strategic goals converge, it becomes possible to resolve even the most complex historical challenges. The fact that the Azerbaijani flag flies today in Shusha, Khankendi, and other towns and villages of Karabakh is the most significant outcome of that historic journey," the analyst concluded.

World.title: Baku unveils Patriotic War exhibition and new Victory Hall (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. As part of a joint project between the Baku City Executive Authority and the Ministry of Culture, a ceremony was held at the National Museum of the History of Azerbaijan to unveil an exhibition dedicated to the Patriotic War and the newly created Hall of Victory.

The ceremony, attended by prominent figures from the country’s scientific and cultural communities, representatives of the education sector and the general public, as well as the families of martyrs and veterans, was opened by the director of the National Museum of the History of Azerbaijan, Academician Naila Valikhanli, who welcomed the participants and provided information about the museum’s new exhibition and the Hall of Victory.

Speaking at the event, Eldar Azizov, Head of the Executive Authority of the City of Baku, stated: "Six years ago we endured 44 days of turmoil and anxiety, which culminated in a glorious victory. For the first time in the last 200 years, our people have succeeded in regaining their occupied lands. Over the years, the enemy has remained the same, and the people have remained the same. However, at the heart of our Glorious Victory this time lies the personal contribution of President Ilham Aliyev, his brilliant intellect, and his policies."

At the ceremony, Minister of Culture Adil Karimli noted in his speech: “The historic victory won by the Azerbaijani Army under the leadership of the Victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev is a triumph of our people’s will, unity, and love for the Motherland. Today, with deep respect, we honor the bright memory of our martyrs and express our gratitude to our veterans and all heroes."

The event highlighted that the exhibition features not only historical materials but also modern technological and interactive solutions. It features a simulation game for younger visitors, modern information displays, and an immersive hall illustrating the large-scale restoration and reconstruction efforts underway in the liberated territories, as well as the process of the Great Return.

The main focus of the exhibition is to demonstrate that Azerbaijan’s historic Victory, the restoration of its territorial integrity, and the postwar process of nation-building were achieved thanks to the resolute political will, far-sighted leadership, and strategic vision of President and Victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev. Through the use of modern technology, these historical processes are presented to visitors in a more vivid and interactive manner.

Elbay Gasimzade, Chairman of the Board of the Union of Architects of Azerbaijan; Maleyka Majidova, mother of a martyr; and Famil Melikov, a veteran of the Patriotic War, spoke about the historical significance of the war and the unity and solidarity of Azerbaijani people. It was noted that, thanks to the heroism of the Azerbaijani Army under the leadership of President Ilham Aliyev, Azerbaijani lands were liberated from occupation. Currently, large-scale restoration and reconstruction work is underway in these territories, and the return of former internally displaced persons to their homelands is proceeding rapidly.

At the conclusion of the event, copies of the book “History of the Patriotic War: Restoration of Azerbaijan’s Territorial Integrity – The Factor of Personality,” published in English and Russian and dedicated to important historical events that took place in the period following the Patriotic War, were presented. The book is a joint project of the Executive Authority of the City of Baku and the Institute of History.

World.title: Uzbekistan, US think tank review mining investment cooperation
World.content:
Photo: the Ministry of Mining Industry and Geology of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Uzbekistan and the US think tank Center for the National Interest (CFTNI) held talks in Tashkent on November 4 to explore expanded investment in the mining and geological sectors.

According to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Mining Industry and Geology, First Deputy Minister Feruza Khamidova met with the CFTNI delegation to outline priorities for mineral resource development.

The delegation included Center President Paul Saunders, Senior Fellow Andrew Kuchins and Marsha Olive, head of the Central Asia Colloquium at Johns Hopkins University.

The discussions focused on the efficient development and use of mineral resources that are important for industrial production, as well as opportunities to attract investment into Uzbekistan's mining and geological industries.

Moreover, the participants considered prospects for expanding cooperation in these sectors and identifying potential areas for future investment engagement.

The Center for the National Interest is a Washington, DC-based foreign policy think tank that focuses on international affairs, US foreign policy and geopolitical developments. It conducts research, organizes policy discussions and brings together experts, policymakers and business representatives to examine issues affecting US interests and international relations. Its engagement with Uzbekistan provides an opportunity to discuss the country's mineral resources and investment prospects with US policy and regional experts.

World.title: Breaking: New wave of bomb threats hits passenger flights across Europe
World.content:
Bomb threats have affected at least 15 flights in Europe today, in the largest disruption this week after similar threats were made on Monday and Tuesday.

Thursday's disruption particularly affected low-cost carriers flying over Italy, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic, as well as France, Brussels and Austria.

No explosives have been found on any of the affected flights, and the source of the threats is yet to be determined.

The first reported affected flight was an Aer Lingus plane flying from Dublin to Rome, diverted to an air base at Évreux, France, following a bomb threat.

Seven flights and cruise ship disrupted in Europe by bomb threats Seven flights across Europe were grounded on Tuesday, after receiving separate bomb threats.

All 151 passengers and six crew members are safe and military bomb defusal teams are examining the plane, officials said.

Soon afterwards, three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, had to make emergency landings because of bomb threats on board.

Two of the flights, one from Copenhagen and the other from Madrid, landed safely at Sofia's Vasil Levski Airport, airport officials said.

The third flight, from London's Stansted Airport to Sofia, had been diverted and landed safely at the airport in Plovdiv — Bulgaria’s second-largest city — Plovdiv Airport CEO Krassimir Peshev said.

Bulgaria's transport ministry later said inspections carried out on the three planes identified no issues.

Italian local media also reported at least four flights over Italy had been affected, including two heading to Milan, one which had taken off in Milan, and one heading to Rome.

The alerts did not disrupt operations at Rome's Fiumicino airport, the company managing the airport said.

Two Finnair flights from Helsinki were affected, including one to Rome and one to Vienna. (Reuters: Denis Balibouse)

The Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was successfully escorted into the city by Italian Air Force units, and a Finnair spokesperson said it "nevertheless landed as normal". It has been checked by bomb squad units.

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw was diverted to Vienna.

An Aegean Airlines flight from Thessaloniki and a Ryanair flight from Porto both landed safely at their destination in Milan, local media said.

Finnair said its flight from Helsinki to Vienna, operated by Jettime, also received a threat but landed normally in Vienna.

Romania's intelligence agency said another Wizz flight from Milan to Bucharest had received a bomb threat but landed safely in Bucharest.

Czech police said on X that four planes heading to Prague were affected by bomb threats.

No explosives were found on those planes after landing, local media cited a police spokesperson as saying.

Poland's LOT airline said its flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels after a security warning. (Reuters: Kacper Pempel)

Poland's LOT airline also said its flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels after a security warning, but the threat was not confirmed.

Crew and security services carried out inspections of the plane and no dangerous or suspicious items were found.

It was the third day this week in which bomb threats disrupted air traffic over Europe, with about 10 flights targeted on Tuesday.

Those threats — which turned out to be hoaxes — forced the closure of a Warsaw airport and the deployment of Italian air force jets to protect flights.

On Monday, a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton airport to Sofia was diverted following a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.

World.title: Union pushes for mandatory sentences after alleged assault on Mount Isa police
World.content:
The Queensland Police Union (QPU) is calling for mandatory minimum sentencing for serious assaults on police after an alleged attack that left an officer with a cut jaw.

A male officer was taken to hospital after he and two colleagues were allegedly involved in an altercation in the city about 2:30am on October 30, a Queensland Police Service (QPS) spokesperson said.

Two men, aged 26 and 24, have been charged over the alleged assault and are set to face court.

Shane Prior says the officer sustained cuts and substantial injuries to his cheek and nose. (Supplied: Queensland Police Union)

QPU president Shane Prior said reforms were needed to better protect police.

"If you assault a police officer … there is one place for you, and that is inside a prison cell," Mr Prior said.

"As far as I'm concerned, that meets community expectations."

The union leader and former frontline officer said he had since spoken with the Mount Isa staff involved, including the injured officer.

Mr Prior said he sustained "injuries to his cheekbone and upper jaw [and] a deep laceration to the top area of his lip and nose".

'We've got to do something differently'

Mandatory minimum sentencing reforms for serious assaults on emergency workers were referred to the Queensland Sentencing Advisory Council by then attorney-general Yvette D'Ath.

The report found that more than 90 per cent of serious assaults on emergency workers, examined in the previous 10 years, resulted in a custodial sentence.

Shane Prior wants the state government to introduce mandatory minimum sentencing for serious assaults on police. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Mr Prior said it did not go far enough.

"We've got to do something differently," he said.

Data from the Queensland Sentencing Board in 2025 showed aggravated serious assaults on police had increased.

In the 2019-2020 financial year, 220 matters involved a sentencing for aggravated serious assault on police by adult perpetrators.

In the last financial year, that grew to 360.

Between 2020 and 2025, 48 per cent of sentenced matters involving serious assault on police resulted in imprisonment while 20 per cent were wholly suspended, the data showed.

'Doesn't stand up'

Griffith University senior law lecturer Simon McKenzie acknowledged the need for worker safety but said mandatory minimum sentencing would not deter assaults.

"The idea that someone is having a disagreement with a police officer and think, 'Maybe I'll assault them, but maybe I won't, because of the mandatory minimum' doesn't really stand up to scrutiny," he said.

Simon McKenzie says there is little evidence to show mandatory minimum sentencing would reduce assault rates. (Supplied: Griffith University)

Dr McKenzie said such reforms would likely lead to higher prison populations and a less efficient justice system.

"It really reduces the likelihood that people will plead guilty because there's no point if you get the mandatory minimum … so you might as well roll the dice," he said.

The state government last month passed mandatory minimum sentencing laws for bail breaches, which take effect at the end of this month.

In a statement to the ABC, Attorney-General Deb Frecklington would not rule out whether similar laws for assaults on police were being considered.

She said the government was steadfast in its commitment to make Queensland safer.

"We've always said we will continue to strengthen laws where required," Ms Frecklington said.

World.title: Woman alleged to have stalked Greens senator appears in court
World.content:
A woman has appeared in a Perth court accused of stalking and threatening WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John.

The 40-year-old is charged with one count of aggravated stalking with intent to intimidate, and demanding property by written threats.

She appeared in the Perth Magistrates Court on Thursday, and was granted bail with conditions, including that she not contact Senator Steele-John.

However, her identity was suppressed by Magistrate Clare Stanyer due to an "ongoing matter".

Jordon Steele-John became a senator in 2017. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The woman is next due in court on February 25.

'Workplace investigation'

Separately, Senator Steele-John took leave from parliament in October after a group of current and former party staffers wrote to Greens leader David Shoebridge about "multiple allegations of serious misconduct" by the senator, relating to his "behaviour in the presence of women".

Senator Steele-John has denied the allegations, saying rumours had been weaponised by a faction of the Greens.

The allegations are now the subject of an external "workplace investigation" by Perth law firm Modern Legal, commissioned by the WA branch of the Greens.

The inquiry will investigate Senator Steele-John's "individual behaviour and allegations", and a "crisis comms" document about how the WA Greens would manage allegations about him.

The investigation is scheduled to last six weeks, with a final report due in eight weeks.

Jordon Steele-John's behaviour is under investigation. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Senator Shoebridge has previously said he would not prejudge the inquiry, and that it was appropriate for Senator Steele-John to take leave.

Senator Shoebridge's office declined to comment on the ongoing court matter, and the inquiry.

Senator Steele-John's office has been contacted for comment.

World.title: 'Completely dead': How Trump himself 'killed' the MAGA movement
World.content:
Former Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene says the results of the US midterms are not simply the end of an era but also the end of the MAGA movement she once championed and that only one person is to blame.

Ms Greene is adamant that person is US President Donald Trump.

Marjorie Taylor Greene was once one of MAGA's loudest voices. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

"The MAGA movement's completely dead, and Trump himself is the one that killed it," Ms Greene told 7.30.

She said that might mean a period of upheaval in US politics as the landscape shifts to a Democrat-controlled House and Senate and the Republican Party looks to rebuild after the historic midterms loss that also turned the traditionally red state of Texas blue.

Democrat James Talarico flipped the Texas Senate seat in an historic election. (Reuters: Kaylee Greenlee)

"Does that mean that Americans change the way they feel on issues and the things they want? I don't think so," Ms Greene said.

"[But] how that gets reorganised, I think that'll take some time to see what everybody wants.

"Everyone asks, 'Are we having a third party? Who's going to be the new leader of Republicans?' I think those answers don't come easily and are actually going to have to take some time to sort themselves out."

Ms Greene said that might mean a calmer United States and the removal of the partisanship and divisiveness that Trumpian politics has brought with it.

Majorie Taylor Greene says the MAGA movement is now dead. (Reuters: Andrew Kelly)

"The ground is changing, and issues that are important to the populist right are also important to the populist left," she said.

"What looks interesting to me for the future is where there can be common ground found between the left and the right, and people come together and work on those issues.

"That's what younger generations want.

"Many Americans are tired of the constant drama and fearmongering and insanity that gets shoved into their lives from Washington DC."

Sun sets on the Trump era

Ms Greene was formerly a huge supporter of Mr Trump but the pair fell out over her calls for the Epstein Files to be properly investigated.

Marjorie Taylor Greene has called for the release of the remaining Epstein Files. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

She says the midterms results are a rebuke of Mr Trump and, in her words, were a "referendum" on his leadership.

"Last night was a referendum on Donald Trump and Donald Trump only," Ms Greene told 7.30 in Washington.

"He told everyone for the past year, 'Vote like I am on the ballot,' and the American people did."

She accused him of turning his back on those who put him into the White House for the second time.

Marjorie Taylor Greene says the midterm elections were a referendum on Trump's leadership. (AP: Karl DeBlaker)

"The White House became a revolving door of foreign leaders," she said.

"The dinners he had existed with the big tech CEOs, leaders of major industries, the defence industry and so forth.

"Those are the people that he constantly entertained ... he pretty much forgot about all the people that showed up to the MAGA rallies over and over for him."

President Donald Trump next to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Elon Musk, and surrounded by top executives of AI firms. (AP: Jacquelyn Martin)

Asked if this result meant the end of the Trump era, Ms Greene was clear.

"Yes, of course," she said.

"He's now a lame duck.

" This is the second half of his second administration by our constitution. He cannot run for president again. He's also ... in his 80s now, so this Trump era is definitely on its way to sunset. "

'Like it or not', Israel an issue

The US involvement with Israel was a major factor in the midterm results, says Ms Greene. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

Cost of living, corruption allegations, immigration and the actions of ICE agents all played a part in how Americans voted but Ms Greene said the issue of the United States' support for Israel in multiple wars in the Middle East also had an impact.

The war with Iran, in particular, has caused global oil prices to rise and seen Americans, along with citizens of many other nations, find pain at the pump.

Ms Greene said the US involvement with Israel could not be ignored.

"It was a top issue whether people like it or not," she said.

"Our government leaders and most of my colleagues that I served in Congress with, the administration, the president himself, have basically lent themself to be used by foreign countries, government and military.

" It's not just Israel. If you filled that in with any other country, it would be equally as offensive. "

Majorie Taylor Green says Trump is now a "lame duck". (Reuters: Umit Bektas)

However, she said that Israel's actions in Gaza made this worse.

Israel's war was triggered by the October 7, 2023 terrorist attacks led by Hamas, which resulted in 1,200 deaths.

A UNICEF report released in June said that at least 20,179 children were killed in Gaza in the two years since October 7, 2023.

Ms Greene said the number of child deaths had left Americans "disgusted".

"These aren't terrorists," she said.

" We're talking about kids. And most Americans are so absolutely horrified and disgusted that our tax dollars, by the billions, go to that country every single year, that our military produced weapons and ammunition have been used to murder kids. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: WA farmers say reported canola crop failures could cost millions
World.content:
Farmers are eyeing legal action after some reported losses of crops of a genetically modified canola line potentially in the millions of dollars across Western Australia.

A specialist agribusiness law firm has received dozens of enquiries from WA grain growers this season, all alleging that the glyphosate-resistant TruFlex canola variety failed after planting.

An implanted gene developed by agricultural giant Bayer, TruFlex helps canola plants survive weed control chemicals like glyphosate, commonly known by the brand name Roundup.

The gene is, in turn, implanted into strains developed by individual chemical companies, which sell to wholesalers supplying individual farms.

Mark Fowler farms near Williams, 170 kilometres south-east of Perth, with additional land further east near Wickepin.

Farmers and agronomists have reported significantly reduced plant strength in some varieties. (Supplied: Courtney Piesse)

Parts of his business are located in a strip of WA's agricultural zone, which has received little rain this season, coupled with severe frost events.

Mr Fowler, who is also WAFarmers Grains Council president, said particular canola varieties he planted this season had underperformed, and he remained convinced the weather was not to blame.

Mark Fowler says there is significant damage to some of his crops. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

"We have got about 3,500 hectares of canola, and about 1,100 of that is the two varieties that have got this issue — and that could cost us up to as much as $1 million. That is not a cost we can accept," Mr Fowler said.

The complaints centre on Emu and Hunter varieties from Nufarm Seeds, and the InVigor LR405 40P strain produced by BASF.

Bailiwick Legal associate director Matilda Lloyd said the firm had been contacted by more than 40 growers reporting problems with their plants.

Mark Fowler says the damage will come at a significant cost. (Supplied: Mark Fowler)

Ms Lloyd said farmers believed some varieties had lost their tolerance for glyphosate.

"We've got some farmers who have a large majority of their program with this variety," she said.

"Their losses could be in the millions of dollars."

Matilda Lloyd says dozens of growers have contacted her legal firm. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

A BASF spokesperson said the company was aware of reports of crop underperformance, and was working with growers and agronomists to understand each reported case.

"The cause has not been determined, and our technical team is on the ground investigating," the spokesperson said.

A Nufarm spokesperson said the company was conducting similar inquiries.

"A number of agronomic and seasonal factors may be relevant," their spokesperson said.

Bayer said the company was aware of reports regarding canola performance and was gathering relevant facts.

Farmers protected by consumer law

Consumer Protection told the WA Country Hour that farmers had a right to seek compensation for seed that did not perform as stated on the label.

Commissioner for Consumer Protection Trish Blake said producers were protected by the same laws as consumers.

"In Western Australia, farmers have a unique position where they are protected, just as consumers are — so that means all the consumer guarantees apply to farm products," Ms Blake said.

Trish Blake says farmers should collect as much evidence as possible. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"So in this instance, the grain must be of an acceptable quality, and it must be fit for purpose and match any descriptions that the manufacturer sold it to them under."

The commissioner, WAFarmers and Bailiwick Legal urged farmers to collect as much information as they could.

"If there are multiple farmers who are experiencing the same thing, having that gathering of all of their experiences will start to show the grain is the problem — not something the grower has done," Ms Blake said.

World.title: Murder trial hears claims Frances Crawford wanted husband to leave RAAF
World.content:
A former RAAF pilot accused of killing his wife told his boss she “didn’t want him to be in the Air Force anymore” and changed his work duties for her before she died, a jury has heard.

Robert Crawford is on trial in the Supreme Court in Brisbane, charged with the murder of 49-year-old Frances Crawford.

The 49-year-old denies killing her and has pleaded not guilty.

In July 2024, Ms Crawford's body was found at the bottom of a retaining wall on their Upper Lockyer property beside an overturned ride-on lawn mower.

Prosecutors allege Mr Crawford caused her death, before manipulating the scene to look like an accident.

On Thursday, Mr Crawford's commanding officer in his squadron, Mark Seery was called to give evidence.

Mr Seery told the jury in 2023 and 2024 Mr Crawford discussed his marriage issues with him and often became upset.

"He said they were having difficulties," he said.

Psychologist Frances Crawford died at her Upper Lockyer home in July 2024. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

The jury has previously heard during this period the couple went through a separation, due to Ms Crawford discovering Mr Crawford had been unfaithful.

Mr Seery told the jury he was not aware of specific problems, but recalled Mr Crawford once telling him Ms Crawford began taking medication which was "creating disruption between them".

He told the jury Mr Crawford also divulged his job was a source of tension in his relationship, and he claimed Ms Crawford no longer wanted him to travel.

"She didn't want him to be in the Air Force anymore," he said.

The jury was shown text messages between Mr Seery and Mr Crawford sent in February 2024.

In the messages, Mr Crawford said "big joint counselling session went better than I thought it would" and he was planning to move back into the family home the following month.

He went on to say in another message, "still a long road ahead".

The court heard Mr Crawford's job was a source of tension in the relationship. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

After the couple reconciled, Mr Seery told the jury, Mr Crawford expressed still having difficulties, which centred around him travelling for work.

He told the jury Mr Crawford said his wife took issue with a trip he took to Townsville.

"We had discussed bringing him back sooner," he said.

After this trip, Mr Seery told the jury he allowed Mr Crawford to take regular days off on a weekly basis, to help ease the stress at home.

In more text messages shown to the jury, Mr Seery thanked Mr Crawford for going on a last-minute trip to Papua New Guinea in the weeks before Ms Crawford's death.

Mr Seery said: "I hope it hasn't stressed the home front too much."

Mr Crawford replied "it wasn't fun when I told her, but it was good for me to get away tbh".

He went on to say "I feel happy when I come to work".

Mr Seery told the jury he believed Mr Crawford was "eager to get home".

Jurors in the trial this week visited the house where Frances Crawford was found dead. (Queensland Police Service)

After this, he told the jury Mr Crawford arranged to do "local flights only" which meant "not flying overnight" anywhere.

The jury has already heard Mr Crawford told police he believed his wife was trying to move the lawnmower that night because sprinklers were due to come on.

Earlier Detective Sergeant Troy Weston gave evidence about tests he did on the sprinkler systems.

Sergeant Weston told the jury he found timers had been set for the afternoon and evening but conceded he did not run the sprinklers with water, to check if they operated correctly.

He also admitted he did not know Mr Crawford advised there was another sprinkler system, which would go off randomly, and also did not research how the sprinkler system worked.

"I didn't read the instructions," he said.

The trial continues.

World.title: Raiders 'couldn't have offered any more' to want-away Hudson Young
World.content:
Ricky Stuart says the Canberra Raiders "bent over backwards" to keep Hudson Young at the club, as the star back-rower touched down in Port Moresby ahead of a potential move the the PNG Chiefs.

Canberra stunningly pulled their $4.4 million, four-year offer to the Blues star on Monday.

Young travelled to Papua New Guinea this week, with the 2028 expansion club having already offered the six-time Kangaroo international $900,000 per year.

That tax-free package would have meant he would take home far more in his pay packet than the Raiders' offer, but the NRL established Young's market value at $1.1 million, which has since been revised to $1 million.

ARLC chairman Peter V'landys told Nine Newspapers that players can seek to challenge their "official" market value and make their own submissions to the salary cap auditor.

"Let's say a player wanted to be with his family or there are other specific reasons," V'landys said.

"We just don't want the salary cap rorted. However, we know that at times there are exceptional circumstances, so we take those exceptional circumstances into account.

"We won't have a situation where people manipulate the salary cap.

"The unfortunate thing is with the tax-free status of PNG, we have to be extra cautious with the market value of the players there."

Hudson Young has played nine State of Origin matches for the Blues. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Raiders' $1.1 million per season offer was understood to be the biggest in the club's history, with Stuart saying the club could go no higher.

"We couldn't have offered Hudson any more," Stuart told 666 ABC Radio Canberra.

"I mean, we bent over backwards to try and keep Hudson and it would have been unfair on the club if we had went any further.

"We were at a stage where it was probably too much, yet we look after our players and we do everything we possibly can for them.

"But it gets to a stage where you've got to make a decision [and] my position and [Raiders CEO] Don Furner's position is we have to look after the club."

The 28-year-old made his NRL debut with the Raiders in 2019 and has played 155 NRL games for the Green Machine.

Stuart acknowledged that Young was well within his rights to seek out new opportunities, and that all the clubs agreed with the expansion to PNG and the challenges that would hold for the rest of the competition.

However, the veteran coach was under no illusions why Young was looking for pastures new.

Ricky Stuart says money was the driving factor moving forward. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

"Money," Stuart said.

"Absolutely it is [all about money].

"That doesn't bother me one bit. If Hudson wants to make that decision and take those tax-free dollars, you've got to understand he's got to live in Papua New Guinea."

It was put to Stuart that Young, who is currently recovering from an Achilles rupture that he suffered against South Sydney in July, may well look for a release from his contract for the 2027 season, with the Chiefs not coming in until 2028.

Stuart said any decision on that would be up to the player's management, but bemoaned the "messy" process that allowed players to sign a year in advance for a new club.

"Unfortunately … with our rules and the regulations, the guidelines we have with our ability for players to go off and sign at another club 12 months in advance, it makes it very messy," he said.

"I don't agree with that interpretation or the guidelines we've got in the competition. I think it makes it very messy and I feel very, very sorry for the fans, because you got some of your favourite players, players you want to watch, players you want to keep with your club in 12 months' time playing elsewhere.

"I think it's very unfair on the fans, but it is what it is."

Hudson Young has played for the Raiders since 2019. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

Stuart, despite acknowledging that players moving on was just business, said he did take it "personally" when players move on.

"I do take it personally, and I take it very personally about coaching this team, this club," Stuart said.

"I do find it difficult at times, but you got to lose the emotion and see the business side of it.

"I'm not disgruntled with the fact that Hudson's looking elsewhere, that's his choice and decision.

"But what my club's done is give him probably the highest offer that's ever been offered to a player at this club in its time. It was a very, very generous offer, probably too big of an offer. But we did it [and] now he's knocked it back.

"We've got to move forward. We've got to move on."

ABC/AAP

World.title: Teen charged over motorhome fire that left man inside critically injured
World.content:
A teenage boy has been charged in relation to a motorhome fire that left a man living inside with critical burns.

Police allege the motorhome was set alight in the early hours of October 29.

They allege a 14-year-old Wallsend boy was responsible, charging him today with damage property by fire/explosives greater than $15,000 and reckless grievous bodily harm.

He appeared before the Children's Court today and was refused bail.

At the time of the fire, witnesses said they heard loud bangs and explosions before it was swallowed up by a fireball.

In a statement at the time, Fire and Rescue NSW said there had been reports of gas bottles involved in the fire.

Police praised bystanders afterwards, saying the blaze was suspicious.



Forensic officers declared the motorhome a crime scene.

Police investigate the fire. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

The 69-year-old occupant was described by locals as a quiet man who had fallen on hard times.

One resident said complaints had been made to the council about the motorhome being parked in local streets.

Police said a resident pulled the man out of the burning vehicle to safety.

NSW Ambulance paramedics treated the man for burns before he was taken to John Hunter Hospital and later flown to Royal North Shore Hospital.

He remains there in a critical condition.

The teenager is due back in court again next Friday.

World.title: Besieged Labor MP’s alleged debts mount under fresh legal threat
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsWAWA Parliament Besieged Labor MP’s alleged debts mount under fresh legal threat Hamish Hastie and Connor McGoverne November 5, 2026 — 9:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Riverton MP Jagadish Krishnan is facing another demand for more than $1 million, this time from a Perth-headquartered mining and construction conglomerate that also owns Indian Rugby Premier League franchise the Chennai Bulls. AvidSys, the Indian-Australian-owned Guatam family business, sent Krishnan a letter of demand in June, seeking $1.93 million. Riverton MLA Jagadish Krishnan. Hamish Hastie The allegedly unpaid money relates to the proposed sale of the GP network Krishnan founded, Spectrum Health Group, to AvidSys, which fell through last year. AvidSys’ parent company Avid Global Holdings alleged Krishnan’s company promised to cover the legal and professional costs associated with the sale.



The demand adds to the financial pressures the WA Labor MP is already facing, after WAtoday and 9News revealed he was being sued in a New Jersey court for $1.2 million over an allegedly unpaid loan secured in 2024. Krishnan, known under his nickname Dr Jags, also used his family home in Mosman Park, 18 kilometres from the electorate he represents in Parliament, to secure a $330,000 loan with an interest rate of 3.5 per cent a month, Landgate documents show. A June 15 letter from Clayton Utz lawyers on behalf of Avid Global Holdings demanded $1,932,020. “In or about late October 2025, you represented to our client that you would pay all of our client’s legal and other professional costs incurred by our client in connection with the Transaction,” it said. “Since that time, you repeated the Representation to our client on a number of occasions in numerous telephone conversations.



“You knew or intended that our client would so act; and our client now suffers detriment because the assumption has not been fulfilled. AvidSys chairman Ansh Gautam. “It would be unjust for you to retain that benefit without making payment.” That payment was demanded within five days of the date of the letter. AvidSys founding director and chairman Ansh Gautam declined to comment but confirmed the letter had been sent.



Krishnan said he’d made all financial declarations as required by parliament, declaring the AvidSys issue a “private matter” he was trying to resolve. Related Article Exclusive

WA Parliament Labor’s Riverton MP spends nearly entire salary on electorate expenses “My legal representatives have sought more information from Avid Global Holdings regarding their initial correspondence sent in June, but have not received a response since June,” he said. Krishnan resigned from all his directorships ahead of entering politics. He told 9News last year that he had “been out of business for almost four years”. Before the sale of Spectrum Health to AvidSys fell through last year, the latter company issued a press release heralding the deal, while declaring Krishnan would stay on as an advisor.



“Following the acquisition by AvidSys Group, Dr Jags Krishnan will continue to support Avid Health and drive the integration and future growth of the business” the statement said. The intrigue in the MP’s financial dealings intensified after this masthead found he had spent almost his entire parliamentary salary on electorate expenses. Premier Roger Cook said he had spoken to Krishnan about his disputes. “Since my return from my trade mission to China, I have spoken with Dr Krishnan, and he advised these are private commercial legal matters that he will continue to defend,” Cook said. Spectrum Health Group is understood to be in the process of being sold in a deal believed to be worth $47.5 million to rival GP network Family Doctor, owned by Melbourne businessman Rodney Aziz.



“All dealings will be closed on full settlement, which is due at the end of the month,” Krishnan said. He refused to detail how much money he would make from the sale, citing commercial confidence. The American businessman suing Krishnan over the alleged $1 million unpaid loan also claimed he spent thousands on the politician’s accommodation, a limousine trip and an evening Hudson River cruise past the famous Statue of Liberty. Cook said he had reminded Dr Krishnan of the standards expected of members of parliament around the disclosure of gifts. Krishnan has maintained he has met his declaration obligations as an MP.



Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti backed Krishnan on Thursday. “He’s been an excellent member for Riverton, working for his community, delivering for his community, and he’ll continue to be a very good member for Riverton,” she said.

A 14-year-old boy has been arrested over a horrific group attack in Ellenbrook that was filmed and shared over social media, as the community rallies around the young boy who was savagely bashed and threatened with a knife. Confronting footage of the assault, which is understood to have occurred at Coolamon Oval early on Sunday morning, has spread across social media, prompting a warning from police against online users identifying the boys involved – and their families – in the comments section. Loading Midland District Detective Inspector Gary Butler told Radio 6PR police were investigating the attack and were working with the victim’s family on an official complaint. “A number of the people involved, their parents have come forward,” he said.



On Thursday afternoon, a WA Police spokesperson revealed a 14-year-old boy had been arrested and was assisting police with their inquiries. “Detectives are continuing to investigate the involvement of further parties,” they said. It is understood the incident started ostensibly as a robbery, with the attackers allegedly demanding the boy’s vape, before then telling him to hand over clothes. Butler said the 13-year-old boy at the centre of the assault was lucky to not have any more severe injuries, and was “holding up well at the minute, and we’re providing all the support we can give to him”. “Hopefully by this afternoon, we can provide the community some reassuring outcomes as to how we’ve progressed this investigation and put some calm back into the community,” he said.



In a statement, WA Police said the 13-year-old was allegedly assaulted by several juveniles believed to be known to him at the reserve on Coolamon Boulevard. “It is further alleged a knife was produced, threats were made and property was stolen from the victim,” the statement read. “The victim received minor injuries and later attended St John of God Midland Public Hospital for medical treatment.” WA Police said officers became aware of vision of the incident circulating online and commenced inquiries. “Police understand the incident has caused considerable concern within the community and ask

members of the public to remain calm and allow detectives to conduct their investigation,” WA police said in a statement.



“Members of the community are strongly urged not to take matters into their own hands, threaten

retaliation or publish the names, photographs or personal information of people believed to be involved.” Editor's pick Updated

Courts Jordon Steele-John’s ex granted bail on stalking charges as WA Greens inquiry begins There has been an outpouring of support for the young boy at the centre of the attack, with offers to help the family and plans for a fundraising car cruise. Tania Lawrence, the federal MP for Hasluck, said she was “absolutely heartbroken” to see the vision of the boy being assaulted. “I can’t begin to imagine what he and his family have been through,” she posted to social media.



“No person should ever experience something so horrific, and no family should have to endure such heartbreak. “What happened to this young man is shocking and traumatising, but the kindness and compassion we’ve seen from people across our community is a reminder of just how much we care for one another.” One of the most concerning moments in the video came when one of the attackers brandished a large knife as the boy continued to be bashed on the ground. On Wednesday, Police Minister Reece Whitby said the presence of the knife meant “one wrong move could have had tragic consequences that might have ended a life and might have resulted in a very serious outcome for those young people involved”. Whitby vowed “serious consequences” for the attackers.



“We will make sure that the law is enforced because this is unacceptable,” he said. Editor's pick Exclusive

Weather WA stalls on heatwave health plans ahead of scorching summer The video’s proliferation on social media also spurred debate about Labor’s “post and boast” legislation, which has stalled in the upper house. Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas accused the government of “sitting on their hands” for not bringing the legislation forward, however Whitby laid blame at the feet of the opposition and Greens for the delay. The Greens have previously raised concerns about the legislation’s stifling effect on protests.



Speaking to 6PR, Butler urged social media users to refrain from naming the alleged perpetrators or their families in the comments section. “It’s certainly something that we don’t condone, and for a number of reasons,” he said. “Can people be 100 per cent sure who they’re naming? And, you know, we don’t want innocent people to be caught up in this. “It’s very easy to sit on your phone and type things, but we really need to think of A, the community, and B, the family and then their extended family, because violence isn’t the answer.”

Multiple flights in Europe made emergency landings on Thursday after being diverted because of bomb threats, authorities said. The incidents followed hoax bomb threats earlier this week that prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, a military escort.

At least eight flights from Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw were confirmed to have been targeted with bomb threats, most diverted to other airports for emergency landings, while others landed safely at their destinations. So far, inspections have not turned up hazardous or suspicious materials.

Czech police said they deployed at Prague’s Vaclav Havel Airport to prepare for the landing of four planes after receiving a threat of explosive devices on board. Police said that “all necessary security measures have been activated.”

The path of flight EI402 going from Dublin to Rome, after it was diverted following a bomb threat. FlightRadar24

Earlier, a flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in western France because of a bomb threat, the French prime minister’s office said. The flight landed safely at the base in Evreux in Normandy, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office said. All 151 passengers and six crew members were safe, and military bomb disposal teams were examining the plane, the office said.

World.title: ‘A dumping ground for blood oil’: Pressure mounts on Canberra over Putin trade ties
World.content:
PoliticsFederalBlood Oil ‘A dumping ground for blood oil’: Pressure mounts on Canberra over Putin trade ties Rob Harris November 5, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. An international coalition of organisations has written to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese demanding urgent legislation to stop petrol and diesel refined from Russian crude oil in third countries entering Australia. The B4Ukraine Coalition – a group of nearly 100 civil society organisations campaigning to strip Russia of economic resources for its war – estimates Australia has imported $16.5 billion worth of petroleum products made partly from Russian oil since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, potentially generating $1.7 billion in tax revenue for the Kremlin. Almost 70 per cent of oil exported to Australia from Brunei’s Hengyi refinery in the first seven months of the year was Russian-derived, a Finnish think tank has found. Marija Ercegovac The call comes as Australia’s forestry industry raises separate concerns that up to 100,000 cubic metres of imported timber products each year could contain Russian-sourced material, exposing further weaknesses in Canberra’s sanctions enforcement. The coalition accused the federal government of failing to act despite repeated warnings and an August Senate inquiry calling for stronger sanctions enforcement. Australia imported an estimated $480 million worth of fuel made from Russian crude oil in the first seven months of this year alone, according to figures cited in the letter.



“With two months having passed since the report’s publication, and 12 months since we first called for action, we are concerned that the Government has yet to outline concrete steps to address this issue,” executive director Nezir Sinani wrote. Related Article Blood Oil Putin’s blood oil profits untouched by Australia’s toothless sanctions The coalition wants Australia to ban imports from any refinery or port that has received Russian crude or refined petroleum products in the preceding six months, closing a loophole that allows Russian oil to enter Australia through blending, re-exporting or further processing. Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organisations chair Kateryna Argyrou said Australia was falling behind its closest allies, with European restrictions redirecting Russian-linked fuel towards other markets. “Our allies have shown a ban can work. With Europe now closed to this fuel and our door still open, Australia is becoming a dumping ground for blood oil,” she said.



The European Union prohibited fuel refined from Russian crude oil in third countries in January, followed by Britain in May. Research by the Kyiv School of Economics found European imports of petroleum products from 11 refineries processing Russian crude oil fell 69 per cent in the three months to April following the EU ban. Indian refineries cut exports of Russian-derived fuel to Europe by 97 per cent, redirecting almost all such products elsewhere. Related Article Energy Australia scoured the world for fuel supplies. It’s working Australia became an increasingly important destination for Indian refineries and remained the primary market among countries sanctioning Russia for fuel exported from Brunei’s Hengyi refinery. At Hengyi, Russian crude oil reportedly accounted for 68 per cent of the oil processed for products exported to Australia in the first seven months of 2026, up from 24 per cent during the corresponding period in 2024.



Australia banned direct imports of Russian crude and petroleum products in 2022, but the restrictions do not automatically prevent Russian oil being refined elsewhere before being exported to Australia. Argyrou rejected suggestions tougher sanctions would threaten Australia’s fuel supplies, adding that Europe and the UK incorporated transition periods, and Australia could do the same. “A phased ban with a clear timetable is very different from no ban at all,” she said. “Relying on fuel made from Russian oil isn’t fuel security either.” Meanwhile, the Australian Forest Products Association has joined Nationals MPs in demanding tougher action following Senate estimates evidence that the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry does not necessarily consider Russian timber a breach of Australia’s illegal logging laws. A departmental trial found that about one in four timber products tested did not match their declared species, origin or both. Yet the department confirmed it had tested no consignments for Russian content this year and had the equivalent of just 2.2 full-time staff working on compliance.



Association acting chief executive Richard Hyett said Russian-sourced timber could be entering Australia’s construction industry through blended products including plywood. “This latest evidence suggests significant volumes of Russian timber continue to find their way into the Australian market, despite existing sanctions,” he said. Energy Minister Chris Bowen has previously declared Australia neither needs nor wants Russian fuel and that Moscow should not be rewarded for its invasion of Ukraine. But campaigners argue those declarations require enforceable restrictions, urging Albanese to commit to a ban on Russian-derived fuel, introduce legislation and establish an implementation timetable. “Closing this loophole would ensure that its trade policy better reflects that commitment and that Australian fuel imports do not continue to help finance Russia’s war of aggression,” the B4Ukraine letter states.



A Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade spokesperson said Australia was working alongside partners in the G7 Price Cap Coalition to restrict the Kremlin’s energy revenues. The spokesperson said Canberra had imposed nearly 1900 sanctions targeting Russia and its supporters – including almost 300 shadow fleet vessels – and expected businesses to ensure their supply chains did not inadvertently fund Moscow’s war effort. While declining to comment on potential future sanctions, a government source said ministers were carefully considering the Senate committee’s recommendations and would table a formal response in due course. World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation Secrecy orders protecting teachers accused of misconduct Caroline Schelle November 5, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Victorian teachers accused of serious misconduct are increasingly having their identities kept secret by a disciplinary panel dominated by fellow educators, who have overruled the state teaching watchdog’s lawyers. The Victorian Institute of Teaching (VIT) held four disciplinary hearings this year, and all were subject to a non-publication order that temporarily or permanently prevented details of allegations, the school or a teacher’s name from publication. Non-publication orders are increasingly being issued at hearings for teachers accused of serious misconduct. iStock Formal disciplinary hearings are held in front of a three-person panel who probe allegations of serious misconduct, incompetence or lack of fitness to teach. These panels decide whether a teacher is barred from the profession, suspended or face another consequence. Internal data from the watchdog, obtained by this masthead, shows in two disciplinary hearings held this year lawyers representing the VIT argued against non-publication orders that keep details from the public but the panel, comprising registered teachers, issued the order anyway.



The VIT’s boss, Martin Fletcher, acknowledged change was necessary, while legal and education experts said the issues raised questions of when a teacher should be identified as a public safety measure and when it could unfairly jeopardise their career. One teacher, currently subject to an interim suspension, is accused of six counts of misconduct that include writing a teen student a song, favouring her with gifts and sending messages of a personal nature over five years. A hearing in July was told the song was titled “Sparkle in the Dust” and the teacher asked the teenager to “keep it close to [their] heart, as people always misconstrue” what it meant. After the teen finished high school, he asked her out for coffee via WhatsApp and said: “I just can’t leave it like this, it hurts too much.” In another message, he said: “Who knows, 20 years from now we might just pick up where we left off.” Lawyer Alice Cooney, representing the VIT, argued for publication of the allegations and the teacher’s name in the interests of transparency.



However, the three-person panel suppressed the teacher’s name until it had reached a determination. Internal VIT data shows that since 2015 there have been 19 formal disciplinary hearings, but no permanent suppression orders were issued before 2023. In 2023, a permanent order was made to protect the identity of a teacher who gained their registration by fraud because of “significant mitigating circumstances”, the watchdog said. Temporary non-publication orders have been on the rise for the past three years when details were suppressed in half of the eight cases. This year, there have been four hearings with details kept secret in three. Last year, former Carey Grammar teacher Eleanor Louise Yorke was barred from the profession after sending tens of thousands of messages to a student and beginning a romantic relationship after they graduated. It was the only disciplinary case heard that year and not subject to any secrecy orders.



The VIT data shows that of the seven hearings held between 2024 and 2026, only two featured legal practitioners. The rest were composed entirely of registered or retired teachers. The teaching watchdog’s chief executive, Martin Fletcher, acknowledged reforms to how serious disciplinary matters were carried out was needed, and the process was under way. Former teacher Eleanor Yorke has been barred from teaching after admitting to an inappropriate relationship with a student. This included a modern conduct framework to ensure hearings were fair, efficient, transparent and featured a diversity of perspectives. “Community confidence in professional regulation depends not only on the decisions that are made, but on the clarity and integrity of the processes used to make them.”



Fletcher added it was a balancing act between transparency and ensuring victims or witnesses were not harmed or discouraged from taking part in the process. Changes being considered include legal practitioners sitting on panels, enhanced training for those selected for panels, better case management and clearer decision-making structures. Improving guidance for procedural matters including non-publication orders are also on the agenda. VIT lawyers can argue a suppression order shouldn’t be issued if they are based on concerns about embarrassment, reputational damage or other consequences associated with proceedings. They can also argue against non-publication orders that relate to information already in the public domain, or where the risk identified is considered to be remote or speculative.



The University of Melbourne’s Jason Bosland said there should be public scrutiny of any regulatory proceeding, and that included naming a teacher accused of misconduct. “It would also give the opportunity to other survivors or victims to come forward with their experiences,” he said. He believed a non-publication order should only be made when absolutely necessary, and said there was a public interest in knowing the outcomes and details of the hearings. But Swinburne University education academic Janine Forbes-Rolfe believed a teacher’s name shouldn’t be published until a determination was reached. “In terms of reputational damage, that would be quite immense,” Forbes-Rolfe said.



She said teachers held a privileged position and had to abide by high standards, but if allegations were substantiated, they should be named. “I’m sometimes a little bit concerned in terms of the narrative that occurs … why are we focusing on the very small numbers of bad actors as opposed to the broader positives of the profession,” Forbes-Rolfe said. The Victorian Institute of Teaching suspended 29 teachers on an interim basis when they were assessed as posing an unacceptable risk of harm to children in the 2025-2026 financial year. World.title: Two figures emerge alongside Kanga in move that could blow up VRC boardroom
World.content:
Updated SportRacingVictorian racing Two figures emerge alongside Kanga in move that could blow up VRC boardroom Danny Russell Updated November 5, 2026 — 7:47pm ,first published November 5, 2026 — 7:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
