John Kanga will have to undergo a thorough vetting process before his carefully timed Melbourne Cup week re-emergence is cleared for a run at the Victorian Racing Club board. The colourful identity nominated to join the famous Flemington organisation’s board on Wednesday night, little more than a year after quitting his Melbourne Racing Club post amid a cloud of controversy. Former MRC chairman John Kanga at Caulfield Racecourse. Getty Images Kanga resigned as MRC chairman on the eve of last year’s Caulfield Cup carnival after questions from The Age about his past. The looming elections have the potential to divide the VRC committee room and reshape the club’s future amid a growing industry push for mergers.



VRC chairman Neil Wilson has resigned, creating a vacancy on the board, while three sitting directors - chair elect Vin Cox, treasurer Glenn Carmody and Michael Saadie - are up for re-election. Another figure, former Josh Frydenberg adviser Claire Ewart-Kennedy, confirmed to The Age she had nominated for a director’s role. Two sources with inside knowledge of the process, but unable to comment on behalf of the VRC, said they understood Nicholas Tzaferis, a former adviser to Jeff Kennett and Denis Napthine, had also joined the election race. Tzaferis, who was contacted for comment, has worked as an executive for The Lottery Corporation and Tabcorp. The Victoria Racing Club oversees the Melbourne Cup at Flemington. Getty Images



All candidates will front the VRC’s remuneration and nominations committee in coming days to prove their suitability to stand. “Nominations for election to the Victoria Racing Club board will be communicated to members in the coming weeks, following the completion of the club’s standard eligibility and governance processes,” the VRC said in a statement. The current board was split last month in a secret vote to anoint Wilson’s successor. Loading The Age reported that VRC vice chairman Michael Ramsden lost 5-6 to Cox in a ballot that included votes cast by Wilson and VRC CEO Kylie Rogers.



Members were told in a club statement that Cox would assume the role at December’s annual general meeting. But first he must survive an election at the end of this month to retain his seat, before heading off a potential board room coup. A 5-6 vote is easily overturned once a new director replaces Wilson on the board. The emergence of Kanga has several ramifications. He has previously been pro-mergers. But the horse owner and jockey mentor denies his nomination is aligned to power broker and MRC vice chairman Jonathan Munz.



“I am an independent candidate,” Kanga said. Related Article Racing integrity John Kanga’s resignation came after questions from The Age “I respect Jonathan and agree with most of his views on what is best for the industry, but he is not involved in my campaign and did not encourage me to run as a candidate.” The Age reported last year that Munz hosted Wilson, Kanga and Carmody at a secret meeting in his Toorak mansion to discuss a potential merger of the Victoria and Melbourne racing clubs. Wilson rejected the suggestion and has staunchly defended the need for the VRC, which hosts Melbourne Cup week, to stay independent.



“The government and RVL [Racing Victoria] have encouraged club mergers and intuitively, there are big cost savings to be made,” Kanga said in a statement on Thursday. Related Article Victorian racing Legal feuds, boardroom battles and a 24-year-old taking on racing’s elite “I have heard $30-$50 million reported. The club executive and board would need to do proper due diligence first and have the support from members. “If it did happen, you would apply part of the savings towards immediate benefits to members, such as lower food and drink prices.” During his time at Melbourne Racing Club, Kanga became popular among members after his board saved Sandown Racecourse from being sold for housing development, moved the mounting yard back in front of the Caulfield members’ stand and scrapped plans for a new $250 million grandstand.



But he also cut through with rank-and-file racegoers by cutting beer and food prices at MRC racetracks. Kanga resigned as Melbourne Racing Club chair on the eve of last year’s Caulfield Cup carnival after questions from The Age about loans and the use of his car in a 22-kilogram cocaine trafficking case in 2014. John Kanga was popular with racegoers at Caulfield, for reducing the cost of food and beverages. Getty Images Kanga said he had resigned “to ensure the focus remains where it belongs – on racing, our members, staff, and delivering a world-class spring carnival”. The Age does not suggest Kanga was involved in any criminal activity, and he has never been accused of any crime.





The board was then thrown into turmoil when Barbara Saunders resigned in support of Reilly, citing concerns about the club’s governance. Seven MRC directors left the club after Kanga began his leadership tilt, while the club’s executive team was also stripped bare. The club was also criticised for not running due process before appointing Munz’s associate Tanya Fullarton as chief operating officer or hiring Munz’s track consultant Kenneth Neff. The jobs were not advertised, and no interviews were held. Both are still at the MRC. After Munz replaced Kanga on the board, Fullarton was appointed MRC CEO.



Ewart-Kennedy, who manages cropping and livestock farms near Nagambie and is Strathbogie Shire deputy mayor, said she had been a VRC member for 28 years. Related Article Melbourne Cup It took 166 races for a trainer to nail the Cup trifecta. And Ciaron Maher’s not stopping there In addition to working with Frydenberg, she has also worked as an adviser to former Victorian premier Ted Baillieu. “The reason I’m running is that I don’t believe the members have a strong enough voice in the direction of the VRC, and we need to have real value demonstrated for members – not just for the spring racing carnival – the cost of living crisis is real for everyone and for the VRC to thrive the members deserve greater accessibility, accountability & real buy in to what is happening with our club,” she said. Furniture company owner and former Melbourne Football Club vice president Bill Guest has also been floated by several sources as a potential nominee. He is yet to confirm.



With Bridget McArthur News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday. 

CORRECTION Correction: A previous version of this story said Claire Ewart-Kennedy is a former chief of staff to Josh Frydenberg and former Victorian premier Ted Baillieu. She was an adviser to them, and was chief of staff to John Pesutto, Tim Wilson and Damian Drum.

Exclusive PoliticsWAWA Parliament Besieged Labor MP’s alleged debts mount under fresh legal threat Hamish Hastie and Connor McGoverne November 5, 2026 — 9:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Riverton MP Jagadish Krishnan is facing another demand for more than $1 million, this time from a Perth-headquartered mining and construction conglomerate that also owns Indian Rugby Premier League franchise the Chennai Bulls. AvidSys, the Indian-Australian-owned Guatam family business, sent Krishnan a letter of demand in June, seeking $1.93 million. Riverton MLA Jagadish Krishnan. Hamish Hastie The allegedly unpaid money relates to the proposed sale of the GP network Krishnan founded, Spectrum Health Group, to AvidSys, which fell through last year. AvidSys’ parent company Avid Global Holdings alleged Krishnan’s company promised to cover the legal and professional costs associated with the sale.



The demand adds to the financial pressures the WA Labor MP is already facing, after WAtoday and 9News revealed he was being sued in a New Jersey court for $1.2 million over an allegedly unpaid loan secured in 2024. Krishnan, known under his nickname Dr Jags, also used his family home in Mosman Park, 18 kilometres from the electorate he represents in Parliament, to secure a $330,000 loan with an interest rate of 3.5 per cent a month, Landgate documents show. A June 15 letter from Clayton Utz lawyers on behalf of Avid Global Holdings demanded $1,932,020. “In or about late October 2025, you represented to our client that you would pay all of our client’s legal and other professional costs incurred by our client in connection with the Transaction,” it said. “Since that time, you repeated the Representation to our client on a number of occasions in numerous telephone conversations.



“You knew or intended that our client would so act; and our client now suffers detriment because the assumption has not been fulfilled. AvidSys chairman Ansh Gautam. “It would be unjust for you to retain that benefit without making payment.” That payment was demanded within five days of the date of the letter. AvidSys founding director and chairman Ansh Gautam declined to comment but confirmed the letter had been sent.



Krishnan said he’d made all financial declarations as required by parliament, declaring the AvidSys issue a “private matter” he was trying to resolve. Related Article Exclusive

WA Parliament Labor’s Riverton MP spends nearly entire salary on electorate expenses “My legal representatives have sought more information from Avid Global Holdings regarding their initial correspondence sent in June, but have not received a response since June,” he said. Krishnan resigned from all his directorships ahead of entering politics. He told 9News last year that he had “been out of business for almost four years”. Before the sale of Spectrum Health to AvidSys fell through last year, the latter company issued a press release heralding the deal, while declaring Krishnan would stay on as an advisor.



“Following the acquisition by AvidSys Group, Dr Jags Krishnan will continue to support Avid Health and drive the integration and future growth of the business” the statement said. The intrigue in the MP’s financial dealings intensified after this masthead found he had spent almost his entire parliamentary salary on electorate expenses. Premier Roger Cook said he had spoken to Krishnan about his disputes. “Since my return from my trade mission to China, I have spoken with Dr Krishnan, and he advised these are private commercial legal matters that he will continue to defend,” Cook said. Spectrum Health Group is understood to be in the process of being sold in a deal believed to be worth $47.5 million to rival GP network Family Doctor, owned by Melbourne businessman Rodney Aziz.



“All dealings will be closed on full settlement, which is due at the end of the month,” Krishnan said. He refused to detail how much money he would make from the sale, citing commercial confidence. The American businessman suing Krishnan over the alleged $1 million unpaid loan also claimed he spent thousands on the politician’s accommodation, a limousine trip and an evening Hudson River cruise past the famous Statue of Liberty. Cook said he had reminded Dr Krishnan of the standards expected of members of parliament around the disclosure of gifts. Krishnan has maintained he has met his declaration obligations as an MP.



Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti backed Krishnan on Thursday. “He’s been an excellent member for Riverton, working for his community, delivering for his community, and he’ll continue to be a very good member for Riverton,” she said.

On Thursday afternoon, a WA Police spokesperson revealed a 14-year-old boy had been arrested and was assisting police with their inquiries. “Detectives are continuing to investigate the involvement of further parties,” they said. It is understood the incident started ostensibly as a robbery, with the attackers allegedly demanding the boy’s vape, before then telling him to hand over clothes. Butler said the 13-year-old boy at the centre of the assault was lucky to not have any more severe injuries, and was “holding up well at the minute, and we’re providing all the support we can give to him”. “Hopefully by this afternoon, we can provide the community some reassuring outcomes as to how we’ve progressed this investigation and put some calm back into the community,” he said.



In a statement, WA Police said the 13-year-old was allegedly assaulted by several juveniles believed to be known to him at the reserve on Coolamon Boulevard. “It is further alleged a knife was produced, threats were made and property was stolen from the victim,” the statement read. “The victim received minor injuries and later attended St John of God Midland Public Hospital for medical treatment.” WA Police said officers became aware of vision of the incident circulating online and commenced inquiries. “Police understand the incident has caused considerable concern within the community and ask

members of the public to remain calm and allow detectives to conduct their investigation,” WA police said in a statement.



“Members of the community are strongly urged not to take matters into their own hands, threaten

retaliation or publish the names, photographs or personal information of people believed to be involved.” Editor's pick Updated

Courts Jordon Steele-John’s ex granted bail on stalking charges as WA Greens inquiry begins There has been an outpouring of support for the young boy at the centre of the attack, with offers to help the family and plans for a fundraising car cruise. Tania Lawrence, the federal MP for Hasluck, said she was “absolutely heartbroken” to see the vision of the boy being assaulted. “I can’t begin to imagine what he and his family have been through,” she posted to social media.



“No person should ever experience something so horrific, and no family should have to endure such heartbreak. “What happened to this young man is shocking and traumatising, but the kindness and compassion we’ve seen from people across our community is a reminder of just how much we care for one another.” One of the most concerning moments in the video came when one of the attackers brandished a large knife as the boy continued to be bashed on the ground. On Wednesday, Police Minister Reece Whitby said the presence of the knife meant “one wrong move could have had tragic consequences that might have ended a life and might have resulted in a very serious outcome for those young people involved”. Whitby vowed “serious consequences” for the attackers.



“We will make sure that the law is enforced because this is unacceptable,” he said. Editor's pick Exclusive

Weather WA stalls on heatwave health plans ahead of scorching summer The video’s proliferation on social media also spurred debate about Labor’s “post and boast” legislation, which has stalled in the upper house. Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas accused the government of “sitting on their hands” for not bringing the legislation forward, however Whitby laid blame at the feet of the opposition and Greens for the delay. The Greens have previously raised concerns about the legislation’s stifling effect on protests.



Speaking to 6PR, Butler urged social media users to refrain from naming the alleged perpetrators or their families in the comments section. “It’s certainly something that we don’t condone, and for a number of reasons,” he said. “Can people be 100 per cent sure who they’re naming? And, you know, we don’t want innocent people to be caught up in this. “It’s very easy to sit on your phone and type things, but we really need to think of A, the community, and B, the family and then their extended family, because violence isn’t the answer.”

World.content:

Multiple flights in Europe made emergency landings on Thursday after being diverted because of bomb threats, authorities said. The incidents followed hoax bomb threats earlier this week that prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, a military escort.

At least eight flights from Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw were confirmed to have been targeted with bomb threats, most diverted to other airports for emergency landings, while others landed safely at their destinations. So far, inspections have not turned up hazardous or suspicious materials.

Czech police said they deployed at Prague’s Vaclav Havel Airport to prepare for the landing of four planes after receiving a threat of explosive devices on board. Police said that “all necessary security measures have been activated.”

The path of flight EI402 going from Dublin to Rome, after it was diverted following a bomb threat. FlightRadar24

Earlier, a flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in western France because of a bomb threat, the French prime minister’s office said. The flight landed safely at the base in Evreux in Normandy, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office said. All 151 passengers and six crew members were safe, and military bomb disposal teams were examining the plane, the office said.

World.title: ‘A dumping ground for blood oil’: Pressure mounts on Canberra over Putin trade ties
World.content:
PoliticsFederalBlood Oil ‘A dumping ground for blood oil’: Pressure mounts on Canberra over Putin trade ties Rob Harris Updated November 5, 2026 — 8:53pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. An international coalition of organisations has written to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese demanding urgent legislation to stop petrol and diesel refined from Russian crude oil in third countries entering Australia. The B4Ukraine Coalition – a group of nearly 100 civil society organisations campaigning to strip Russia of economic resources for its war – estimates Australia has imported $16.5 billion worth of petroleum products made partly from Russian oil since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, potentially generating $1.7 billion in tax revenue for the Kremlin. Almost 70 per cent of oil exported to Australia from Brunei’s Hengyi refinery in the first seven months of the year was Russian-derived, a Finnish think tank has found. Marija Ercegovac The call comes as Australia’s forestry industry raises separate concerns that up to 100,000 cubic metres of imported timber products each year could contain Russian-sourced material, exposing further weaknesses in Canberra’s sanctions enforcement. The coalition accused the federal government of failing to act despite repeated warnings and an August Senate inquiry calling for stronger sanctions enforcement. Australia imported an estimated $480 million worth of fuel made from Russian crude oil in the first seven months of this year alone, according to figures cited in the letter.



“With two months having passed since the report’s publication, and 12 months since we first called for action, we are concerned that the Government has yet to outline concrete steps to address this issue,” executive director Nezir Sinani wrote. Related Article Blood Oil Putin’s blood oil profits untouched by Australia’s toothless sanctions The coalition wants Australia to ban imports from any refinery or port that has received Russian crude or refined petroleum products in the preceding six months, closing a loophole that allows Russian oil to enter Australia through blending, re-exporting or further processing. Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organisations chair Kateryna Argyrou said Australia was falling behind its closest allies, with European restrictions redirecting Russian-linked fuel towards other markets. “Our allies have shown a ban can work. With Europe now closed to this fuel and our door still open, Australia is becoming a dumping ground for blood oil,” she said.



The European Union prohibited fuel refined from Russian crude oil in third countries in January, followed by Britain in May. Research by the Kyiv School of Economics found European imports of petroleum products from 11 refineries processing Russian crude oil fell 69 per cent in the three months to April following the EU ban. Indian refineries cut exports of Russian-derived fuel to Europe by 97 per cent, redirecting almost all such products elsewhere. Related Article Energy Australia scoured the world for fuel supplies. It’s working Australia became an increasingly important destination for Indian refineries and remained the primary market among countries sanctioning Russia for fuel exported from Brunei’s Hengyi refinery. At Hengyi, Russian crude oil reportedly accounted for 68 per cent of the oil processed for products exported to Australia in the first seven months of 2026, up from 24 per cent during the corresponding period in 2024.



Australia banned direct imports of Russian crude and petroleum products in 2022, but the restrictions do not automatically prevent Russian oil being refined elsewhere before being exported to Australia. Argyrou rejected suggestions tougher sanctions would threaten Australia’s fuel supplies, adding that Europe and the UK incorporated transition periods, and Australia could do the same. “A phased ban with a clear timetable is very different from no ban at all,” she said. “Relying on fuel made from Russian oil isn’t fuel security either.” Meanwhile, the Australian Forest Products Association has joined Nationals MPs in demanding tougher action following Senate estimates evidence that the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry does not necessarily consider Russian timber a breach of Australia’s illegal logging laws. A departmental trial found that about one in four timber products tested did not match their declared species, origin or both. Yet the department confirmed it had tested no consignments for Russian content this year and had the equivalent of just 2.2 full-time staff working on compliance.



Association acting chief executive Richard Hyett said Russian-sourced timber could be entering Australia’s construction industry through blended products including plywood. “This latest evidence suggests significant volumes of Russian timber continue to find their way into the Australian market, despite existing sanctions,” he said. Energy Minister Chris Bowen has previously declared Australia neither needs nor wants Russian fuel and that Moscow should not be rewarded for its invasion of Ukraine. But campaigners argue those declarations require enforceable restrictions, urging Albanese to commit to a ban on Russian-derived fuel, introduce legislation and establish an implementation timetable. “Closing this loophole would ensure that its trade policy better reflects that commitment and that Australian fuel imports do not continue to help finance Russia’s war of aggression,” the B4Ukraine letter states.



A Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade spokesperson said Australia was working alongside partners in the G7 Price Cap Coalition to restrict the Kremlin’s energy revenues. The spokesperson said Canberra had imposed nearly 1900 sanctions targeting Russia and its supporters – including almost 300 shadow fleet vessels – and expected businesses to ensure their supply chains did not inadvertently fund Moscow’s war effort. While declining to comment on potential future sanctions, a government source said ministers were carefully considering the Senate committee’s recommendations and would table a formal response in due course. World.title: US election lesson, don’t take voters for granted
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters US election lesson, don’t take voters for granted November 5, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Matt Davidson To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. The most important lesson of the past few years of American politics is that neither Republicans nor Democrats can take particular constituencies of voters for granted anymore. The gains made by Republicans among minority and working-class voters in 2024 proved a great shock to Democrats, who considered these groups part of their traditional support base.

The Democrats’ midterm victories in states such as Texas, Georgia and South Carolina (″⁣Democrats sweep to power at midterms in rejection of Trump, Republicans″⁣, 4/11) indicates that the GOP’s long-established hold on the South has been broken, and that southern Republicans can no longer ignore Americans’ growing distrust of Donald Trump. In the future, both Democrats and Republicans will need to appeal to a broad range of voters, instead of narrow sectional interests. For Republicans, this means that they may now need to distance themselves from Trump, whose aggressive deportation campaigns and foreign militarism have toxified the Republican brand. For the first time since the beginning of the Trump era, even Republicans can now see that their emperor is wearing no clothes.

Nikhil Dhanabal, Clyde North Will repudiation reach these shores?

Is it too much to expect that the repudiation of Trumpian values by Americans might also translate into an Australian repudiation of the same values promoted by the likes of Pauline Hanson? Australia’s reputation as a decent, respectful and compassionate country depends on it.

Ross Corben, Knoxfield Perhaps, the reinvention of Trump looms

Donald Trump may spend the next two years reinventing himself. The following possibilities come to mind: become a statesman – a novelty too difficult to bear; idle his time away as a lame duck – bullies are not big on placidity; behave like a dog with distemper – certainly has the right temperament having previously shown signs of extreme agitation, unprovoked aggression and a urge to snap and bite people or objects; join a circus. The world awaits.

Pack Raphael, Vermont



Result might have foreign consequences

Shane Wright had the Australian and global economy in mind when sounding the alarm on a weakened Trump (″⁣An even more unpredictable Trump is worst nightmare″⁣, 5/11). That’s serious enough, but the geopolitical order of the world now faces greater jeopardy. Questions abound. Will Trump lash out at Iran? Will he abandon Ukraine? Will he curry favour with China? Amid all this foreboding there may be an unexpected ray of light. In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump made the surprising announcement that by the end of the year the United States would cease freely supplying arms to Israel. Whatever the outcome of Israel’s post-election negotiations for power, it seems that the incoming regime will no longer be able to rely on unconditional support from the White House. All who are concerned about justice for Palestine might dare to imagine that the United States will stop shielding Israel from independent scrutiny of its anti-Palestinian policies and practices. Could decades of Israel’s impunity be coming to an end? One can only hope so.

Tom Knowles, Parkville Good use for a fine word

Great to see US correspondent Michael Koziol use that wonderful word shellacking when describing the size of the Democrats’ victory (″⁣Republicans must break from Trump″⁣, 5/11).

Rod Moran, Brighton Hallelujah, this cup runs over

My cup is usually half empty, but following the US midterm elections my cup is now full to the brim and runneth over. Hallelujah!

Craig Calvert, Montmorency THE FORUM Taking politics out of it

When will we ever learn? The article ″⁣This is why airport rail is a mess″⁣ (5/11) says it all.

Whether it’s decisions about AUKUS, or Snowy Hydro 2, or airport rail, or the SRL, or the Western Sydney airport, politicians need to be removed from the decision-making process, full stop. The role of politicians should be to establish capital works priorities to align with their policies and/or electoral commitments. We need fully independent, transparent bodies, similar to the RBA, to be established at both federal and state level that are accountable for the costing and implementation of these priorities with the boards of these bodies to be bipartisan, government appointments.

The bodies would determine the locations of routes, construction methods etc to achieve the lowest cost, or most cost-effective outcome. While this might introduce another layer of bureaucracy, it should alleviate the poor allocation and/or waste in public funds that we see occurring, with the total capital available in a government’s budget being allocated based on established priorities and directions and not political whims or political benefit.

Roger East, Balwyn North



Safety at the polls

Anybody who saw the aggressive and intimidatory behaviour by third-party campaigners at pre-polling booths at the 2025 federal election will be delighted the Victorian Electoral Commission is employing security squads to patrol booths at the state election (″⁣Election watchdog deploys security squad to curb bad behaviour on booths″⁣, 4/11). A parliamentary committee investigating the 2025 election received 360 submissions detailing aggressive acts towards voters, volunteers and electoral officials.

Former independent MP Zoe Daniel said the battle for her seat was so toxic, she feared for her safety. The established norms for conduct at polling places (and beyond) was broken. The VEC is determined to ensure that at the November poll, everyone ″⁣plays by the rules″⁣.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne New strategy needed

As the excellent comments from Age readers highlight, slowly strangling the economy through interest rate rises that punish the least likely offenders (mortgagors and the financially strapped) is a disastrous strategy for the government (“Duo labour on, but mud sticks”, 5/11) and society itself.

Instead of focusing on macro solutions to cut spending and demand by individuals, businesses and governments, could an option be to cut off the head of inflation at the source. The inflation rate is simply the rate of increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) which in turn measures the change in the cost of a basket of goods and services bought by a hypothetical consumer. This seems an artificial and badly flawed measure to begin with, as a typical consumer is impossible to define. However, the government (using a range of carrots and sticks and compensatory measures if necessary) could limit price increases to 2.5 per cent a year for products and services that make up this basket of items. Job done.

A fairer, more timely solution for all sections of society.

Peter Thomson, Brunswick Data centre backlash

It is interesting to note that one of the factors in the US midterm elections was the concern over data centres. Americans have turned the tide against the Republican Party. Why are our governments so enthusiastic about data centres? Have they had a mandate from the Australian electorate for them? Are they paying attention?

Christine Baker, Rosanna Freeway jam doesn’t beckon

Your correspondent (Letters, 5/11) sees the Suburban Rail Loop as “throwing good money after bad″⁣. Have they tried the Monash freeway (commonly known as Monash Car Park in peak times) and other major roads in areas without train lines as a way to travel from one area to another? Have they imagined getting from Frankston to Box Hill by public transport?

The SRL is decades overdue as it is, and those affected by a lack of such facilities would appreciate support from people in areas well-serviced by public transport.

Everyone would love to enjoy the benefits that come with good, safe, environmentally beneficial, more economical in the long run, travel infrastructure. It is no fun sitting in almost stopped traffic on our “freeways″⁣ for many kilometres. An expensive, unpleasant exercise, with no alternatives for many.

Marianne Dalton, Balnarring Ticket to Box Hill?

If the Labor government is replaced in Victoria there may be many inquiries and investigations conducted. Perhaps a thorough and well-funded one will be set up to find someone who actually wants to catch a train from Cheltenham to Box Hill.

Don Relf, Mentone



Promises, promises

Despite justified criticism of the state debt, there seems to be a lot of expensive electoral promises.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick Evidence please, RBA

Using Michele Bullock’s own reasoning expressed a while ago, decisions on interest rates take a number of months to have an effect on the economy. So when has the RBA given enough time over the past few interest rate rises to allow for these rises to bed in and slow the economy? How can they assess the impact of one when they immediately add another rise after only one month. Somewhere down the track we may find out whether all of them were necessary. And, if it turns out that only a couple were needed, will we get an apology from the RBA for the financial impost that they put on household budgets?

Greg Tuck, Warragul DJs, it’s all your own fault

Early this year, I needed new makeup. I stood at the door of David Jones, surveying the sea of make-up counters before me, dreading I’d need to go to each one to compare their offerings.

So I walked across Bourke Street Mall to the newly opened Mecca. An assistant greeted me, I told her what I wanted and she asked me to wait, then returned with several to choose from. What a great customer-focused business model.

David Jones (and other department stores) have brought about their own potential demise. Once, you could go to the knitwear section, the evening wear section etc; now the stores resemble a posh market, with floor spaces marked off for specific designer labels, even physical walls in some areas. This indicates a lack of understanding of what a customer seeks, making us do all the work.

And don’t tell me we all want to shop online. There’s great merit in seeing, feeling and trying on. Yes, I’m a Boomer, but I also have spending power (apparently).

These stores could do with a dedicated shopper like me on their board, not just bean-counters who are only interested in the bottom line and thus think nothing of killing off a 188 year-old business, and with it a satisfying shopping experience.

Margaret O’Connor, Balwyn There was no other

David Jones used to be destination store where you would see lift operators, a pianist playing in store and exceptional customer service.

Sadly, it’s declined significantly over the years and while it saddens me that it’s in administrators hands many customers are not in the least surprised.

There was no other store like David Jones.

Panagiota Frangopoulos, Malvern Dole equals poverty

Living on the dole equals living in poverty. Continued rate rises and more unemployment creates big social problems down the line. Everyone should receive a living wage, not the pitiful unemployment benefits.

Chris Hooper, Castlemaine



Follow Perth’s path

The airport link seems to be bedevilled by indecision and obfuscation.

Generally, we agree on the need for it, but getting a plan in place seems to be beyond our government’s control. Costs are enormous, government indecision stultifying, funding – whether public or private – hidden behind closed doors, planning for actual routes, a party room ″⁣hot potato″⁣.

To copy many other cities, such as Perth, we should be using our current infrastructure- running the line/s up the middle of the Tullamarine Freeway. North Melbourne station would be a better starting point for the line- further connections could be added over time.

Using current infrastructure is less damaging to communities and the environment on any other touted routes, funding/costs will be enormous but that is the reality. An efficient and sustainable transport system will benefit most Victorians and overseas visitors.

Denis Shandley, Drysdale Holiday for the arts

It’s great to hear Australia now has its own songbook (5/11). The time is well overdue for a major step to be taken to recognise Australia’s amazing range of artists in all fields. What is needed is a public holiday – Arts Day – being preceded by a week of major arts activities.

We have a holiday for a horse race, a football match and a King’s birthday (on the wrong date) and yet continue a glaring gap in acknowledging Australian artists with so many who have an international recognition. It’s time to drop remaining traces of our cultural cringe like a hot scone.

Des Files, Brunswick National anthem options

Either Waltzing Matilda or I Still Call Australia Home should have been our national anthem, songs to which most people know the words, and catchy tunes as well.

Marie Nash, Balwyn Rock-solid case

Australia finally has its own songbook. But how on earth was Goanna’s Solid Rock left out? This is one rock-solid Australian anthem. Surely we can stretch the list to 11. Some things are too important to leave out. Justice needs to be done!

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING US elections

Americans heard Donald Trump loud and clear when he pleaded with them to “pretend I’m running ... because I am on the ballot”. Credit where credit is due.

Jenny Bone, Surrey Hill Democracy is alive and well, and living in the most unlikely corners of the US.

Matthew Hamilton, Kew Lame duck a l’orange anybody? Or maybe he’s just a Christmas turkey.

Philip West, Jan Juc



Americans voted for change. Democrats have claimed control of the Senate, now they must deliver and make America sane again.

Elizabeth Osborne, North Hobart, Tas It seems Donald Trump was right, the Iran war did achieve regime change.

Emilio Bedin, Narre Warren My faith in Americans has been restored.

Phil Alexander, Eltham Blue wave powered by an orange undertow.

Peter Rushen, Carnegie As Donald Trump said, ″⁣I wasn’t on the ballot” but you were on the nose.

Ian Holton, Yarraville



Looks like the voters actually did imagine Donald Trump was on the ballot, and voted accordingly.

Trevor Sheridan, Charmhaven, NSW Re the US mid-term elections, I have been daydreaming of a great outcome: Trump leaves a note saying: ″⁣Obviously I am not appreciated by losers in America, so I have left to join Vladimir in Moscow. He has told me I would be King of Russia.″⁣

John Hennessy, Montmorency Furthermore

I don’t want to vote for any of the major parties. Could The Age please profile the minor parties and the independents?

Paul Spencer, Ascot Vale Before teachers can teach kids how to hold a pen/pencil correctly, someone (old, most likely) will have to teach the teachers.

Peter Neuhold, Elsternwick

World.title: Secrecy orders protecting teachers accused of misconduct
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation Secrecy orders protecting teachers accused of misconduct Caroline Schelle November 5, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victorian teachers accused of serious misconduct are increasingly having their identities kept secret by a disciplinary panel dominated by fellow educators, who have overruled the state teaching watchdog’s lawyers. The Victorian Institute of Teaching (VIT) held four disciplinary hearings this year, and all were subject to a non-publication order that temporarily or permanently prevented details of allegations, the school or a teacher’s name from publication. Non-publication orders are increasingly being issued at hearings for teachers accused of serious misconduct. iStock Formal disciplinary hearings are held in front of a three-person panel who probe allegations of serious misconduct, incompetence or lack of fitness to teach. These panels decide whether a teacher is barred from the profession, suspended or face another consequence. Internal data from the watchdog, obtained by this masthead, shows in two disciplinary hearings held this year lawyers representing the VIT argued against non-publication orders that keep details from the public but the panel, comprising registered teachers, issued the order anyway.



The VIT’s boss, Martin Fletcher, acknowledged change was necessary, while legal and education experts said the issues raised questions of when a teacher should be identified as a public safety measure and when it could unfairly jeopardise their career. One teacher, currently subject to an interim suspension, is accused of six counts of misconduct that include writing a teen student a song, favouring her with gifts and sending messages of a personal nature over five years. A hearing in July was told the song was titled “Sparkle in the Dust” and the teacher asked the teenager to “keep it close to [their] heart, as people always misconstrue” what it meant. After the teen finished high school, he asked her out for coffee via WhatsApp and said: “I just can’t leave it like this, it hurts too much.” In another message, he said: “Who knows, 20 years from now we might just pick up where we left off.” Lawyer Alice Cooney, representing the VIT, argued for publication of the allegations and the teacher’s name in the interests of transparency.



However, the three-person panel suppressed the teacher’s name until it had reached a determination. Internal VIT data shows that since 2015 there have been 19 formal disciplinary hearings, but no permanent suppression orders were issued before 2023. In 2023, a permanent order was made to protect the identity of a teacher who gained their registration by fraud because of “significant mitigating circumstances”, the watchdog said. Temporary non-publication orders have been on the rise for the past three years when details were suppressed in half of the eight cases. This year, there have been four hearings with details kept secret in three. Last year, former Carey Grammar teacher Eleanor Louise Yorke was barred from the profession after sending tens of thousands of messages to a student and beginning a romantic relationship after they graduated. It was the only disciplinary case heard that year and not subject to any secrecy orders.



The VIT data shows that of the seven hearings held between 2024 and 2026, only two featured legal practitioners. The rest were composed entirely of registered or retired teachers. The teaching watchdog’s chief executive, Martin Fletcher, acknowledged reforms to how serious disciplinary matters were carried out was needed, and the process was under way. Former teacher Eleanor Yorke has been barred from teaching after admitting to an inappropriate relationship with a student. This included a modern conduct framework to ensure hearings were fair, efficient, transparent and featured a diversity of perspectives. “Community confidence in professional regulation depends not only on the decisions that are made, but on the clarity and integrity of the processes used to make them.”



Fletcher added it was a balancing act between transparency and ensuring victims or witnesses were not harmed or discouraged from taking part in the process. Changes being considered include legal practitioners sitting on panels, enhanced training for those selected for panels, better case management and clearer decision-making structures. Improving guidance for procedural matters including non-publication orders are also on the agenda. VIT lawyers can argue a suppression order shouldn’t be issued if they are based on concerns about embarrassment, reputational damage or other consequences associated with proceedings. They can also argue against non-publication orders that relate to information already in the public domain, or where the risk identified is considered to be remote or speculative.



The University of Melbourne’s Jason Bosland said there should be public scrutiny of any regulatory proceeding, and that included naming a teacher accused of misconduct. “It would also give the opportunity to other survivors or victims to come forward with their experiences,” he said. He believed a non-publication order should only be made when absolutely necessary, and said there was a public interest in knowing the outcomes and details of the hearings. But Swinburne University education academic Janine Forbes-Rolfe believed a teacher’s name shouldn’t be published until a determination was reached. “In terms of reputational damage, that would be quite immense,” Forbes-Rolfe said.



She said teachers held a privileged position and had to abide by high standards, but if allegations were substantiated, they should be named. “I’m sometimes a little bit concerned in terms of the narrative that occurs … why are we focusing on the very small numbers of bad actors as opposed to the broader positives of the profession,” Forbes-Rolfe said. The Victorian Institute of Teaching suspended 29 teachers on an interim basis when they were assessed as posing an unacceptable risk of harm to children in the 2025-2026 financial year. World.title: 'Appalling' family violence system made survivors question leaving abuse partners, new report shows
World.content:
A new report has found responses to requests for help after leaving abusive partners made some women consider whether staying and tolerating the abuse would have been preferable.

The report, released on Thursday, examined five women's experiences with the system dealing with family violence between 2021 and 2024.

That included reviewing their agency records involving police, Oranga Tamariki, refuges and specialist family violence services, the Ministry of Social Development, health services, housing providers, courts, education providers, and legal services.

Lead author, University of Auckland law lecturer Julia Tolmie, said while some practitioners provided valuable support, they found multiple agencies were "punitive, judgemental, and demanding."

"Some of these participants, three out of five, spontaneously said they had lost so much, and the systemic response had been so terrible, they looked back and wondered if they'd done the right thing in leaving their abusive relationships.

"One of the women who said that actually left because she thought her partner was going to kill her.

"Even though she was facing life-threatening violence in her relationship, she'd ended up at different points in time with such an appalling response that she felt it would have been potentially better to stay and endure that than what she'd had to experience with the family violence response system."

One of the report's participants Ngākau* who lived with permanent injuries from intimate partner violence, was repeatedly required to obtain medical certificates to access financial and educational support.

"They would sit down ... all love and caring ... [you would] say your story and then what you needed help for ... and I soon learnt that ... you would never hear from them again," she said.

" ... when I got into emergency transitional housing ... I would get random phone calls ... some ... NGO, talking about my housing and it was the same narrative every time."

The report stated Ngākau's agency records showed she was contacted many times over the three-and-a-half-year period she was in emergency housing to discuss her accommodation needs, before she was given a "lecture" on the difficulty of meeting those needs and a ranking score for her level of need. But no further action was taken.

Tolmie said all of the women they followed were repeatedly referred between services without receiving meaningful help.

"All of our participants ended up homeless in consequence of intimate partner violence.

"A number of them were living in vehicles at one point in time or in emergency accommodation for years. Some of them couldn't care for their kids because they weren't materially able to provide for them at different points in time, which is absolutely heartbreaking."

Māori-centred approach

However, the report found three participants who were involved with Kaupapa Māori practitioners and providers had positive experiences.

*Māreikura went through a programme for homelessness, Manaaki Tangata e Rua, offered by Te Puea Memorial Marae in Auckland.

"She sort of fell through the cracks of the mainstream family violence safety system and ended up in this programme provided by Te Puea and received a very different response from what victim-survivors were experiencing in the mainstream system.

"She had a holistic, relational response that was deeply mana-enhancing. Very quickly, she was in her own home and put back onto her feet."

She said a Māori-centred approach could improve outcomes for everyone affected by family harm, not only Māori.

"All victim-survivors need this kind of response. One which isn't founded on distrust of them and who they are, which isn't fragmented, which is practically helpful."

She said the report's findings supported years of research that the system had serious shortcomings and needed urgent changes.

"When we look at what's working within the system, we can see pockets of safe practice at Kaupapa Māori service providers and practitioners, or certainly that's what we have seen in this report."

The report called for more funding for Kaupapa Māori services and a Māori-centred response throughout the system.

World.title: 'Reckless and foolish': Shane Jones weighs in on Michael Laws in final campaign debate
World.content:
New Zealand First's deputy Shane Jones has rebuked fellow candidate Michael Laws for his "reckless and foolish" jibe about women, suggesting the controversy could yet have consequences.

"That remark has been very distractful," Jones said. "There'll be more to be said about it, no doubt, after the election."

Jones' comments came during the final televised debate of the election campaign on Thursday night, hours after party leader Winston Peters said Laws' future in New Zealand First was yet to be decided.

Watch the full debate here:

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407946321112

Laws was roundly criticised by all political parties after a clip surfaced from his online talk show in which he mocked the appearance and demeanor of Opportunity candidate Kayla Kingdon-Bebb.

"Must be hell dating people like that, just quietly," Laws said. "Can you imagine what it's like post-sex?"

Speaking at TVNZ's Q+A People's Debate, Jones was asked for his views on the comments.

"It was a reckless and foolish thing to have said," Jones said. "And you can imagine what my four daughters and my wife said."

Asked if he would be happy to work with Laws in caucus, Jones deferred: "I'll leave all that up to Winston."

The controversy was only briefly touched on during the colourful debate, which produced some unlikely alliances between political rivals.

Labour's Kieran McAnulty at the People's Debate. TVNZ/Supplied

Labour's Kieran McAnulty, a former volunteer firefighter, argued against an outright ban on private fireworks sales, instead suggesting restrictions on when they could be set off.

That would stop people letting them off "at 1:30AM on a random Tuesday", he said.

"At the risk to my political career, I actually think Kieran's right about this," ACT leader David Seymour responded.

Seymour and Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick both opposed a social media ban for under-16s and argued for tighter curbs on harmful algorithms.

Swarbrick drew a laugh when she said she "largely" agreed with Seymour, "although probably for different reasons".

"We have overlapping views while maintaining our distinct identity," Seymour replied to more laughter.

TVNZ/Supplied

Only Swarbrick and Te Pāti Māori's Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke backed scrapping the fast-track law, and they were also the only two who wanted to bring back a fees-free year at university.

Maipi-Clarke called for funding for Māori media to cover Parliament, while Jones accused RNZ of bias against him and Peters.

McAnulty said the coalition had tilted New Zealand too far towards the United States and away from China, and he said Labour would take a different approach.

Nobody raised a hand for automatically adjusting income tax brackets for inflation each year, though National's Nicola Willis said more tax relief would follow once the books were balanced.

National's Nicola Willis and Opportunity's Qiulae Wong at the People's Debate. TVNZ/Supplied

Willis also crossed swords with Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong over research and development funding, with the latter accusing the coalition of prioritising cuts over investment.

Wong said New Zealand should aim to spend 3 percent of GDP on research and development: "If we don't fund the science and the research of today, we won't have the Rocket Labs."

Willis challenged Wong on where the money would come from, asking whether she would take funding away from areas such as special needs education

"I would rather you take it from the oil and gas industry," Wong replied.

World.title: Waikato medical school's ethnicity plan 'almost offensive to Māori', GP leader says
World.content:
Audio player for " Waikato school proposes removing ethnicity based admission " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2358368%2Fwaikato-medical-school-s-ethnicity-plan-almost-offensive-to-maori-gp-leader-says

Waikato school proposes removing ethnicity based admission Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

A plan from New Zealand's newest medical school to remove ethnicity as a priority admission factor has been dubbed regressive, disappointing, frustrating and offensive.

Set to take its first cohort in 2028, the University of Waikato said a decision on the selection process would be made next year.

General Practitioners Aotearoa chair Dr Buzz Burrell said it's astonishingly disappointing.

"It's both backwards and naive and we were heard that what they instead are going to do is to make sure that applicants are committed to Māori health, that should be a given.

"That should be a basic requirement of every doctor working in New Zealand. That's almost like being committed to breathing. It's a completely meaningless statement.

"It's a retrograde step. It's a naive step and it's an unhelpful step. And certainly, almost offensive to Māori in this country and offensive to the statistics, which are not good."

General Practitioners Aotearoa chair Dr Buzz Burrell. Social Media

He said having Māori and Pasifika representation was highly important.

"About 6 percent of the country's doctors are Māori, whereas about 18 percent of the population is Māori.

"And if we look at the health statistics for Māori in particular, Māori men, they die seven years younger than non-Māori men, and the women, Māori women are dying six years younger than non-Māori women.

"They're really quite confronting statistics, and it very much is important that Māori people do have Māori doctors."

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton said promoting access to entry meant a wider cross section of people could access those courses.

"The standards required to successfully complete those courses and that training remain as high as they ever have."

She said through priority entry they were gradually seeing the number of Māori and Pasifika doctors and dentists increase, and removing that was regressive.

"Given all of the good things that are proposed about this medical school, inclusion in terms of rurality, a focus on graduate entry, a hope to include community-based and smaller hospitals, supporting training and development for this new generation of doctors would be great so it's just really disappointing and frustrating that they're not taking current, good practice and best evidence to inform their admissions policy."

She had written to the university to say the association was disturbed at the changes and the resignation of the medical school's academic lead Dr Rawiri Keenan.

The university responded saying the difference in view with Keenan was not about whether there would be a substantial number of Māori students in the programme, but about the way they would be selected - on the basis of ethnicity or on the basis of "demonstrated competence to serve Māori communities".

"The good news about this government being supportive of a third medical school is, is not such good news, if it's going to put checks, balances, limits on, I guess, the kind of processes that a medical school can run in order to ensure that it's reflective of our broader society," Dalton said.

Pro vice-chancellor of health at the University of Waikato Professor Jo Lane said the focus was to select students and produce doctors who were committed to working in primary care in regional and rural areas. He said the student selection process was still under development, but it would aim to reflect New Zealand's communities.

Jo Lane. Supplied

"Our admissions process is structured around a single pathway, with applicants receiving points across overlapping priorities rather than being considered through separate admission pathways."

He said a final decision on selection criteria would be made next year.

Meanwhile, the University of Auckland said it had defined admission pathways and criteria, based on specific, evidence-informed policies.

"These policies are developed within programme and university regulations, as well as in alignment with legal and regulatory expectations.

"As an example, the University runs its Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme because of the evidence it works. It also aligns with the Australasian Medical Council accreditation standards."

The University of Auckland. RNZ / Ke-Xin Li

University of Otago pro-vice-chancellor of health sciences Associate Professor Megan Gibbons said it had an admissions policy for health professional programmes that's designed to promote equity for students from underrepresented priority groups.

"Not only Māori and Pacific students, but also those from rural, low socioeconomic, refugee communities - with an academically strong focus.

"All students meet the same minimum academic standards to enter medicine and must meet and pass exactly the same academic requirements of the degree programme each year to progress and successfully graduate."

Gibbons said the pathways did not lower standards or guarantee entry, they ensured that once standards were met, selection decisions reflect long-term workforce needs that the market and open competition have repeatedly failed to meet on their own.

"This policy has led to record numbers of Māori and Pasifika students entering health professional programmes.

"However, despite this progress, there remains significant under-representation of Māori and Pacific health practitioners in the workforce."

World.title: All aboard: National's big blue bus continues its final push towards Auckland
World.content:
Sheep's wool on Wednesday, human hair on Thursday, Christopher Luxon has once again wielded clippers during his three-day election roadie to Auckland, aboard National's big blue bus.

This leg takes him from Hawke's Bay to Bay of Plenty, and RNZ political reporter Lauren Crimp is along for the ride. Here's her diary of the day's events.

8.15am: First order of business in sunny Napier is a haircut. Not Luxon's - he's the one behind the clippers.

The metaphor for the party not wanting to leave the job half done continues. A Young Nat sporting a half-shaved head had Luxon finish the job.

Sam says he's happy with the result (despite journalists pointing out a few tufts still left), and would recommend Luxon as a barber and as a Prime Minister.

9am: Breakfast at FG Smith's Eatery.

Ticket for National's 'No New Taxes' Express. RNZ/Lauren Crimp

Luxon chats with locals and delivers a slice of cake - complete with a sing song - to the birthday boy, one of the travelling journalists, whom RNZ has agreed not to name. The journalist graciously blows out the candle.

9.45am: Luxon hands out the day's tickets, as everyone boards the bus.

Yesterday's 'Stick To The Plan' Express has today become the 'No New Taxes' Express.

9.49am: The first play of National's AI parody tax song.

10.36am: Luxon makes a special announcement on the bus microphone: "I've just received some very positive news.. financial statements for the three months to September are out this morning and the good news is the deficit was $1.3b smaller than forecast just at the PREFU".

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407946032112

Young Nats cheer and clap accordingly.

12.25pm: The tax song starts back up, as we roll into Taupō.

Luxon is chatting with reporters at the back of the bus and says he wants to make a bunch of different versions of the song, including a country one. It's not the first time he's brought this up.

Reporters suggest he can do that if he wants, because he's the boss. Luxon doesn't reckon and has a laugh about it.

"It turns out you crawl your way through the bowels of the political system in New Zealand... to realise you're probably about the 17th most powerful person."

1pm: Luxon walks one of the main drags in Taupō, popping his head in to shops and cafes, dishing out handshakes and selfies.

National leader Christopher Luxon poses for selfies with Taupō supporters. RNZ/Lauren Crimp

He meets an American and enthusiastically remarks about the US midterm results, which the Democrats dominated. She replies, "Unfortunately", but Luxon doesn't appear to hear.

1.10pm: Labour's Taupō candidate, Chris Flatt, happens to show up on the same street at the same time, lurking metres behind Luxon.

He says he saw the bus and told reporters his conversations on doorsteps have revealed a mood for change.

1.27pm: A woman walks past Luxon, who is mid-conversation, and starts yelling: "Go Winston, go Winston, Winston Peters for Prime Minister... down with National, down with National!"

Luxon doesn't bat an eye. A pharmacy manager tells Luxon she let her staff go and vote for National on company time.

1.35pm: Lunch stop at Brumby's cafe. Luxon opts for Coke Zero (standard) and a sandwich (unusual - he normally goes for a pie).

Depart Taupō for Rotorua.

2.04pm: The Young Nats' first bus singalong of the day to Justin Bieber (yesterday, it was Taylor Swift).

National leader Christopher Luxon addresses party supporters in Rotorua. RNZ/Lauren Crimp

They backed it right up with 'Unwritten' by Natasha Bedingfield. It's nice to see a millennial favourite adopted by the next generation(s).

5.30pm: Luxon rallies party faithful alongside incumbent candidate Todd McClay at a Rotorua pub decked out in National blue.

He thanks the crowd for being "true-blue believers".

World.title: Oil spill after major fire at Auckland power substation
World.content:
Auckland Council is responding to an oil spill after a large fire at a Vector electrical substation in the Auckland suburb of Penrose on Thursday.

The fire broke out on Thursday afternoon, throwing a black plume of smoke across the city.

One person was taken to Middlemore Hospital in a serious condition and two others to Auckland City Hospital in a moderate condition.

The fire has since been extinguished and power has been restored for all but one customer. Up to 12 fire engines were at the scene at the fire's peak and thousands were without power.

Auckland Council team leader compliance Kevin Reeve said council was working alongside the Harbourmaster and FENZ to work out the extent of the oil spill after the fire and how to manage it.

"Our pollution response team and Healthy Waters are onsite, and investigations are ongoing.

"Once we've confirmed the extent of the discharge, we will be able to provide an update on the environmental monitoring required."

Three Vector workers were carrying out maintenance at the facility "when there was an incident" Fire and Emergency assistant district commander Barry Thomas told 1News.

A spokesperson for Vector told RNZ an investigation into the cause of the incident will be undertaken.

"We remain focused on the welfare and wellbeing of the crew."

Fire and Emergency said crews would rotate through the evening and continuing to monitor the site for hot spots overnight.

'All you could see was billowing, black smoke'

Auckland Resident Kerry Prendeville was driving on Southern Motorway heading towards the Auckland city centre in the afternoon.

"All you could see was billowing, black smoke," he said.

Passing Penrose, he said he could see the electricity substation well ablaze.

"I undid my window, and it was super hot. The heat was like an intense outdoor bonfire, that sort of hot heat you feel you can't get too close to it."

A close up at the scene of a fire in Penrose, Auckland. RNZ / Luka Forman

Louise Kyle, who lived near the fire, said that after her power went out in the afternoon and she could see rising smoke outside.

"It was probably by that point maybe 150-plus feet in the air, black, thick, dense smoke. She said when she rushed to her car to leave the area, she could taste the smoke.

"By the time I'd managed to get myself downstairs and into the car, by that point you could definitely feel it in the back of your throat."

Kyle said her car was covered in black ash.

Mieke Thompson-Pain, who was near Mt Wellington when the fire erupted, said she was almost brought to tears by the scale of the blaze.

"I was driving over to my friend's house and my dad was in the car and he told me 'look, there's black smoke in the sky' and it was massive," she told RNZ.

She said her friend's sister ran up the road fearing her own home was affected.

"It was very scary... I was almost brought to tears... it was just so large and, you know, you can't even imagine how many lives it's been impacting."

World.title: Four face insider-trading charges related to computer chip maker Rakon
World.content:
Four people face charges of insider trading related to computer chip maker Rakon, which delisted from the NZX in May, after shareholders accepted a takeover offer.

The Financial Markets Authority said Rakon was not a party to the proceedings heard in the Auckland District Court on Thursday.

"People need to be able to trust that our markets are fair," FMA head of enforcement Margot Gatland said.

"Insider trading undermines that trust and confidence, which is why tackling insider conduct is a priority for the FMA."

Michael Walter Daniel was charged under sections 240(1), 241(1), (242)(1) and 244 of the Financial Markets Conduct Act and s 66(1) of the Crimes Act.

"These are serious allegations and I am working through them carefully with my legal advisers," Daniel told RNZ.

"The charges concern events surrounding discussions about a potential takeover of Rakon, over three years ago [in late 2023], which ultimately did not proceed," he said, adding the charges were not related to the recent takeover completed in May.

He declined to offer additional details about the case.

Paul Louis Smit was also charged under the Financial Markets Conduct Act.

Two other individuals were granted interim name suppression.

World.title: NAS weighs in more than 33kg heavier than Paul Gallen
World.content:
Nelson Asofa-Solomona has landed another low blow on Paul Gallen, claiming that even his premiership-winning former Cronulla teammates want the Sharks legend laid out on Friday night.

A day after the Big Nasty riled his rival by dragging Gallen's wife into the verbal sledging, Asofa-Solomona got even nastier as he lobbed explosive accusations about the Sharks' only grand final-winning captain.

"There's been so many people jumping in my DMs," Asofa-Solomona said on Thursday.

"People that have played with him, people that have played against him, people who have worked with them in the past. They were telling me all these stories about him and saying 'Yeah, bro, please do a job on him.'

"That was my plan all along anyway."

Nelson Asofa-Solomona says his plan is to knock Paul Gallen out. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

The Cronulla-Melbourne rivalry is one of the fiercest in the NRL, with the two sides featuring in a series of spiteful encounters either side the Sharks' stirring 2016 grand final triumph over the Storm.

Having already copped a drugs spray from Asofa-Solomona (3-0, 3KOs) in light of the Cronulla peptides saga, Gallen (16-2-1, 8KOs) will be livid after the ex-Storm star's latest verbal jabs.

Asofa-Solomona would not be drawn on specifics but said Gallen's former State of Origin teammates and "work colleagues" were among those who he claimed had reached out to him in the hope of doing over the 2014 series-winning Blues skipper.

"I can't say too much, but probably just stuff to do with money and bits and pieces," Asofa-Solomona said.

"But, look, he's grown up in a different era. He's a bit of a different cat, but the new era is here."

Asofa-Solomona's inflammatory allegations came after the two heavyweights featured in a spicy weigh-in at Sydney's TikTok Entertainment Centre.

The ex-New Zealand Test enforcer promised Gallen he would proudly take the mantle of NRL-boxing crossover king on Friday night.

"And if it's not a knockout, I don't want it," the 200cm, 137.56-kilogram behemoth said.

"That's the only result I'm here to get. I'm here for a highlight-reel finish."

Nelson Asofa-Solomona is much heavier than Paul Gallen. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

But the retiring Gallen, 45, is having none of it, despite weighing in at 104.18kg.

"I'm really proud I'm fighting a bloke now, 30-odd kilos heavier than me, 15 years younger than me and I'm still willing to compete — and I'll win this fight, at my age," he said.

"That's what I'm proud of, and this is a no-lose situation for me. I'm going to get paid a ton of money and go home happy and healthy and live the rest of my life with my family.

"That's my goal in life and that's what I'm here to do."

What time is the fight?

Paul Gallen and Nelson Asofa-Solomona meet on Friday, November 6, with the main card getting underway from 7:00pm AEDT.

How can I watch the fight?

The fight is exclusive to Fox Sports and Kayo's pay per view channel, Main Event and will cost $69.95.

ABC Sport will live-blog the fight card.

Who else is fighting?

World.title: Netball blindsided by leak of likely inclusion at Brisbane Olympics
World.content:
Netball has been blindsided by a leak of its likely inclusion at the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games.

Media reports by NewsCorp suggest it is "near the top of the list" in priority for the 2032 organising committee, which is permitted to put forward up to six local sports to feature as one-offs at the Games.

Cricket, surf lifesaving, rugby league and lawn bowls are also in the frame.

This would set netball up for a historic Games debut. Despite being part of the Commonwealth Games since 1998, it has tried and failed at least four times to join the Olympic programme previously.

Loading Instagram content

The endorsement is a positive sign, the significance of which is not lost on Netball Australia, who have garnered more than 115,000 signatures on their petition since officially launching a bid to join the Brisbane Games in 2021.

In January, a survey conducted by independent market and social research agency Insightfully, found 66 per cent of Australians support netball's inclusion at the Olympics. It polled 10 points higher than any other sport.

However, key figures at Netball Australia were tight-lipped on Thursday, for fear of speaking out of turn and jeopardising their chances.

Earlier this week, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) revised its timeline for determining which sports and disciplines would make it onto the programme for the Brisbane Games.

In December, the IOC will make recommendations in three different categories: existing disciplines to have automatic inclusion; existing or proposed disciplines that require further assessment; and candidate disciplines eliminated from consideration.

A formal verdict will be handed down in April next year after votes are taken at the IOC session in the Dominican Republic.

Former Australian defender turned-commentator Bianca Chatfield shared her initial reaction with ABC Sport.

"Everyone is really shocked that it's come out and there has been this leak," Chatfield said.

"I was so excited when I saw the news, but then I dug deeper and realised it's not official.

"We're all just holding on with hope that the news is real and that it'll come to fruition next year."

Bianca Chatfield (left) faces New Zealand in the 2013 Constellation Cup. (Getty: Michael Dodge)

Chatfield said the Olympics always felt out of reach as an option for netball, but the sport deserved its chance to shine at the Games.

"It would mean everything to the sport, there's been a lot of work done behind the scenes," she said.

"For the athletes especially it would be a once in a lifetime opportunity to have a crack at an Olympic gold medal.

"The Olympics was just something that we never thought would happen so the fact it's a tangible thing now, we'd all be absolutely stoked to see it happen."

Bianca Chatfield now works as a commentator and presenter in the game. (Getty: Graham Denholm)

The Australian team's recent form sees it on the brink of losing the world number one ranking for the first time since 2013, but that lapse in dominance could perhaps help a greater cause.

The Diamonds missed the Commonwealth Games final for the first time in Glasgow, falling to Jamaica in the semifinals before rallying to claim bronze. They also conceded the Constellation Cup to New Zealand for just the fourth time in 16 series.

"I do think a competitive environment really helps [our Olympic case]," Chatfield said.

"As we're seeing internationally, with the rise of teams like Jamaica and New Zealand, it's not a forgone conclusion that Australia would get the gold."

Federal Minister for Communications and Sport Anika Wells, who is also vice chair on the board of the Brisbane 2032 committee, pledged her support at the Queensland Media Club on Thursday.

She also told ABC Sport that it was feasible that multiple team sports like cricket and netball could be selected, despite there being pressure to remain inside the overall 10,500 athlete quota.

Sports Minister Anika Wells fronts the media. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"Today I am publicly committing my support to netball as part of Brisbane 2032," Wells said.

"Netball is quintessentially Australian and the leading team sport for women and girls here and across our region.

"It connects communities, it creates leaders, it builds confidence and inspires dreams.

"It would be a massive moment for the million little girls and women, and increasingly men and boys, who pull on their netball bibs and get out to play."

Former Diamond Kathryn Harby-Williams is the CEO at ANPA. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Chief executive of the Australian Netball Players' Association Kathryn Harby-Williams said the athletes welcomed the news.

"It would be an incredible opportunity for the athletes if it is true, to compete at one of the biggest sports events in the world," Harby-Williams told ABC Sport.

Meanwhile, a Netball Australia spokesperson said it would follow due process.

"We are focused on putting our best foot forward with the Brisbane 2032 Organising Committee and the IOC and we respect their processes," a statement read.

"We will continue to advocate for netball and our incredible community across the globe.

"There are countless Australian netball players who dream of one day becoming an Olympian and we believe Brisbane 2032 would be the perfect stage for those dreams."

World.title: Swans 'need to be better' as club launches investigation in culture
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say they have commissioned a "comprehensive examination of the club's AFL program" as they grapple with another off-field incident.

On Monday, Papley, a high-profile forward and one of the team's most experienced players, allegedly returned a positive roadside test for methylamphetamine, and will appear in court this month for driving with a suspended licence.

The club has penned a letter to members from chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich saying the club commissioned the review in September and will feature "a board endorsed independent process".

"What is already clear from our work to date is that the actions and attitudes of some within our club has damaged and diminished the many great things we do, and the great people who do them," the statement read.

"This is unacceptable and must change.

"We have a long and proud history but clearly, we have work to do to get back to the standards we have long set. We will make the necessary changes that are required and will work to be better.

"The standards we expect of every player and employee, on and off the field, are central to who we are. They reflect the behaviour rightly expected of professional athletes and public role models.

"The incident involving Tom Papley this week and the separate incident in Melbourne in August, fall a long way short of those expectations."

If Papley's second sample is positive, the 216-gamer is likely to face an AFL penalty separate from any legal sanction.

Pavlich admitted the embattled AFL club had a "long way to go" when he spoke briefly to reporters outside the club headquarters in Moore Park on Thursday, conceding the Swans had again let down the football community.

"We're bitterly disappointed that we're here talking about this today," Pavlich said.

"We're really disappointed in Tom himself. We voiced that pretty directly to him yesterday.

"We apologise unreservedly to our members, fans and corporate partners.

"We've let them down again. We must be better.

"It's a really disappointing time for the footy club, but given this is a police matter, we cannot make any further comment."

Tom Papley (centre) allegedly returned a positive roadside test for methylamphetamine on Monday. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Papley's looming court appearance comes after the Swans suspended five players for breaching club behavioural standards last August.

Vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down for the remainder of the AFL season and missed the finals.

"We're looking at that right now," Pavlich said, when asked if the Swans had a culture problem.

"We've been identifying that over the last eight weeks.

"We've started some deep work on that with our AFL men's department, independent advisers helping us through that.

"These are the questions we are asking ourselves right now and asking our players."

Pavlich added "we need to be better".

"This is not something that anyone is stopping short of, knowing that we've got a long way to go," he said.

"We've got some deep work to do to understand how we can get better."

Second test results to take weeks

Papley was pulled over by police in Sydney's Centennial Park on Monday for random testing.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test, with checks revealing his licence was suspended due to non-payment of a parking fine.

A secondary sample of oral fluid was taken for further analysis, with the results from the second test expected to take at least four weeks.

Papley was issued a 24-hour driving prohibition and will appear before Waverley Local Court on November 26.
